Between 1945 and 1947 the Soviet Union made Japanese prisoners of war work on it; a plaque honouring them was put up at the theatre in 1996, when Islam Karimov was President of Uzbekistan. It opened its doors to the public in November 1947, to celebrate 500 years since the birth of Alisher Navoi, regarded as the greatest figure of Chagatai literature. The hall holds 1,400 people, and the main stage measures 540 square metres.

Gottfried Böhm (d. 2021) designed the pilgrimage church of Maria, Königin des Friedens in Neviges (Velbert, Germany), built from 1966 and consecrated in 1968. Devotion to a wonder-working image of the Immaculate Conception there goes back to 1681. The church is regarded as the most influential and widely recognised of Böhm's works. On 23 September 1978 Cardinal Karol Wojtyła came to the "Mariendom" together with German and Polish bishops, led by Primate Cardinal Wyszyński and Cardinal Höffner. Twenty-three days later Wojtyła was elected Pope John Paul II.

Villa Méditerranée stands in Marseille's 2nd arrondissement, in the La Joliette neighbourhood next to MuCEM. Stefano Boeri designed it within Euroméditerranée, an urban renewal scheme. It opened in 2013, the year Marseille was European Capital of Culture, at first as a conference venue: a 9,000 sqm centre for exhibitions and research looking over the port, intended for cultural and research events on Mediterranean subjects. Boeri imagined it as a place where the region's many identities could meet and blend, with the sea as its point of reference. An artificial dock lets the 36-metre-high conference space look down onto a broad square of water. Since 2022 it has been home to Cosquer Méditerranée, a museum built around a replica of the Cosquer Cave.

Aspire Tower, also called The Torch Doha, is a skyscraper hotel 300 metres tall in Doha's Aspire Zone. Architect Hadi Simaan and AREP designed it with the engineers Ove Arup and Partners, and it was the focal point of the 15th Asian Games, which Qatar hosted in December 2006. Its structure is a reinforced-concrete cylinder core, 1 to 1.8 metres thick and 12 to 18 metres across, ringed on every floor by radiating cantilevered steel beams. An energy-efficient glass skin helps keep temperatures comfortable in the desert climate. Midmac and Six Construct, a BESIX subsidiary, finished it in November 2007 for €133,395,000. Inside are a five-star hotel, a health club, a museum of sport, a revolving restaurant and an observation deck. The pool sits 80 metres above the ground, cantilevered from the core and reaching 12 metres beyond the facade.

Charles Correa designed the British Council's headquarters in India, a New Delhi building that took him five years, from 1987 to 1992. It brings together a library, an auditorium, an art gallery and the Council's offices. Correa set these out over several floors as layers, meant to recall three centuries of contact between India and Britain. Walking through, one moves from a spiral that stands for Bindu, the cosmic centre of energy, past a traditional Islamic Char Bagh, to a European emblem inlaid in marble and granite that represents the Age of Reason. Across the front, the British artist Howard Hodgkin made a mural of a banyan tree whose branches spread over the walls, worked in black Kadappa stone and Makrana marble.

Barcelona's Dispensario Central Antituberculoso was planned as a centre to coordinate the fight against tuberculosis across the country. Designed in 1934, it was finished in 1938, in the middle of the Spanish Civil War. Josep Lluís Sert, Josep Torres Clavé and Joan Baptista Subirana designed it with other members of GATCPAC. To meet its functional needs, the building takes in as much fresh air and sunlight as possible throughout. Two linked wings form an L, with the caretakers' quarters standing apart, and a courtyard garden ties the parts together, acting both as the entrance and as a buffer against the surrounding city. Each part has a steel and concrete structure, faced with light panels in a range of materials. It is now recognised as heritage architecture for its history in Spain and its design.

The Apollo Pavilion, also called the Pasmore Pavilion, is a public artwork in Peterlee, a County Durham new town. It was designed by Victor Pasmore, a British artist and architect, and completed in 1969. The town was designed around this central abstract artwork and pavilion, named after the Apollo space programme to echo that programme's optimism. Cast in place in reinforced concrete, it is made of broad geometric planes of white concrete, with two oval murals as its only decoration. It spans a small lake that frames a large geometric sculpture by Pasmore, first serving as a footbridge between the estate's two halves. It remains a rare British attempt to fuse art and architecture at large scale. After a £400,000 restoration it was formally unveiled on 11 July 2009; Grade II* listing came in December 2011.

Denys Lasdun's building for the Institute of Education, now part of UCL, was designed for the University of London and dates from 1970 to 1976. Plans for new premises on Bedford Way had been drawn up in 1960, but only part of Lasdun's first scheme was completed. The building proved controversial for the way it was set into the existing pattern of squares and terraces; Lasdun argued that it respected that plan, even if its language was more Brutalist. Its fire escape stairs are expressed on the outside, nodding to Louis Kahn and Wells Coates, while Lasdun's masterplan laid a new, partly public square over car parking. The library finally moved into an extension in 1992, taking the name Newsam Library after Peter Newsam, the Director who oversaw the new construction. The building is listed Grade II*.

The terminal at Beijing Daxing International Airport is nicknamed "the starfish" for its shape: six curving spokes radiating from a central hub. Zaha Hadid Architects designed it with ADPI, a French planning firm, and partners, and BIAD, the Beijing Institute of Architectural Design, carried it out; it was still being built when Zaha Hadid died. Work on the airport started on 26 December 2014 under chief engineer Guo Yanchi, and the terminal's concrete structure was capped by March 2017. Nearly five years and CN¥80 billion (US$11.4 billion) later, the project had a 700,000 m2 terminal, the largest airport terminal in a single building anywhere, on 47 km2 of land. Opening day came on 25 September 2019, six days before the People's Republic of China turned 70, at a ceremony attended by Xi Jinping.

Eun Young Yi won the international competition for Stuttgart's new city library in 1999. Work ran from 2010 to 24 October 2011 and cost about 80 million euros, 4 million of them for the interiors. Yi designed a plain cube on a square plan, 44 metres long and 40 metres tall, with nine floors above ground and two below. The frame is precast concrete, with glass brick panels set into it. At the centre is the "heart", an archaic four-storey space with no specific library function. Behind the outer glass front sits a second, membrane-like glass skin, with a walkable gap between them that ventilates the building. Plan, elevation and section all keep to a 0.97-metre grid. Inspirations included the Pantheon, a 1785 proposal for the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Noah's ark and Kubrick's A Space Odyssey.

Blues Point Tower stands in McMahons Point near North Sydney: 83 metres tall, with 144 apartments on 24 levels. Harry Seidler received the commission in 1958 from Dick Dusseldorp, through Dusseldorp's company Civil & Civic. Because planning rules then counted balconies toward the floor-space ratio, the design was changed in 1959 to French balconies, and that is how it was built. Completed in 1962, when its first residents moved in, it was the first high-rise apartment block to be strata titled and stayed Australia's tallest residential building until 1970. Following Albers, Seidler avoided static symmetry and plain grids, offsetting elements to create "visual tension", which shows in the tower's window pattern. Its heritage listing calls it a "conspicuous, though unpopular" example of the Internationalist style, and North Sydney Council added it to its local heritage register in 1993.

Miles Warren designed the Dorset Street Flats in Christchurch in 1956, a year after starting his own practice. On a 771-square-metre site, the original scheme held eight one-bedroom flats with built-in furniture and fittings, a ninth made from an old stable block, four garages, courtyards and a shared laundry. Warren drew on modernism and on New Brutalism, which he had met in Britain in the 1950s. The flats are credited as an early work of the Christchurch School and one of New Zealand's first attempts at building in load-bearing concrete block. Critics and fellow architects praised the work, but public reception was cooler: the flats were compared to a prison and nicknamed "Fort Dorset". Heritage New Zealand listed them in Category 1 in 2010, and a restoration by Young Architects' Greg Young won a 2023 New Zealand Architecture Award.

The Adam Art Gallery, Te Pātaka Toi in Māori, is a purpose-built gallery at Victoria University of Wellington, on its Kelburn Campus. Ian Athfield designed it. It sits between three university buildings, Old Kirk, Hunter and the Student Union, and over the "Culliford stair", which was already in place. New Zealand's Governor General, Sir Michael Hardie Boys, formally opened it on 21 September 1999. That year Athfield Architects received two NZIA Resene awards for the building, both in the Community & Cultural category: a branch architecture award and a colour award. In 2025 the gallery received the Enduring Architecture Award at the NZIA's Wellington Architecture Awards.

1 Bligh Street is a 30-storey office tower in Sydney's central business district, looking out over Circular Quay, the harbour and the Harbour Bridge. Germany's Ingenhoven Architects designed it with Australia's Architectus. The Green Building Council of Australia gave it a six-star green rating. A sewage plant in the basement recycles 90 percent of its waste water, the roof carries solar panels, and chilled beams handle the air conditioning. It was the first major Australian high-rise with a full double-skin facade and external louvres. On the south side, a naturally ventilated atrium runs the full 120-metre height, bringing daylight to every office floor. In 2012 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat named it Best Tall Building in Asia & Australasia, and it also won the International Highrise Award and the Harry Seidler Award for Commercial Architecture.

The Centro per l'arte contemporanea Luigi Pecci in Prato was founded in 1988 by the curator Amnon Barzel and the industrialist Enrico Pecci, in memory of Pecci's son Luigi. Since it first opened that year it has staged more than 250 exhibitions, events and learning programmes for students and adults. Italo Gamberini designed the original building. In 2016 Maurice Nio enlarged it with a U-shaped wing wrapped around an open-air amphitheatre for 800 people. The new wing holds 3,000 square metres of galleries, an archive, a library, an auditorium that doubles as a cinema, a bookshop and a restaurant. Besides its permanent collection of contemporary art, the centre has a sculpture garden and an area set aside for temporary shows.

Dudley Zoo is credited to Berthold Lubetkin and the Tecton partnership; it was an entirely new zoo, commissioned from Tecton by London Zoo alongside Tecton's buildings for London Zoo's reserve park at Whipsnade. The engineer Ove Arup acted as Tecton's structural consultant on it, as he did on the Penguin Pool at Regent's Park Zoo in London. The zoo was made up of twelve animal enclosures and was an early example of Modernism in Britain. Every original enclosure still stands apart from the penguin pool, which was pulled down in 1979. The Twentieth Century Society sees in these playful pavilions a reminder that architecture should answer more than material needs, and should also set out to inspire and delight.

In central Cardiff, St David's Hall (Neuadd Dewi Sant in Welsh) serves officially as the national venue for concerts and conferences in Wales, hosting the Welsh Proms every year and the BBC Cardiff Singer of the World every two years. Seymour Harris Partnership had to fit a 2,000-seat auditorium, with all its foyers, bars, offices and backstage rooms, onto a tight city-centre plot. Space was so short that it had to be built into and over the St David's Shopping Centre, then planned and partly built, which explains its unusual form. Angular grey concrete covers nearly all of the exterior; Building Design called the style "complex late brutalism". The first concert was held on 11 September 1982. Cadw gives it interim Grade II protection. It closed in September 2023 when RAAC was found in the roof.

Alex Gordon, who went on to become a prominent south Wales architect, designed Cyncoed Methodist Church in Cardiff. Its foundation stone went down in November 1965; the church dates from 1966, the year it was dedicated, in September. It follows the International Modern style that Mies van der Rohe pioneered, with a rectilinear form built of glass and buff brick. A large extension went up at the back in 1992. The church was listed in 2001; the listing praises it as an individually accomplished design that helps to set the architectural benchmark for Welsh religious buildings after the war.

Henry Hobson Richardson designed the Converse Memorial Library (or Building) in Malden, Massachusetts. Elisha S. and Mary D. Converse gave it in memory of their son Frank Eugene Converse, killed in what is described as the first bank robbery and murder in North America. Built from 1883 to 1885, it forms an L, faced in brown Longmeadow sandstone, with a tower at the inner corner and a deeply arched entrance porch in the short arm. The main library room measures 50 by 36 feet, lined in richly carved white oak beneath a high vaulted ceiling. Richardson also designed the furniture, made by A. H. Davenport and Company of Boston. It was his last library and is often ranked among his finest works. It housed Malden Public Library until 1996 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1987.

Built to show widescreen Cinerama films, the Cinerama Dome in Los Angeles opened on November 7, 1963. The French architect Pierre Cabrol, lead designer at Welton Becket and Associates, proposed the design; as a student at MIT he had worked with R. Buckminster Fuller. Crews worked around the clock, and the whole build took just 16 weeks. It is the world's only geodesic dome in concrete, assembled from 316 hexagonal and pentagonal panels in 16 sizes, each about 12 feet across and weighing around 7,500 pounds. Inside are a loge with stadium seating and floating stairways of architectural note. When it opened, its curved screen, 32 feet high and 86 feet wide, was the largest of its kind anywhere. The dome was made a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument in 1998.

Benaroya Hall fills a whole city block in central Seattle. LMN Architects of Seattle designed it, and it cost $120 million when it opened in September 1998; in 2001 it received the American Institute of Architects' National Honor Award. It has two auditoria: the S. Mark Taper Foundation Auditorium, with 2,500 seats, and the Illsley Ball Nordstrom Recital Hall, seating 536. Cyril Harris designed its acoustics, which draw heavily on technology, and the main hall rests on rubber pads that isolate it from the outer shell. The hall stands right over the Great Northern Tunnel, the city's main rail corridor, and beside the Downtown Seattle Transit Tunnel, whose Symphony station is built into it. The lobby displays glass art, including Crystal Cascade by Dale Chihuly. The hall has helped the Seattle Symphony double its budget and its number of performances.

Toronto Reference Library is the largest public reference library in Canada, holding books, manuscripts, microfilm and more. Raymond Moriyama's design was revised after months of talks with local government and approved in April 1974, slightly reducing its size, height and bulk and switching its cladding to brick. It opened at Yonge Street and Asquith Avenue on 2 November 1977. Upper levels step back from the street to form a pyramid. The structure is steel-reinforced concrete, clad in orange-red brick to match its neighbours, with glazing toward Yonge Street. A heat pump system recovers heat from lights, visitors and sunlight. The curved, skylit atrium lets air move freely, with plants and water inspired by the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. A 2009–2014 renovation added a glass cube with a larger lobby, shop and café, recalling Moriyama's 1973 proposal.

The Cinquantenaire Arcade in Brussels began with the Belgian government's plans, under King Leopold II's patronage, for the 1880 National Exhibition, held 50 years after the Belgian Revolution. Gédéon Bordiau conceived that exhibition's single arch. After his death in 1904, Leopold II chose the French architect Charles Girault to rework it; Girault made it a triple arch but kept Bordiau's quadriga. Leopold II inaugurated the arcade on 27 September 1905, in time for 75 years of Belgian independence. The arch is 30 metres wide and 45 metres high, with three equal bays. On top, Thomas Vinçotte's bronze quadriga, Brabant Raising the National Flag, has horses by Jules Lagae. A wall closed the back of the colonnade in 1905, and from 1912 Jean Delville covered it with a 360 m2 mosaic frieze. Protection followed on 29 June 1984.

Head office of CEC Bank, the CEC Palace stands on Calea Victoriei in Bucharest, facing the country's National Museum of Romanian History. Construction started on 8 June 1897 and ended in 1900, with the bank paying for both the land and the building from its own funds. The site had earlier held the ruins of the Saint John the Great monastery and an inn beside it. The design came from Paul Gottereau, who had studied at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris, while the Romanian architect Ion Socolescu oversaw construction. Eclectic in style, the palace is crowned by a dome of glass and metal. Its entrance is an arch carried on two pairs of composite columns, and each of the four corners has gables, coats of arms and a Renaissance dome.

At 97 metres, the Administrative Palace in Satu Mare is the tallest building in Transylvania and among the tallest in Romania. Work began in 1972; Nicolae Porumbescu from Iaşi was the main architect, assisted by Ludovic Gyüre of Satu Mare, and more than 1,000 workers took part before it was completed in 1984. Built in the brutalist style, it pairs one large main tower with three smaller ones. The smaller towers were meant to stand for the three ethnic groups of Satu Mare County, Romanians, Germans and Hungarians, and the main tower for the bond between them. Today it houses several public bodies, among them the county council, the prefecture, the city hall and the culture office.

The Haludovo Palace Hotel was the architectural and social heart of Haludovo, a resort at Malinska designed by the Croatian architect Boris Magaš and built from 1969 to 1972, as tourism on the Yugoslav Adriatic boomed. Covering about 25 hectares, Haludovo was planned as a self-contained tourist town rather than one hotel. The Palace held the commanding place of a castle, long blocks of rooms at the edge read as city walls, and clusters of small atrium villas formed a settlement inside. Shared rooms centred on a double-height atrium ringed by a gallery, where tall, thin concrete columns branched into arches. Similar concrete forms recur across the site as pergolas, sunshades and roofs. Guccione set up the Penthouse Adriatic Club in the Palace, with a casino aimed mainly at foreign guests. Historians count Haludovo among Magaš's key works.

Sofia Central Railway Station is the main passenger station of Bulgaria's capital and the largest in the country. Transproekt, with Milko Bechev as lead architect, designed the new terminal. Work began on 23 February 1971 on the plaza and gardens of the 1888 station, so that trains could keep running during construction. The station was picked as one of 30 buildings to be renovated, rebuilt or newly built for the 30th anniversary of the 1944 Bulgarian coup d'état. Spread over two levels below ground and three above, it held 365 rooms and spaces and used white marble extensively. It was inaugurated on 6 September 1974 before the country's elite, with Zhivkov, Bulgaria's de facto ruler, cutting the ribbon. A full renovation followed in 2016.

Kuala Lumpur Railway Station went up between 1910 and 1917 on the site of an earlier station. It was the city's rail hub for the Federated Malay States Railways and then Malayan Railways (KTM), until Kuala Lumpur Sentral largely replaced it in 2001. Its designer, Arthur Benison Hubback, a British assistant to the Director of Public Works, drew on the region's Anglo-Asian architecture. The main block blends Western and Mughal elements in a "Raj" style close to Indo-Saracenic. Horseshoe and ogee arches and large corner chhatris (six, plus two added later) make it comparable to contemporaries such as the Sultan Abdul Samad Building. Unlike similar buildings in bare brick, it is fully plastered and painted in pale colours. Its original glazed roofs were partly open to let out locomotive smoke. It reopened as a railway museum on 31 August 2007.

Mimar Sinan built the Caferağa Medrese in Istanbul in 1559 for Cafer Agha, while Suleiman the Magnificent was sultan. It lies below the forecourt of the Hagia Sophia, in the historic heart of the Sultanahmet district, so it falls inside the UNESCO World Heritage conservation area covering the whole district. Visitors enter through a main gate into an inner courtyard, with the former teaching rooms set around it. In 1989 the Turkish Cultural Service Foundation converted the medrese into a tourist centre, with 15 rooms for classes and exhibitions, a large hall and a garden. Traditional Turkish crafts such as calligraphy and ceramics are taught, made and sold there.

Ben Gurion Airport's Terminal 3 was inaugurated on 28 October 2004, when Prime Minister Ariel Sharon spoke, and opened to passengers a month later, replacing Terminal 1 as Israel's main gateway. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) designed the main building, while Moshe Safdie & Associates and TRA (today Black & Veatch) were responsible for a link building and the airside gates and departure areas. Hamid Kia, SOM's lead architect, aimed to capture the emotion of arriving in and leaving Israel. In Safdie's connector, arriving and departing passengers share one space and see each other through glass, with views to the Judean Hills and a garden of the Seven Species. An inverted dome hangs over the departures rotunda under a white fabric ceiling that softens daylight. Walls are faced in Jerusalem stone, set against white concrete, glass and aluminium.

Bab Al Bahrain, Arabic for "Gateway of Bahrain", stands in Customs Square in Manama's central business district and marks the main way into the Manama Souq. It opened in 1949 to a design by Charles Belgrave, the British adviser to the emir, who saw how much trade mattered and pushed for a gateway at the edge of the market, beside the landing jetties for dhows. It once stood on the shoreline, but heavy land reclamation in the second half of the 20th century has left it several kilometres inland. The square is regarded as the region's first formal public space. A 1986 refurbishment added Islamic architectural features. Today the monument is essentially one large arch with a road running beneath it, flanked by two side arches for people on foot.

Deira's Clock Tower in Dubai dates from 1965. Otto Bullard designed it with Ziki Homsi, a Syrian architect who was a partner in the Architecture Design Construction (ADC) Office. Meant as a symbol for Dubai, it was placed in Deira because, before the Dubai–Abu Dhabi Road existed, the main roads into the city came together there. Its roundabout leads onto the Al Maktoum Bridge, the first land crossing ever built between Deira and Bur Dubai, and the tower is now a well-known landmark of the area. Its form came from Bullard's own ideas and was not meant to show a drill bit or anything else. The Daily Telegraph included it in a list of the 17 most beautiful clock towers in the world.

Moscow Cinema stands on Charles Aznavour Square, on Abovyan Street, in Yerevan, Armenia's capital. Tiran Yerkanyan and Gevorg Kochar designed it, and it opened in 1936 where the Saint Paul and Peter Church had stood until the Soviet authorities demolished it earlier that decade. Kochar came back in 1960 to redesign the building with Telman Gevorkyan. In 1983 the facade was redone with scenes from well-known Soviet-Armenian films such as Sayat Nova, Pepo, Chapayev and David Bek. The Golden Apricot Yerevan International Film Festival, held every year since 2004, uses it as its main venue. Today it has four halls, the red hall (491 seats), the blue hall (350), the small red hall (49) and the gallery (35), plus an open-air theatre on its east side.

The Tbilisi City Assembly Building is a clock-towered building on the south side of Freedom Square in Georgia's capital, and it houses the City Assembly, or sakrebulo. The first building went up in the 1830s under Imperial Russian rule and has been rebuilt several times since, changing its appearance over two centuries. Until 1879 it held the Chancellery of the Chief Policemaster and the police department. In 1878 a competition was held to remodel it as the City Hall, and Paul Stern's entry won. Its exterior follows the Exotic style popular at the time, in a Neo-Moorish manner. A tower was added in 1910, and the building was enlarged again in 1912.

On Cusco's main square the Incas built the temple of Kiswarkancha, palace of Viracocha, who ruled the Kingdom of Cusco about a century before the Spanish arrived. Building the cathedral was entrusted to Juan Miguel de Veramendi in 1560; Juan Correa replaced him a year later and worked until 1564. In 1615 Miguel Gutiérrez Sencio, a follower of Vitruvius and Giacomo Barozzi who admired the sober Herrerian style of El Escorial, took charge with Francisco Becerra, and the cathedral was finished in 1654. It was built of local stone, with red granite blocks reused from Sacsayhuamán. Its three naves share one height, as at Lima and Jaén, and fourteen cruciform pillars set out twenty-four rib vaults. The facade is Renaissance, the interiors Baroque, late Gothic and Plateresque. Since 1983 it has been within Cusco's UNESCO World Heritage centre.

This Catholic cathedral stands on the southwest of Quito's Plaza de la Independencia. With the church before it, it held the bishop's seat from 1545 until 1848, when Quito became an archdiocese. It was built of stone through the minga, a custom of communal hauling, carving and masonry. Its three naves, with semi-ogival arches on square pillars, have a layout typical of the sixteenth century, and some experts call it Gothic-Mudéjar for its pillars, arches and carved, coffered ceiling. The main door turns away from the plaza because a deep gorge, the quebrada de Sanguña, blocked extension southwest. In 1797–1799 it gained the Carondelet Arch, the work of Spanish military engineer Antonio García. Glazed green ceramic covers three domes, over that arch, the high altar and the transept. After a 1987 earthquake, the city restored its deep foundations using micropiles.

The President of Colombia lives and works in the Casa de Nariño in Bogotá. Its name means the House of Nariño; it was built on the site of the house where Antonio Nariño was born and dedicated in 1908. Julián Lombana and Gastón Lelarge, who was born in France and had studied under Charles Garnier, designed it. They pushed the property out as far as Eighth Road, reorganised the inside on two levels, laid out wide halls and gave the front carved stone. The Swiss sculptor Luigi Ramelli made all the ornament. New additions led to a second dedication in 1980. Fernando Alsina, an architect and auditor at the Ministry of public works, handled restoration. In the garden stands the Observatorio Astronómico de Bogotá, built in 1802–03 to a design by Domingo de Petrés, a Capuchin friar and architect.

Bharat Mandapam is an exhibition hall within New Delhi's Pragati Maidan complex. The complex opened in 1972, the hall in 2023, before the G20 summit the city hosted that year. It stands where Raj Rewal's Hall of Nations stood, once hailed as the world's first and, at the time, largest space-frame in reinforced concrete. That hall was torn down in 2017, controversially, while courts were still weighing its heritage status. In 2016 Arcop of Delhi and Aedas of Singapore, led by Sanjay Singh and the Spaniard Simón Núñez de Arenas Fraile, won the contest to plan and design the exhibition halls and convention centre. The complex has 390,000 square metres of built-up area, a meeting hall for 7,000 and six exhibition halls with 150,000 square metres of display space. The National Buildings Construction Corporation built it for over ₹2,600 crore.

Yashobhoomi is a convention centre in Sector 25 of Dwarka, Delhi. By area it is the largest in India and in Asia, and among the world's biggest MICE venues. Its first phase opened on 17 September 2023. Fifteen convention centres, counting the main auditorium, the Grand Ballroom and 13 meeting centres, can hold 11,000 people together. Indian culture shaped the auditorium's decoration: terrazzo floors inlaid with brass in rangoli patterns, hanging metal cylinders that absorb sound, and lit patterned walls. Automated seating lets its floor switch between flat and tiered. The ballroom ceiling follows a petal theme, with seating both inside and out. The complex reuses all of its treated wastewater, harvests rain and has solar panels on every roof, measures that earned a Green Cities Platinum rating from the Indian Green Building Council.

The Christuskirche, or Christ Church, is a Lutheran church and landmark in Windhoek, belonging to Namibia's German-speaking Evangelical Lutheran Church. Gottlieb Redecker designed it, and it was raised as a symbol of peace once the Germans had fought wars against the Herero and Nama. Work began with a foundation stone on 11 August 1907, and the church was dedicated on 16 October 1910. It is built of quartz sandstone, mined near the Avis Dam, while the portico uses Carrara marble shipped from Italy. Neo-Romanesque, Art Nouveau and Gothic Revival influences meet in the design, and the spire rises 24 metres. Emperor Wilhelm II gave the coloured stained lead glass windows in the sanctuary.

The Acropolium, or Cathedral of Saint Louis, crowns Byrsa Hill in Carthage, Tunisia, near the ruins of the Punic, then Roman, city, over the remains of a temple to Eshmun, the Punic god of healing. Built in 1884–1890 under the French protectorate, it became the primatial church of all Africa when that title was revived for Cardinal Lavigerie. He dedicated it to Saint Louis, who died near this spot in 1270 during the Eighth Crusade. The abbot Pougnet drew the plans, mixing Byzantine, Gothic and Moorish ideas on a Latin cross 65 metres by 30. Two square towers frame the front; a large cupola ringed by eight short towers covers the crossing, and a smaller one tops the apse. It has 284 stained glass windows. Worship has ended, and it now hosts events and concerts of Tunisian and classical music.

This monumental grave in Monastir, Tunisia, holds the remains of Habib Bourguiba, known as the father of Tunisia's independence, who died on 6 April 2000. It was built in 1963, while he was still alive, in a modern Arab-Muslim style, and enlarged in 1978. The mausoleum closes the main alley, some 200 metres long and 30 wide, in the western section of the cemetery of Sidi El Mézeri, the city's main burial ground. Two minarets, each 25 metres tall, flank the building, and a golden dome sits between two green ones. Its entrance gate and the gate setting it apart from the cemetery are both works of Tunisian art. A small museum inside keeps his desk from Carthage's presidential palace, with his pens, passports, identity card, glasses, photographs and clothes, Western and traditional, including the jebba, chéchia and fez.

In Alexandria's Anfoushi district, this thirteenth-century mosque is also a mausoleum and Sufi shrine, named after the mystic Abu'l Abbas al-Mursi, who lived in that century and lies here beside members of the Ashraf family. In 1934 King Fouad I ordered a courtyard of 3,200 square metres taking in the mosque-shrines of Yaqut al-Arshy and Al-Busiri, with this mosque at its centre. The Italian architect Mario Rossi helped plan its design and decor, and building took sixteen or eighteen years. The exterior especially is Neo-Mamluk, drawn from late Mamluk work. Four of the granite pillars, of a harder granite designed in Italy, carry the heavy main dome; four smaller domes stand for the saint and his disciples. The minaret rises about 73 metres. It inspired the far larger Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi, completed in 2007.

Cape Town Stadium was built when South Africa hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup and hosts football and rugby union; since 2021 a sponsor has named it the DHL Stadium. It sits on the Green Point Common, between Signal Hill and the Atlantic, near the city centre and the Victoria & Alfred Waterfront. Work began in March 2007 and took 33 months, with the contractors Murray & Roberts (now Concor) and WBHO, at a cost of R4.4 billion, about US$600 million. GMP Architects of Germany designed it with two local practices, Louis Karol Architects and Point Architects. It seated 64,100 for the World Cup. Afterwards, temporary rows on both sides of the top tier gave way to event suites and clubrooms, cutting capacity to 55,000. Greenpoint Park was completed within a year of the tournament, as promised in public consultation.

The Capital Museum, a public art museum run by the city of Beijing, opened in 1981; in 2006 it moved into its present building. Cui Kai and Jean-Marie Duthilleul shaped its great roof and the sloping entrance square. The stone outer wall was meant to recall the walls and towers of old Chinese cities. Before the museum's north gate, a danbi, a huge stone carved with dragons, phoenixes and imperial objects, is set into the ground. Inside the reception hall stands a decorative archway from the Ming dynasty, showing the central axis common in Chinese architecture. The oval Bronze Exhibition Hall leans outward from the ground through the outer face of the museum, a slant meant to evoke ancient objects being dug up.

Digital Beijing, a 57-metre block, was built as a data centre for the 2008 Summer Olympics and opened on 3 November 2007. Of the big Olympic Green facilities, only it hosted no events, and it was the one major Olympic building by a Chinese architect. Pei Zhu, interested in how digital technology relates to traditional Chinese design, made a sustainable building that reads as a circuit board from the sides and a bar code from the ends. Four narrow 11-storey slabs vary in thickness, the eastern one thickest and set apart by the widest gap. They are faced in dark stone from northern China and some aluminium made to look like stone. At night, green LEDs blink downward across the east front. Inside, a translucent fibre-reinforced plastic floor, first made as a substitute for costly jade, takes projected images.

This building in Taipei's Zhongzheng District serves as the Republic of China's presidential office. Uheiji Nagano designed it while Japan ruled Taiwan (1895–1945), and it first housed the Office of the Governor-General. Work ran from 1 June 1912 to 31 March 1919 and cost 2.8 million yen. The 130-metre front faces east down Ketagalan Boulevard, as Japanese architects tended to turn key buildings to the sunrise at the end of long avenues; that, with a free mix of Renaissance, Baroque and neoclassical elements, typifies their colonial work. Tokyo raised the central tower from six storeys to eleven; at 60 metres, it stood higher than anything else in the Taipei Basin under Japanese rule. A restoration involving about 81,000 workers ended in late 1948, leaving it little changed. In 1998 it was declared a national historic monument.

Made of bamboo, Bug Dome was a shelter put up in Shenzhen, China, for the 2009 Shenzhen and Hong Kong biennale of urbanism and architecture. Its makers called themselves WEAK!: Hsieh Ying-Chun, a Taiwanese architectural activist focused on collaborative and sustainable building; Roan Ching-Yueh, architect, art critic and curator; and the Finnish architect Marco Casagrande, founder of C-lab. Homes that insects build inspired it. It was made to shelter underground gigs, poetry readings and talks during the biennale. The structure used bamboo and a 'weak concrete' of cement mixed with soil. All its materials came from around the site and would return to nature once the dome was no longer needed. After the biennale, illegal workers who had come from China's countryside kept using it as a gathering place, many of them living in nearby shelters and abandoned buildings.

The Yuz Museum sits in the West Bund area of Shanghai's Xuhui District and is operated by the Yuz Foundation, a non-profit. It was founded by the Chinese-Indonesian businessman, philanthropist and art collector Budi Tek. The Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto designed the museum inside a renovated aircraft hangar of the former Longhua Airport. Its premises cover more than 9,000 square metres. The great hall made from the old hangar alone exceeds 3,000 square metres and suits the many large art installations, while the other galleries add over 1,000 square metres for contemporary painting, sculpture and photography. The museum opened on 17 May 2014.

Chengdu Museum is a public city museum in Chengdu, in China's Sichuan province. It stands on Tianfu Square's western edge, near the Jincheng Art Palace, the Sichuan Art Museum, the Sichuan Provincial Library and the Sichuan Science and Technology Museum. Sutherland Hussey Harris, with the Beijing-based practice Pansolution, won first place in a 2007 international contest to design a new museum for the city. The building was finished in 2016 under the name Chengdu Museum New Hall. It has 65,000 square metres of floor space and shows historic artefacts on six floors. It is the city's largest comprehensive museum, holding nearly 200,000 objects that span from the Neolithic period to the Republic of China.

The Auditorium Building, on South Michigan Avenue (number 430) in Chicago's Loop, is an early mixed-use skyscraper. Adler & Sullivan, the partnership of Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan, designed it, with help from Frank Lloyd Wright, who had joined the firm. It was built in 1887–1889. At first it combined the Auditorium Theatre with offices and a hotel; the theatre survives, while the rest now holds classrooms for Roosevelt University. It is mostly 10 storeys, with a 17-storey, 73-metre tower to the south. The front, mainly darker granite and lighter limestone, falls into three horizontal bands. Grillages and pyramid-shaped footings support an iron and steel frame. The theatre takes up 40% of the volume, with 4,200 seats on three levels. It is listed as a Chicago Landmark, a National Historic Landmark and on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Climatron, a greenhouse inside a geodesic dome, belongs to the Missouri Botanical Garden in St. Louis. Frits W. Went, then the garden's director, started it, and T. C. Howard, of the Raleigh, North Carolina firm Synergetics, designed it; it was finished in 1960. It was the world's first greenhouse to be fully air-conditioned, and no geodesic dome before it had been enclosed in rigid Plexiglas panels. The half-sphere, 42 metres across and 21 high, has no inner partitions: climate controls alone create the range of conditions of a lowland rain forest. Aluminium tubes in compression and aluminium rods in tension hold up the frame. The architects won the R. S. Reynolds Memorial Award for 1961, worth $25,000, for their use of aluminium. Later, 2,425 panes of heat-strengthened glass with a Saflex interlayer and a low-emissivity coating replaced the Plexiglas.

Biosphere 2 is an Earth system science research facility in Oracle, Arizona. Built in 1987–1991, the 3.14-acre structure was meant to be a materially closed ecological system, testing whether such systems could sustain human life in outer space; it remains the largest ever made. It held a rainforest, an ocean with a coral reef, mangroves, savannah and a fog desert, plus farmland and a human habitat. Above ground, steel tubing and frames carry high-performance glass. Pearce Structures, the firm of Buckminster Fuller's associate Peter Jon Pearce, designed and made the frame and glazing. Patented airtight seals by Pearce and William Dempster kept leakage below 10% a year. Rather than resist the huge forces of a fixed volume, the building used large diaphragms in domes called 'lungs'. Facing demolition, it passed to the University of Arizona for research in 2007.

The Denver Public Library system's flagship, the Central Library, stands in Downtown Denver's Golden Triangle, south of the 16th Street Mall and beside the Denver Art Museum. In the 1990s city voters approved $91.6 million in bonds to extend the Fisher/Hoyt building. The 540,000-square-foot addition, commissioned in 1990 and opened in 1995, was designed by Michael Graves, later the 2012 Driehaus Prize winner, with the Denver firm Klipp Colussy Jenks DuBois. It is one of the biggest libraries in the country, with over a million visitors a year. Its seven-storey exterior is finished in limestone and pre-cast concrete with copper accents; the postmodern design draws on abstracted classical forms, colours and materials. Edward Ruscha painted murals inside, and fossils are set in the floor of Schlessman Hall. The 23rd G8 Summit met here in 1997.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this Prairie Style house in Wichita, Kansas, in 1915 for Henry Justin Allen, a former Kansas governor, and his wife, Elsie. It was one of his last Prairie Houses. Outside and in, it shows the influence of the prairie and of Japanese architecture; at that time Wright was also busy with the Imperial Hotel in Japan. A horizontal water table of grey Carthage marble eases the step from ground to house, and the brick walls pair white horizontal joints with flush ochre head joints. The roof, laid with Ludowici tiles, stresses horizontal lines and has a Japanese-inspired starting course. The living and dining rooms enclose a sunken garden of lilies and koi. The house also had the first firewall in a home. It joined the National Register of Historic Places on 7 March 1973.

The Dreischeibenhaus, roughly 'three plates building' in English, is a 95-metre office tower on August-Thyssen-Straße in Düsseldorf's Hofgarten district. It was also called the Thyssenhaus, because the Thyssen and ThyssenKrupp groups had their headquarters there. Built from 1957 to 1960, it brought Helmut Hentrich worldwide recognition and was among the first skyscrapers finished in Germany after the Second World War. It remains one of the country's best-known high-rises, a major example of post-war International style modernism and a symbol of the Wirtschaftswunder, Germany's post-war 'economic miracle'. It contrasts with its neighbour, the Düsseldorfer Schauspielhaus on Gustaf-Gründgens-Platz. A full refurbishment in the early 1990s gave it a new curtain wall that kept the original look while handling heat and moisture better. After another renovation, led by HPP Architects of Düsseldorf in 2013, it offers 35,000 square metres of gross floor area.

On completion, Berlin's Detlev-Rohwedder-Haus was Europe's largest office building. It went up from February 1935 to August 1936 for the German Ministry of Aviation (Reichsluftfahrtministerium), headed by Hermann Göring, in just 18 months, with workers on double shifts and Sundays. Its architect, Ernst Sagebiel, also rebuilt Tempelhof Airport on a similar scale. His severe, linear manner, starker than Albert Speer's more classical leanings, was called 'Luftwaffe modern' for his close ties to the Luftwaffe. A reinforced concrete skeleton is faced in limestone and travertine from at least 50 quarries. Seven storeys hold 112,000 square metres, 2,800 rooms, 7 kilometres of corridors, over 4,000 windows and 17 stairways. The German Democratic Republic was founded in its Festsaal on 7 October 1949. The Finance Ministry's Berlin branch arrived in 1990, and after a major refit the building became its headquarters in 1999.

The Stockholm Court House (Stockholms rådhus) stands on Kungsholmen in central Stockholm. Credited to Carl Westman, it was designed in the National Romantic style and completed in 1915. Westman's earlier building for the Swedish General Medical Association in Stockholm, of 1904–1906, was the first in that style; the Court House and the Röhss Museum in Gothenburg are two other prominent examples. Castles of the Vasa era shaped its architecture, and it closely resembles the medieval Vadstena Castle. The building has proved quite inflexible for its purposes. The Stockholm City Court sat here from 1915 to 1971, and the Stockholm District Court has used it since 1971.

Brasília's Military Cathedral, dedicated to St. Mary Queen of Peace, serves Roman Catholics in Brazil's capital. It stands on the west side of the Monumental Axis, between its N1 and S1 lanes, near the Urban Military Sector. Pope John Paul II laid its foundation stone in 1991, while visiting Brazil. The Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer designed the church, which was inaugurated on 12 September 1994. Its triangular form recalls a tent. The cathedral belongs to the Military Ordinariate of Brazil, whose archbishop is Marcony Vinícius Ferreira.

Frank Lloyd Wright, born in Richland Center, Wisconsin, in 1867, designed this Mayan Revival warehouse in his home town. He did the work instead of paying a bill he owed to Albert Delvino German. The building was meant for storing and selling goods wholesale, and plans also called for a teahouse restaurant, shops and an art gallery. Work started in 1917 and ended in 1921. Facing one of the town's main streets, it is built mostly of concrete with a brick veneer, and carries a Mayan-style concrete frieze said to derive from masks of the rain god Chac. It is on the National Register of Historic Places, and in 2017 its condition was assessed and a preservation plan drawn up.

MOMAT, Tokyo's National Museum of Modern Art, is the leading museum for collecting and showing modern Japanese art. It stands in Chiyoda, Tokyo, and is known for twentieth-century works, including artists in Western styles and in Nihonga. Founded in 1952 under the Ministry of Education, it was Japan's first national art museum. Kunio Maekawa was the architect of the building. Later, on two occasions, the museum bought neighbouring sites and expanded. Its latest redesign was conceived by Yoshirō Taniguchi, whose son Yoshio Taniguchi designed the extension to New York's MoMA.

Also called the Recinto Ferial, the Centro Internacional de Ferias y Congresos de Tenerife opened in May 1996 on the seafront of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, in Spain's Canary Islands. It covers more than 40,000 square metres. Santiago Calatrava, architect and engineer, designed it as a multipurpose building for the island's major fairs, exhibitions and conferences. The Great Hall on the top floor takes up 12,000 square metres; nowhere else in the Canaries is there a bigger covered space. This main room is 190 metres long, 70 wide and about 20 high, built of glass, iron and concrete. Capacity reaches 15,000 people, and entry is through an arch 50 metres long. World Trade Center Tenerife also has its headquarters here.

This park at La Pobla de Lillet, Spain, was built in 1905–1906 to a design by the Modernista Antoni Gaudí. Staying in Lillet with Joan Artigas i Alart, a textile magnate whose estate, Font de la Magnèsia, lay on the Llobregat river, Gaudí designed the gardens to thank his host. He sent some workers from Park Güell, and the two share clear likenesses in style and structure; as there, the design merges fully with nature. An artificial grotto, a Gaudí trademark, echoes his grotto at the Parc de la Ciutadella cascade. Gospel symbols recur: Saint Matthew's angel at la Cascada, Saint John's eagle at the Coix arch bridge over the Llobregat, Saint Mark's lion at la Pèrgola and Saint Luke's bull at the Bull Fountain. Nearly abandoned by 1971, the gardens were restored in 1992 under the Reial Càtedra Gaudí.

Malmö Opera was known until 1992 as the Malmö City Theatre, housing several organisations. Asked in the 1920s to design a new theatre, Sigurd Lewerentz proposed a classical scheme, but new trends in Swedish architecture pushed the design towards functionalism. Lewerentz designed it with David Helldén and Erik Lallerstedt, and it was built from 1933 to 1944; it opened on 23 September 1944 and was considered the most modern theatre in Northern Europe. Separate volumes for different uses meet a monumental, classical language, above all in the marble-clad columns and large windows of the entrance front. Among Scandinavia's largest, the 1,511-seat auditorium is an enclosed amphitheatre meant to give the best view, and can shrink to four sizes with retractable walls. Max Reinhardt's influence led to a revolving stage 20 metres across. It has been listed since 13 December 1994.

Green Library, formally the Cecil H. Green Library, is Stanford University's main library and part of the SUL system. It holds 4 million volumes, mostly in the humanities and social sciences. Approved in 1913 and completed in 1919, a big new library building now forms Green Library's older part. Its design broke early and clearly with the look of Stanford's Main Quad. A larger annex came in 1980, when the library was renamed for Cecil H. Green. The original section is now called the Bing Wing, after Peter Bing, who gave a large sum to repair it after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake.

Berlin's Altes Stadthaus, or Old City Hall, served as an administrative building and is now used by the Senate. Ludwig Hoffmann, the city's chief of construction, designed it to supplement the Rotes Rathaus; construction ran from 1902 to 1911 and cost 7 million marks. Over the central bay facing Judenstraße, a tower about 80 metres high climbs from a square base; its dome carries Ignatius Taschner's 3.25-metre copper Fortuna on a gilded globe. The grey muschelkalk facades follow Palladian principles and draw on the Palazzo Thiene in Vicenza. Since other buildings once hemmed it in, Hoffmann designed it to be seen up close rather than from afar. At its heart is a three-storey barrel-vaulted Jugendstil hall for 1,500 people. A full refurbishment in the 1990s replaced about 180 sculptural pieces outside, and the original mansard roof was rebuilt in 1998–99.

Werner March designed this building in Berlin for the Kingdom of Yugoslavia's legation in the German Empire, and it was built from 1938 to 1940. March is best known for the Olympiastadion in Berlin and other Reichssportfeld buildings for the Summer Olympics, whose overall planning he also led. His 1938 design has an angular plan and an austere, closed character. Two wings follow the streets to form an L, and the tiled roof uses Mediterranean-style monk-and-nun tiles. Its address is Rauchstraße 17–18, in the embassy quarter of Tiergarten, and it is a listed building. The legation moved in during October 1940 but used it for only six months. Since 1999 the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) has occupied it.

Leighton House, in west London's Holland Park, was the home of Frederic Leighton (1830–1896), a wealthy Victorian painter, President of the Royal Academy and creator of the popular Flaming June. His friend George Aitchison built him a combined house and studio on the private Ilchester Estate between 1866 and 1895. Red Suffolk brick with Caen stone dressings gives a restrained Classical look. The principal room, a first-floor studio, faced north, measured 45 by 25 feet at first and had a large central window for painting light. In 1877–79 a two-storey Arab Hall was added for tiles Leighton had gathered in the Middle East; Aitchison and Walter Crane said La Zisa palace in Palermo was its model. The historian J. Mordaunt Crook called it one of the most innovative Victorian houses. An £8 million refurbishment was unveiled on 15 October 2022.

The Adam Mickiewicz Theatre stands on Theatre Square in the Old City of Cieszyn, Poland. Ferdinand Fellner and Hermann Helmer, architects from Vienna, designed it, having already designed 48 theatres in cities including Berlin, Vienna, Łańcut and Toruń. Finished in 1909, it opened as the Deutsches Theater; in October 1930 the German sign was taken down from the front. The five-storey, 16,944-cubic-metre building follows late Viennese Baroque under a tall mansard roof with a turret and dormers. It had 770 seats and standing places (630 seats today), with a rotating stage, an iron fire curtain, a boiler room, a power station, a ballet hall and stores for sets and costumes. White, gold and red dominate the interior. A whisper on stage could be heard in the ninth row of the second balcony, where shell-shaped sound catchers were placed.

Bush House, a Grade II listed building in London, sits where Kingsway ends to the south, between the Strand and Aldwych. Irving T. Bush won approval for his plans in 1919; the building was conceived as a big new centre of trade, and the American architect Harvey Wiley Corbett designed it. Building ran from 1925 to 1935. Corbett gave London a massive office block, essentially American in style, yet within the city's strict building codes. Built of Portland stone, it was declared in 1929 the costliest building on earth. At the entrance, two statues by the American artist Malvina Hoffman symbolise Anglo-American friendship, and an inscription reads 'To the friendship of English speaking peoples'. Broadcasting from the building lasted 70 years, from winter 1941 to summer 2012. King's College London has used it since taking the lease in 2015.

Fresno City Hall, in Fresno, California, is a post-modern futurist building designed by the Canadian architect Arthur Erickson, who shaped its look for the local architect William Patnaude. It stands at the north end of the twelve-block civic corridor called the Mariposa Mall, with the Fresno County Courthouse closing the southern end. A new design, with two separate peaks at the centre under a big sloping roof, went to the city council and passed by four votes to two. The five-storey exterior uses glass and matte stainless-steel panels below an angular roofline meant to recall the nearby Sierra Nevada's peaks. In the chamber, daylight falls through a skylight set in the gap between the two peaks. The building was dedicated on Presidents' Day, 17 February 1992.

100 Eleventh Avenue is a 23-storey apartment tower in Manhattan at 19th Street and Eleventh Avenue. The developers, Craig Wood and Curtis Bashaw, hired the French architect Jean Nouvel, with Beyer Blinder Belle as executive architects, and it was completed in 2010. The tower follows a curve running the full length of the site, giving every apartment a street front and views. On the south and west, Nouvel drew a pixelated curtain wall inspired by an insect's compound eye: 1,647 different panes join into 'megapanels' tilted at varied angles, so transparency shifts across the face. That curtain wall is among New York's most technologically advanced, yet the building also refers to West Chelsea's masonry industrial traditions; black brick clads the north and east sides. Described as a conceptual heir to Nouvel's Arab World Institute in Paris, it is LEED certified.

Frist Campus Center is a focal point of campus social life at Princeton. It combines the former Palmer Physics Lab with a modern addition finished in 2001. Venturi, Scott Brown & Associates, the practice of Denise Scott Brown and Robert Venturi, himself a Princeton graduate, designed this expansion of the Collegiate Gothic Palmer Hall. The new volume fills the courtyard of the old C-shaped building and runs across its open side to form a new east front. Money from the Frist family's fortune in private hospitals paid for it. Room 302, a lecture hall, has been restored to how it was when Albert Einstein lectured there. The building also stood in for the fictional Princeton–Plainsboro Teaching Hospital in exterior shots for the television series House.

Caja Mágica, Spanish for 'Magic Box', is a multi-purpose stadium in Madrid, also called the Manzanares Park Tennis Center. The French architect Dominique Perrault designed the sports complex, and since 2009 it has hosted the Madrid Open tennis tournament. One structure covers three courts, each with its own adjustable roof that can sit in several positions, open fully or close completely. The cube-shaped building is made mainly of steel, aluminium, concrete and glass. Its centre clay court, officially the Estadio Manolo Santana, holds up to 12,442 spectators. The budget was first set at 120 million euros, but the final construction bill reached 294 million.

550 South Tryon, formerly the Duke Energy Center, is a Charlotte skyscraper 786 feet (240 metres) tall, with 48 floors, or 54 counting mechanical floors. On completion in 2010 it was Charlotte's largest building by floor area and its second tallest, the 63rd tallest in the US, and the world's tallest to use precast double tees. Those tees, a method usually seen in parking decks, form the floors around a core of concrete poured in place; the concrete reaches 18,000 psi. Batson-Cook Construction built it, with TRC International of Sarasota, Florida, as structural engineers. Water-saving plumbing, rainwater stored for the cooling tower and a green roof earned it LEED Platinum. Gabler-Youngston Architectural Lighting Design planned the facade lighting: hundreds of programmable colour-changing LED and metal halide fixtures. No building in the Levine Center for the Arts is taller.

Waterloo's Canadian Clay and Glass Gallery, in Ontario, is a public art gallery and the only one in Canada devoted solely to showing and collecting contemporary Canadian ceramics, glass, enamel and stained glass. In October 1986 a national competition invited eight firms from across Canada to submit designs. John and Patricia Patkau, architects from Vancouver, came first and turned the site, where Erb and Caroline Streets meet, from an old hockey arena into a cultural building. Work started in 1991, and the gallery opened in June 1993. In June 1997 Patkau Architects received a Medal of Excellence for the design in the Governor General's Awards for Architecture. Five galleries offer 6,088 square feet of exhibition space. The City of Waterloo owns, manages and maintains the building in Uptown Waterloo.

BULAC, the Bibliothèque universitaire des langues et civilisations, is a major academic library in Paris Rive Gauche, open to the public since 2011. It covers every language and civilisation outside the Western world, with more than a million documents in all languages, drawn from the former collections of over 20 libraries. Building began in summer 2008 to a design by the architect Yves Lion. The library spans five floors, three of them public, with 910 seats. The Île-de-France region is responsible for the building and paid two-thirds of the roughly 80 million euros of funding; the French State paid the rest.

In Pacific Grove, California, at the Monterey Peninsula's western tip, Asilomar Conference Grounds, now a conference centre, was originally built for the YWCA. Early in 1913 came the news that Julia Morgan would design the new campgrounds, in Arts & Crafts style, alongside her work on the Oakland YWCA building. Work started that spring; the Social Hall and Longhouses were done by August, in time for 300 girls at the first summer programme. From 1913 to 1929 Morgan designed 16 buildings here, and 11 still stand; her final design, Merrill Hall, was dedicated in 1928. The name joins the Spanish asilo ('refuge') and mar ('sea'), the winning idea of Helen Salisbury, a Stanford student. California's state government bought the site in 1956 and had John Carl Warnecke design seven more buildings. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1987.

Bakkehaugen Church stands in the Tåsen neighbourhood of Oslo, Norway. Ove Bang won the architectural competition announced in 1938, and the church is credited to him and Erling Viksjø. The Second World War and a shortage of money held up construction, and Bishop Johannes Smemo consecrated the church on 20 December 1959. It is built of natural concrete in a triangular shape like a boathouse, with a bell tower standing on its own. The Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage has listed the church, and Norwegian law protects it.

Aon Center rises 62 stories, or 858 ft (262 m), at 707 Wilshire Boulevard, downtown Los Angeles; it was formerly known as the United California Bank Building and as First Interstate Tower. Charles Luckman designed it as a rectangular office tower clad in bronze and trimmed in white, notably slim for a skyscraper in an earthquake-prone region. Site work started in late 1970, and it was done by 1973. No building in the world outside New York and Chicago was then taller, and it stayed the tallest in Los Angeles until 1989, when Library Tower, today U.S. Bank Tower, was completed. A fire in the tower became especially severe because it had no sprinklers, which office towers did not need when it was built; Los Angeles then changed its codes so that every high-rise must have them.

The Coliseum Theater opened in Seattle on January 8, 1916, as a cinema. B. Marcus Priteca designed it, and it was the city's first theater built purely to screen films, as well as one of the earliest cinemas anywhere to aim for architectural grandeur. In 1931 the Journal of the Royal Institute of Architects gave it the title of the world's first movie palace. Elaborate terra cotta covers the outside, and the original interior was just as ornate. It has had a National Register of Historic Places listing since 1975 and is an official landmark of the city. The cinema closed on March 11, 1990, after a screening of Tremors, and the building became a Banana Republic clothing store of 15,000 square feet (1,400 m2), which opened in 1994.

The B.J. Ricker House in Grinnell, Iowa, is a historic home whose importance lies in being early work by Walter Burley Griffin. Building began in 1911, but trouble with millwork and labour held back completion until 1912. It is a two-story brick house on a rectangular plan, raised on a high cement basement, with four broad brick piers marking its corners. Over the main block sits a gable roof that seems to hover. On the south side, a veranda is laid out as a Greek cross in plan. In 1979 the house gained a National Register of Historic Places listing.

Le Corbusier designed Villa Savoye with his cousin Pierre Jeanneret, while Charlotte Perriand handled the interior and furnishings. Built from reinforced concrete between 1928 and 1931, it began as the Savoye family's country retreat, and its design carried his "Five Points", the core rules of his new aesthetic. Unlike his earlier town villas, here he could shape all four sides around the view and the sun's path. The plan rests on the Golden section's principal ratios. Even the curved glass at the ground-floor entrance follows a car's turning circle. A ramp, seen from nearly everywhere inside, climbs to the living area and salon on the first floor, then runs outdoors from the roof terrace to the second-floor solarium. In July 2016 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site with 16 other Le Corbusier buildings in seven countries.

Surottam Hutheesing, then president of the Ahmedabad Mill Owners' Association, asked Le Corbusier to design the group's new headquarters, finished in 1954. A ceremonial ramp leads into a triple-height entrance hall left open to the wind. The third floor holds a top-lit auditorium under a roof canopy, enclosed by a curved wall, and a generous lobby. The east and west faces are brise-soleil, or sun breakers, among the many formal devices Corbusier invented: they keep out harsh sun yet let air move and views pass through. These free façades are rough shuttered concrete, while the north and south walls, in rough brick, are almost solid. His notion of a house that is also a palace gave form to the institution's public and private sides. Experiments tried here later helped Harvard's Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, among others.

Mies van der Rohe designed the Farnsworth House in the International Style as a weekend retreat for Edith Farnsworth, a nephrologist and physician, and it was completed in 1951. The house is lifted 5¼ feet (1.6 m) above the floodplain. Eight steel columns carry its concrete floor and roof slabs and split it into three bays running west to east. The walls are glass set between steel mullions, and the western third is an open-air veranda. Inside, the plan is mostly open, with a minimal colour scheme broken only by an off-centre utility core and a movable wardrobe. That core holds the kitchen, bathrooms and services, with living, dining and sleeping areas arranged around it. Now a National Historic Landmark, the house has shaped other houses and Mies's own later work, and has featured in books, films and exhibitions.

Mies van der Rohe designed S. R. Crown Hall for the College of Architecture at IIT, a school he headed for twenty years, and it was completed in 1956. Except near the entrances, the exterior is entirely steel and glass. Its curtain wall has three horizontal tiers of glass panes between steel columns and mullions. Four girders, carried on four pairs of columns, lift the roof 18 feet (5.5 m) over the main floor. That floor is mostly one open space with half-height partitions, and apart from two mechanical shafts it has no interior columns. Large renovations in the 2000s corrected faults in the design, brought in new mechanical systems and improved the building's energy efficiency. Chicago has made it a city landmark, and it is also a National Historic Landmark.

The Seagram Building is a 38-story tower, 515 feet (157 m) tall, that first housed the headquarters of a Canadian distiller, the Seagram Company, after its completion in 1958. Mies van der Rohe designed it in the International Style with Robert Allan Jacobs, Ely Jacques Kahn and Philip Johnson, and Phyllis Lambert, whose father Samuel Bronfman was Seagram's CEO, strongly shaped the design. The tower fills half its site and stands 90 feet (27 m) back from Park Avenue. It was the world's first office building faced in extruded bronze, and the first New York skyscraper with plate glass windows running full height. The building helped shape the city's 1961 Zoning Resolution, which let developers add floor area in return for plazas. In 1989 the Four Seasons Restaurant, the lobby and the exterior became official city landmarks.

Mies van der Rohe designed the Neue Nationalgalerie and its sculpture gardens, which opened on 15 September 1968 south of the Tiergarten, in West Berlin as it was then. A black-painted square plate of pre-stressed steel, 1.8 m thick, forms the roof and rests on only eight cruciform columns, two to a side, set back from the corners. Thanks to an 18 m cantilever, the glazed gallery wall stands well clear of those columns. Inside, the hall rises 8.4 m and is planned on a square grid of 3.6 m. After work by David Chipperfield Architects finished in 2021, the museum opened again that August with an exhibition of the American sculptor Alexander Calder.

The original Johnson Wax Headquarters in Racine consists of two Frank Lloyd Wright buildings. The Administration Building was completed in April 1939; the Research Tower followed in November 1950. The first is a version of the streamlined Art Moderne style, its brick facade curving and its windows made of Pyrex glass tubes. Its main space is a great workroom where concrete shell columns are topped by large "calyxes". The tower alternates square floors with circular mezzanines, all cantilevered out from a structural core. The glass tubes caused trouble: once the building was done, the caulking between them began to peel, and leaks went on for several years. The headquarters holds the Twenty-five Year Award of the American Institute of Architects and is a National Historic Landmark.

In 1924 Gerrit Rietveld built the Rietveld Schröder House at Prins Hendriklaan 50, Utrecht, for Mrs Truus Schröder-Schräder, a mother of three. Of all De Stijl buildings it ranks among the best known, and arguably the only true one. Mrs Schröder wanted the living space to work either open or divided, and panels that slide and revolve made both possible. On the facades, planes and lines are deliberately kept apart so they seem to glide past each other. Colours were picked to strengthen this plastic effect: white and grey surfaces, black frames to windows and doors, and a few linear elements in primary colours. Only the foundations and balconies are concrete; the walls are brick and plaster. It became a listed monument in 1976 and joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2000.

Aino Aalto and Alvar Aalto designed and built Villa Mairea in Noormarkku, Pori, for Harry and Maire Gullichsen as a rural retreat, villa and guest-house; construction ran from 1938 to 1939. Its plan is a modified L-shape, a type the Aaltos had used before. The interiors were led mainly by Aino Aalto, rich in wood, stone and brick and fitted with custom cabinetry, lighting and textiles. The structural grid varies both ways, and the round steel columns stand at random, in one case tripled, clad in wood strips or bound in rattan. Early in 1938 Frank Lloyd Wright's newly acclaimed Fallingwater gave fresh inspiration. Sigfried Giedion called the house "a love poem". In July 2026 UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site with 12 other Aalto works.

Säynätsalo Town Hall is a complex of two main buildings grouped round a central courtyard. One is a U-shaped block with the council chamber and administrative offices; the other holds a community library and flats. Alvar Aalto was given the commission after a 1949 design contest, and the building was finished in December 1951. He set it into Säynätsalo's wooded hillside, making a three-story building that wraps a raised courtyard. Finnish vernacular building and the humanism of the Italian Renaissance both shaped the design. Crowning the town hall is the double-height council chamber, capped by Aalto's "Butterfly" trusses. Aalto kept to a narrow palette, mostly brick with touches of timber and copper, and even laid the bricks slightly out of line so their shadows enliven the surface. Grass stairs form a simple amphitheatre that recalls ancient Greek and Italian architecture.

Philip Johnson built the Glass House in New Canaan in 1948–49 as his weekend retreat. In 1947 he had curated a Museum of Modern Art exhibition of Mies's work that included a Farnsworth House model. The house is 56 ft long, 32 ft wide and 10.5 ft high (17 × 9.8 × 3.2 m), and its outer walls are charcoal-painted steel and glass. The interior is one open space divided by low walnut cabinets. Only a brick cylinder enclosing the bathroom reaches the ceiling. The idea was to erase the line between inside and outside, and Johnson once said of the landscape, "I have very expensive wallpaper." In 1997 it was made a National Historic Landmark. It now belongs to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, and guided tours begin at the visitors center, 199 Elm Street.

The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum documents the atomic bombing of Hiroshima in World War II and stands inside Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, at the centre of the city. Kenzō Tange was the architect of its main building, and the park itself was planned and designed by Tange at Tange Lab. The site was once the busiest commercial and residential district downtown; the park was laid out on an open field left by the explosion. From the building there are views of the Memorial Cenotaph, the Peace Flame and the A-Bomb Dome. Between 1955 and 2005 the museum received 53 million visitors, more than a million a year on average. Once the East Wing had reopened, the Main Hall closed for seismic retrofitting and stayed shut until 25 April 2019.

Wanting a contemporary design for its library, Phillips Exeter Academy commissioned Louis Kahn in 1965, and the building opened in 1971. No secondary school library in the world is larger: it holds 160,000 volumes on nine levels, with shelves for 250,000. Kahn arranged it as three square rings, one inside another. The outer ring, of load-bearing brick, includes the four outside walls and the carrel desks right behind them. The inner ring is an atrium whose walls have huge circular openings showing several floors of book stacks, and two massive concrete cross beams at its top spread the light from the clerestory windows. The brick piers thicken toward the bottom, where they carry more weight, and the windows widen near the top, where the piers are thinner. In 1997 it received the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award.

Louis Kahn's Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth is known above all for the silvery daylight that washes across its vaulted gallery ceilings. Construction started in summer 1969, and the building opened in October 1972, soon earning an international name for architectural excellence. It is made of 16 parallel vaults, each 100 ft long, 20 ft wide and 20 ft high inside (30.6 × 6 × 6 m). A slot along the top of each vault lets natural light into the galleries. Using post-tensioned concrete just five inches thick, Komendant made gallery vaults that need support only at the four corners. The vault ends are concrete block, faced in travertine inside and out.

Louis Kahn designed the Jatiya Sangsad complex, seat of Bangladesh's National Assembly, initially for the Parliament of Pakistan. Spread over 210 acres (840,000 m2), it is among the world's largest legislative complexes, and Kahn planned all of it, lawns, lake and MPs' housing included. He aimed to express Bengali culture and heritage while using space well. Kahn died with it about three-quarters built; work went on under David Wisdom, who had worked for him, until its completion on 28 January 1982. The main building has nine blocks: eight outer ones of 110 feet and a central octagon of 155 feet. Huge walls are cut deep by porticoes and large geometric openings, and daylight bounces off surrounding walls and the octagonal drum into the Parliament Chamber. Water features echo Bangladesh's riverine landscape. It won the 1989 Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Paul Rudolph designed the Yale Art and Architecture Building, now called Rudolph Hall, while he chaired the architecture department, and the School of Architecture moved into it in 1963; it has stayed there ever since. Among his best-known works, it is a spatially complex Brutalist structure in concrete. Rudolph's design reflected the close integration between Yale's various fine art departments. In 2008 the building was extensively renovated and extended by a team that included the New York architect Charles Gwathmey, a Yale graduate and Rudolph mentee. The work, inside and out, returned the building to its "original 1963 intention", with historically correct windows and better lighting and furnishings.

Kenzō Tange began designing Yoyogi National Gymnasium in 1961 with the engineer Yoshikatsu Tsuboi, for the 1964 Summer Olympics in Tokyo. Approval of the bid came 20 months before the games, construction took 18 months, and the building opened on October 10, 1964. When built, it had the largest suspended roof span in the world: two reinforced concrete pillars hold a pre-stressed steel net with steel plates fixed onto it. The roof's overall curve helps shield the building from strong winds. It inspired the design of Munich's Olympic Stadium for the 1972 games, and when Tange won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1987 the citation counted it "among the most beautiful buildings of the 20th century". In 2021 Japan made it an Important Cultural Property, calling it a monumental postwar work with an energetic exterior and grand interior.

Moshe Safdie, an Israeli-Canadian-American architect, designed Habitat 67, a housing complex beside the Saint Lawrence River at Cité du Havre in Montreal. It grew out of his master's thesis at McGill University, and a revised version went up for Expo 67, the 1967 World's Fair. The complex stacks 354 identical prefabricated concrete modules, each 11.7 × 5.3 × 3 m, to form three pyramids reaching 12 residential storeys. Each unit has at least one private garden terrace, roughly 20 to 90 square metres, set on the roof of the storey beneath. The goal was to combine suburban gardens, fresh air and privacy with the density and economics of a city apartment block. August Eduard Komendant, a pioneer of prestressed concrete, was the structural engineer. Safdie wanted affordable housing, but demand has made the units dearer than planned.

MASP is well known for its headquarters, a concrete and glass building of 1968 by Lina Bo Bardi. A city landmark and an emblem of modern Brazilian architecture, it also houses one of the world's most-visited art museums. Because a view of downtown had to stay open, Bardi imagined the building lifted off the ground. Its main volume hangs 8 meters up, carried by four bright red concrete pillars joined by two huge concrete beams along its length. The 74-metre (243 ft) gap between the pillars was the widest free span anywhere at the time. In the Pinacoteca, each painting hung on its own glass sheet fixed in a rough concrete block, a "crystal easel", set out in a loose grid. In 2003 the building was registered as national patrimony by Brazil's Institute for Historic and Artistic Heritage.

SESC Pompéia occupies what was once a factory for steel drums and refrigerators in São Paulo. From 1977 to 1986 Lina Bo Bardi converted it for the non-profit Serviço Social do Comércio into a leisure and recreation centre for the working class. It was among her largest and most important projects and an early case of adaptive reuse. Her priority was to keep and amplify the life that neighbours had brought to the place, so she insisted the industrial buildings stay. She stripped old plaster and sandblasted the walls to expose the factory's rough concrete, and had rough windows knocked through and fitted inside with bright red sliding screens. At the back she added two concrete sports towers, pierced by globular windows and linked by eight walkways. The building is valued for both its architectural and social qualities.

The Greater London Council commissioned Trellick Tower, and Ernő Goldfinger designed it in the Brutalist style; it opened in 1972. Planned to replace outdated social housing, it was designed to improve on his earlier Balfron Tower in Poplar, in East London, and was his final major project. The long, thin main block has 31 floors. A separate tower for lifts and services joins its access corridors on every third storey and rises two floors higher, and includes a projecting plant room for the main heating system.
