Goldfinger included space-saving touches such as sliding bathroom doors and light switches set into the door surrounds. He argued that building high should free the ground so that children and adults could enjoy the earth. Grade II* listed since 1998, the local landmark has kept its concrete facade as a result.

The Sydney Opera House stands on Sydney Harbour's foreshore. Jørn Utzon won an international design competition in 1957, but the Ministry's criticism of cost, time and what it saw as impractical designs ended with him resigning in 1966. An Australian team headed by Peter Hall completed it, and Queen Elizabeth II formally opened it on 20 October 1973. In its modern expressionist design, large precast concrete "shells" form the roofs above a monumental podium. In mid-1961 the design team settled on making every shell a section of one sphere, 75.2 metres in radius, so arches of varying length could share one mould. From afar the shells look plain white, but they carry a subtle chevron pattern of 1,056,006 glossy white and matte cream tiles. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2007.

Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya is the museum of Sabarmati Ashram, Gandhi's ashram in Ahmedabad, on the banks of the Sabarmati River. Charles Correa began designing it in 1958, and it was his first important commission. As first built, it was made up of 51 modular units of 6 by 6 metres, arranged around a water court. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated the complex in 1963. The collection includes tens of thousands of letters written to and by Gandhi, along with photographs and books. Before this building, the museum had been housed in Gandhi's own cottage in the ashram, Hridaya Kunj.

Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa designed the Kandalama Hotel, built between 1992 and 1995. The six-storey hotel has 152 rooms and sits beside the Kandalama Reservoir, 12 km (7.5 mi) from Dambulla. The hotel wraps around a cliff, and a big porte-cochère shaped like a cave, set against the cliff's western side, is one of its main design features. Bawa wanted a planned sequence of spaces and views on arrival, so the distant view of Sigiriya appears only after guests enter the lobby. It was the first building outside the United States to be certified green under LEED, the first hotel anywhere to earn that certification, and the first hotel in Asia accredited to the Green Globe standard. The project met opposition, at first over ecology and later over its perceived harm to local culture.

Hassan Fathy built New Gourna, or New Qurna, between 1946 and 1952 to rehouse the people of Qurna, halfway between el-Gezira on the Nile and the Colossi of Memnon, on the main road leading to the Theban Necropolis. It was also an experiment in low-cost, environmentally friendly building. Fathy chose appropriate technology, above all mud brick construction. For its look he drew on traditional Nubian forms he had seen on a 1941 trip there, such as enclosed courtyards and vaulted roofs. The villagers were reluctant to move, since it cut them off from their trade in archaeological finds. The design, mixing traditional materials and methods with modern principles, was never finished, and of the original village only a few houses, the market and the mosque survive. In 2010 the World Monuments Watch named it among the most endangered sites.

Kolumba stands on the historic site of St. Kolumba church in Cologne, lost in World War II, and takes in the chapel "Madonna of the Ruins" (1950) by Gottfried Böhm. Atelier Zumthor won the competition in 1997; planning ran until 2003, the cornerstone was laid on 1 October that year, and Cardinal Meisner consecrated the building on 15 September 2007. Zumthor built directly on the original foundations and remains of St. Kolumba. A perforated grey brick facade wraps like a cloak around the museum and the old church. The bricks, fired specially for the project, blend with the stone and brick of the destroyed Romanesque church and with the concrete blocks of the post-war years. A ground-floor walkway crosses the excavation. The galleries use daylight and avoid artificial light. It won Germany's DAM Prize for Architecture in 2008.

Row House in Sumiyoshi, also called Azuma House, is a private home in Sumiyoshi-ku, Osaka, designed by Tadao Ando early in his career. Completed in 1976, this small two-story house of cast-in-place concrete began to show elements of the style that became his own. It has no exterior windows, because the owner wanted to feel he was not "in Japan". To make up for the lost light, Ando added an inner courtyard crossed by a walkway. The house divides into three equal rectangles: rooms fill the two closed ones, and an open courtyard takes the middle. That courtyard brings in daylight, air and the weather, and joins the living spaces to each side. Upstairs, a bridge crosses it to link the bedrooms.

Sendai's city government held an open competition in 1995, won by Toyo Ito, and the Sendai Mediatheque opened in January 2001. The structure combines three elements: plates, tubes and skin. Seven floor plates rest on a forest of 13 irregular tubes that appear to rise fluidly through the building. Each plate is a honeycomb of steel sections filled with lightweight concrete, which lets it span between the unevenly spaced supports without beams and stay very thin. The tubes look continuous, but they were made in floor-height pieces and assembled one floor at a time. The main south facade is double-glazed and forms part of the climate control system. Ito cites Mies's Barcelona Pavilion and the Dom-ino house of Le Corbusier as precedents. The building survived the earthquake of March 2011 almost undamaged.

Lloyd's of London, the insurance institution, is housed at 1 Lime Street in a building sometimes called the Inside-Out Building. The firm Richard Rogers & Partners designed it, and construction ran from 1978 to 1986. It is a leading case of radical Bowellism, with ducts, lifts and other services placed outside to make the most of the space inside. Around a central rectangular space stand three main towers and three more for services. Galleries overlook the Underwriting Room and form a 60-metre (197 ft) atrium lit through a vast barrel-vaulted glass roof. No UK building had glass lifts like its 12 before, and Archigram's work of the 1950s and 1960s shaped it strongly, as it did the Pompidou Centre. In 2011 it became the youngest structure ever listed Grade I. Its exposed outside pipes have made upkeep very expensive.

Norman Foster's HSBC Main Building in Hong Kong is a suspended steel structure. Work finished on 18 November 1985, and the official opening followed on 7 April 1986. Costing around HK$5.2 billion, or some US$668 million, it was then the world's most expensive building. It rises 178.8 metres through 47 storeys above four basement levels. Its five steel modules were prefabricated by Scott Lithgow Shipbuilders in the UK and shipped out. The frame is eight clusters of four steel columns clad in aluminium, rising from the foundations through the core, with triangular suspension trusses locked into these masts at five levels. The aim was a social dimension on each floor, with talk flowing between levels to make "a village in the sky". Mirrors atop the atrium reflect sunlight indoors, and cooling uses seawater rather than fresh water.

Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao stands on the bank of the Nervion, the river that crosses Bilbao on its way to the Cantabrian Sea. The outer curves are meant to look random; Gehry said this randomness was "designed to catch the light". 33,000 titanium plates form the outer skin. Its atrium, called The Flower by Gehry for its shape, organizes the whole museum. Nineteen galleries hold 120,000 sq ft (11,000 m2) of exhibition space. Ten have a classic orthogonal plan and read from outside as stone-faced; the other nine are irregular and appear as swirling, titanium-clad organic forms. It opened as part of Bilbao's revitalisation, and its impact on the district became known as the Bilbao effect. The 2010 World Architecture Survey of experts named it more often than any other building as a major work completed since 1980.

The Jewish Museum Berlin is Europe's largest Jewish museum. Against other entrants' cool, neutral spaces, Daniel Libeskind proposed a radical zigzag nicknamed "Blitz" (lightning). The twisting building is reachable only by a tunnel from the old building. A line of empty "Voids", about 20 m (66 ft) tall, slices through it. Three axes stand for the paths Jewish life in Germany has taken: continuity within German history, emigration, and the Holocaust. The second leads to the Garden of Exile, set on tilted ground, where oleaster grows high above reach on 49 pillars; 48 hold Berlin soil and one holds soil from Jerusalem. The bare concrete Tower, unheated and uncooled, is lit only by a small slit in the roof. Finished empty in 1999, it drew over 350,000 visitors before its exhibits went in and it opened on 9 September 2001.

Norway's national opera house, home to its National Opera and Ballet, stands where the Oslofjord ends, in central Oslo's Bjørvika district. Judges picked Snøhetta's design from 350 entries. Construction began in 2003 and ended in 2007, early and 300 million NOK (about US$52 million) under a 4.4 billion NOK budget. Clad in white granite and Carrara marble, the sloping outer surfaces make the building seem to rise from the water, and the roof descends to the ground as a broad plaza that people can climb for views across Oslo. In the lobby, minimally framed 15 m windows face the water, and thin angled columns hold up the roof. Oak warms the interior against the cool white outside. It took the culture award at the 2008 World Architecture Festival and the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture in 2009.

Herzog & de Meuron's Elbphilharmonie, or Elphi, is a concert hall on the Elbe's Grasbrook peninsula, in Hamburg's HafenCity quarter. Its new upper part has been likened to a hoisted sail, a wave, an iceberg or a quartz crystal. It rests on Kaispeicher A, an old brick warehouse from 1963, but stands on its own foundation, with the same footprint, a glassy skin, a wavy roof line and about a thousand curved windows. At 108 metres (354 ft) it is Hamburg's tallest inhabited building. A curved escalator climbs from the east entrance to the Plaza, an 8th-floor observation deck on top of the brick base. In the Great Concert Hall, 2,100 listeners surround the performers in vineyard style, and Yasuhisa Toyota's acoustics use some 10,000 individually shaped drywall plates. Estimated at about €200 million, construction finally cost €870 million.

The Louvre Abu Dhabi, an art museum on Saadiyat Island, may use the Louvre name until 2047 under a March 2007 deal between France and the UAE; the Louvre has described it as France's biggest cultural venture abroad. Abu Dhabi's authorities chose Jean Nouvel as architect in 2006, and in the 2006–2007 concept phase his team shaped a "seemingly floating dome" whose web pattern filters the sun, meant to recall light through the fronds of date palms in an oasis. The dome is built from 7,850 aluminium stars of varied sizes in eight tessellated layers. The museum comprises 55 buildings, 23 of them galleries, made to resemble the region's low-rise homes. Tidal pools and a watertight basement suggest a "museum in the sea" yet shield art and visitors from the corrosive marine environment. It was inaugurated on 8 November 2017.

Known widely as Las Setas, "The Mushrooms", for its look, the Metropol Parasol project began in 2004 to bring life back to the Plaza de la Encarnación in Seville. The square had been a car park for years, regarded as a dead zone between the city's more popular tourist spots. Credited to J. Mayer H., the redevelopment ran from 2004 until March 2011 at a total cost just above €102 million, over twice the original plan. Built of crossed wooden beams, it is said to be the world's largest timber-framed structure. Roman remains, left exposed where they were found, are shown below in its underground Antiquarium. It was a finalist for the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture in 2013.

In 2007, after a competition, Zaha Hadid was named design architect of the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, a complex of 619,000 sq ft (57,500 m2) known for a flowing, curving style that shuns sharp angles. Its fluid form grows out of the folding of the site's natural topography and the wrapping of the centre's individual functions. Each function, and each entrance, is expressed as a fold in one continuous surface. Spread over eight floor levels are a museum, workshops, a conference centre, temporary exhibition spaces and a 1,000-seat auditorium. President Ilham Aliyev held an official soft opening on 10 May 2012. In 2014 the centre won the Design Museum's award for Design of the Year, despite concerns raised about human rights, making Hadid the first woman to win that competition.

Andrea Palladio designed Villa La Rotonda on the edge of Vicenza in northern Italy. Work started in 1567 but ended only in 1605; after Palladio died in 1580, the new owners hired Vincenzo Scamozzi to complete it. The plan is square and fully symmetrical, with a projecting portico on each of its four faces. Each portico has a pediment crowned with statues of classical gods and carried on six Ionic columns. At the centre is a round domed hall, which gives the villa its name. Palladio had planned a tall half-round dome, but Scamozzi built a lower one with an oculus, drawing on the Pantheon in Rome. The design is turned 45 degrees off the compass points so that each room gets sun. Together with Palladio's other works, it is protected as part of a World Heritage Site.

Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall opened on 23 October 2003 in downtown Los Angeles, becoming the fourth hall of the city's Music Center. It seats 2,265 and is home to the Los Angeles Philharmonic as well as the Los Angeles Master Chorale. The auditorium blends two seating types: the vineyard layout of Hans Scharoun's Berliner Philharmonie and the classic shoebox of halls such as the Vienna Musikverein. Douglas-fir lines the walls and ceiling, with oak underfoot. Minoru Nagata designed the acoustics, and his protégé Yasuhisa Toyota oversaw their completion; both sound and architecture have drawn praise. A stone exterior was planned first, but cost cuts brought a cheaper stainless steel skin. Gehry worked with CATIA, software normally used in designing French fighter jets, and meant the angular forms to evoke the movement of music and of Los Angeles itself.

Le Corbusier designed the main building of Tokyo's National Museum of Western Art, his only representative work in the Far East. Finished in reinforced concrete in March 1959, it marked restored ties between France and Japan after the Second World War. His Japanese apprentices Kunio Maekawa, Junzo Sakakura and Takamasa Yoshizaka drew the details and ran the site. The plan is square, with the main galleries lifted on pilotis to the first floor, a layout shaped by his Sanskar Kendra museum in Ahmedabad, designed at the same time. Entry is through the double-height 19th Century Hall, lit by a north-glazed pyramid skylight. Four daylight troughs designed for the painting galleries are no longer used, and the galleries are lit artificially. Prefabricated concrete panels clad the outside. In 2016 it joined 16 other Le Corbusier works on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

The National Museum of African American History and Culture, nicknamed the Blacksonian, is a Smithsonian museum on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. After a 2006 site choice, a design by Freelon Group, Adjaye Associates and Davis Brody Bond won in 2009, and it was built in 2012-2016. It had to fit a 5-acre site, earn LEED Gold and meet federal security rules. Its ten storeys, half underground, give 350,000 square feet. Above ground, three stacked trapezoids form an upside-down step pyramid, inspired by the top of a sculpture by Olowe of Ise and echoing a Yoruba Oba's crown. Outward-leaning frames carry a bronze scrim pierced with patterns from historic iron grilles in Charleston and New Orleans. A 200 ft porch of plate girders and box columns covers the entrance. It was overall Beazley Design of the Year for 2017.

Zaha Hadid's Guangzhou Opera House, in Guangdong, China, opened on 9 May 2010. Her "double pebble" was named the winner in November 2002, and ground was broken early in 2005. It was conceived as two rocks washed by the Pearl River, and the result resembles a pair of smooth boulders faced in 75,000 polished panels of granite and glass. A freestanding concrete auditorium sits inside a steel frame clad in granite and glass; building it took more than five years. The complex holds a theatre of 1,800 seats, a multipurpose theatre, an entry hall and a salon, with a covered walkway of shops and restaurants between the two main blocks. Jonathan Glancey of The Guardian called it "at once highly theatrical and insistently subtle." It stands in a new business district and is the largest performing centre in southern China.

The Scottish Parliament Building stands at Holyrood in central Edinburgh. Work began in June 1999, and members held their first debate there on 7 September 2004; its Spanish architect, Enric Miralles, died before completion. Leaf motifs shape the Garden Lobby roof, and the chamber, committee rooms and Tower Buildings have large windows toward Holyrood Park, Salisbury Crags and Arthur's Seat. Scottish gneiss and granite line floors and walls, and the furniture is oak and sycamore. The roof rests on laminated oak beams linked by 112 stainless steel joints, no two alike, and hung from the walls on steel rods. Bay windows inspired by the leaf motif and the stepped Scottish gable jut from the members' offices, each with a seat and shelves for reflection. On summer nights, windows open so the concrete can cool. It won the 2005 Stirling Prize.

Lever House is a 307-foot office tower at 390 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, built in 1950-52 for the soap firm Lever Brothers. Designed in the International Style by Gordon Bunshaft and Natalie de Blois of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it followed only the UN Secretariat as a New York high-rise clad in a glass curtain wall. A public courtyard fills the ground level under a second floor raised on columns; above, a slab takes the northern quarter of the site, meeting the 1916 zoning rules without setbacks. Higher up, heat-absorbing glass and stainless steel wrap every side. The facade echoes Mies; the lifted courtyard draws on Le Corbusier. It turned Midtown's Park Avenue from masonry apartments to modern offices, and several buildings worldwide copied it. Nearly replaced by a 40-storey tower, it became a city landmark in 1982.

Torre Velasca is a 26-storey skyscraper in Milan by the BBPR partnership, completed in 1958 and opened in 1961. It rises 106 metres to the roof, and its mushroom-like outline stands out against the city skyline. The shape answers a practical need, keeping the lower floors narrow on the ground while giving the upper floors more room. The upper part is cantilevered out on exposed diagonal trusses, a deliberate reference to the fortresses of late-medieval Lombardy and to the Castello Sforzesco's Filarete Tower. The frame is reinforced concrete faced with stone. It is seen as one of Italy's rare post-rationalist brutalist buildings. Italian architects valued its dialogue with its setting, and in 1961 IN/ARCH, the National Institute of Architecture, gave BBPR its regional award for Lombardy. Since 2011 it has been protected as a historic building.

I. M. Pei designed the Louvre Pyramid in Paris as a glass-and-metal entrance and skylight for the museum. President François Mitterrand announced the Grand Louvre project in 1981, Pei was chosen in 1983, and the pyramid was finished in 1989. It was built because the old layout could no longer handle growing daily crowds. Daylight passes through it into an underground visitor hall, where people can still see the palace and reach its wings through access galleries. Built entirely of glass segments and metal poles, it stands 21.6 metres high on a square base 34 metres a side, covering 1,000 square metres. The faces rise at 51.52 degrees, close to the angle of ancient Egyptian pyramids. Its construction sparked years of heated aesthetic and political debate, but it now stands as a Paris landmark and the museum's emblem.

The Museum of Modern Art of Rio de Janeiro, known as MAM, sits in the northeast of Flamengo Park in the Centro district, on Guanabara Bay. Affonso Eduardo Reidy (1909-1964) designed the concrete Modernist building, with his partner Carmen Portinho as chief engineer; Burle Marx designed the gardens. A strong rhythm of external pillars, linked by longitudinal beams, leaves the gallery level free of inner columns and structural walls. Since the park is built on landfill in the bay, the footings reach 20 metres down. Gallery windows face north and south, and aluminium shutters on the north side control the low winter light. A broad spiral ramp rises to a roof terrace with a restaurant, bar and lounge facing Sugarloaf and the bay. In July 1978 a fire destroyed 90% of the collection.

Dresden's Bundeswehr Military History Museum is the military museum of Germany's armed forces, set in a former arsenal in the Albertstadt. The armoury was built from 1873 to 1876 and turned into a museum in 1897. By 2001 attitudes had shifted, and a competition sought an extension that would make visitors rethink how they see war. Daniel Libeskind added a transparent silver arrowhead jutting from the old Neo-Classical building's centre. It holds a five-storey viewing platform 29 metres high that looks over modern Dresden and points to where the fire bombing of the city began. His studio says the open new facade stands for democratic society, against the rigid old block and the authoritarian past it represents. After six years of building work, it opened in October 2011, focusing on the human side of war and on German military technology.

St. Joseph's Church is part of the rebuilding of Le Havre, destroyed by the British in the Second World War, which the city entrusted to Auguste Perret and his studio from 1945 to 1964. Raised from 1951 to 1957/58, the church is a memorial to five thousand civilians killed and a sanctuary for Saint Joseph. Concrete and centrally planned, it was conceived as a beacon: its central tower, 107 metres tall, dominates the skyline and is visible from the port and at sea, especially when lit at night. Perret brought in his former colleague Marguerite Huré for the stained glass. From seven base colours she mixed fifty hues, setting the strongest at the foot of the tower and lighter ones above, so light seems to come from on high. UNESCO made Perret's Le Havre a World Heritage Site in 2005.

Yale University's Center for British Art, in central New Haven, holds the largest and widest-ranging collection of British art outside the UK. It began in 1966, when Paul Mellon, a 1929 graduate of Yale College, gave his British art to the university along with an endowment and money for a building. Louis I. Kahn designed that building where York Street meets Chapel Street, opposite one of his earliest works, the Yale University Art Gallery of 1953. It was finished after his death and opened on 15 April 1977. Matte steel and reflective glass form the outside, while travertine, white oak and Belgian linen line the rooms. Kahn aimed for intimate galleries in soft natural light, letting in all the daylight he could and keeping electric lamps for dark days and evenings. Entry is free six days a week.

The National Museum of Qatar in Doha opened its current building on 28 March 2019, replacing a 1975 one on the same site. French architect Jean Nouvel, a Pritzker Prize winner, drew on the desert rose, a crystal found in Qatar. His building wraps around the old palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani, a twentieth-century structure restored by the Berlin firm ZRS Architekten Ingenieure. The museum covers 430,000 square feet and is built from 539 interlocking discs; the hollows between them shade visitors from the desert heat. About 76,000 panels of glass-fibre-reinforced concrete clad the building. Its 1.5 million square foot site lies at the south end of the Corniche, where the building rises out of the sea, reached by two footbridges and a road bridge. At reopening it had LEED Gold and a four-star GSAS sustainability rating.

Saint-Pierre, a concrete building in Firminy, France, is Le Corbusier's final major work. He designed it as a church for the model town of Firminy Vert but died in 1965, before construction began. Local political quarrels then stopped the project between 1975 and 2003, the year local authorities named the crumbling concrete shell "architectural heritage" and funded its completion. The French architect José Oubrerie, who had studied under Le Corbusier for years, completed it in 2006, 41 years after his teacher died. Because the secular French state cannot pay for religious buildings, it now serves as a cultural venue. In Vanity Fair's World Architecture Survey of 2010 it ranked second among the top buildings of the twenty-first century, with four votes, and Peter Eisenman named it the most significant structure since 1980.

Devoted to California's art, history and natural science, the Oakland Museum of California stands at 1000 Oak Street. Three smaller museums in the area, including the Oakland Art Gallery, merged to form it in 1969. In 1961 voters approved a $6.6 million bond to start developing its site overlooking Lake Merritt in the city centre. The building was the first major commission for Kevin Roche and John Dinkeloo's firm; Dan Kiley did the landscape and Geraldine Knight Scott the gardens. It stands as a key mid-century modern example of blending indoor and outdoor space. Three concrete tiers hold art, history and natural science in turn, plus temporary galleries, an auditorium and a restaurant, while roof gardens, patios, sculpture, a lawn and a koi pond fill the outdoors. Mark Cavagnero Associates renovated and enlarged it from 2009 to 2013.

Kaleva Church is a Lutheran church on a small hill in Tampere, Finland, where the main streets Teiskontie and Sammonkatu meet. Reima Pietilä won the 1959 competition held by Tampere's Lutheran church board; his partner Raili Paatelainen, his wife from 1963, joined the project later, and it was built in 1964-66. Slip forming produced its 17 slender hollow concrete U-shapes, each 35 metres tall, with full-height glazing between them. The plan resembles a fish, an ancient Christian symbol, and the main hall rises 30 metres and seats 1,120. Because Finnish grain elevators were then often slip-formed too, the church picked up the nickname "Silo of the Souls". All the furniture is lacquered Finnish pine. Seen as a key work of post-war Finnish modernism, it was protected under the Church Act in 2006.

Helsinki Central Library Oodi, known as Oodi (Finnish for "ode"), is a public library close to Helsinki Central Station, beside the Helsinki Music Centre and Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art. Finnish firm ALA Architects won the 2012 design competition against 543 rivals, with Ramboll Finland on structure. It opened on 5 December 2018, the eve of Finnish Independence Day. The second floor is mainly for work, learning and making things, while the third, called Book Heaven, holds about 100,000 books plus magazines, films, sheet music and games; purpose-built robots carry returned books to its automated shelves. It is rated very energy-efficient thanks to local materials and passive solar design, using almost no energy. A large sloping timber wall forms an overhang, a feature described as an ALA trademark. In 2019 IFLA named it the best Public Library of the Year.

Rafael Moneo's Kursaal, a congress centre and auditorium in San Sebastián in the Basque Country of Spain, opened in 1999. In 1989 six architects, Moneo, Norman Foster and Arata Isozaki among them, were invited to a consultation, and Moneo's "Two Stranded Rocks" was chosen. It takes the form of two large prisms rising from a platform. Each of these "cubes" wraps an inner prismatic structure in double translucent glass panels on a metal frame. The bigger cube, closer to the sea, holds the auditorium of about 1,800 seats. A wide terrace between them faces Zurriola Beach and the Urumea's mouth. It hosts the San Sebastián International Film Festival, Spain's largest, founded in 1953. At first its effect on a city of classical French-style buildings was judged negative; in 2001 it won the EU Prize for Contemporary Architecture.

Robert Venturi designed this house in Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, for his mother Vanna, and it was built from 1962 to 1964 as one of the first prominent works of postmodernism. With five rooms and a height of only about 30 feet, it still shows a monumental front, because Venturi deliberately played with the elements that signal scale. "Hole in the wall" windows and a non-structural applied arch openly defied Modernist rules, ideas he set out in Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966), written as he designed the house. Its pitched roof, central hearth and chimney, and closed ground floor set firmly on the ground all reject the flat roofs, columns and glass walls of Modernism. Vanna, a widow near 70, needed daily life on one level, so every main room is on the ground floor.

Michael Graves's Portland Building, a 15-storey city office block in downtown Portland, Oregon, stands beside City Hall. Graves won it in a large competition with Philip Johnson among the three judges. Opened in 1982 at a cost of $29 million, it was the first big postmodern office tower, ahead of Johnson's AT&T Building. Varied colours and surface materials, small windows and bold ornament set it sharply apart from the office towers of its day, and its design has been seen as a rejection of the Modernist principles laid down in the early 20th century. Portlandia, a hammered-copper statue, was placed above the front entrance in 1985. It won an AIA honor award in May 1983 and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2011. A later unitized curtain wall replaced its leaky envelope, keeping to Graves's original.

Aino and Alvar Aalto designed this public library in Vyborg, now in Russia, which was built from 1927 to 1935 while the city, then called Viipuri, belonged to Finland. Their first scheme followed Nordic Classicism, influenced by Gunnar Asplund's Stockholm City Library, but over five years of development, from 1928 to 1933, it turned fully modernist. Deep round skylights spread daylight over the desks without glare, and a stepped, sunken reading and lending hall opens up several levels. The auditorium's wavy ceiling of red-hearted pine was shaped for precise acoustics. It was the first Finnish public library with its own children's wing and open shelves, and Aino Aalto led the child-sized interiors and furniture there. War damage and a decade of neglect destroyed the wave ceiling; a restoration costing nearly 9 million euros was finished in late 2013.

Bertrand Goldberg designed Marina City, a mixed-use residential and commercial complex in Chicago. Its two 65-storey apartment towers, each 587 feet tall, opened in 1963 and were at completion the world's tallest residential buildings and tallest reinforced concrete structures. The lowest 19 floors form an open spiral car park with about 896 valet spaces. Above, each residential floor has a round corridor around a 32-foot lift core, with 16 wedge-shaped flats set around it. Each flat ends in a 175-square-foot semicircular balcony behind a full-height glass wall, so all living rooms and bedrooms have one. Planned as a "city within a city", it offered a theatre, gym, pool, ice rink, bowling alley, shops, restaurants and a small marina at river level, which gives it its name. It is widely credited with starting the return of residents to American inner cities.

The Fondation Maeght, a museum of modern art, sits on a hill above Saint-Paul de Vence about 25 km from Nice. Marguerite and Aimé Maeght founded it in 1964. The Catalan architect Josep Lluís Sert, recommended by Joan Miró, designed the building, first imagined as an artists' village rather than a museum. Sert modelled the plan on a Mediterranean village gathered around a central chapel, and kept the natural slope, setting galleries, patios and gardens on terraces at different levels. Half-vaulted roofs act as "light traps" that catch sunlight and spread it through glass. Two large white impluvia collect rainwater for the pools and cool the galleries with their shade. Artists added works built into the site, such as the Giacometti courtyard, Miró's Labyrinth and mosaics by Chagall and Braque. France's Ministry of Culture has labelled it "20th Century Heritage".

Adolf Loos designed Villa Müller in Prague, built in 1930, as a home for František Müller, an engineer and co-owner of the Plzeň building firm Kapsa-Müller, which specialised in reinforced concrete and new building methods. The architect Karel Lhota introduced Müller to Loos and, because Loos was in poor health, also helped with the design. Outside, Loos gave the house a white cubic facade; inside, he set out to separate this public face from the private life of the family, so the rooms are richly finished in marble, wood and silk with comfortable furniture. The villa is a clear example of his Raumplan, or spatial plan, in which rooms sit at different levels according to their use and symbolic weight, an idea that shapes the exterior as well. After restoration in 1998, it reopened as a museum in 2000.

VM Houses are two side-by-side apartment blocks in Ørestad, Copenhagen, with footprints shaped like a V and an M. Per Høpfner, the developer, teamed with Dansk Olie og Naturgas and hired PLOT, the practice of Julien De Smedt and Bjarke Ingels, though the pair had never built anything this large; it became their first major project. The 95-unit M House was done in 2004, the 114-unit V House a year later. Drawing on Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation, the design favours daylight, privacy and views: instead of looking at the neighbouring block, each flat gets diagonal views of the landscape, and short corridors cut through like bullet holes. About 80 flat types suit different needs. Høpfner noted that VM "may look crazy" but still came in on budget. In 2006 it won the Forum AID Award as Scandinavia's best building.

Robert Mallet-Stevens built Villa Cavrois in Croix in 1932 for Paul Cavrois, a Roubaix textile industrialist. The owners, who commissioned it in 1929, gave him free rein, and for the first time he controlled every detail of a project, treating the house as a total work of art. Its design guidelines named "air, light, work, sports, hygiene, comfort and efficiency". The look is fully modern, with large windows, flat roofs, clean lines and no ornament, yet its plan follows the 17th- and 18th-century French château: two symmetrical wings, for the parents and for the children and staff, flank a central hall. Its brick, modelled on Dudok's Hilversum town hall, was made by the firm Bonzel in 26 different moulds. Listed as a historic monument in 1990, it was bought by the French state in 2001 and restored from 2004.

Gunnar Asplund designed Stockholm Public Library. He joined the committee discussing it in 1918; a scheme followed in 1922 and work started in 1924. Taking partial inspiration from Claude Nicolas Ledoux's Barrière Saint-Martin, he set aside early ideas for a dome and chose a rotunda, its tall drum giving the exterior a monumental feel. Classical elements were reduced to abstract geometry and most ornament removed. The building illustrates his gradual shift from classicism to functionalism and is also held up as the model of Nordic Classicism, or Swedish Grace. No Swedish public library had open shelves before it, letting readers fetch books without staff help, an idea Asplund studied in America. Prince Eugen attended its opening on 31 March 1928, but for lack of money the west wing, closing the near-square base around the rotunda, followed only in 1932.

Mountain Dwellings, in Copenhagen's Ørestad district, was designed by the Danish practice PLOT (BIG and JDSA). Homes sit on a multi-storey car park for 480 cars, climbing the sloping roof from street level to the 11th floor to form an artificial south-facing mountainside. One layer of 80 L-shaped penthouses covers the slope, each with a terrace and small garden on the roof of the flat below; the L-plan and courtyard were inspired by Jørn Utzon's Kingo Houses. Garage ceilings reach up to 16 metres, and the undersides of the flats are clad in aluminium painted in Verner Panton's exact colours. Perforated aluminium sheets shield the garage from wind and rain yet let in light and air; varied hole sizes turn them into a giant image of Mount Everest. It was named best residential building at the 2008 World Architecture Festival.

The Met is a 66-storey condominium tower on Sathorn Road in Bangkok, credited to WOHA and completed in 2009. At 228 metres, it was in 2012 Thailand's tallest condominium and the city's fourth-tallest building. Its 370 flats are spread over six towers joined by sky bridges, and the gaps between them hold sky gardens and pool terraces. The architects meant it as a model for tall buildings in a tropical climate with little wind, reworking the standard high-rise made for cold, windy places. Openings through it are meant to strengthen breezes to cool the homes, and every unit is cross-ventilated, so residents can choose to live without air conditioning. Sunshades, overhangs and walls of living plants filter the sun and stop interiors overheating. It won the German Architecture Museum's International Highrise Award in 2010 and RIBA's Lubetkin Prize in 2011.

Richard Neutra designed this Palm Springs house in 1946 as a desert retreat from harsh winters for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr., the Pittsburgh department store owner who also commissioned Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater. Julius Shulman's 1947 photographs and Slim Aarons's 1970 image "Poolside Gossip" made it famous, and it has been credited with helping to define the modernist look of the resort city. In 1993 the Harrises began a five-year restoration with Marmol Radziner + Associates to return it to Neutra's design. They also bought adjoining plots, more than doubling the grounds of the 3,200-square-foot house to bring back the desert buffer Neutra had planned. Palm Springs lists it as a Class 1 Historic Site, and in 2008 a Los Angeles Times poll of experts ranked it among the ten best houses in Los Angeles despite its location.

Otto Wagner designed Kirche am Steinhof, also known as the Church of St. Leopold, as the Catholic oratory of the Otto-Wagner-Spital in Vienna, and it is ranked among the world's most important Art Nouveau churches. He built it between 1903 and 1907, at 63, with Koloman Moser's mosaics and stained glass and Othmar Schimkowitz's angels. Unusually, it lies on a north-south axis at the top centre of the hospital grounds. Because it served mentally ill patients, Wagner consulted doctors and nurses: corners are mostly rounded, few crosses show, emergency exits are set into the side walls, running water replaces holy water stoups, and men and women had separate doors. The floor falls about 26 centimetres to the altar, a gentle rake for clearer views. The dome is hidden from inside, yet the nave holds a six-second echo.

Rudolph M. Schindler designed this West Hollywood house as a shared home and workplace for two young families. With Chace as builder to save money, work ran from November 1921 to June 1922 and cost $12,550. The house was new for what it lacked: no usual living room, dining room or bedrooms, just two sleeping baskets on the roof. Its plan joins two L-shaped apartments based on a campsite Schindler had seen the year before. One flat concrete slab is both foundation and finished floor, and the walls are concrete panels cast on top of it and tilted up, separated by 3-inch strips of concrete or of clear or frosted glass. Its concrete and sliding canvas used industrial materials in a fresh way, and its open plan, merging inside and out, set an example for California architecture.

Built in Paris between 1928 and 1932, the Maison de Verre (House of Glass) was the work of Pierre Chareau, a furniture and interiors designer, Bernard Bijvoet, a Dutch architect, and the metalworker Louis Dalbet. It is called France's first house made of steel and glass; glass block was the third main material. Translucent glass-block walls, with a few clear panes, form the outside. Inside, sliding, folding or pivoting screens of glass and plain or perforated metal reshape the rooms. Three ideas guide the design: honest materials, varying transparency, and industrial fittings set against more traditional furnishings. The ground floor held a medical practice for Dr Jean Dalsace. An elderly top-floor tenant would not sell, so the three lower floors of the existing building were torn down and the new house slotted in beneath, leaving the top flat alone.

Willem Marinus Dudok designed Hilversum Town Hall for the town council, and it was completed in 1931. His first sketches date from 1924, for a raised site the town had bought in 1923. Set in a park, the light-coloured building rises out of water, stressing the garden city image Hilversum wanted. Its plan joins two squares: one courtyard lined with offices, the other edged by low rooms and crossed by a service road. Dudok's earlier work came from the Amsterdam School, but the dramatic massing, asymmetry and overhanging eaves here show a clear debt to Frank Lloyd Wright and the Prairie School. Until the 1960s public radio aired its bell live each hour, a sign of the town's place as the Dutch media centre. By its restoration in 1989-1995, frost had damaged nearly all the soft, porous original bricks.

Parliament House in Canberra is where Australia's Parliament meets. In a competition of 329 entries from 29 countries, the Philadelphia practice Mitchell/Giurgola won, and Romaldo Giurgola directed work on site; the credited architects are Mitchell/Giurgola & Thorp, and a joint venture of Concrete Constructions and John Holland built it. The scheme set most of the building beneath Capital Hill and crowned it with a giant spire holding a large Australian flag, its legs tracing the triangular capitol Griffin had envisaged. Two curved walls divide the plan into quarters: the formal entrance, the House of Representatives, the Senate and the executive wing. Because the walls are sunk into the hill, the building seems to rise from the land, and people can walk on grass roofs above their representatives. Elizabeth II opened it on 9 May 1988; it cost over $1.1 billion.

Fernsehturm Stuttgart, a 216.61-metre TV tower credited to Fritz Leonhardt, was the first telecommunications tower anywhere to be built of reinforced concrete. That made it the prototype for the modernist needle tower with a "basket" at the top, a type later copied worldwide. It stands on the 483-metre Hoher Bopser hill in Degerloch, southern Stuttgart. The project drew criticism: opponents disliked the new construction method and the expense, since a plain 200-metre antenna array would have cost only 200,000 DM. Work started on 10 January 1954 and took 20 months, and Süddeutscher Rundfunk, now SWR, put the tower into service on 5 February 1956. It cost 4.2 million DM, a sum visitor income matched within five years. The foundation is 27 metres across. Despite the early controversy, it soon became a well-known Stuttgart landmark and tourist attraction.

MuCEM, the Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations, is a national museum of ethnology in Marseille, built under the Euroméditerranée regeneration project. Rudy Ricciotti designed it with Roland Carta, using "stone, water and wind". It sits on reclaimed land at the harbour entrance beside the old J4 port terminal. A channel parts it from Fort Saint-Jean, a 17th-century stronghold restructured in the same project and joined to it by a high 130-metre footbridge. The museum is a 15,000-square-metre cube inside a lattice shell of fibre-reinforced concrete, with galleries on two levels, a 400-seat auditorium below ground and a rooftop restaurant looking over the bay. François Hollande opened it in 2013, Marseille's year as European Capital of Culture, and it took the Council of Europe Museum Prize in 2015. The final bill reached 350 million euros, against 160 million planned.

Vladimir Shukhov's broadcasting tower in Moscow, also called the Shabolovka Tower, comes out of the Russian avant-garde and went up from 1920 to 1922, during the Civil War. The first plan was a nine-section hyperbolic tower 350 metres tall, 15 metres more than the Eiffel Tower, weighing about 2,200 tons against the Eiffel Tower's 7,300. War and scarce resources forced the design down to 148.5 metres and 240 tons. Six sections sit one on another, each a separate single-cavity hyperboloid of rotation made from straight beams whose ends rest on circular foundations. The steel diagrid shell catches very little wind. It was raised without cranes or scaffolding, using only winches. After a campaign to save it, Russia's Ministry of Culture said it would stay standing, and in September 2014 Moscow City Council placed a preservation order on it.

The Louisiana Museum of Modern Art lies on the Øresund coast, some 30 km north of Copenhagen. Its name goes back to the estate's first owner, Alexander Brun, who named it after his three wives, each called Louise, and in 1855 built the villa that still holds part of the museum. Vilhelm Wohlert and Jørgen Bo walked the grounds for a few months to see how new building would best fit the land. The result, opened in 1958, was three buildings linked by glass corridors. It is a modernist Danish landmark known for uniting art, architecture and landscape. Between its two wings, a sculpture garden has pieces by Calder, Moore and Arp. No museum of modern and contemporary art in Scandinavia draws more visitors: over 700,000 a year.

Frank Lloyd Wright's former apprentice E. Fay Jones designed Thorncrown Chapel in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, built in 1980, and its design recalls Wright's Prairie School. Jim Reed, a retired schoolteacher, commissioned it as a non-denominational pilgrimage chapel for meditation, and the design drew on Sainte-Chapelle, the Gothic church in Paris pierced by many stained glass windows. To protect the wooded site, he ruled that no structural piece could be bigger than two men could carry through the trees. Made from materials native to the region, such as treated Southern pine and flagstone, it is 48 feet high, 24 feet wide and 60 feet long, with 425 windows totalling 6,000 square feet of glass. It looks open to the air but is an enclosed, air-conditioned room for up to 100 people. The AIA gave it its Twenty-five Year Award in 2006.

Montreal's Biosphere, an environment museum, occupies the old US pavilion from Expo 67 in Parc Jean-Drapeau. R. Buckminster Fuller, working with Shoji Sadao and Geometrics Inc., designed the geodesic dome. Fuller's first idea was a larger dome with a geodesic sphere hung inside for his "World Game". The built dome, 76 metres wide and 62 metres tall, had two layers joined by a lattice of struts and was closed with cells of steel and acrylic. Shades regulated the inside temperature, an attempt to copy how the human body keeps its own. A 41-metre escalator, said to be the longest unsupported one anywhere, carried visitors to the exhibits. A welding fire in May 1976 burned off the acrylic bubble but spared the steel truss. Since June 1995 the museum has filled enclosed buildings by Éric Gauthier set within the old frame.

The Interlace is a complex of 1,040 apartments on the boundary of Bukit Merah and Queenstown in Singapore. Ole Scheeren and OMA designed it, and RSP Architects Planners & Engineers saw it through to completion; commissioned in 2007, it was finished in 2013. Instead of the usual towers of dense cities, it looks like Jenga blocks stacked at odd angles. Thirty-one linked six-storey blocks are staggered in a hexagonal pattern around eight courtyards and piled up to four high in the centre, for a maximum of 24 floors, so nearly every home gets a wide view. The layout seeks daylight and shared spaces. Units run from 74 to 590 square metres, with penthouses topping each block. It took the 2014 Urban Habitat Award and was named World Building of the Year at the 2015 World Architecture Festival.

Robson Square is a civic centre and public plaza in downtown Vancouver holding the Provincial Law Courts, UBC Robson Square, government offices and public space reaching to the Vancouver Art Gallery. Arthur Erickson recast the project as a tower lying down, "the B.C. Centre on its back". Built in 1979-83, it covers three city blocks with 1,300,000 square feet. In the southern block, the 42-metre Law Courts hold 35 courtrooms under a 420-by-115-foot glass roof on a steel space frame. As usual for Erickson, concrete dominates, softened by environmental design. Working with Cornelia Oberlander and Bing Thom, a former student, he created one of the first green roofs: offices sit beneath the plaza garden, and waterfalls flow past windows and skylights, cooling the air and covering street noise. In 2011 the RAIC awarded it the Prix du XXe siècle.

Museo Tamayo, dating from 1981, stands in Chapultepec Park in Mexico City. Abraham Zabludovsky and Teodoro González de León, both from Mexico, designed the building, and the design brought both men the National Award of Science and Art, Fine Arts section, in 1982. The institution is a public museum of contemporary art. It puts on contemporary shows that draw both on its own holdings of modern and contemporary work and on pieces gathered by the artist Rufino Tamayo, who founded it. The modern holdings include work by many major figures, among them Francis Bacon, Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Salvador Dalí, Barbara Hepworth, Mark Rothko, Georgia O'Keeffe, Roy Lichtenstein and Andy Warhol.

Known as MAC, the Niterói museum of contemporary art is one of the main landmarks of Niterói, in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Oscar Niemeyer designed it with the structural engineer Bruno Contarini, a past collaborator, and it was finished in 1996. The saucer-shaped building, likened to a UFO, rests on a cliffside above a beach. It rises 16 metres, and its cupola, 50 metres across, contains three floors. A reflecting pool of 817 square metres rings the cylindrical base, which Niemeyer said sits in it "like a flower". A broad ramp climbs to a Hall of Expositions that holds sixty people, and two doors open onto a viewing gallery with views of Sugarloaf Mountain, Rio de Janeiro and Guanabara Bay. The museum keeps 1,217 works from the collector João Sattamini.

Also called the building of the Ministry of Education and Health, the Gustavo Capanema Palace houses government offices in downtown Rio de Janeiro. Lúcio Costa worked on its design with Roberto Burle Marx, Jorge Machado Moreira, Carlos Leão, Ernani Vasconcellos and Affonso Eduardo Reidy; Oscar Niemeyer worked on it as an intern in Costa's office, and the group asked Le Corbusier to oversee the work. Begun in 1939 and finished in 1945, it housed Brazil's new education and health ministry. Though 15 storeys tall, it feels light, lifted three floors on pilotis over open ground. An inner concrete frame let both broad sides be fully glazed, and adjustable brises-soleil, the first such system anywhere, shade the northern glass. As Brazil's first modernist project, it is on the country's UNESCO tentative list.

Pedregulho is a planned community of flats in Rio de Janeiro's São Cristóvão district, officially named Conjunto Residencial Prefeito Mendes de Moraes. Affonso Eduardo Reidy designed it, with his partner Carmen Portinho as chief engineer. It was planned in 1946 for lower-paid civil servants of Rio, then Brazil's Federal District. The main block, a long serpentine slab on pilotis, has 272 flats on seven floors; Reidy tried to give each a view of Guanabara Bay. Two gangplanks lead to the single entrance on the third floor, whose central position reduced the need for lifts. That floor holds offices, a children's theatre, a nursery and a kindergarten; the original complex also had a school, pool and health centre. It took first prize at the 1st São Paulo Biennial's international architecture competition in 1951 and its serpentine block was restored in 2010–2015.

Founded by the state government in 1905, the Pinacoteca is São Paulo's oldest art museum; it shows Brazilian work from the 1800s onward alongside other cultures and now occupies three buildings. The main one was designed by Ramos de Azevedo with his chief collaborator Domiciano Rossi in a monumental manner close to Italian eclecticism: three floors around two inner courtyards that bring in air and light. It was never finished; the planned dome was never built, and bare brick still shows outside and in the courtyards. From 1993 to 1998 Paulo Mendes da Rocha led a major renovation, with Eduardo Argenton Colonelli and Weliton Ricoy Torres, that fitted it for international exhibitions; the three won Latin America's Mies van der Rohe Prize for it.

Argentina's largest library, the Mariano Moreno National Library, sits in the Recoleta district of Buenos Aires. Its site opened up after the Unzué Palace was pulled down in 1958 for political reasons, and the grounds were then reserved for a new main building. The brutalist design dates from 1961 and came from Clorindo Testa, Alicia Cazzaniga and Francisco Bullrich, yet work on site only started in 1971. Repeated changes of government and bureaucracy, together with some indifference to cultural matters, slowed the project, and the library was finally inaugurated on 10 April 1992.

Eero Saarinen designed the main terminal at Washington Dulles, in Chantilly, in 1958, and it is admired for a graceful form that suggests flight. A catenary roof hangs over it, covering a wide space with no columns in the way, and in 1966 the American Institute of Architects recognised the terminal's design concept. It was built with no concourses or gates. Aircraft stood at remote stands, and passengers rode out to them in mobile lounges that rose to the level of the plane; some are still in use. In 1996 the terminal was extended to 1,240 feet (380 m), the length of Saarinen's original design and slightly more than twice the 600 feet (180 m) first built. Taiwan's Taoyuan airport based its original terminal on this one.

The TWA Flight Center stands at JFK airport in Queens, New York. Eero Saarinen and Associates designed it for Trans World Airlines; completed in 1962, it worked as a terminal for four decades. The central headhouse is covered by a thin concrete shell shaped like a pair of bird's wings and carried on four Y-shaped piers. Inside is an open space on three levels, whose big windows faced the tarmac before the hotel towers and Terminal 5 rose. Two red-carpeted tubes run out from the headhouse for departures and arrivals, and the terminal was an early user of enclosed jetways for passengers. Both inside and out, the headhouse is a New York City landmark, and since 2019 it has formed part of the TWA Hotel. The building is also on the National Register of Historic Places.

Rising 630 feet (192 m) over St. Louis, Missouri, the Gateway Arch is a weighted catenary sheathed in stainless steel, the tallest arch anywhere and the highest structure in Missouri open to visitors. Eero Saarinen designed it in 1947 for a two-stage competition; in the first stage Carl Milles advised him to give each leg a triangular base instead of a square one. On 18 February 1948 the jury chose his scheme unanimously, praising its "profoundly evocative and truly monumental expression". Work ran from 12 February 1963 to 28 October 1965 and cost $13 million. The arch is built from 142 prefabricated steel pieces, each 12 feet long, whose double skins were filled with concrete and prestressed with 252 tension bars. A monument to America's push west, it is a National Historic Landmark.

The Frederick C. Robie House, now a museum, stands in Chicago's Hyde Park, on the campus of the University of Chicago. Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in the Prairie style, and it was finished in 1910. Its open plan is built from two large rectangles, called "vessels", set off from each other. Outside walls are mostly Roman brick, trimmed with concrete and cut-stone ornament and pierced by art glass windows. Terraces step across several levels. Where comparable houses carried their roofs on load-bearing walls beneath, here the roofs are cantilevered out from the core. The house had wide influence, helping spread picture windows, projecting roofs and attached garages through home design. It is a National Historic Landmark as well as a city landmark, and belongs to the World Heritage Site The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright.

Unity Temple, in Oak Park, Illinois, is home to a Unitarian Universalist congregation. Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in the Prairie style, and it is often named as an early work of modern architecture. An auditorium at the north end and a church house, Unity House, at the south are joined by an entrance pavilion, all of reinforced concrete. The Portland cement surface was washed back to show the gravel inside, and clerestory windows sit deep near the top. Unlike other churches of the time it has no spire; flat, overhanging concrete slabs form the roof. The auditorium is a Greek cross with stair towers at its corners and two levels of seats around a central pulpit. Abstract patterns stand in for overtly religious images. It is a National Historic Landmark and part of a World Heritage Site.

The TD Centre is a group of skyscrapers in Toronto's Financial District: six towers and a pavilion wrapped in bronze-tinted glass and black-painted steel. On paper Ludwig Mies van der Rohe was design consultant to the local firms John B. Parkin and Associates and Bregman + Hamann Architects, but the design was in effect entirely his, and it was his last major work before he died in 1969. The buildings stand on a granite plinth, ordered in three dimensions by a mathematical 1.5 m² grid. Saint-Jean granite pavers follow the grid and carry on into the glass tower lobbies and the banking pavilion, so inside and outside run together. Ontario has protected the complex under its Heritage Act since 2003.

Still widely called the John Hancock Center, 875 North Michigan Avenue is a 100-storey Chicago skyscraper, 1,128 feet (344 m) tall, on the Magnificent Mile. It came from Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, with Bruce Graham as chief designer and Fazlur Rahman Khan as structural engineer. When it topped out on 6 May 1968, only New York's Empire State Building was taller, and nothing in Chicago matched it. Offices and restaurants share it with about 700 condominiums, and on completion it held the world's highest home. The X-braces outside show that the skin is part of a "tubular system"; the bracing helps tall towers perform and opens up the floor plans. It was the first tower with a "sky lobby", where residents change from express to local lifts. The American Institute of Architects gave it its Twenty-five Year Award in 1999.

Built for the Philadelphia Saving Fund Society, the PSFS Building in Center City, Philadelphia, was the first International Style skyscraper in the United States; it is also called the Loews Philadelphia Hotel. George Howe and William Lescaze designed it, leaving out the domes and ornament of older banks and of the city's architecture. The T-shaped tower was planned to bring as much light as possible to the office floors and to give weight to the banking section at its base. Its spine of lifts and services was shown on the outside, a skyscraper first, instead of hidden in the middle. Only one American high-rise had air conditioning before it. A red neon PSFS sign on top, seen from 20 miles (32 km), has become a city emblem. The building was named a National Historic Landmark in 1976 for its architecture.

The Ford Foundation Building is a 12-storey office block in East Midtown Manhattan. Kevin Roche designed it with his engineering partner John Dinkeloo, and it was finished in 1967 in a late modernist manner. It is a glass and steel cube on concrete piers faced in Dakota granite, with weathering Cor-Ten steel, now a deep tan, on the overhanging parts. Most upper floors sit in narrow wings on the north and west sides of a public atrium, much like Spanish courtyard buildings. The atrium covers a third of an acre, is 100 feet square and 160 feet high, and was planted by Dan Kiley with trees, shrubs and vines, the first such space in a Manhattan office building. Restored in 2015–2018, it now bears the name Ford Foundation Center for Social Justice, and both building and atrium are city landmarks.

The Wainwright Building is a 10-storey terra cotta office building, 135 feet (41 m) tall, on Chestnut Street in downtown St. Louis. Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan designed it, and it was built in 1890–1891. It is seen as one of the first skyscrapers fully expressed in architectural terms. The design follows Sullivan's ideas on tall buildings: a base, shaft and attic modelled on the parts of a classical column, and a wish to stress height. Under the deep cornice runs a wide frieze of stylised celery leaves, a motif from Sullivan's System of Architectural Ornament, and the spandrels and main doorway are ornamented too. Frank Lloyd Wright saw it as the first time a tall steel office building had been given human expression as architecture. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1968 and a city landmark in 1972.

The Glass Pavilion was commissioned in 2000, when the Toledo Museum of Art picked SANAA to house its glass collection; it was the first job the firm won in the United States. Front Inc. was brought in to help the architects work out the technical side of the glass wall systems, and the curved glass panels were shipped from China. The pavilion covers 74,000 square feet and opened in August 2006 to warm praise from critics. In a review for The New York Times, Nicolai Ouroussoff praised its delicate composition and placed its curving maze of glass at the end of a line of monuments that starts with the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

Toyo Ito designed the Hachioji library, the newer of Tama Art University's two libraries; it is regarded as an architectural achievement for both its idea and its construction. Between the main gate and the centre of campus, it took three years to build and opened in 2007. It is of steel and concrete, with two floors above a basement. The ground floor follows a gentle three-degree slope, and rows of simple arches carry the structure. Each arch is plate steel reinforced with concrete, 200 mm thick, with a maximum span of over 12 metres, and with the glass walls around them the arches follow the land. Fujie Kazuko's furniture and shelves suit the sloping floors. The Guardian's Claire Shaw reported 38,000 visitors to the old library in 2006 and 86,000 visits to the new one in 2012.

The Suzhou Museum, in Suzhou in China's Jiangsu province, holds ancient Chinese art, painting, calligraphy and handmade crafts. Its building is by the Pritzker Prize winner I. M. Pei with Pei Partnership Architects; work began in 2002 and it opened on 6 October 2006. Pei mixed traditional Chinese design and local Suzhou character with modern means. Sloping roofs, white stucco walls and a black, white and grey palette recall the old city, while the roof adds glass, a steel frame in place of timber rafters, and "China black" granite instead of brick tiles. Daylight through this roof is tempered by metal sunshades. Octagons, rhombuses and triangles are the basic shapes of the design. North of the courtyard lies the Humble Administrator's Garden, Suzhou's biggest classical garden.

The Harbin Opera House, or Harbin Grand Theatre, is a performing arts centre with several venues in Harbin, Heilongjiang Province, China. MAD, the Chinese practice led by Ma Yansong, designed the 850,349-square-foot building as the focus of Cultural Island, an arts district beside the Songhua River and its wetlands on the city's edge. White aluminium panels cover the whole exterior, and paths cut into the façade let visitors climb to the top for the view. Inside are white walls, skylights and timber. Ma wanted the snow-white form to feel calm, unlike the tall, imposing landmarks of many Chinese cities, and saw it as an extension of the wetlands, waterways and snowy ground. It won ArchDaily's 2016 Building of the Year award, a 2016 WAN Performing Spaces Award and a 2017 IALD Award.

Tai Kwun occupies the old Central Police Station compound in Central, Hong Kong. Its 16 historic buildings, dating from 1841 to 1925, make up three declared monuments: the former police station, the former Central Magistracy and Victoria Prison. After the prison closed in 2006, the government teamed up with the Hong Kong Jockey Club in 2008 to conserve the site; work began in 2011, and at HK$1.8 billion it became one of the territory's costliest revitalisation projects. The scheme, credited to Herzog & de Meuron, restored all 16 heritage buildings and added two new ones whose design draws on the site's old brickwork. Taking the compound's old everyday name, it reopened on 29 May 2018 as a centre for heritage and the arts, and in 2019 received an award of excellence from UNESCO's Asia-Pacific heritage conservation awards.

Menara Mesiniaga, also called Mesiniaga Tower, is an office building in SS16, Subang Jaya, in the Malaysian state of Selangor. Ken Yeang designed it as an office for IBM, in a high-tech architectural manner. Building began in 1989 and finished in 1992. The tower responds to the local climate and shows Yeang's key principles for "bioclimatic skyscraper" design. Among the strategies it uses are a shaded façade, terraces set back into the building, planting across the exterior and a swimming pool on the roof. The design brought Yeang the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1995, and it also received the International Award of the Royal Australian Institute of Architects and a design award from the Malaysian Institute of Architects.

Rose Seidler House in Wahroonga, a Sydney suburb, was a family home and is now a heritage-listed house museum. Harry Seidler designed it for his parents, Rose and Max, and the builder Bret R. Lake finished it in 1950. Only Rose's name is on it because she began the commission and made the main decisions as client. Its International modernist design looked futuristic in the Australia of its time, and it is held up as a fine example of mid-century modern home design. It uses just four materials: concrete, timber, glass and natural bush stone. A bi-nuclear plan separates living rooms from bedrooms and bathrooms, linked by a playroom and deck that can be used flexibly, and every room but the main bathroom looks fully outside. It was placed on the New South Wales State Heritage Register in 1999.

The Shine Dome in Canberra, first called Becker House, is a local landmark known for its unusual structure. Its nickname, "The Martian Embassy", plays on both its shape and Canberra's role as the capital, where foreign embassies are based. Sir Roy Grounds of the firm Grounds, Romberg and Boyd designed it. On completion in 1959 its dome, 45.75 metres across, was the largest in Australia. The approved scheme called for a reinforced concrete dome of 710 tonnes resting on 16 slender supports. The shell is about 60 cm thick at the supports and thins to 10 cm at the crown, and it stands on its own with no inner walls holding it up; building it was a considerable technical feat. It took its present name in 2000, after John Shine gave one million dollars toward renovating the dome.

Fed Square, as Melbourne's Federation Square is usually called, is a venue for the arts, culture and public events beside the city centre. Its 3.2 hectares at Flinders and Swanston Streets, facing Flinders Street station, sit over busy railway lines. On 28 July 1997 a group led by Lab Architecture Studio of London won the competition alongside the landscape architects Karres en Brands, with Bates Smart as local executive architects in the second stage. Gently angled "cranked" geometry shapes plans and façades alike. The cladding mixes zinc, perforated zinc, sandstone and clear and frosted glass in a camouflage pattern based on pinwheel tiling. The main square is paved with 470,000 ochre sandstone blocks from Western Australia, and beneath it, above the tracks, lies the "labyrinth", a passive cooling system. It opened on 26 October 2002.

The Royal National Theatre on London's South Bank is Denys Lasdun's best-known work and among the most notable Brutalist buildings in Britain. It holds three theatres. The main auditorium, named after the company's first artistic director Laurence Olivier, is modelled on the ancient theatre at Epidaurus, with an open stage and 1,160 seats in a fan. The main material is a pale concrete chosen to suit the stone of Somerset House and Waterloo Bridge. Cast in rough timber formwork, it keeps the board grain on surfaces inside and out. On its opening, the historian Mark Girouard called the style "an aesthetic of broken forms". In 1988 the future Charles III described it as a clever way to put a nuclear power station in central London without anyone objecting. Despite such controversy, it has been Grade II* listed since 1994.

Set on the University of East Anglia campus in Norwich, England, the Sainsbury Centre is a museum of world art. Completed in 1978, it was among the first major public buildings by Norman Foster and Wendy Cheesman. The main building is a large clad steel box on sloping grass. One face is almost all glass, exposing the prefabricated frame, and inside the museum reads as one huge open room, with no partitions to interrupt daylight and artificial light. Services, lighting, toilets and maintenance routes are tucked into triangular towers and trusses, or between the outer skin and inner aluminium louvres. The slope let an enlarged basement open onto a man-made lake through a curved glass front. Chris Abel sees it as typical of Foster's early "universal space", designed for change. It was Grade II* listed in 2012.

The Isokon Building, or Lawn Road Flats, is in Belsize Park in the Camden borough of London. The Canadian engineer Wells Coates designed the reinforced concrete block for Molly and Jack Pritchard, with 32 flats at first and 36 today. Designed in 1929–1932, it opened in July 1934 as an experiment in minimal urban living. Every compact "Existenzminimum" flat had a tiny kitchen, since a shared kitchen sent meals up by dumbwaiter. Its simple living spaces drew strongly on Coates's experience of Japan and came with built-in Isokon furniture. Residents included Walter Gropius, Marcel Breuer, László Moholy-Nagy and Agatha Christie. Avanti Architects carefully refurbished it in 2003 for a housing association. Its smooth outer finish is the palest pink, as at first, not the white assumed from black and white photographs. It has been Grade I listed since 1999.

Sir John Soane's Museum, by Lincoln's Inn Fields in London, was once the home of the neo-classical architect John Soane. Made Royal Academy Professor of Architecture in 1806, he then bought No. 13, the house beside his own and today the museum, and rebuilt it in 1808–09 and 1812. After that he treated it as an architectural laboratory, reworking the interiors again and again. The best-known spaces, the dome area, colonnade and museum corridor at the back, are mostly lit from above, a small-scale echo of his top-lit banking halls at the Bank of England. Convex mirrors set into the domed Breakfast Room ceiling have influenced architects worldwide. More than 30,000 architectural drawings sit alongside models, paintings and antiquities such as the Sarcophagus of Seti I, all to be kept as nearly as possible as Soane left them.

Cartier SA set up the Fondation Cartier in 1984 as a centre for contemporary art. Ten years later it moved into a glass building designed by the Pritzker Prize winner Jean Nouvel on Boulevard Raspail, in Paris's 14th arrondissement. It stands where the American Center for Students and Artists once was, and Lothar Baumgarten laid out the modern woodland garden around it. Its ground floor is eight metres (26 ft) tall and glazed on all four sides. Here the foundation showed established artists, gave young artists their first shows and added work to its collection. By 2014 it had dropped a plan to move away and asked Nouvel to enlarge the Raspail premises instead. It stayed there until 2025, when it moved to the Palais-Royal area, reopening on 25 October 2025.

The Millau Viaduct is a cable-stayed bridge of many spans that crosses the Tarn gorge just west of Millau, in southern France. The engineer Michel Virlogeux and the English architect Norman Foster led its design team. Its structure reaches 343 metres (1,125 ft), and for more than twenty years, until late 2025, no bridge in the world was taller. After wind tunnel tests, the road deck was reshaped and the pylons were refined in detail. The deck was built on the plateaus at both ends and slid out over the pylons by bridge launching. Construction took three years, with the formal opening on 14 December 2004 and traffic two days later. In 2006 it won the Outstanding Structure Award of the International Association for Bridge and Structural Engineering.

The Pavillon Le Corbusier, on the Zürichhorn in Zürich, is a museum devoted to Le Corbusier and the last building he designed. It marks a sharp turn from his concrete and stone to steel and glass: early drawings showed a concrete building, but in 1962 the scheme switched to steel. Prefabricated steel parts are used extensively, with multicoloured enamelled panels on the central core. The frame is built of 2.26-metre cubes assembled on site, with walls, windows, ceilings and floors screwed onto it. Over it all hovers a separate roof against rain and sun, prefabricated in the largest possible pieces, joined on the ground in two welded halves and craned 9 metres up onto its pillars. Le Corbusier died in 1965, and the building opened as the Centre Le Corbusier on 15 July 1967.

Park Güell brings together parks, gardens and architectural elements in Barcelona's Gràcia district. As the city expanded around 1900, the Catalan industrialist Eusebi Güell asked Antoni Gaudí, a leading figure in Catalan modernism, to design it. Güell first meant it as an upmarket housing estate on the model of the English garden city. Work ran from 1900 to 1914, and the public was let in from 1926. The heart of the park is a terrace edged by a winding bench in the form of a sea serpent, designed by Josep Maria Jujol, whose curves make nooks where people gather. As at Colònia Güell, Gaudí used inverted catenary arches to keep loads in compression. UNESCO listed it in 1984 among the Works of Antoni Gaudí, saying it anticipated and influenced many of Modernism's forms and techniques in the 20th century.

After winning a 1984 competition, Carme Pinós and Enric Miralles designed Igualada's New Cemetery, near Barcelona; it was built in 1985–1994 to replace the Old Cemetery. It is widely held to be among the most poetic Catalan buildings of the 20th century. The architects aimed to explore how people accept life's cycle and to link past, present and future. The scheme is partly an earthwork reshaping the land and partly an image of life as a river. Crossed, rusting steel poles at the entrance serve as gates and recall Calvary's crosses; from there a processional "street" descends, walled by repeated concrete burial niches, its concrete floor set with railway sleepers. It is meant to lead mourners down into a "city of the dead" where living and dead draw close. Miralles, who died in 2000, lies in one of its tombs.

Often simply called the Holocaust Memorial, this Berlin memorial remembers the Jews murdered by Nazi Germany. Peter Eisenman designed it with Buro Happold for a site in Mitte, one block south of the Brandenburg Gate. On a sloping 1.9-hectare site stand 2,711 concrete stelae laid out on a grid. Each is 2.38 m by 0.95 m, and they rise anywhere between 0.2 and 4.7 m, so long, narrow, straight alleys run between them over rolling ground. In Eisenman's own text, the stelae are meant to create an uneasy, confusing mood, picturing a seemingly ordered system cut off from human reason. An underground "Place of Information" lists about 3 million victims' names, from Yad Vashem. Built in 2003–2004, it was inaugurated on 10 May 2005, six decades after the Second World War ended in Europe.

By the Schie in Rotterdam, the old Van Nelle Factory is held up as a leading work of functionalist modernism and of Nieuwe Bouwen, the Dutch modern movement. Leendert van der Vlugt, of the firm Brinkman & Van der Vlugt, designed it together with J.G. Wiebenga, a civil engineer then expert in reinforced concrete, and it went up between 1925 and 1931. It is claimed to be the first building in the world with a curtain wall prefabricated in a factory. The plant processed tea, coffee and tobacco, and later rice and chewing gum. In 1932 Le Corbusier described it as the finest sight of the modern age. Eric Gude planned its conversion to new uses in 1997, and Wessel de Jonge coordinated the renovation that started in 2000. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.

The Chapel of Saint Benedict is a Roman Catholic church in Sumvitg, in the Surselva region of the canton of Graubünden, Switzerland. It exists because an avalanche in 1984 wiped out the Baroque chapel that had stood on the site, after which Disentis Abbey chose to put up a new one. A design competition followed, and Peter Zumthor won it; the engineering was by Jürg Buchli with Jürg Conzett. Work on the chapel began in 1985 and ended in 1989, and the whole project cost CHF 600,000.

The Fondation Beyeler's museum in Riehen, near Basel, houses the modern and traditional art collected by Hildy and Ernst Beyeler. The two art dealers set up the foundation in 1982 and asked Renzo Piano to design a home for their private collection; it opened on 18 October 1997 with 140 modern classics, 23 of them by Picasso. At the founder's request, white walls, pale wood floors and daylight make the rooms calm. Four porphyry walls, each 115 metres long and 7 metres apart, run north to south and set out the plan. On them rests a light glass roof, enamelled white underneath, that admits north light, screens east and west sun, and overhangs to shade the glass fronts, which look out to the vines and cornfields of the Tüllinger Hills. An extension by Peter Zumthor was completed in 2026.

The Secession Building in Vienna is an exhibition hall for contemporary art. Joseph Maria Olbrich completed it in 1898 as the built manifesto of the Vienna Secession, rebel artists who had split from the long-standing fine art establishment, and it became the movement's landmark. Karl Wittgenstein, father of the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein, paid for it. Over the entrance runs the movement's motto, which says that each age deserves its own art and art deserves its freedom, and beneath it three gorgons stand for painting, sculpture and architecture.
