His son's toy robot gave him the idea. Sumet called it possibly post-high-tech: it dresses a finished object in abstract machine parts instead of exposing its workings. The floor plates shrink in steps up to the 18th floor, a profile that gives the robot its look and meets setback rules requiring an 18-degree slope from each edge of the plot. Two rooftop antennas double as lightning conductors, and two 6-metre lidded eyes, of reflective glass with lids of metal louvres, are windows for the top executive meeting and dining rooms. Finished in 1986 for US$10 million, it was chosen by MOCA in Los Angeles as one of 50 seminal buildings of the century.

Sirius, in The Rocks in Sydney, was designed in 1978–1979 by Tao Gofers, an architect at the state's Housing Commission, and is a prominent Australian example of Brutalism. Its repeated geometric forms respond to the Japanese Metabolist movement. The complex rehoused public tenants pushed out by a disputed redevelopment of the historic Rocks area in the 1960s and 1970s. The only high-rise in The Rocks, it held 79 homes of one to four bedrooms. Gofers meant to paint it white to match the Opera House close by, but a tight budget left it unpainted. In 2017 the state government refused heritage listing against its Heritage Council's advice and offered the building for sale. In 2018 the World Monuments Fund listed it as at risk, and the NSW Australian Institute of Architects gave it its Enduring Architecture Award.

One Central Park, in the Sydney suburb of Chippendale, is a pair of mixed-use towers, the opening phase of the Central Park renewal scheme, developed by Frasers Property and Sekisui House. Carlton & United Breweries once occupied the Central Park site, which Frasers bought in 2007. Ateliers Jean Nouvel teamed up with PTW Architects on the architecture. Botanist Patrick Blanc worked with the Nouvel office on the vertical gardens, with LED art by Yann Kersalé; rising more than 50 metres, they are the tallest in the world. Motorised mirrors on the west tower's roof follow the sun and send daylight up to a cantilever 100 metres above, hung from the 28th floor of the east tower, which reflects it down to the gardens and atrium. Opened officially in December 2013, it won the CTBUH award for Best Tall Building Worldwide.

Eliel Saarinen designed Helsinki Central Station, which opened in 1919. His winning competition scheme, titled "A winged wheel standing on a globe", was purely national romantic: heavy walls, eight bears, one tall pointed tower and many smaller ones, and a finely drawn stone gateway to the main platform. It provoked calls for a modern, rational style in major public buildings. Back in Finland in 1904, Saarinen dropped romanticism and redrew the station on rational lines. Large concrete vaults roof the halls and show clearly in the outer form; built with the Hennebique system patented in France in 1892, they were then the largest reinforced concrete structure the state had commissioned. The granite-clad station is known for its clock tower and Emil Wikström's Lantern Bearers statues; the main front and the stone figures at the entrance are red Hanko granite.

The Slovak Radio Building in Bratislava is an upside-down pyramid, nicknamed Radio Diamant by locals. Miloš Chorvát won the design competition, yet the client picked the second-placed scheme by Štefan Svetko, Štefan Ďurkovič and Barnabáš Kissling. The project started in 1967 and was finished in 1983. Its designers deliberately avoided the standard tall-building recipe of the time, a low block joined to an office tower, and aimed for a more expressive form with its own character. It was among the first big buildings in Slovakia framed in steel, when prefabricated concrete panels were the norm. Svetko called it a temple of word and music. The building stands 80 metres high, and inside is a concert hall for 522 people with a large organ. Slovakia listed it as a cultural heritage monument in 2017.

This memorial cemetery in Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina, honours the city's Yugoslav Partisans who died in the Second World War. It lies at Bijeli Brijeg, on the slopes of Hum hill, on the Neretva's right bank. At Džemal Bijedić's initiative, the Belgrade architect Bogdan Bogdanović was given charge of the design. Civil engineer Ahmet Ribica ran the drilling and blasting of the hill and the construction of the monument. Josip Broz Tito opened it on 25 September 1965, twenty years after Mostar was freed and the Mostar Battalion was founded. In 1992 war and dynamite left the cemetery badly damaged, and in 2006 Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed it a national monument.

The academic area of IIT Kanpur brings together the institute's central library, department buildings and research centres with the auditorium, tutorial block and lecture hall complex. Student hostels, the Student Activities Centre and the sports complex lie outside it. The institute moved to this site beside the Grand Trunk Road, near Kalyanpur in Kanpur district, in 1963. Achyut Kanvinde designed the campus, which spreads over 4.3 square kilometres; it was planned and landscaped for environmental freedom and for ease of movement and communication. The academic area is one part of this campus.

Chandigarh's Government Museum and Art Gallery was built to hold artefacts that came from the Lahore Museum at the partition of India. Its collections include Gandharan sculpture, sculpture from ancient and medieval India, and Pahari and Rajasthani miniature paintings. Le Corbusier designed it with three associate architects, among them Pierre Jeanneret; design work ran from 1960 to 1962 and building from 1962 to 1967. Le Corbusier designed three museums: this one, Sanskar Kendra in Ahmedabad and Tokyo's National Museum of Western Art. Its pivoting entrance, metal-clad door, built-in furniture, display systems and sculptural concrete gargoyles are typical of the city's architecture, and a mural by Satish Gujral brings colour to the reception of an otherwise stark concrete building. Chief Commissioner M. S. Randhawa opened the museum on 6 May 1968.

Nek Chand Saini, a government official, began the Rock Garden of Chandigarh in secret in his spare time in 1957. He collected materials from demolition sites and chose a forested gorge near Sukhna Lake for his vision of a divine kingdom, Sukrani. The work broke the law, but stayed hidden until officials found it in 1975. By then it had grown into a set of linked courtyards crowded with hundreds of concrete dancers, musicians and animals clad in pottery. Chand built up each form in a cement and sand mix from recycled matter, then finished it in burnished pure cement combined with waste such as bangles, broken glass, crockery and slag. When demolition loomed, he won public opinion over, and the garden opened to all in 1986. It is now praised as a pioneer of environmental art and recycling.

Mazar-e-Quaid, whose name means 'Tomb of the Leader', is the resting place of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, who founded Pakistan. After Fatima Jinnah blocked a 1957 proposal, she chose Yahya Merchant, a Bombay architect and personal friend of Jinnah, as designer. His scheme is a domed, cube-like block faced in white marble, raised on a platform on a gardened hill above Karachi. It measures 75 by 75 metres in plan and 43 metres high, sits on a 4-metre plinth, and has curved arches, copper grilles and a doorway in each wall. The marble suggests purity, and the plain geometry is meant to make Jinnah seem larger than life. It has been described as traditional in style, lightly touched by modernism. The foundation stone was laid on 31 July 1960, and Yahya Khan opened the mausoleum on 18 January 1971.

Patan Museum occupies an old residential courtyard of Patan Durbar, a palace of the Malla kings who once ruled the Kathmandu Valley, inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The palace stands on the site of a Buddhist monastery and has been renovated many times. The Austrian architect Götz Hagmüller restored the museum, Mary Shepherd Slusser curated its collection, and King Birendra Bir Bikram Shah opened it in 1997. Most pieces are cast bronzes, chiefly Hindu and Buddhist gods, along with gilded copper repoussé, crafts Patan is known for. In 2017 the restored Sundari Chowk courtyard joined the museum, making space for the Seamann Gallery and the Frozen Wall. There the floor is laid in mud, the traditional Nepalese finish, where the rest of the museum has tiles.

Hilton Istanbul opened in 1955, and no Hilton outside the United States has been running longer. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it; the design is credited jointly to Gordon Bunshaft and the Turkish architect Sedad Hakkı Eldem. The hotel is an eleven-storey rectangular slab, 21 by 100 metres, on a green slope looking over the Bosphorus, close to Taksim Square. Bunshaft's modern lines meet Ottoman and Turkish elements brought in by Eldem, whose flying-carpet canopy over the main entrance is an example of Orientalism. Cement, glass and steel came from Germany, marble and ceramics from Italy, and window castings, air-conditioning and lifts from the US. Finished in a record 21 months, it became the biggest hotel in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, and the project played a part in the US–Soviet Cold War rivalry.

KAPSARC, the King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center, is a Riyadh-based body that researches and advises on climate, sustainability and the economics of energy. Its campus in the Saudi capital is split in two, with homes on the west side and the research and office complex to the east. Zaha Hadid designed that 70,000 square metre complex, with support from Event Communications, after a 2009 design competition. Five buildings interlock within it: one for research, one for computing, a conference centre, a library and a prayer space, the Musalla. The complex opened in October 2017 and holds LEED Platinum certification.

Education City Mosque is part of the Qatar Faculty of Islamic Studies, in its Minaretein building on the Hamad Bin Khalifa University campus. The building also holds teaching and staff space and a research centre. Designed by Mangera Yvars, it was finished in 2013. It rests on five big columns standing for the five pillars of Islam, each carrying a verse from the Qur'an. It follows the Islamic idea of the kulliyya, in which all knowledge comes from faith: the plan traces a spiral, and paths lead from the teaching spaces to the mosque. A four-storey ablution cascade below the mosque marks a symbolic divide between the two and helps keep it cool. It was named best religious building at the 2015 World Architecture Festival, was nominated in 2016 for the first RIBA international prize, and has won sustainability awards.

The Nubia Museum in Aswan, formally the International Museum of Nubia, is an archaeology museum devoted to Nubian culture and heritage. Designed by the Egyptian architect Mahmoud El-Hakim, it was built following the UNESCO campaign to save the monuments of Nubia and opened on 23 November 1997. It stands on a rocky hill, built in local stone, and its layout and look draw on the region's ancient temples, fortresses and houses. Of its 50,000 square metres, 7,000 are building; the rest is gardens and public space, among them a botanical garden of Egyptian plants. Three floors serve display and housing, plus a library and information centre. Because it sits on a steep cliff, the museum can hold a full-scale design of the Nile, from Ethiopia and Sudan down to Egypt. In 2001 it won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

The University of Constantine, in Algeria, was established in 1969 and laid out to plans by the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer. Niemeyer was in touch with the Ecotec design office, headed by Mehnaoui Abdelhamid, and the Ecotec company built the campus. President Houari Boumedienne, in power from 1965 to 1978, commissioned the project, and it was coordinated by Seddik Benyahia, who served as the minister for higher education and research from 1971 to 1977. The campus lies on the road that links Mohamed Boudiaf Airport with the city centre, and is made up of more than six buildings.

Maqam Echahid in Algiers opened on 5 July 1982, twenty years after Algeria became independent. Three stylised concrete fins, shaped like standing palm leaves, meet halfway up and rise to 96 metres, sheltering an "Eternal Flame" beneath them. At the edge of each leaf stands a soldier statue marking a stage in the country's struggle for independence. The Canadian company Lavalin built it from a model made at the Fine Art Institute of Algiers under Bashir Yelles's leadership. Several artists were involved: the painter Yelles, the Polish sculptor Marian Konieczny and the calligrapher Abdelhamid Skander. The fins' curved geometry, a clifftop site and the region's high seismic risk made it a real technical challenge; building took seven months and 20 days, from 15 November 1981. Its esplanade holds a crypt, an amphitheatre and, underground, the National Museum of El Mujahid.

Kamalapur railway station in Dhaka is the largest station in Bangladesh and its busiest transport hub, a gateway to the capital. It opened in 1968. Design work began under the American architect Daniel Dunham, who had come to what was then East Pakistan with the Louis Berger Group, and was continued by Robert Boughey. For the roof they devised an unusual concrete parasol structure. Seen from outside, the terminal is a rhythmic row of gently tapering, arched shells that recalls the tropics and an umbrella sheltering people from the monsoon rain. Under this one shared canopy are the ticket office, administrative offices, and places for passengers to rest and wait. The roof is made up of 36 slender concrete domes, carried on columns 59 feet tall, each of which spreads four branches upward to hold it.

The Gate of Europe, or Puerta de Europa, is a pair of office towers in Madrid, standing either side of the bus station at Plaza de Castilla, close to Chamartín railway station and the Cuatro Torres Business Area. Philip Johnson and John Burgee, both American, designed them. The Kuwait Investment Office commissioned the towers, which explains their first name, the KIO Towers; Fomento de Construcciones y Contratas built them, and Leslie E. Robertson Associates handled the structural engineering. Each tower has 26 floors and leans at 15 degrees, and the pair were the world's first skyscrapers built on a slant. Construction ran from 1989 to 1996.

The SEC Armadillo, first named the Clyde Auditorium, hosts concerts and conferences beside the Clyde in Glasgow, Scotland. Foster + Partners designed it as an extension of the city's exhibition and conference centre, the SECC, and it formed part of a broader remaking of Glasgow's old industrial waterfront. Work started in September 1995 and the building opened in September 1997. Arup carried out the engineering, from civil and structural to mechanical, electrical and geotechnical design, and Arup's published account documents its system of curved shells and supporting steelwork. Those overlapping curved forms earned the building its nickname, which later became its recognised name, and its sculpted roofline has sometimes been likened to the Sydney Opera House. Seating can be arranged for events of different sizes, up to about 3,000 people.

Generali Tower in Milan, also called Hadid Tower after its designer, the Anglo-Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid, and nicknamed lo Storto, "the Twisted One", is an office skyscraper finished in 2017. It reaches 177.4 metres over 44 floors, plus three below ground, with about 67,000 square metres of floor space. Its shape warps as it rises: each floor changes in size and in the direction it faces along the tower's axis. The frame is concrete and composite, with a central core doing the main work against sideways forces. Underneath, a concrete raft 2.5 metres thick sits on 64 piles grouped below the main load points, and a free-form steel podium for commercial use wraps the base. The tower holds offices of Assicurazioni Generali, and in October 2019 the American Concrete Institute ranked it first for excellence among high-rise buildings.

Herzog & de Meuron designed Roche Tower (Building 1) in Basel for the drug maker Hoffmann-La Roche. It rises 178 metres over 41 floors, and on opening it overtook Zürich's Prime Tower by 52 metres to become the highest building in Switzerland. Building began in 2012; it opened on 18 September 2015. It cost CHF 550 million and offers 74,200 square metres of floor space for around 2,000 staff. The tower rests on 143 piles up to 24 metres deep, capped by a foundation slab meant to steady it in earthquakes. It was engineered for a magnitude 6.9 quake, beyond the legal minimum and equal to an event expected statistically once in 1,500 years. A closed-cavity façade needs less cleaning, shades the interior and keeps views open, while groundwater cooling and waste-heat recovery serve the heating, cooling and ventilation.

Place Ville Marie is an office and shopping complex in downtown Montreal, with four office buildings and an underground shopping plaza, a hub of the Underground City. The main tower went up in 1962 in the International style as the head office of the Royal Bank of Canada. Cross-shaped in plan, it rises 47 storeys to 188 metres. It was among the first built works of Henry N. Cobb, a founding partner of Pei Cobb Freed & Partners, and was disputed from the outset for its nearness to many landmarks and the changes it would bring downtown. Design historian Mark Pimlott saw its boldest move in putting almost half its floor area below the street, sheltered from extreme weather. Since most of it stands over railway tracks, it was built to resist vibration, making it Montreal's most earthquake-resistant office tower.

Montreal's Tour de la Bourse (Stock Exchange Tower) rises 48 storeys where Victoria Square meets Saint Jacques Street. Luigi Moretti and Pier Luigi Nervi designed it, and it is considered International Style. The first plan, made in the boom years around Expo 67, called for three identical towers set in a triangle. Finished in 1964 at 190 metres, it was Canada's tallest building until 1967, and no reinforced concrete tower was taller until Chicago's Lake Point Tower in 1968. A bronze-tinted anodised aluminium curtain wall, renovated in 1995, contrasts with slightly leaning precast concrete columns at the four corners, giving a gently convex look. Mechanical floors split it into three roughly equal blocks; at those levels the corners are cut back in an octagon, leaving small outdoor gaps behind the columns. The Montreal Exchange still occupies floors 3 and 4.

Kyushu National Museum opened on 16 October 2005 in Dazaifu, near Fukuoka, next to Dazaifu Tenman-gū. No new national museum had opened in Japan for more than a century, and it was the first to put history ahead of art. Kiyonori Kikutake designed the building, made of wood and glass and set among hills; work on it finished in 2004. Its collections of Japanese artefacts, especially ceramics, follow Kyūshū's past from prehistoric times through the Meiji era, with particular weight on its rich history of exchange with neighbouring China and Korea. Temporary shows fill the third floor and the permanent collection the fourth. Most Japanese museums hire outside help for conservation, but this one has a large suite of conservation labs and staff of its own and acts as the main conservation centre for all of western Japan.

Muziekgebouw aan 't IJ, the "Music Building on the IJ", is Amsterdam's main hall for contemporary classical music. Designed by the Danish architects 3XN, it opened in 2005 on top of the IJtunnel, ten minutes on foot from Amsterdam Centraal. The Bimhuis belongs to the building and is partly built into it. Besides one large concert hall there is a smaller hall that also serves for conferences, talks and exhibitions, and music is played elsewhere in the building too, in the atrium and on three big balconies over the restaurant. The Kleine Zaal, formerly the Bamzaal, contains a microtonal 31-TET organ designed by Adriaan Fokker. In 2006 the building received the Urban Land Institute Award for Excellence in its Europe category.

Tokyo Sea Life Park is a public aquarium in Kasai Rinkai Park, in Tokyo's Edogawa Ward, and took over from the Ueno Aquarium at Ueno Zoo. To mark the zoo's hundredth year, a plan was announced for the largest aquarium in Japan, and the new building, designed by Yoshio Taniguchi, opened officially in 1989. Around 650 species live in 47 tanks. Tuna live in a big round tank with a viewing space at its centre, and the ring-shaped Voyagers of the Sea tank, holding 2,200 cubic metres, was Japan's biggest indoor tank when built. In its first year the aquarium drew 3.55 million visitors, far above the previous Japanese record of 2.4 million, set in 1987 at Suma Aqualife Park. In January 2019 the park set out a basic plan to add a new facility on its grounds.

Tour Perret in Amiens, France, is a 29-storey residential tower, now 110 metres tall, which has been called the first skyscraper in France. Design began in 1942, after the centre of Amiens was badly damaged in the Second World War, as part of a large rebuilding scheme led by Auguste Perret. Perret meant the tower for offices, but the authorities overruled him. At first 104 metres high, it was the tallest building in France and the first there over 100 metres. A clock belfry planned for the top was dropped after delays and rising costs. Only in 2005 was the tower completed, with Thierry Van de Wyngaert's Hourglass of Light: a cube of 192 glass panels with electrically adjustable transparency, lit by twelve neon rings that change colour through the day. It became a listed historic monument in 1975.

Rohm Theatre Kyoto, officially Kyoto Kaikan, is a venue for concerts and other performances in Kyoto, Japan, whose design is credited to Kunio Maekawa. Its main hall first opened in 1960 with 2,005 seats. The venue closed in 2012 and spent four years being redeveloped, reopening in January 2016. Besides the main hall it has two more performance spaces, for 700 and 200 people. Its survival owes much to Rohm, the Kyoto semiconductor company, which gave ¥5.25 billion toward the refurbishment and so saved this landmark from possible demolition. In return the company received the naming rights.

Raffles City Chongqing, by Moshe Safdie (2019), groups eight skyscrapers on a 9.2-hectare site in Yuzhong District, at the point of the peninsula where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers join. Safdie also designed Marina Bay Sands in Singapore, which looks much like it. The scheme draws on Chinese sailing vessels and honours the city's past as a trading centre. Across the tops of four of the towers runs The Crystal, a closed horizontal skyway 300 metres long. The towers are reinforced concrete, with steel columns wrapped in concrete and steel floor spans, and the outer skin uses about 3,000 glass panels and close to 5,000 aluminium ones. The whole project holds 1.12 million square metres, including 150,000 m² of offices, 1,400 homes, a hotel and a 235,000 m² shopping mall. It won the China Tall Building Innovation Award.

Zorlu Center, in Istanbul's Beşiktaş district, is a complex of high-rise buildings with mixed uses, finished in 2013 to designs by Tabanlıoğlu Architects and Emre Arolat Architects. The two firms won a competition for which more than 100 practices applied and 13 were picked to take part. It sits where the Bosphorus Bridge's European approach meets Barbaros Boulevard. The group is described as four towers with five functions, among them a public square, housing, a hotel and offices; there is also an upscale shopping mall and a Cinemaximum multiplex. The design is said to start from the idea of a historical town square, with bold lines framing the sky and wide greenery. It is home to Zorlu PSM, Turkey's largest performing arts centre, and Turkey's first Apple Store; the complex has a 2,300-seat concert hall and a 770-seat theatre.

Torre BBVA México, once known as Torre BBVA Bancomer, is a skyscraper of offices standing on Paseo de la Reforma, in the Colonia Juárez neighbourhood of Mexico City. It is the head office of BBVA México, which is the biggest bank in the country and belongs to the Spanish financial group Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria. The design is credited to LegoRogers, a joint effort of two practices, Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners and Legorreta + Legorreta. Completed in 2015, the 50-storey tower reaches 235 metres (771 ft), and when it was finished it ranked as Mexico City's second tallest building.

The Lighthouse in Glasgow is a conversion of the former Glasgow Herald newspaper offices. The design is officially credited to the firm Honeyman and Keppie, with Charles Rennie Mackintosh among the contributing artists; it was the first building he worked on for them. Work started in February 1894 and was finished by summer 1895. The building draws on the Queen Anne and Scottish baronial styles, while its proportions and window layout are seen as typical of Mackintosh. He also contributed to the interiors; his influence is said to be strongest in the editor's room. The newspaper stayed until 1980, when it moved to Albion Street. Page and Park Architects later renovated and extended the A-listed building for £13 million, and Queen Elizabeth II reopened it in July 1999 as The Lighthouse, Scotland's Centre for Architecture and Design.

Tokyo Skytree, in Sumida, Tokyo, serves both as a broadcasting tower and an observation tower, with Nikken Sekkei as lead architects. As of 2019 it was described as the world's tallest self-supporting broadcasting tower and the second tallest structure of any kind made by people. Its design, made public on 24 November 2006, rested on three ideas: blending neofuturistic design with traditional Japanese beauty, helping to revive the city, and contributing to disaster prevention. The base works like a tripod, and from about 350 m upward the structure turns cylindrical for panoramic views. A central reinforced-concrete shaft helps it resist earthquakes. The lattice is painted 'Skytree White', a colour based on aijiro, a pale bluish white from Japanese tradition. The 634 m height was chosen because 6, 3 and 4 can be read as 'Musashi', the area's old name.

Jørn Utzon designed this water tower for Svaneke, a small town on the Danish island of Bornholm, and it was completed in 1952. It was his first successful project; he would later design the Sydney Opera House. Utzon sketched the idea at once on a paper serviette. The unusual form takes its cue from the old sea marks that once helped ships find their way. A pyramid-shaped tank rests on three slim legs of reinforced concrete that meet at the top, and a concrete stair placed in the centre winds gracefully up from the ground. Of five Utzon works that can be called concrete architecture, this one came first. Changes to the water supply took the tower out of use in 1988, and since 1990 it has been protected as a listed building.

Václav Aulický (architect) and Jiří Kozák (structural engineer) designed the Žižkov Television Tower, a Prague transmitter put up from 1985 to 1992. It rises on a hill in Žižkov, the district it is named after, high over the old city skyline, and is a work of high-tech architecture. Its plan is a triangle: at the corners rise three steel tubes with double walls, filled with concrete. Together they hold nine pods and three decks of broadcast equipment. One pillar climbs much higher than the other two, giving the radio antennas height and lending the tower its rocket-and-gantry look. It is 216 m tall. Official criticism was impossible at the time, but unofficially it was called megalomaniac and jarring on the skyline, and blamed for wrecking part of a Jewish cemetery, centuries old, at its foot.

Moscow's White House, formally the House of the Government of the Russian Federation, holds the main offices of Russia's government and of the prime minister. Dmitry Chechulin designed it, and construction ran from 1965 to 1981; it was built for the Supreme Soviet of Russia and the People's Control Committee. Its overall form follows his 1934 draft for the Aeroflot building. He had wanted to build on Taganka Square, but the embankment site was picked for its views along the high Moskva riverbank. No multi-storey building before it had paired monolithic stiffening cores with a uniform prefabricated frame of reinforced concrete. Outside, it was lined with claydite concrete panels that had been faced with marble beforehand. It was a centre of resistance in the failed coup of August 1991, and was repaired after heavy damage in the 1993 constitutional crisis.

King Power Mahanakhon, first called MahaNakhon, is a skyscraper of mixed uses in the Silom/Sathon business district of Bangkok. Its development team included the German architect Ole Scheeren, a former partner at the Office for Metropolitan Architecture, along with Pace Development, David Collins Studio and IBC. Ground was broken on 20 June 2011 and the tower was finished in 2016. In form it is a square prism, with cube-like cuts winding round its sides in a rough spiral. This 'pixelated' ribbon peels back the outer skin to show an inner layer and makes balconies that look over the city, while glass walls split into horizontal and vertical bands add to an 'unfinished' look. At 314.2 m and 77 floors, it was recognised by the CTBUH as Thailand's tallest building on 4 May 2016. Its homes rank among Bangkok's priciest condominiums.

Joensuu City Hall is a brick building in the centre of the Finnish town, designed by Eliel Saarinen and finished in 1914 in a mix of Romantic Nationalism and late Art Nouveau. It stands on Rantakatu street on the bank of the Pielinen River. Inside are the city's central administration, a restaurant and the city theatre, said to be the most easterly professional theatre in the European Union. On completion, on 14 November 1914, the building kept quite close to Saarinen's drawings, above all in its façades. The sculptor Johannes Haapasalo designed the statues on the front. In March 1966 a fire came close to destroying the hall, and it was renovated in 1998.

The London Central Mosque, also called the Regent's Park Mosque, sits at Regent's Park's edge, in the City of Westminster. In 1969 an open international competition for its design drew more than a hundred entries from Muslim and non-Muslim designers alike; Sir Frederick Gibberd was the architect. John Laing & Son began work early in 1974 on the main complex, with prayer halls for men and women, a library, offices and living quarters, and it was finished in July 1977 for £6.5 million in all. A golden dome makes it easy to spot. Inside, the dome carries Islamic sacred geometry, and small stained glass windows ring its base, holding turquoise 16-pointed stars. More than 5,000 men can pray in the main hall, while women use a balcony above it. It was listed Grade II* in 2018.

Inside the Moscow Kremlin stands the State Kremlin Palace, a large modern building once unofficially called the Kremlin Palace of Congresses. Nikita Khrushchev initiated it as a modern venue for Communist Party meetings. Work began in 1959, and the hall opened on 17 October 1961, with the Soviet Communist Party's 22nd Congress. Its Soviet modernism broke with Stalinist design. It is made of glass and concrete and reaches 17 metres below ground, and its façades are clad in anodised aluminium and white marble from the Urals. At the centre is an auditorium of 6,000 seats. Its spare form and the aim of opening the interior to the outside reflected the fresh architecture of the Khrushchev Thaw. Several heritage buildings were cleared for it, among them the old neoclassical State Armoury and some rear wings of the Great Kremlin Palace.

Also called the MI6 Building, the SIS Building at Vauxhall Cross holds the headquarters of Britain's foreign intelligence service. It stands at 85 Albert Embankment, by Vauxhall Bridge on the Thames. Terry Farrell won a competition for the site; his first proposal was an urban village. His design looked to 1930s industrial modernism, Battersea and Bankside power stations among it, and to Mayan and Aztec temples. Its many layers create 60 separate roof areas; 25 kinds of glass went into it, and 12,000 m² of glass and aluminium in total. Because MI6's work is sensitive, large parts lie below street level, linked by underground corridors. It was finished in April 1994, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 14 July. In a favourable 1992 review in The Guardian, Deyan Sudjic called it an 'epitaph for the architecture of the eighties'.

Kaknästornet, the Kaknäs Tower, is a telecom tower in Stockholm's Ladugårdsgärdet area and a major hub for Swedish television, radio and satellite broadcasting. The architect Bengt Lindroos designed it, and it was finished in 1967. It is 155 metres tall, or 170 metres counting the antenna at the top. For a few years it was the Nordic region's tallest building, until Näsinneula in Tampere, Finland, opened in 1971. It takes its name from Kaknäs, the old name of the area. The tower used to welcome visitors, with an information centre, a gift shop, indoor and outdoor viewing decks and a restaurant, but since 2018 it has been shut to the public for good, because the security repairs needed would have cost too much.

In Sofia, the National Palace of Culture, known as NDK, is a multi-purpose centre for conferences and culture. It opened on 31 March 1981 to mark 1,300 years of the Bulgarian state. Alexander Georgiev Barov (1931–1999), working with Ivan Kanazirev, led its design team of architects from Bulgaria and abroad. Its 123,000 m² of usable space is spread across three underground levels, eight floors and four terraces with panoramic views. Hall 1, the largest, seats more than 3,000. Inside, one consistent visual language runs throughout: geometric motifs and dark colours, with more than 80 monumental works that Bulgarian artists created especially for it, from murals and mosaics to sculpture, woodcarving and metalwork. In July 2005 it was named the world's best congress centre of the year, an International Association of Congress Centres award.

Wellington's Te Papa, whose name means 'the treasure box' in Māori, serves as New Zealand's national museum. It opened in 1998, following the merger of the National Art Gallery and the National Museum of New Zealand. Pete Bossley of Jasmax Architects was the designer and Fletcher Construction the builder, and the design followed bicultural principles drawn from the Treaty of Waitangi. The building sits on reclaimed Cable Street land. To firm up the soft fill, weights as heavy as 30 tonnes were dropped from heights of up to 30 metres in a crossing grid, compacting it 16 metres down. Base isolation, developed in New Zealand, guards against earthquakes; some isolators can be seen underground in 'Quake Braker'. The 36,000 m² building cost NZ$300 million by opening, and in 2000 Architecture NZ readers voted it Building of the Decade.

This brewery for Fix on Syngrou Avenue in Athens is one of Takis Zenetos's early works; he has been called Greek architecture's 'enfant terrible'. It has been named, together with one of Valsamakis's first apartment buildings, among buildings of the period that differ radically from what others were building at the time. In 1994 the former brewery was sold to the metro operator Attiko Metro, which planned an underground car park with a park on top. About 40 percent of the building had been pulled down when fierce protests made the car park investor give way: he kept to the part already cleared, where a lower building went up, and the rest was donated so it could later become a museum of modern art. Today the site is home to Athens's National Museum of Contemporary Art.

Belgrade's Sava Centar serves as an international centre for congresses, culture and business. Its origins lie in 1975: after the first OSCE conference, in Helsinki, President Josip Broz Tito agreed that Belgrade would host the following summit, yet the city had no hall for so many delegates. Stojan Maksimović led the team as project author and chief designer, and was given just a month to produce the concept. Work began in April 1976; building took 11 months, and Tito opened it on 14 May 1977. Its 100,000 m² overall (69,720 m² usable) hold a 4,000-seat theatre hall and 15 conference halls. Critics praised the sharp lines and unusual outline, the wide spans, the cascading terraces, the concrete brise-soleils and the brightly coloured exposed structure. It was declared a cultural monument in 2021.

The basilica of Las Lajas, a Roman Catholic minor basilica, stands within the Guáitara River canyon at Ipiales in Colombia. It was designed by Lucindo María Espinosa Medina (1871–1945), a self-taught cabinetmaker, builder and architect from Pasto in Nariño. The present church, in a neo-Gothic style, was begun on 1 January 1916 and paid for with gifts from local worshippers. It rises 100 m from the floor of the canyon, and a bridge 50 m tall links it to the far side. Pilgrims come from Colombia and neighbouring Ecuador because of a Marian apparition said to have happened in the 18th century. The first shrine on the spot, of straw and wood, dates from the middle of that century, and a brick chapel 7 m long replaced it in 1795/96.

Istanbul Modern, formally the Istanbul Museum of Modern Art, opened on 11 December 2004 as Turkey's first gallery of modern and contemporary art. On 4 May 2023 it reopened in a new building by Renzo Piano, close to its first home in Karaköy, inside the Galataport complex in Beyoğlu. Piano pictured it as a 'flying vessel' on the water. Its facade is made of 300 grey aluminium modules, some concave and some convex, which he likened to a fish leaping from the water; they play with the changing light and the reflections of the Bosphorus. A highly transparent ground floor ties the museum to Tophane Square and the renewed Galataport waterfront. A central staircase is the main circulation spine, and a roof terrace has a 'Reflection Pool' only 5 cm deep that mirrors the sky and city.

Built over the water of the Sea of Marmara, off the shore at Florya in Istanbul's Bakırköy district, this historic presidential residence was made for Mustafa Kemal Atatürk to relax in. Istanbul's municipality commissioned the architect Seyfi Arkan in 1935; the house was finished on 14 August of that year and presented to Atatürk as a gift. Arkan worked in the Bauhaus style, and the mansion is seen as an example of Early Republican Turkish architecture. Steel piles sunk into the sea floor carry it, and a timber pier links it to the sandy shore some 70 m off. On a single level, in an L-shaped plan, are a reception hall, reading room, bedrooms and bathroom. After renovation, it opened to visitors as a museum in 1993.

The Palace of Serbia houses several government ministries and hosts state visits by foreign leaders. The accepted design came from a group of Zagreb architects: Vladimir Potočnjak, the lead architect, drew its H-shaped exterior with Dragica Perak, Zlatko Nojman and Anton Urlih. The first plans followed Socialist realism, as Yugoslavia was then allied with the Soviet Union, but after the Tito–Stalin split of 1948 much changed. When work restarted in 1955, Mihailo Janković took over: his new project was modernist, he designed the interior, and he oversaw construction until it was finished in 1959. Its brick-filled concrete frame is faced in white Brač marble. Its H-shaped base, about 65,000 m², makes it Serbia's biggest building by area. In front of the middle wing, a lower, glass-domed central annex of 8,000 m² holds the Main Salon, with space for 2,000 guests.

The Museum of the Future fills seven floors in Dubai's Financial District, exploring what lies ahead for science, technology and innovation. Killa Design won the 2015 design competition; the building is credited to Shaun Killa Design, engineered by Buro Happold, and claimed to be among the world's most complex structures. It is a torus whose windows form Arabic calligraphy by the Emirati artist Matar Bin Lahej, setting out words about the future by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. The shell on top is built from 1,024 panels of fire-retardant composite with a stainless steel skin, each shaped differently in 3D to make up the script. New parametric and BIM tools were developed for it, including a growth algorithm that grew the inner steel frame digitally. It opened on 22 February 2022 and was certified LEED Platinum in February 2023.

Erich Mendelsohn designed the Red Banner Textile Factory in St Petersburg; the project's senior architect, Hyppolit Pretreaus, with E. A. Tretyakov and S. O. Ovsyannikov, later partly redesigned it. It was built from 1926 to 1937. In 1925 Mendelsohn had become the first foreign architect asked to work in the USSR, on the strength of his dynamic Expressionist buildings. A model showed a large factory, close to his earlier hat factory at Luckenwalde but more functionalist in look. The primitive building methods of the day could not realise it in full, so the design was altered freely. Mendelsohn disowned the result, though he often used the model to explain his approach to industrial architecture. The factory's power station, built in 1926, is officially listed as Russian heritage, and after a change of owners the exterior was restored by early 2018.

Shakespeare's Globe is a London reconstruction of the Globe Theatre, the Elizabethan playhouse of 1599 for which Shakespeare wrote his plays. The new theatre, founded by Sam Wanamaker, stands some 230 m from the first one in the old open-air style. Theo Crosby of Pentagram was the architect and Buro Happold the structural and services engineer, and the design rested on research by the historical adviser John Orrell. As in the original, a thrust stage pushes into a circular yard, wrapped by three raked tiers of seats. It is framed entirely in English oak, joined by mortise and tenon, without structural steel, making it in that sense a genuine 16th-century timber frame. Its thatch is claimed to be the first and only roof of its kind allowed in London since the Great Fire of 1666. It was completed in 1997.

MSN Warsaw, the city's Museum of Modern Art, is devoted to modern and contemporary art. Its road to a building was long: Christian Kerez won a first competition in February 2007, picked from more than 100 designs, but the City ended his contract in May 2012. A two-stage tender in 2013–14 then chose the New York practice Thomas Phifer and Partners. Their purpose-built museum stands on the north side of Plac Defilad in the city centre, beside Warsaw's Palace of Culture and Science, and opened on 25 October 2024. In a September 2025 interview with ARTnews, the director, Joanna Mytkowska, said the new building had already become a landmark in central Warsaw, and that it reflects several layers of Polish history: wartime destruction, the communist era and the transformation that followed.

Wales Millennium Centre, Wales's national arts centre, stands in Cardiff Bay. Jonathan Adams of the local firm Percy Thomas Architects designed it, and Arup Acoustics served as acoustic designer and building engineer. Adams aimed for a building that spoke of 'Welshness' and would be known at once, made from materials bound up with the history of Wales: slate, metal, wood and glass. Multi-coloured slate from Welsh quarries covers the outside, cut by narrow windows so the layers read like rock strata in sea cliffs. A bronze-coloured dome clad in stainless steel covers the Donald Gordon Theatre, which seats 1,896. On its front, above the main entrance, lines by the poet Gwyneth Lewis appear in Welsh and English, made by the windows of the upstairs bars and lit at night. Its two phases opened in November 2004 and January 2009.

Louvain-la-Neuve in Belgium is home to the Musée Hergé, devoted to Georges Remi, the cartoonist known as Hergé, creator of Tintin, Quick & Flupke and Jo, Zette and Jocko. It sits centrally, beside the green Parc de la Source. Christian de Portzamparc, the French winner of the Pritzker Prize, designed the futuristic building, and the cartoonist Joost Swarte did its interiors. Its first stone went down on 22 May 2007, a century after Hergé was born, and it opened in June 2009. Over three floors are nine exhibition rooms, a café, a shop and a small cinema. The visit begins on the top floor; a long walkway then passes between a view of the lobby and, on the other side, an oak forest outdoors. The address, Rue Labrador 26, is where Tintin first lives in the books.

Quebec City's Grand Théâtre de Québec, a complex for the performing arts, was planned to celebrate two anniversaries: the Canadian Centennial in 1967 and the 1864 Quebec Conference, a key step toward Confederation in 1867. Building restarted late in 1967, but it opened officially only on 16 January 1971. Of its two halls, Salle Louis-Fréchette has 1,885 seats and honours the French-Canadian author Louis-Honoré Fréchette. Jordi Bonet, a Catalan artist based in Quebec, was commissioned for a lobby mural in 1969. In 2020 a restoration by Lemay and Atelier 21 wrapped the building in glass held by a steel frame, protecting both its architecture and Bonet's sculpted mural built into the façade. In 2021 the theatre won the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada's Innovation in Architecture Award, partly for innovations made in the spirit of honouring Victor Prus's original building.

The Israel Goldstein Synagogue serves a Jewish congregation at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, on its Edmond J. Safra campus at Givat Ram. Two Israeli architects designed it in an organic style: Heinrich Heinz Rau, born in Germany, and David Resnick, born in Brazil. It was consecrated on 7 August 1957, when the new campus site at Givat Ram was still largely undeveloped. Outside, it reads as a concrete hemisphere resting on eight arches, 3.73 m high. Inside, the floor is a raised platform and there are no windows, yet light is described as rising from below on every side. The domed prayer space holds 100 worshippers. In 1964 the design won the Rechter Prize of the Israeli Architects Association, and in 1975 it appeared in a series of Israeli stamps on 'Architecture in Israel'.

The Matenadaran in Yerevan is the largest centre for keeping, studying and sharing Armenian manuscripts, acting as museum, archive and research institute. In October 1939, soon after the decision to bring the manuscripts to Yerevan, the Soviet Armenian authorities asked the city's chief architect, Mark Grigorian, to design it. Building ran from 1945 to 1957–58, halted from 1947 to 1953 for lack of skilled workers, and the interiors were finished between 1957 and 1959. A plain cube 22.4 m tall, faced in local grey basalt, it sits on a slope at the north-eastern end of Mashtots Avenue and closes the view along it. Grigorian wanted national architecture expressed as strongly as possible: the tall arched entrance between two narrow niches follows the 12th-century gavit of the Holy Apostles church at Ani, and the interior also draws on medieval gavits.

Toronto's Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts, a theatre of 2,071 seats, stands at the corner of Queen Street West and University Avenue, across from Osgoode Hall. The National Ballet of Canada and the Canadian Opera Company are based there. Of ten proposals, the modernist scheme of Diamond Schmitt Architects, a Canadian firm headed by Jack Diamond, was picked. A gala concert opened it on 14 June 2006. The horseshoe auditorium rises in five tiers, modelled on European opera houses and especially the National Theatre Munich. So that audiences do not hear the traffic, the subway and streetcars next door, or sirens heading to nearby hospitals, the hall sits on 489 rubber pads. The glass City Room faces both streets, while the other three sides wear dark brick. Inside is an unusual glass staircase.

Havana's memorial to José Martí, Cuba's national hero, stands in Vedado, at the northern edge of the Plaza de la Revolución. After seizing power, Batista pushed it ahead but passed over the competition winner for the third-placed scheme. That team was led by Raoul Otero de Galarraga and included Enrique Luis Varela, a friend of Batista who served as his Minister of Works, and the Princeton professor Jean Labatut. The 109 m tower, designed by Labatut under Otero de Galarraga, is a five-pointed star faced in grey Isla de Pinos marble. Work started in 1953, the centenary of Martí's birth, and was completed in 1958. A lift serves a closed viewing deck at the top, Havana's highest point. Facing the plaza is Sicre's 18 m white marble statue of Martí, carved on site and ringed by six half-height columns.

In Old Montreal, Pointe-à-Callière is a museum devoted to the city's archaeology and history, its design credited to Dan Hanganu. It was founded in 1992 to help mark Montreal's 350th birthday. Its entrance building, L'Éperon, stands above the spit of land where French settlers, among them Jeanne Mance and Paul de Chomedey, Sieur de Maisonneuve, landed in 1642. Before the museum, the Royal Insurance Building stood here, and from 1871 to 1917 it was also the city's second Customs House. The new building was raised on pilings so that the archaeological finds underneath would remain undisturbed and protected. Some remains exposed while it was being built were kept in place and now form part of the permanent display on Montreal's past. Over fifty national and international awards have gone to the museum, including awards for architecture and museography.

The Italian architect Aldo Spirito designed St Paul's Cathedral in Abidjan, mother church of the city's Roman Catholic archdiocese. Pope John Paul II consecrated its first stone on 11 May 1980, on his first pastoral journey to Côte d'Ivoire, and came back in August 1985, on his second visit, to consecrate the finished cathedral. Its most visible feature is a tall concrete structure in the form of a giant human figure. The cross structure, winged on both sides, is held by seven cables tied back to the triangular main building, so that it seems to be pulled toward the lagoon. The materials are concrete, steel, travertine, stone and stained glass. The cathedral stands on a small hill with wide views over the city and the Bay of Cocody, and holds 5,000 people, 3,500 of them seated.

New Delhi's Old Parliament House, once the Council House and now officially Samvidhan Sadan (Constitution House), housed India's Parliament from 26 January 1950 until 18 September 2023. It was designed by the British architects Herbert Baker and Edwin Lutyens and built from 1921 to 1927. Lutyens suggested a circular plan, which he judged the most efficient shape for the triangular plot. Its style mixes classical architecture inspired by Greece and Rome with structural features and ornament from Indian architecture. Outside stood 144 sandstone columns. A round central chamber formed the core, with three semicircular halls around it for the Chamber of Princes, the Central Legislative Assembly and the Council of State. Broad gardens surrounded the building, and jali, latticed sandstone railings, enclosed its boundary. On 28 May 2023 a new Parliament House beside it was inaugurated and took its place.

Toronto's Ontario Science Centre is a museum of science and a teaching organisation, for now based at Harbourfront Centre. Raymond Moriyama, a local architect, was engaged to design it; it was his first big project after setting up on his own. The first buildings, drawn up early in the 1960s, were Brutalist. Construction was not done by 1967, and the public could enter only from 26 September 1969. Set into a ravine cut by one branch of the Don River, the complex was a chain of buildings at several levels on steep ground, linked by escalators, with big windows onto the forest and river. At the glass front entrance, a large steel cable structure was left exposed. In June 2024 the Government of Ontario shut it after engineers reported a high risk that the roof could fail.

The Union Buildings are the official seat of South Africa's government and hold the offices of the President. Though outside central Pretoria, they occupy its highest point, and are a national heritage site. Herbert Baker designed them in the English monumental style, in light sandstone, and they stretch 285 m. A semicircular colonnade in the middle joins two side wings, meant to stand for the coming together of a people once divided. The site was a disused quarry, and its old diggings were used to form the amphitheatre, set with trees, ornamental pools, fountains, balustrades and sculptures. Baker used local materials wherever he could: granite quarried on the site and Buiskop sandstone for the courtyards. It took 1,265 workers three years to build, and it was finished in 1913 at a cost of £1,310,640, plus £350,000 for the land.

Now known as Bumi Siliwangi, Villa Isola is an Art Deco building on the north side of Bandung, West Java's capital. The Dutch architect Wolff Schoemaker finished it in 1933 for Dominique Willem Berretty, a Dutch media tycoon who founded the Aneta press agency. Built as Berretty's own house, it was turned into a hotel when he died and now holds the rectorate of the Indonesia University of Education. Schoemaker, a committed Art Deco designer, combined it with local ornament and let indigenous Javanese philosophy shape the design. The building lies on a north–south axis, with Mount Tangkuban Perahu to its north and Bandung to its south. Circles are the main motif, inside and out, gardens included. Besides linking to the terraces, the east and west corridors channel air, shielding the rooms from the tropical heat.

Melbourne's Royal Exhibition Building, built in 1879–1880, belongs to the international exhibition movement, which ran over 50 exhibitions worldwide from 1851 to 1915. Local architect Joseph Reed beat seventeen other entries to the £300 first prize. Its materials are brick, timber, steel and slate, and its styles Romanesque, Byzantine, Lombardic and Italian Renaissance; the dome follows Florence Cathedral. The plan, on a French Beaux-Arts scale, is a Latin cross: two long nave-like wings run east and west of the central dome, with a shorter one to the north, and windows in the drum light the crossing. Its foundation stone was laid on 19 February 1879, and it opened 18 months later, on 1 October 1880. Australia's first Parliament was opened there on 9 May 1901. In 2004 it was the first Australian building to gain UNESCO World Heritage status.

Known as the Casablanca Cathedral or the Church of the Sacred Heart, this former church stands west of Casablanca's Arab League Park, in Morocco. Paul Tournon, a French architect, designed it in the Art Deco style, and it was built in 1930. Although people commonly call it a cathedral, it never actually was one, since no bishop ever had his seat there. After Morocco gained independence it stopped being used for worship in 1956, and it was later turned into a cultural centre that is open to visitors.

Founded in 1854 as Melbourne Public Library, State Library Victoria is the oldest public library in Australia and among the earliest free libraries in the world. A competition for the building went to Joseph Reed, a recently arrived architect; his firm and its successors designed most later extensions. The first stage, the central section of the Swanston Street wing, was opened in February 1856 holding 3,800 books. Built in many stages, the complex filled the whole block in 1992. The Domed Reading Room, opened in 1913, is a separate work by Norman G. Peebles of Bates Smart. Six storeys tall and octagonal, it is 34.75 m wide and as high; when finished, its dome was the world's largest. Refurbished, it reopened in 2003, now named the La Trobe Reading Room, with skylights that copper had hidden since 1959 revealed again.

Built in 1593–1596 to guard the Old Port of Mombasa, Fort Jesus was ordered by Spain's King Felipe II, who also reigned over Portugal, and designed by the Italian Giovanni Battista Cairati. Cairati drew on the Italian architect Pietro Cataneo; Gaspar Rodrigues was master builder. Though the design is Renaissance, local Swahili people are believed to have supplied the masonry techniques, materials and labour. From above, the fort is shaped like a man: a rough square with a bulwark at each corner, regarded as a high point of late Renaissance military fortification. No European-style fort outside Europe had been built to resist cannon fire before it. The walls stand 18 m high; the Portuguese built them to 15 m, and the Omani Arabs added 3 m when they captured it. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 2011.

Wellington's Old Government Buildings, on Lambton Quay in Pipitea, are a four-storey heritage complex of 143 rooms built of wood, and the Southern Hemisphere's largest timber-framed building. They were finished in 1876 on ground won from Wellington Harbour, to house New Zealand's young government and public service. William Clayton was the architect; Scoular and Archibald were the contractors. Concrete and timber were planned, but concrete then cost too much, so timber alone was used. As Italianate Neo-Renaissance design normally meant stone, the building copies stone: it was meant to look like an Italian palace in stone, signalling strength and stability as a symbol of nationhood. Its native kauri timber cannot be replaced, as the public kauri forests that remain are protected for good. Victoria University's Law Faculty took a 50-year lease, and the buildings reopened in January 1996.

Perth Arena, which trades as RAC Arena, sits in central Perth, Western Australia, and is used mainly for basketball. Ashton Raggatt McDougall designed it jointly with Cameron Chisholm Nicol, basing the design on the Eternity puzzle. It holds up to 13,910 for tennis, 14,846 for basketball and up to 15,000 for concerts. Its facilities include a retractable roof, 36 corporate suites, five function spaces and a 680-bay car park below ground, and touring trucks can drive right onto the floor. Perth City Link began with the arena; that 13.5-hectare renewal scheme sank the Eastern Railway to tie the central business district to Northbridge. Building it drew controversy as time ran over and costs rose from an estimated $150 million to $550 million. Elton John gave the opening concert on 10 November 2012.

The Palais Garnier, also called the Opéra Garnier, is a 1,979-seat opera house in Paris's 9th arrondissement. Napoleon III's Second Empire launched a competition for a new opera house on 30 December 1860, and the building rose for the Paris Opera between 1861 and 1875 at the emperor's wish. Its eclectic style mixes Baroque, Palladian classicism and the Renaissance. Masonry walls carry the structure, with iron floors, vaults and roofs hidden from view. Seventeen kinds of material make up the façade, worked into multicoloured marble friezes, columns and statues, many showing Greek gods. Inside, corridors, stairs, alcoves and landings weave together so crowds can circulate and meet at the interval. A white marble ceremonial staircase, its balustrade in red and green marble, splits into two flights rising to the Grand Foyer.

The United Nations Secretariat Building is the skyscraper at UN headquarters in Manhattan's Turtle Bay, home to the offices of the Secretariat, the UN's executive organ. Ten architects led by planning director Wallace K. Harrison designed it in the International Style, and after long debate Harrison picked a scheme drawn from proposals by Oscar Niemeyer and Le Corbusier. The tower is a rectangular slab, 22 by 87 metres, running north to south. Its broad east and west faces are glass curtain walls, the first on any skyscraper in New York City. The first glazing, heat-absorbing blue-green glass, was chosen mainly to cut heat on the west face, which took most of the sun. The narrow ends, faced in Vermont marble, rise without a single opening. Staff began moving in on 21 August 1950, and work was finished in June 1951.

Maisons Jaoul is a pair of houses by Le Corbusier in Neuilly-sur-Seine, a wealthy suburb of Paris. They were drawn in 1937 but not built until after the war, in 1954–56, for André Jaoul and his son Michel. They rank with the most significant of his post-war buildings, using raw, unpainted béton brut concrete alongside roughly finished brickwork. With their vaults, the houses mark a new direction in his architecture and can be seen as his first "New Brutalist" work. Brick walls carry the load and close in each house on every side. At the request of André Malraux, the French state has protected the Maisons Jaoul as historical monuments since 1966.

The Port House, also called the Port Authority Building (Havenhuis in Dutch), is a government building in Antwerp, Belgium, built from 2009 to 2016. Zaha Hadid designed it, and it opened in 2016, the year she died; it is her only government building. Its lower part, a disused fire station that is a protected copy of an old Hanseatic house, could not be pulled down, so it became part of the project; the extension sits right on top. Shaped like a ship's hull with a jutting bow, the extension is cut like a diamond toward the Kattendijk dock, a nod to Antwerp's diamond trade. Its skin of transparent and opaque triangular facets lets the architects control how much sun gets in. According to project manager Joris Pauwels, concrete pillars and 900 tonnes of steel carry the glass offices.

Torre de Collserola stands on Barcelona's Tibidabo hill, part of the Serra de Collserola. Norman Foster designed it together with two Spanish civil engineers, Julio Martínez Calzón and Manuel Julià Vilardell, and Cubiertas y MZOV S.A. built it in 1991 for the 1992 Summer Olympics. It is a hybrid: a pod gives usable floors, as on many towers, while guy wires hold it sideways, as on a mast. The hollow reinforced-concrete shaft, slip-formed, measures just 4.5 m across and narrows to 3 m to carry a telescoping radio mast. Thirteen floors, ringed by open stainless-steel grilles, hang from the shaft on three main steel trusses; the pod tops out at 152 m and the antenna at 288.4 m. The upper guys use three sets of seven parallel aramid-fibre cables with resin sockets. Visitors may go up to the tenth floor.

The Miho Museum is an art museum in the Shigaraki area of Kōka, Shiga Prefecture, southeast of Kyoto. It was commissioned from I. M. Pei by Mihoko Koyama and her daughter Hiroko, and Pei came to call the design Shangri-La. The building sits in hilly, wooded country, and about three-quarters of its 17,400 square metres lies below ground, cut into a rocky mountaintop. A large roof of glass and steel covers it, while the walls inside and out and the floors are a warm beige limestone from France, the same stone Pei had used for the Louvre's reception hall. As new works joined the collection during construction, he kept revising the galleries. The Shumei Cultural Foundation has run the museum since it opened in 1997.

Berlin's Fernsehturm, or Television Tower, was built in the city centre from 1965 to 1969 by the East German government, both to broadcast and to stand as a symbol of communist power. Walter Ulbricht, head of the ruling Socialist Unity Party, allowed a tower modelled on Stuttgart's television tower and on Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. Many architects took part, among them Hermann Henselmann, Fritz Dieter and Günter Franke. The concrete shaft rose 248.78 metres; the working group VEB Ipro devised a way to piece the ball together from 120 segments on the ground. The sphere holds a viewing platform and a revolving restaurant. At 368 metres with its antenna, it is Germany's tallest structure. Sun on the tiled stainless-steel dome usually reflects as a Greek cross, which Berliners dubbed the "Pope's Revenge". It became an official monument in 1979.

NEMO Science Museum, whose name is Latin for 'nobody', is the largest science centre in the Netherlands and stands in Amsterdam. The museum's history goes back to 1923, but since 1997 it has occupied a building that Renzo Piano designed. Its exhibitions spread over five floors and are made to be handled and tried out rather than only looked at. The fifth floor, called the upper deck, holds a cafeteria and a play area for children and gives a wide view over the surrounding city.

Frankfurt's Museum für Moderne Kunst, or MMK, was founded in 1981. Hans Hollein won its design competition in 1983, three years after his entry for the city's Museum für angewandte Kunst came a close second to Richard Meier's winning scheme. Groundbreaking was put off until 1987, and the museum, built for about $38 million, opened to the public on 6 June 1991. Hollein shaped the building to its three-sided plot, so the big rooms at the narrow end are wedge-shaped, giving 3,500 m² of galleries. That triangular form earned it the popular nickname Tortenstück, or 'piece of cake'. Its three storeys match the height of the buildings around it. Exhibitions fill three main levels, and offices sit on a mezzanine over the entrance and the café.

Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret began designing this Geneva block of flats in 1928, and Immeuble Clarté was built in 1931–32. Across eight storeys it holds 45 free-plan apartments, each differing in layout and size. For Le Corbusier it was an important early project, a chance to test modernist ideas on a residential building, and that line of thinking later fed into the Unité d'Habitation. After it was again threatened with demolition in the early 1980s, it was listed as a historic monument in 1986. In July 2016 it joined a group of his other works on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

The Pinakothek der Moderne is a museum of modern art in the Kunstareal, in central Munich. Stephan Braunfels won the competition for it in 1992, his first major competition win, and after seven years of building it was inaugurated in September 2002, one of the biggest new museums in the country. Its straight-edged façade of white and grey concrete is broken by big windows and tall columns that hold up a broad canopy roof. A domed rotunda at the centre links the building's four corners, each given to one collection: art, architecture, design and works on paper. On the first floor, where the art hangs, daylight from above is topped up by computer-controlled lamps to keep the light even and almost free of shadow against grey floors and white walls.

The Weisman Art Museum belongs to the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. In 1993 it moved into its present home by Frank Gehry, finished that November, and was renamed after Frederick R. Weisman, an art collector and philanthropist. MSR Design served as the architect of record. Set on a bluff that looks over the Mississippi where the Washington Avenue Bridge ends on the east side, it is a major campus landmark. The building shows two faces. Toward the south and east, a brick front fits in with the historic buildings of Northrop Mall. Toward the north and west, curving and angled sheets of brushed steel form an abstract fish and waterfall. The design is seen as highly significant because it came before computer-aided design was widely used. A major addition, again by Gehry, followed in 2011.

Near Palmachim and Yavne in Israel, the Soreq Nuclear Research Center carries out research and development. The American modernist Philip Johnson designed its building, and the project was his first commission from a government. The institute's facilities include a 5 MW AMF reactor of the pool type using light water, supplied by the United States in the late 1950s through the Atoms for Peace program, a 10 MeV proton cyclotron, and large laboratory and testing areas. Johnson worked very closely with Zetlin, a leading practitioner in his field, on designing and building the reactor. Johnson never visited the site, yet he called it "my temple in the desert."

Kunsten Museum of Modern Art Aalborg, a modern Scandinavian design, was built from 1968 to 1972 to plans by the Finns Elissa and Alvar Aalto and the Dane Jean-Jacques Baruël. The design was chosen from 144 entries sent to a Nordic architecture competition by 15 January 1958. Covering 6,000 m², the museum rises like a ziggurat against the hills. The plan is square, ground-floor galleries ringing a central exhibition area. Skylights, reflectors and pale materials spread the Nordic light through the rooms; the long, two-sided skylights admit southern sun only within an angle of 56 degrees but open fully, at 90 degrees, to the north. The outer walls combine marble, glass, wood and copper sheet; inside, most floors are Carrara marble. Around it are an amphitheatre, a terrace and a sculpture park.

In downtown New Haven, Connecticut, the Knights of Columbus Building serves as headquarters for the Knights of Columbus, a Roman Catholic fraternal service organisation. Also called the Knights' Tower, it was designed by Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates and completed in 1969. The 23-storey reinforced-concrete building stands 320 feet (98 metres) tall, the third-tallest in the city. Round towers at its four corners give it a plain geometric shape and stand for the Order's four core principles: Charity, Unity, Fraternity and Patriotism. Those corner towers have also earned it the local nickname "Tootsie Roll Building". It went up at 1 Columbus Plaza, beside the New Haven Coliseum, which the same firm designed and which was demolished in 2007.

London's Natural History Museum displays a huge range of natural history specimens. Its design competition was won by Captain Francis Fowke, a civil engineer, who died soon after, in December 1865. Alfred Waterhouse, hired in February 1866, took over the scheme, reworked the agreed plans substantially and gave the façades his own idiosyncratic Romanesque style, inspired by frequent trips to the Continent. Building ran from 1873 to 1880. Inside and out, terracotta tiles from Gibbs and Canning of Tamworth were used widely to resist the sooty air of Victorian London. The tiles and bricks carry many reliefs of plants and animals, living species in the west wing and extinct ones in the east. The vaulted central hall, sometimes called a cathedral of nature, held a large Diplodocus cast until 2017, when a blue whale skeleton took its place.

Once called One Chase Manhattan Plaza and now 28 Liberty Street, this 60-storey International Style skyscraper stands in Manhattan's Financial District, bounded by Nassau, Liberty, William and Pine Streets. Gordon Bunshaft of SOM (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill) designed it, and it opened in 1961, rising 813 feet (248 m). The tower covers just about 28 percent of a 2.5-acre site. A plaza surrounds it, with a sunken Japanese rock garden by Isamu Noguchi on the south side. On the long sides the columns project from the building, while at the short ends the floors cantilever out from them. At street level the columns form a colonnade around a lobby set back beneath the upper floors. The glass sits in aluminium panels, chosen for durability and performance, between vertical aluminium mullions. The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated it in 2008.

The Mole Antonelliana, a major landmark in Turin, takes its name from its architect, Alessandro Antonelli. Work began in 1863, shortly after Italian unification, and ended in 1889, after Antonelli's death. It was first conceived as a synagogue, but the people of Turin, having watched it climb, called on the city to take over the project, and the city did so. With no steel girder frame, it is the world's tallest building of unreinforced brick. Under the atrium, the ground-floor ceiling uses Catalan vaults, rare in Italy but common in Spain, where they began. On 23 May 1953 a cloudburst and a tornado tore away the top 47 metres of the spire; it was rebuilt in metal faced with stone in 1961. Today the building holds the National Museum of Cinema and is thought to be the tallest museum anywhere.

This Smithsonian museum is given over to the cultures of the Americas' Indigenous peoples. Its architect and project designer was the Canadian Douglas Cardinal (Blackfoot), with GBQC Architects of Philadelphia and Johnpaul Jones (Cherokee/Choctaw) as design architects. Disputes during construction led to Cardinal's removal, yet the building keeps his original intent. Opened on 21 September 2004 after fifteen years in the making, it was the country's first national museum solely for Native Americans. Golden Kasota limestone clads the curving five-storey building, meant to recall rock worn by wind and water over millennia, and simulated wetlands surround it. Its east-facing entrance, prism window and 120-foot-high space for Native performance came from wide consultation with Native peoples. Inside, curved walls leave almost no sharp corners.

Also called the Pinacoteca Agnelli, this art gallery in Turin opened in 2002 at the top of the Lingotto complex, headquarters of Fiat, the Italian car maker Giovanni Agnelli founded in 1899. Part of the complex is Lo scrigno, a steel structure of 450 square metres designed by Renzo Piano and lifted 34 metres above the test track that runs across the factory roof. The permanent collection is a selection of paintings and sculpture from the private holdings of Gianni and Marella Agnelli. Among them are Renoir's Blonde Bather and Manet's La Négresse, alongside works by Matisse, Canaletto, Tiepolo, Canova, Picasso and Modigliani.

Built in 1967 in Ginza, Tokyo, the Shizuoka Press and Broadcasting Center is considered the first realisation of Kenzo Tange's Metabolist movement, which called for a new urban type able to renew itself in an organic, "metabolic" way. It occupies a triangular plot of only 189 square metres and is built around a single column 7.7 metres across, which serves as the core; thirteen offices are attached to it asymmetrically. Tange shaped these offices as cantilevered boxes of steel and glass. The concrete was cast in aluminium formwork that was left in place as cladding. Intended as a prototype for a prefabricated urban megastructure that would keep regenerating, the building left gaps between its office clusters for more offices as demand grew. That never happened, and it has stayed as built.

Home to the McLaren Group and the companies under it, the McLaren Technology Centre sits on a 50-hectare site in Woking, Surrey. Norman Foster and his firm, Foster + Partners, designed the main building, a large glass-walled block shaped roughly like a half-circle. Directly opposite, a formal artificial lake completes the circle, and four further 'ecology' lakes lie nearby. Water is pumped through heat exchangers to cool the building and to carry off heat from the wind tunnels. Inside, the main work space is divided into 18-metre-wide sections called 'fingers', with six-metre corridors called 'streets' between them. The centre brought the group onto one site instead of the 18 it had used before, and staff began working there in May 2003. It was shortlisted for the 2005 Stirling Prize, which went to the Scottish Parliament building.

Kenzō Tange received the commission for a communications building in Kōfu in 1961. The Yamanashi Press and Broadcasting Centre, finished in 1966, became headquarters of the Yamanashi Broadcasting System, holding radio and television studios and newspaper printing presses. It gave Tange one of his few chances to carry out his Metabolist ideals of constant movement and growth, if only at small scale. The building rises from sixteen towers, all five metres across but of different heights, which carry stairs, lifts and services. Large horizontal floor trays span between them and hold the working spaces. Some floor plates were left out to allow later change; gardens have since filled those gaps. The printing plant sits at ground level for easy loading from the street, and the round towers stop at different heights to hint at room to grow upward.

Mode Gakuen Cocoon Tower is a 50-storey school building, 204 metres tall, in Nishi-Shinjuku, Tokyo. When Mode Gakuen asked architects to compete for its new Tokyo site, it ruled that the building must not be rectangular. The winning team, led by Kenzo Tange's son Paul Noritaka Tange, proposed a curved shell of white aluminium and dark blue glass, crossed by a net of white diagonals. Tange Associates said the cocoon form stands for nurturing the students within, and that they hoped the tower would revive the area and link Shinjuku Station with the business district like a gateway. Each floor has three rectangular classrooms around a core of lift, stair and support shaft. Every three floors, a three-storey student lounge sits between the classrooms, facing east, southwest and northwest. Emporis named it Skyscraper of the Year for 2008.

Palazzo Lombardia, meaning "Lombardy Building", is a group of offices in Milan that includes a skyscraper of 43 storeys and 161 metres. Lombardy's regional government has its main seat here, and the complex stands in the Centro Direzionale, Milan's business district, to the north-west of the city centre. Pei Cobb Freed & Partners won an international competition for the design in 2004; Henry N. Cobb was the partner in charge of design. The complex opened on 22 January 2010 and was officially completed on 21 March that year. For a short time afterwards it was the tallest skyscraper in both Milan and Italy, overtaking the Pirelli Tower in Milan and the Telecom Italia Tower in Naples. A 2012 International Architecture Award recognised it as the best new global design.

Officially named the Japan Radio Tower, Tokyo Tower was finished in 1958 in Shiba-koen, Minato, as a communications and observation tower. Tachū Naitō, who designed tall buildings in Japan, was picked for the job and looked to the West, basing his lattice design on the Eiffel Tower. With the engineering firm Nikken Sekkei, he claimed it could survive earthquakes twice as strong as the Great Kantō earthquake of 1923, or typhoon winds of up to 220 km/h. A third of its steel was scrap taken from US tanks damaged during the Korean War. At 332.9 metres it is higher than the Eiffel Tower yet weighs about 4,000 tons, 3,300 less, being much thinner and simpler in build. It was Japan's tallest tower until Tokyo Skytree in 2012. Its white and international orange paint follows air safety rules.

Known today as Torre Emperador Castellana, or simply Torre Emperador, this Madrid office skyscraper went by the name Torre Espacio ("Space Tower" in Spanish) at first. It has 57 floors and stands 230 metres tall. Its design is the work of Henry N. Cobb, an American partner at Pei Cobb Freed, and its builder was OHL. Topping out came on 19 March 2007. At that height it passed the Torrespaña telecommunications tower to become, for a time, the tallest structure in Spain. The Discovery Channel featured the project in its series Build It Bigger because of the skyscraper's unusual form. In 2009 the British Embassy in Madrid moved into the tower.

Also called 9 West 57th Street, the Solow Building rises 50 storeys and 689 feet (210 m) in Midtown Manhattan. Gordon Bunshaft of SOM (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill) designed it, and it was finished in 1974 between 57th and 58th Streets, west of Fifth Avenue, with views over Central Park and the Plaza Hotel. To avoid rectangular setbacks, Bunshaft curved the north and south faces inward from the ground to the 18th floor, above which it rises straight up.
