It was the first major New York building developed with a sloped façade. The curved walls are grey-tinted glass; travertine faces the east and west ends. Narrow window openings several storeys tall show the steel bracing crossing diagonally in front. When it was finished, many critics disliked it, feeling it disrupted the skyline.

Philip Johnson designed the Kunsthalle Bielefeld in 1968 in the International Style, as a museum of modern and contemporary art. It is the only museum he built in Europe. It was paid for by Rudolf August Oetker, a businessman and art patron who had been a Waffen-SS officer. The building is a cube on a square base, with three storeys above ground and two below, giving 1,200 square metres of exhibition space. Its façade is red sandstone. A sculpture garden around it holds sculpture by Rodin, Henry Moore, Richard Serra, Ólafur Elíasson and others. Frank O. Gehry in 1994 and Sou Fujimoto in 2013 each proposed an extension, but neither was built. In 2022 the city council backed a full renovation budgeted at 40.5 million euros; by 2024 Caruso St John had been chosen over 44 rival entries.

Usually called the Javits Center, this large convention hall sits on Eleventh Avenue between 34th and 38th Streets in Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan. James Ingo Freed, of the firm Pei Cobb Freed & Partners, designed it, and its space frame went up from 1979 to 1986. The name honours Jacob Javits, who represented New York in the US Senate. On opening, it took over from the Coliseum at Columbus Circle as New York's main convention venue; the Time Warner Center later replaced the demolished Coliseum. The latest of several expansions, completed in 2021, added 1.2 million square feet, and the new expansion's roof became a 6.75-acre sedum green roof, second in size among extensive green roofs in the country. A new high-performance curtain wall swapped the old 5-by-5-foot façade module for 5-by-10-foot panels, giving a simpler, lighter face.

Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum holds important European, Asian and American art. The collector, philanthropist and arts patron Isabella Stewart Gardner had it built in 1898–1901, modelled on a Venetian palace of the 1400s, and it first opened to visitors in 1903. She was deeply involved in every part of the design, so much that her architect, Willard T. Sears, joked he was merely the structural engineer who made her design possible. Though raised from new materials, the building takes in many pieces removed from Gothic and Renaissance buildings in Europe. Three floors of galleries wrap a garden courtyard set with Roman mosaic and in flower all year, under a glass roof on its original steel frame. An auxiliary wing by Renzo Piano, beside the old building by the Back Bay Fens, was finished in 2012.

One of Japan's major art museums, the Kyoto National Museum stands in the city's Higashiyama ward and focuses on Japanese and Asian art from before the modern era. First called the Imperial Museum of Kyoto, it was proposed in 1889 alongside imperial museums for Tokyo and Nara. Building work ended in October 1895, and the museum opened in 1897. The most prominent building is the Special (or Main) Exhibition Hall, which Katayama Tōkuma designed in 1895. Katayama, who also designed the original buildings of the Nara museum, did much to bring Western, especially French, architecture into Japan. The hall, the Main Gate and the Ticket Area are all Important Cultural Properties. Morita Keiichi designed the Collections Hall in 1966, and work on Yoshio Taniguchi's Heisei Chishinkan wing for the permanent collection was completed in September 2014.

Kobe Port Tower is a landmark of the Japanese port city of Kobe. The Nikken Sekkei Company designed it, and it was completed in 1963. The tower rises 108 metres over eight levels, and its outline is meant to recall a tsuzumi, a Japanese hand drum. It was the first tower to be built with a pipe lattice. Thirty-two red steel staves ring the structure, a symbol of welcoming ships as they return to shore. The first of the sightseeing levels gives views from 75 metres above the ground. The tower closed to visitors again on 27 September 2021 for renovation and earthquake strengthening, and it reopened on 26 April 2024.

Formerly Kingdom Tower, Kingdom Centre is a skyscraper of 99 storeys and 302.3 metres in Riyadh's al-Olaya district. Finished in 2002, it passed the 267-metre Faisaliah Tower to become the tallest tower in Saudi Arabia. Its developer was Prince Al-Waleed bin Talal; its designers, Ellerbe Becket with Omrania, won an international competition. The top third opens into an upside-down parabolic arch crowned by a public skybridge; this opening lets the tower go beyond the local limit of 30 occupied floors. An almond-shaped plan with curving sides helps keep it cool: the narrow ends face east and west, where heat gain is highest. Reinforced concrete carries the first 180 metres and a tubular steel frame the rest. The design took cues from the Gateway Arch, the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Eiffel Tower. It won the 2002 Emporis Skyscraper Award.

Leipzig's Völkerschlachtdenkmal marks the 1813 Battle of the Nations. Funded mainly by donations and the city, it was completed in 1913, a century on. Unconvinced by the winning competition design, the Patriotic Association considered a third round but, to save time, gave Bruno Schmitz the job, then the most respected German architect. He raised the monument on an artificial hill and chose a pyramid form for clear views; the base is 124 metres square. Unlike many monuments of its era, it has no classicist details, drawing instead on ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt. Concrete, used extensively, is faced with granite. In the round crypt, a symbolic tomb for the fallen, sixteen warrior statues guard eight death masks 6 metres high, beneath a 68-metre dome. Of a larger ceremonial complex Schmitz planned, just a reflecting pool and two processional avenues were built.

The National Museum of Finland, in Helsinki, uses objects and cultural history to trace the country's past from the Stone Age to today. The architectural firm Gesellius, Lindgren, Saarinen designed the building, which was constructed between 1905 and 1910 but opened to the public only in 1916. Its outward look echoes the castles and medieval churches of Finland. In style the architecture is national romantic, while the interior is mostly Art Nouveau. In the entrance hall, the ceiling carries frescoes by Akseli Gallén-Kallela on themes from the Kalevala, the national epic, and visitors can see them without paying for entry. The museum closed for a renovation and expansion project, and its reopening was estimated for 2027.

Wangjing SOHO is a group of three curving, asymmetric skyscrapers in Wangjing, Beijing, between the city centre and Beijing Capital International Airport, holding offices and shops. Zaha Hadid designed it. The scheme first had two towers, but concerns about height led to a redesign with three lower ones. The complex, among over a dozen properties SOHO China has developed, had its official opening on 20 September 2014. ArchDaily described three curved towers whose "shimmering" metal skin ties them together as each one seems to "dance" around the others. Pan Shiyi, chairman of SOHO China, said the design was meant to call to mind koi, a traditional Chinese symbol of wealth, luck, health and happiness. A software-driven method for generating panels helped rationalise the manufactured sheet-metal panels and meet stricter demands on cost and manufacturing complexity.

John McArthur Jr. is best remembered for Philadelphia City Hall, though several of Philadelphia's most ambitious buildings from the Civil War era are his too. Construction of the Second Empire-style City Hall began in 1871, and its tower was built from 1874 to 1901. When finished, its 548-foot (167-metre) tower gave the world its tallest occupied building. Until the late 20th century, Philadelphia architects kept to an unwritten agreement that no building should rise above the top of the William Penn statue crowning McArthur's tower. City Hall stayed the tallest building in the city until One Liberty Place was completed in 1987.

Also known as 885 Third Avenue, the Lipstick Building is a 34-floor, 453-foot office tower on Third Avenue between 53rd and 54th Streets, Midtown Manhattan. John Burgee and Philip Johnson designed it for Hines Interests, and it was the first New York project of the developer Gerald D. Hines, completed in 1986. Its shape and colour recall a lipstick tube. The almost elliptical mass steps back twice, above the 19th and 27th floors, under a two-storey granite penthouse; strictly it is polygonal, with more than a hundred sides. Double-height columns lift it at street level, and the façade pairs red Imperial granite with stainless steel. The rounded plan lets people on 53rd and 54th Streets cut across the corners and brings in more light and air. Structural engineer Irwin Cantor's tube system and central core brace it against north winds.

The Humboldt Forum is a museum of human history, art and culture inside the Berlin Palace, on Museum Island in central Berlin. Described as the German equivalent of the British Museum, it shows the Berlin State Museums' collections from outside Europe. The largely baroque palace on the site was badly bombed in World War II and demolished in 1950 under Walter Ulbricht. Three of its baroque facades, designed by Andreas Schlüter and dating from 1713, were rebuilt along with Friedrich August Stüler's dome. The Italian architect Franco Stella added the east wing on the Spree and the passage through the palace forum as plain new work; his modernist Spree facade has drawn wide criticism. The plain, functional interiors were planned to allow later restoration. The foundation stone was laid in June 2013, and the shell was done by June 2015.

In 1994 the city of Vienna asked Zaha Hadid to design and build a three-part scheme renewing an area next to the Danube Canal. Set along the Spittelauer Lände, the buildings engage with and pass over a railway viaduct by the Viennese Modernist Otto Wagner, which is a protected structure. Hadid's practice, ZHA, first drew the mixed-use scheme as five buildings, and it has been described as a "sculpture-like overbuilding" of the old Stadtbahn line. Hadid and the British artist Brian Clarke also worked up a joint proposal, never carried out, in which his glass mosaic and leaded stained glass would have formed part of the cladding and windows; Clarke even developed a new mouth-blown glass for it, which he named 'Zaha-Glas'. Cut back to three buildings and delayed during construction, the project was finished in 2006 without the artwork.

Barcelona's Teatre Nacional de Catalunya, the National Theatre of Catalonia, is a publicly run venue on Plaça de les Arts, opposite L'Auditori and near Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes. Ricardo Bofill i Leví, a Catalan architect of the postmodern school, shaped it as an ancient Greek temple, echoing several National Theatres of the late 19th century. Building work ran from 8 November 1991 to 1996, and the theatre opened on 12 November 1996 with Tony Kushner's Angels in America, directed by Josep Maria Flotats. The design divided opinion, and some critics called it a parody or a mausoleum. Inside are three halls: the Sala Gran, with Greek-style tiered seating for 866; the Sala Petita, whose movable seating takes from 266 up to 500; and the Sala Tallers, a workshop hall that also has movable seating.

The House with Chimaeras, also called Horodetsky House, is an Art Nouveau building in the historic Lypky area of Kyiv. Władysław Horodecki, a Polish architect, built it in 1901–1902 as an upmarket block of flats of his own, one flat per floor, joined by stairs and a lift; he lived on the fourth floor, about 380 m². Built in concrete on a steep slope, it seems to have three floors from the front, while the back shows all six. Its popular name comes from sculpted decorations of exotic animals and hunting scenes, since Horodecki loved to hunt. Emilio Sala made the sculpture inside and out, from frogs, dolphins and mermaids on the roof to chandeliers of huge catfish caught in lotus stems. Since May 2005 it has served the president for official and diplomatic ceremonies.

The Red Town Hall is Berlin's town hall, standing on Rathausstraße near Alexanderplatz in the Mitte district, and it is the seat of the Governing Mayor and of the Senate, the government of the city-state. Hermann Friedrich Waesemann built it between 1861 and 1869 in the manner of the High Renaissance of northern Italy. Its model was the Old Town Hall of Toruń in Poland, and the tower recalls the cathedral tower at Laon in France. The building took the place of several separate medieval buildings and now fills a whole city block. Allied bombing in World War II left it badly damaged, and it was rebuilt to its original plans from 1951 to 1956. Following German reunification, the administration of the reunited city formally moved in on 1 October 1991.

Lille Cathedral is a Gothic Revival church regarded as a national monument. Work on it lasted almost a century and a half. In 1854 a foundation stone was laid and an international competition launched for a design drawing on the Gothic of the early 13th century. Objections were raised to giving a church honouring the Virgin to foreign architects of the Anglican faith, so the project passed instead to Charles Leroy, an architect from Lille. Several generations of architects then built it in stages between 1856 and 1975. It was finally completed in 1999, when a modern facade by the architect Pierre-Louis Carlier and the engineer Peter Rice was put in place, while part of the original programme was given up.

Set in Budapest's City Park, the Széchenyi Medicinal Bath is among Europe's largest spa complexes. Two hot springs supply its water, at 74 °C and 77 °C. Győző Czigler drew up the Neo-Baroque design, but he died in 1905, and when building started in 1909 it was led by Kálmán Gerster and Ede Dvorák, who had worked with him. During planning, which began in the 1880s, the project went by the name Artesian spa; when it opened in June 1913 it was named after István Széchenyi. An extension finished in 1927 brought public baths for men and for women and an outdoor area, and the complex now counts 15 pools indoors and 3 outside. A complete renovation was carried out between 1999 and 2009.

The Office for Metropolitan Architecture designed the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion in Quebec City, with Jason Long and Shohei Shigematsu as lead partners. Built from 2013 and opened in June 2016, the 14,900 m² building holds the MNBAQ's contemporary art, while the Gérard-Morisset Pavilion keeps its historical collection and the Charles Baillairgé Pavilion its modern art. Glass and steel make up most of the structure, chosen to create openness between the museum and the public. A glazed entrance from Grande Allée leads to the rest of the complex, set deeper in Battlefield Park. Inside are 2,741 m² of galleries, a café in the main lobby, a courtyard beside it, a white spiral stair and a gold-coloured lift. During construction the museum's tunnels were renovated and turned into viewing spaces. By the end of 2020 the pavilion had collected many architecture awards.

Museum Folkwang in Essen holds an important collection of art from the 19th and 20th centuries. It was formed in 1922 by joining the Essener Kunstmuseum, founded in 1906, with the private Folkwang Museum that the collector Karl Ernst Osthaus had set up in Hagen in 1902. In March 2007 David Chipperfield won an international competition run by the City of Essen, beating entries from Zaha Hadid, David Adjaye and Volker Staab. His extension was attached to the older building and added 16,000 m² to the museum. It opened in January 2010, as Essen and the Ruhr became European Capital of Culture. The Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Foundation, chaired by Berthold Beitz, paid for the €55m reconstruction. The museum also takes in the German Poster Museum, with about 340,000 posters on politics, economy and culture.

Richard Meier's building for Atlanta's High Museum of Art opened in 1983, and the museum is now the largest devoted to visual art in the American Southeast. Meier's building covers 135,000 square feet (12,500 m²), of which roughly 52,000 square feet is gallery space. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1984, after the building was done, and the High is listed along with his houses and The Atheneum in New Harmony, Indiana, as the work that first brought him notice. In 2005 Renzo Piano added three new buildings, which took the museum to 312,000 square feet, more than twice its earlier size, for $124 million. Those three additions are clad in aluminium panels, in keeping with the white enamel facade Meier had chosen.

The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, a museum and hall of fame, stands in downtown Cleveland beside Lake Erie. I. M. Pei designed the building, which broke ground on 7 June 1993, when Billy Joel, Chuck Berry and Pete Townshend attended, and was dedicated on 1 September 1995. Pei's idea was a tower with a pyramid of glass projecting from it. He first wanted the tower to stand 200 feet (61 m) tall but had to lower it to 162 feet because Burke Lakefront Airport is close by. The building has seven levels, and the inductees are honoured in a special exhibit in a wing that reaches out over the lake. In 2020 the museum announced plans to renovate and enlarge its footprint by a third, with PAU, the firm founded by Vishaan Chakrabarti, to lead the work.

In 1997 Yoshio Taniguchi won the competition for the redesign of New York's Museum of Modern Art, beating nine other architects, Rem Koolhaas, Bernard Tschumi, and Herzog and de Meuron among them. It was his first work outside Japan and became the project he is best known for. His first plan set two structures to the west and east of the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, which was to be enlarged. The result, with 630,000 square feet, almost doubled the room for exhibitions and programmes. Taniguchi wanted to guide people by sight rather than by signs, so he cut openings in walls to reveal their depth and what lay beyond. Time critic Richard Lacayo called it "old-fashioned Modernism", a quietly updated glass-and-steel box. MoMA reopened on 20 November 2004 to a mixed response.

The Pergamon Museum is a listed building on Museum Island in central Berlin. The idea came from Wilhelm von Bode, head of the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, who wanted a new museum close by for ancient architecture, German post-antique art, and Islamic and Middle Eastern art. Alfred Messel started designing the big three-winged building in 1906; when he died in 1909 his friend Ludwig Hoffmann took over. Ordered by Emperor Wilhelm II and built in a Stripped Classicism style, it rose from 1910 through the First World War and the inflation of the 1920s, opening in 1930. Hoffmann toned down the exterior, raising the eaves, flattening the pediment and adding a frieze of metopes and triglyphs. Its chief exhibits are the Pergamon Altar, with a frieze 113 metres long, and the Roman Gate of Miletus.

Seattle's Museum of Pop Culture sits on the Seattle Center campus next to the Space Needle, and the Seattle Center Monorail runs through it. Paul Allen, a co-founder of Microsoft, set it up in 2000 under the name Experience Music Project. Frank Gehry designed the structure, whose sheet-metal construction links it to other works by his firm, such as the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. Gehry recalled that his team gathered pictures of Stratocasters and brought in guitar bodies, drawing on those shapes as ideas developed. The outside mixes many textures and colours, from gold and silver to a "shimmering purple haze". Inside, much of the material is left exposed, across 140,000 square feet on a 35,000-square-foot footprint. The central Sky Church is named in tribute to Jimi Hendrix. Residents met it with praise for Gehry and scorn for the building.

David Chipperfield's East Building is a large new wing for the Saint Louis Art Museum, joined to the gallery that the beaux-arts architect Cass Gilbert built in 1904. The museum board picked Chipperfield in 2005, with Michel Desvigne as landscape architect and the St. Louis firm HOK as architect of record. The 9,000 m² building sits easily beside the older one, its ground floor level with the Gilbert Building's main floor. The dark grey concrete walls were cast and polished on site, flecked with pieces of the same sandstone used on Gilbert's building so the two relate. Concrete caissons in the roof are shaped to temper the daylight entering the galleries. The enlarged museum opened in summer 2013. In the narrow gap between old and new, Andy Goldsworthy made Stone Sea, twenty-five tight-packed limestone arches rising from a sunken courtyard.

Hearst Castle, formally La Cuesta Encantada ('The Enchanted Hill'), is a historic estate at San Simeon on California's Central Coast. The publisher William Randolph Hearst conceived it with his architect Julia Morgan, who worked closely with him for more than twenty years. Building went on almost without pause from 1920 to 1939 and resumed after World War II until Hearst left for good in 1947. Concrete was the main structural material. Hearst bought architectural pieces from Western Europe, above all Spain, including ceilings, fireplaces and whole monasteries, and much was built into the castle. He asked Morgan to base the Casa Grande towers on a church he admired in Ronda. It has 42 bedrooms, 61 bathrooms, indoor and outdoor pools, a cinema and an airfield. Constant design changes and money troubles in the 1930s left it unfinished.

The Mikhailovsky Palace, a grand ducal palace on Arts Square in Saint Petersburg, is built in the neoclassical Empire style. Carlo Rossi drew up its designs in 1817 as part of a wider ensemble that was to take in a square and the new Inzhenernaya and Mikhailovskaya streets. Building took six years and cost 7,875,000 rubles, over half of it on decoration. A central block is flanked by two wings for service rooms. On the facade, a rusticated base supports the portico of the piano nobile: a loggia of eight three-quarter Corinthian columns carrying a triangular pediment, with armour decorations by Stepan Pimenov and Vasily Demut-Malinovsky. Later one wing was rebuilt and became an ethnography museum, and the Benois wing followed in the 1910s. Today it is the Russian Museum's main building, showing early, folk, 18th- and 19th-century art.

Russia's State Historical Museum, devoted to the country's history, stands in Moscow with Red Square on one side and Manege Square on the other. Its site was once taken by the Principal Medicine Store, put up in the Moscow Baroque style on the orders of Peter the Great. After a long competition, the commission went to Vladimir Osipovich Sherwood (also spelled Shervud). His neo-Russian design was built between 1875 and 1881, and the first 11 exhibition halls opened officially in 1883, during a visit by the tsar and his wife. Artists including Viktor Vasnetsov, Ivan Aivazovsky and Henryk Siemiradzki decorated the interiors richly in the Russian Revival style; under Soviet rule these murals were judged gaudy and covered in plaster. Only in spring 2007 did all 40 halls open to visitors for the first time.

Vienna's City Hall, the Rathaus, stands on the Rathausplatz in the Innere Stadt, and houses the mayor and the city and state government. Once the city walls had been cleared between 1858 and 1865 to make way for the Ringstraße, a design competition for a new town hall took place in 1868. Friedrich von Schmidt designed the Gothic Revival building, built from 1872 to 1883. Freestanding, with Renaissance touches, it measures 152 by 127 metres and has 1,575 rooms, 2,035 windows and seven courtyards. The main front has a projecting central bay with a large tower flanked by four smaller ones, over open arcades at ground level. The 98-metre tower is topped by the Rathausmann, a figure standing for Vienna. The Festsaal, the country's biggest historic hall, has a Renaissance barrel vault chosen to avoid a church-like look.

Marin County's government complex in San Rafael, California, was designed by Frank Lloyd Wright with Taliesin Associated Architects (TAA). Its buildings went up from 1960 to 1976. Wright set the main building on the hills: the Administration Building spans three of them, so the road to the car park, now Peter Behr Drive, passes underneath. When Wright died the plans were 90% complete, and TAA, his practice's successor, finished the job, with William Wesley Peters, Wright's son-in-law, among those who took over the design. Pink stucco walls with tiers of arches sit under a blue roof. The Hall of Justice, the longer wing, meets the shorter Administration wing at 120° in a rotunda with a spire, home to a library and cafeteria. The main building, the lagoon and the post office are listed as a National Historic Landmark.

St Peter's Church in Klippan, by Sigurd Lewerentz, stands in a suburban setting on the edge of this small town in Scania, in southern Sweden. Built from 1963 and completed in 1966, it is one of two churches he designed in the last ten years of his life; the other is St Mark's in Björkhagen, Stockholm, from 1956, and together they revived his career in architecture. The church is correctly oriented, with its altar opposite the west doors. Its plan is square, which suggests a closer, more gathered form of worship in the tradition of circonstantes, people standing in a circle, a practice that goes back to early Christianity.

The East Building of the National Gallery of Art in Washington went up in the 1970s on much of the land still left from the original act of Congress, funded by Paul Mellon and Ailsa Mellon Bruce, the children of Andrew Mellon. Completed in 1978 to a design by I. M. Pei, it was opened by President Jimmy Carter on 1 June that year. Pei split the trapezoid-shaped site into two triangles, one for public galleries and the other for a library, a study centre and offices, and the triangle recurs through the building in every dimension. At its heart is a tall atrium, an open court within a sculptural space of 16,000 sq ft, aligned with the West Building's circulation spine and built of the same Tennessee marble. Outside, the building wears pink marble panels 3 inches thick.

Eero Saarinen designed Kresge Auditorium in Cambridge together with his nearby MIT Chapel; a lawn, the Kresge Oval, separates them. Ground was broken in 1953 and the building was dedicated in 1955. It is a thin shell of reinforced concrete, an eighth of a sphere rising 50 feet (15 m), cut back by sheer glass walls so that it lands on just three points. Such thin-shell concrete was new then, and in proportion the dome is thinner than an eggshell. With no interior supports for the dome, all 1,226 seats in the concert hall have a clear view. The dome sits on a round red brick platform, and a lower level holds a 177-seat theatre, rehearsal rooms and offices. Instead of a plaster ceiling, Saarinen and the acoustic firm Bolt, Beranek and Newman hung 'clouds' that absorb and steer sound.

Josef Hoffmann built the Sanatorium Purkersdorf, near Vienna, in 1904–05 for Victor Zuckerkandl, an industrialist, and it is an example of Viennese Secession architecture. It was the first great work he completed. The original furniture came from the Wiener Werkstätte, in which Hoffmann was involved. Silence, light and air, a rational plan and very little ornament were meant to treat new conditions such as hysteria and nervousness. In practice it was closer to a hotel than a hospital and became a meeting place for Viennese society and artists. It broke clearly with the Arts and Crafts style, and its clarity, simplicity and logic looked ahead to the Neue Sachlichkeit. In 1926 Leopold Bauer added a storey against Hoffmann's wishes, harming the original idea; a 1995 exterior renovation removed it and brought back the first appearance.

Eero Saarinen's MIT Chapel is a non-denominational chapel, dedicated in 1955 and completed in 1956. From outside it is a plain brick cylinder with no windows, standing in a very shallow concrete moat. It is 50 feet (15 m) across and 30 feet tall. Saarinen picked rough, imperfect bricks to give the walls texture, and inside, the windowless brick walls undulate. Harry Bertoia's metal sculpture, rising the full height of the room, falls like a cascade of light from the round skylight to a small, plain marble altar. Daylight also rises from shallow slits in the walls, carrying rippling reflections off the moat, and electric lighting adds to this dim glow. The sculptor Theodore Roszak designed the curving spire and bell tower, which were added in 1956.

The University of California, San Diego keeps its main library in the Geisel Library building. William Pereira designed it in the late 1960s to stand where a canyon begins, and it opened in 1970 as the Central Library. He first imagined a mushroom-shaped building framed in steel, but the expected cost of building and running it pushed him to reinforced concrete, which allowed a more sculptural form and opened rooms that trusses would have split. A spheroidal tower at its core puts as many stacks as possible within quick reach of the centre. The tower rises 8 storeys, to 110 ft, and its arches and floors are meant to look like hands raising a pile of books. A later underground addition at the front, funded in 1990 and designed by Gunnar Birkerts, was kept subordinate to the original form.

The Maison du Peuple ('House of the People') stands in Clichy-la-Garenne, a suburb of Paris, and was built from 1935 to 1939. Its makers were the architects Eugène Beaudouin and Marcel Lods, the engineer Vladimir Bodiansky, and Jean Prouvé. It began in 1935, when the mayor, Charles Auffray, held a competition to roof the open-air market on Rue de Lorraine. Beaudouin and Lods wanted to use the site as fully as possible: the market stayed at ground level, and a floor above held offices and a hall seating 1,000. Being fully modular, with movable partitions and a floor and roof that retract, the hall could become a cinema. Among Prouvé's technical ideas were curtain walls, used here for the first time: they bear no load and hang from the frame. The building has been a Monument Historique since 1983.

MVRDV designed the Netherlands Pavilion for Expo 2000 in Hanover, working on it from 1997 to 2000. At 36 m it was the tallest structure at the Expo, built on the theme 'Holland creates Space'. Six Dutch ecosystem landscapes were stacked one on top of another to show how a nation can get the most out of limited space. Visitors entered at ground level and climbed through the displays on large outdoor stairs wrapped around the building. The top level held a small lake ringed by windmills that made power for the pavilion. Standing at 3 Europa Boulevard, it was among the most popular buildings at the Expo and won international praise. Afterwards it stood empty and was partly looted, its windows broken and rubbish everywhere, until in 2020 MVRDV announced plans to turn it into offices and student housing.

Denys Lasdun's Keeling House, finished in 1957, rises 16 storeys on Claredale Street in Bethnal Green, London. Lasdun felt earlier modernist housing overlooked what made neighbourhoods work, and he wanted to recreate the good relations between neighbours he saw in Victorian terraced streets. Instead of a slab or tower, he grouped four blocks of maisonettes, each home much like an East End house inside, around a central service tower, with the wings facing one another to encourage contact. Between the lift and their front doors, residents passed shared drying and storage areas, where he hoped people would meet as easily as in the street. Yet the balconies face outward, keeping homes private. Listed Grade II* in 1993, it was only the second post-war council housing to be listed. Between 1999 and 2001 it became luxury flats.

Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret drew up the Immeuble Molitor in Paris between July and October 1931, and it was built from 1931 to 1934: fifteen apartments on eight storeys. It applies four of the five points of modern architecture: a free plan, columns rather than load-bearing walls, a free facade and a roof garden. The site was only 12 m wide but 24 m deep, and strict zoning rules fixed the parapet height, the street line and even where balconies and bay windows could go. The all-glass facades, identical front and back, drew on the Maison de Verre by Chareau and Bijvoet but added clear openings to its glass brick. Le Corbusier lived here until he died in 1965, in a 240 m² apartment over the top two floors. In 2016 the building joined a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

Villa Schwob, also called Villa Turque, is a house by Le Corbusier in the Swiss town of La Chaux-de-Fonds. The watchmaker Anatole Schwob commissioned it in 1912, and it was finished in 1917, before Le Corbusier moved to Paris. It was the first building in which he used regulating lines as a design principle, and it is the best known of his works in La Chaux-de-Fonds. Brick combined with concrete brings out the house's oriental character. Tall walls around the plot give privacy, and the house is fitted into its sloping site. It has three full main storeys above a basement. In 1995 it was formally listed as a historical monument.

The French Communist Party's headquarters stand at No. 2, Place du Colonel Fabien, in Paris (19th arrondissement). Oscar Niemeyer, who had already designed many buildings for Brasília, was lead architect, and his collaborators included Jean Prouvé, Paul Chemetov and Jacques Tricot. A communist himself, he drew it during Brazil's military dictatorship, when he lived in France as an exile. Designed in 1966 and started on site in 1968, it opened officially in 1971, though the dome outside was not fully finished until 1980. It is made of concrete and shaped in curves. According to Niemeyer, the dome that houses the party's National Council stands for a pregnant woman. In 2007 the building, an example of Brutalist architecture, was classed as a monument historique.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this Usonian house for Isaac Newton Hagan, who owned a local ice-cream firm, and his wife Bernardine. It sits on the south slope of the knoll called Kentuck Knob, above the Youghiogheny River gorge; the name goes back to Little Kentuck, a Fayette County hill so called by an 18th-century settler bound for Kentucky. Redwood and local stone sit under an overhanging copper roof. Equal living and bedroom wings bend apart at 120 degrees and meet at a hexagonal core like a stone chimney, all laid on a grid of equilateral triangles 2.3 feet a side. The house faces west and south for light all year, as Wright held that each room should get sun at some hour. Hexagonal cutouts in the cantilevered eaves ventilate the house and let patches of sun through.

The Humana Building, or Humana Tower, is a 26-storey skyscraper at 500 West Main Street in downtown Louisville, Kentucky, and has served as the headquarters of the Humana Corporation. Michael Graves designed it, and construction ran from October 1982 to May 1985. Each of its sides is handled a little differently, climbing to a sloping, pyramid-like form over the top few floors. The outside is faced in flat pink granite. On the north side, a loggia sits flush with the old Main Street shopfronts, respecting the older buildings downtown. Near the top, a large curved section serves as an open-air viewing deck. The American Institute of Architects gave the building its National Honor Award in 1987, and Time magazine placed it among the ten finest buildings of the 1980s.

The Maison Hermès in Tokyo's Ginza shopping district is the French luxury firm's flagship store and corporate headquarters in Japan. Renzo Piano designed it, with help from the Berkeley firm Bohlin Cywinski Jackson and in collaboration with Takenaka Corporation; it was built from 1998 to 2001. The 6,000 m² building holds workshops, offices, shop floors, exhibition areas and multimedia spaces. It stands exactly 44.55 metres tall, and its facade uses 13,000 glass pieces, each 45 by 45 centimetres, made in Florence, set in Swiss-made supports and assembled in Japan. Every piece can shift four millimetres so the facade can cope with earthquakes. A recess splits the long front in two, forming a courtyard that leads to Ginza Station on the Tokyo Metro, two floors down. Lit up at night, the building is meant to look like a "magic lantern".

The Haus des Rundfunks in Berlin's Westend district is the oldest self-contained broadcasting centre in the world. Hans Poelzig designed it in 1929 after winning a competition; built in 1929–30, it opened on 22 January 1931 to house the Reichs-Rundfunk-Gesellschaft. In plan it is triangular, with two curved sides and a straight, tile-clad front 150 m long. With almost no models to follow, Poelzig put the offices and editorial rooms around the edge, where they shield three large central studio complexes from street noise, an approach still valid today. Chairs in the large studio were made to absorb as much sound empty as occupied, and in the smaller room one hundred panels on the walls could be flipped between an absorbing side and a reflecting one. Germany's first regular television service started here on 22 March 1935.

Mäusebunker, or Mouse Bunker, is the everyday name for Berlin's Research Institutes for Experimental Medicine. It was built for live animal testing, and the animals used were also bred inside, to keep conditions sterile and control as tight as possible. The husband-and-wife team Gerd and Magdalena Hänska began designing it in the years 1965 to 1967, and from 1971 to 1981 Gerd Hänska, working with Kurt Schmersow, carried out the detailed planning and construction. The building was controversial from the start: the public disliked both its sinister look and its use for animal testing. Many international publications have shown it as a leading example of brutalism in Germany. After years of debate it gained protection as a heritage site in May 2023.

Maria Regina Martyrum in Berlin was built on behalf of German Catholics in memory of those martyred for freedom of belief and conscience between 1933 and 1945. It lies about a 20-minute walk from Plötzensee Prison, where Nazi resisters and opponents were executed, now the Gedenkstätte Plötzensee memorial. The diocese of Berlin commissioned Hans Schädel, Friedrich Ebert and Hermann Jünemann. Cardinal Julius Döpfner laid the cornerstone in 1960 and helped consecrate the church in 1963. A campanile marks the entrance to a cobbled ceremonial courtyard, its walls faced in black and grey basalt slabs bearing figural Stations of the Cross. The upper church is sober, with a flat ceiling and indirect light, and Georg Meistermann painted a monumental fresco on the altar wall. A gold-coated concrete wall divides the crypt; its front part is given over to the martyrs.

Alvar Aalto designed the Experimental House at Muuratsalo, in Central Finland, in 1952 as a summer cottage for his second wife, Elissa Aalto, and himself. It stands on the shore of Lake Päijänne, was built during 1952–1954, and remained the Aalto family's summer home until 1994. A provisional courtyard partly encloses the house and, looking out, frames the view through its opening, setting up a contrast between inside and outside, open and closed form. The facade mixes many kinds of reclaimed brick laid in different bonds. Aalto described the group of buildings as both a studio for an architect and a centre for experiments, a place to try out ideas not yet ready for real projects, where nature close at hand might inspire form and structure.

Rødovre Town Hall stands in the middle of Rødovre, a municipality about 9 km west of central Copenhagen. Arne Jacobsen designed it, and it was completed in 1956. It took its cue from the General Motors Technical Center north of Detroit. The complex has two wings joined by a glass corridor. The office wing, three storeys high, measures 91 by 14 metres and is assembled from pillars, floor slabs and precast crossbeams. Dark stone and grey glass in steel-trimmed metal frames make up the facades. Jacobsen also designed the interior and furniture of the tall, rectangular council chamber. The central staircase hangs from the roof by orange-red steel rods; its sides are 5 cm steel plate painted dark grey, and its steps, just a few millimetres thick, are stainless steel with rubber on top for grip.

Villa Göth in Uppsala was completed in 1950 to designs by Bengt Edman and Lennart Holm, as the home of Elis Göth, head of Pharmacia. It is thought to be where the word brutalism comes from: the Swedish architect Hans Asplund is believed to have coined it in 1950 in a joking remark about the house. Built of dark brick, which also forms several inside walls, it has a basement and two floors above. Its materials are shown openly, from the exposed I-beams above the windows at front and back to the ceilings, which carry the tongue-and-groove marks of the boards used as concrete formwork. On the first floor, the bathrooms are shaped in raw concrete, béton brut, after Alvar Aalto's Aalto Vase. The Uppsala county administrative board listed the house as historically significant on 3 March 1995.

Carlo Aymonino and Aldo Rossi designed the Monte Amiata housing complex in Milan's Gallaratese district in the late 1960s. Its nickname, the 'Red Dinosaur', points both to the reddish colour of the buildings and to their oddness. There are five red buildings: two eight-storey slabs, a long three-storey block, another three-storey slab and a linking structure, set around a central yellow open-air theatre and two smaller triangular plazas. Passages, decks, lifts, balconies, terraces and bridges tie the buildings together, giving many walking routes and a complex skyline. The architects imagined it as a small utopian city inside the larger one. They named Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille as a main source, though they meant to improve on it, and Rossi drew on Giorgio de Chirico's paintings for the smaller slab.

Richard Meier's building for the Museum Angewandte Kunst is part of Frankfurt's Museumsufer, or Museum Riverbank. To extend the museum, Meier used the Metzler family villa as the module for his whole scheme. That Neoclassicist house, put up in 1804 as a summer house for the apothecary Peter Salzwedel, has three storeys on a square plan with five window axes per side. Meier turned its plan and domestic character into a museum building of its own, finished in 1987, and joined villa, new wing and park into one ensemble. His forms recall Le Corbusier's houses and Classical Modern architecture. Since spring 2013, when partitions and 1990s additions were removed, the bright, interlocking rooms again look out over the park and the river, and the park links the museum with the Museum der Weltkulturen.

Arne Jacobsen's Munkegaard School in Gentofte, a short way north of Copenhagen, was first planned in 1949 and completed in 1957; it was among Denmark's earliest single-storey schools. The aim was a large school that kept the advantages of a small one. The classrooms were grouped in pairs, every pair with a courtyard or garden of its own, for a feeling of intimacy and wellbeing. Low yellow-brick blocks sit on a rectangular grid, joined by glass-walled cross corridors, and each of the 24 classrooms opens directly onto a courtyard. Besides full-height windows on the courtyard side, clerestories facing south in the split-pitched roofs bring light to the back of each room. Jacobsen designed nearly everything, from desks, chairs and lamps to curtains and gardens. The school was listed in 1996.

Hector Guimard built the Hôtel Guimard in 1909 at 122 avenue Mozart in Paris, after marrying the American painter Adeline Oppenheim. The triangular plot was a real difficulty: too narrow for the outer walls to bear weight, it led to a room layout that changes from floor to floor, and on the upper levels an inclined lift replaces the staircase to save space. The façade was meant to show what went on inside, with a part lit by large windows for his wife's painting and another for his office. Later divided into flats, it no longer has its original room layout or furniture; pieces from it are now in the Petit Palais, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs and Lyon's Musée des Beaux-Arts.

Washington's National Building Museum, covering architecture, design, engineering, construction and planning, fills the former Pension Bureau building. Montgomery C. Meigs, the US Army quartermaster general, designed this brick structure, completed in 1887. Rather than the Greco-Roman models then usual for government buildings in the city, he turned to Italian Renaissance palaces, above all Rome's Palazzo Farnese and Palazzo della Cancelleria, and the result is an important early large-scale case of Renaissance Revival. The interior, 316 by 116 feet (96 by 35 m), centres on a tall columned court and has hosted inauguration balls. Planned before mechanical ventilation, each office had outside windows and also opened onto the court, which took in cool air low down and let hot air out at the roof. It took more than 15 million bricks and became a National Historic Landmark in 1985.

Designed by Renzo Piano, the Tribunal de Paris stands in Batignolles and hears more cases than any other court in France. It brings a number of courts and tribunals, large and small, into a single building. Nicolas Sarkozy announced the move from the Palais de Justice on 29 April 2009, and the contract followed in 2012. The doors opened in 2018, with an official inauguration by Prime Minister Édouard Philippe in April 2019. The tower climbs 38 storeys to 160 metres and offers 120,000 square metres of net floor area, holding 90 courtrooms, 30,000 square metres of offices and 20,000 of public space. With the judicial police headquarters at 36, rue du Bastion and the Paris Bar's offices close by, it forms the Cité judiciaire de Paris.

Renzo Piano designed the Weltstadthaus, a Cologne department store commissioned by the chain Peek & Cloppenburg. Finished in 2005 after a long legal fight over the structural engineering of its core, it sits over the Nord-Süd-Fahrt, a main traffic route, and faces the Schildergasse, Europe's busiest shopping street. Between the late Gothic Antoniterkirche and plain post-war concrete, it has two parts: a rectangular stone block that echoes the angular 1970s buildings nearby, and a partly encircling wood-and-glass shell that flows toward the church. Locals call it the Walfisch, since its shape suggests a ship or a stranded whale. The 4,900 m² glass façade combines 6,800 panes with 66 laminated Siberian larch beams, and a 36 m atrium looks up through five storeys. The design has won several prizes.

The Thomas Jefferson Building, or Main Library, is the oldest Library of Congress building in Washington, D.C., put up between 1890 and 1897. Its design competition went to John L. Smithmeyer and Paul J. Pelz in 1873, but arguments in Congress held work back until a vote in 1886. Smithmeyer did much to win the job, but Pelz seems to have been the main designer and directed most of the exterior. Bernard Green, who superintended construction, and Casey are credited with finishing the interiors and guiding the decoration, and over fifty American painters and sculptors made works for it. Its Beaux-Arts and Classical Revival central block is broadly comparable with the Palais Garnier. Casey and Green raised the Main Reading Room dome from a planned height under 70 ft to 195 ft and gilded it in 23-carat gold leaf.

When bombs hit Royan on 5 January 1945, the town lost its neo-Gothic church of 1877. Its postwar successor, Notre-Dame de Royan, was larger and more ambitious, and drew on the great Gothic cathedrals for its look. The architects were Guillaume Gillet and Marc Hébrard, and the engineers Ou Tseng, René Sarger and Bernard Lafaille; built only of reinforced concrete, it took three years and was done in 1958. The elliptical nave, 45 by 22 metres, seats around 2,000. Prestressed V-shaped concrete members, made with the method named after Lafaille, alternate with very large windows by Henri Martin-Granel, 500 square metres in total. Alongside runs an ambulatory, with a gallery raised three metres and lit by diamond-shaped stained glass of the Stations of the Cross. The church gained historical monument status in 1988.

Werner Ruhnau designed the Musiktheater im Revier, Gelsenkirchen's home for opera, operetta, musicals and ballet, which opened on 15 December 1959 and has been a protected monument since 1997. It has two stages: the Large House with 1,008 seats and the Small House with 336. The Large House is a cube wrapped in 4,500 square metres of glass, through which people can see the cylindrical casing of the auditorium, its stairs and two large works by the French artist Yves Klein. One is a 7 by 20 metre blue sponge relief in a special "Gelsenkirchen Blue", because his International Klein Blue failed on walls this size: the acetone mix evaporated, the paint lost grip and glow, and it was highly flammable. The reliefs, seen through the glass, led the graphic artist Uwe Gelesch to make blue the city's colour.

Martin Elsaesser designed the Großmarkthalle, Frankfurt's main wholesale market for produce, within the New Frankfurt programme. Opened on 25 October 1928 beside the east port on the Main, it measured 220 by 50 metres and stood 17 to 23 metres high, then the biggest single building in the city; it is seen as a major work of expressionist architecture. A 50-metre roof spans the hall freely, formed of Zeiss-Dywidag concrete barrels only 7 cm thick, each a half ellipse 6 m high, realised from 1926 to 1928 by Franz Dischinger and Ulrich Finsterwalder. No monocoque construction in the world was wider then. From October 1941 the Nazis used it to gather Jewish people from Frankfurt and the region for deportation. The market shut on 4 June 2004, and the hall is now part of the European Central Bank's seat.

Hugh Stubbins, an American who had assisted Walter Gropius at Harvard in 1940, designed the Kongresshalle in 1957 for Interbau, an International Building Exhibition, and the conference hall was a gift from the United States. It sits in the Tiergarten beside the Carillon and the new Chancellery, and locals nicknamed it "Jimmy Carter's smile" or "the pregnant oyster". Its roof fell in on 21 May 1980, killing a journalist from Sender Freies Berlin and injuring many others. Rebuilt as it had been, the hall reopened in 1987, ready for Berlin's 750th anniversary. Today it is home to Haus der Kulturen der Welt, Germany's national centre for showing and discussing international contemporary art, with a focus on non-European cultures. In a pool by the entrance stands Large Divided Oval: Butterfly, the heaviest bronze Henry Moore made.

Adolf Loos designed the Rufer House at Schließmanngasse 11, Vienna, in 1922 for Josef and Marie Rufer. It is regarded as the first example of the Raumplan, or spatial plan, which arranges the interior differently from the earlier Free Plan, and though less known than other Loos designs, it set the pattern for his later work. The house is near-cubic, 10 by 10 metres inside. The outer walls bear the load, so inner walls only divide space, and a central column hides the plumbing and acts as a framing device on the second floor. There the living area sits lower, the dining room higher, their volumes overlapping. Outside, ornament is minimal: white walls and slim window frames, balanced by a top frieze and cornice and a low copy of parts of the Parthenon frieze facing the street.

The Hans Otto Theatre, Potsdam's municipal theatre, takes its name from the actor Hans Otto and has its main venue, the Großes Haus am Tiefen See, in the city's cultural quarter on Schiffbauergasse. Paul Böhm designed and built it together with his father, Gottfried Böhm: a five-storey theatre whose shell-shaped roofs cantilever out. Concrete, glass and steel dominate, and a listed gas holder was worked into the structure. Toward the lake, an old chicory mill, likewise listed, joins the theatre and now holds a restaurant. Construction ran from 2003 to 2006 at Schiffbauergasse 11 and cost 26.5 million euros, with Potsdam and Brandenburg's State Development Corporation as clients. The new 485-seat stage opened in 2006, the same year the company's old main venue, the "Blechbüchse", closed for good after fourteen years.

El Capricho, a villa in Comillas, Cantabria, was Antoni Gaudí's design for a summer house for the wealthy Máximo Díaz de Quijano. Built from 1883 to 1885, it was finished a year after the client's death. Gaudí designed few buildings outside Catalonia; this house belongs to his early orientalist period. The tower has been likened to a minaret: four classical columns at the base carry its weight, ceramic tiles alternate yellow sunflowers with green leaves, and the top ends in an arabesque finish. Each of the three floors shows its own material outside, from large stone bricks in the basement to smaller red bricks on the main floor and a sloping tiled roof above. Large windows under pointed Gothic arches bring in daylight. Neglected after the Spanish Civil War, it became a restaurant in 1988 and a museum in 2009.

Siedlung Halen, the Halen Estate, is a housing development in woodland north of Bern, designed and built by the architectural partnership Atelier 5. The work was finished in 1961; sources differ on when it began, giving 1955, 1957 or 1959. Its 82 privately owned houses form three terraces that step down a hillside like stairs. The layout is dense; residents share a pool and other common facilities. An important example of 20th-century Modernism of the Structuralist kind, the estate is listed in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites. The idea of dense low-rise housing reaches back to Roq et Rob, a 1949 scheme by Le Corbusier that was never built, but a more direct source was Atelier 5's pioneering work, and Halen became a model case for the type. It is considered the most influential such project of the 1960s.

Maison Blanche, or Villa Jeanneret-Perret, was the first independent project of Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, later Le Corbusier. He designed it for his parents in his hometown, La Chaux-de-Fonds, and it went up in 1912. Larger and more innovative than its neighbours, it set horizontal planes against the steep alpine slopes, and its plain white walls stood apart from the other houses on the hillside. Inside, rooms gather around the central salon's four pillars, hinting at the open interiors of his later work. Its neo-classical manner breaks with the local Art Nouveau, drawing on his time with Auguste Perret in Paris and Peter Behrens in Berlin. It cost more than planned; his parents had to leave within ten years, and it was sold in 1919. The Association Maison blanche bought and restored it in 2000, opening it to the public in 2005.

The Cecil and Ida Green Building, or Building 54, houses MIT's Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I. M. Pei, an MIT architecture graduate of 1940, designed it with Araldo Cossutta, and it went up in reinforced concrete between 1962 and 1964, its concrete face echoing the older limestone and concrete buildings around it. Cambridge rules then limited the floor count of tall buildings, so the tower stands on stilts, with its first occupied floor about 30 feet (9.1 m) up, letting it reach 277 feet (84 m) with 18 floors. It was the tallest building in Cambridge from 1964 until 2019. The roof carries weather instruments, radio equipment and a white radome around long-range weather radar. In 2019 the troublesome open archway was filled in to form a larger entrance pavilion.

The Gateway West and The Gateway East, two skyscrapers on Beach Road in Singapore's Downtown Core, together make up The Gateway. The complex, 37 storeys and 150 metres tall, was completed in April 1990. The US-based architect I. M. Pei designed the buildings, working with the local firm Chua Ka Seng and Partners Chartered Architects, and T.Y. Lin Structural Engineers of San Francisco also took part. Both towers have a trapezoidal shape, close to the form Pei used for the East Building of Washington's National Gallery of Art. Singapore's National Library Board has described the architecture as "world class".

In the late 1950s Philadelphia's Society Hill was seen as a slum, and the city's planning commission and redevelopment authority chose it for renewal. Pei's team drew up a plan for three 31-storey towers and a low-rise group, the Society Hill Townhouses. The towers, from the firm I. M. Pei and Associates, are built of cast-in-place concrete, and every apartment has floor-to-ceiling windows; the 5-acre (2.0 ha) site holds 624 units. Pei brought a cubist design into an 18th-century setting, with generous green space central to the scheme and traditional townhouses easing the step from classical to modern. Finished in 1964 as rental flats, the apartments became condominiums in 1979. On 10 March 1999 the buildings were placed on Philadelphia's Register of Historic Places.

Harvard's Smith Campus Center, called Holyoke Center until 2013, is a brutalist building on Harvard Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, opposite Harvard Yard's Wadsworth Gate on Massachusetts Avenue. Its main designer was Josep Lluís Sert, who led Harvard's Graduate School of Design at the time. Built in two phases from 1960 to 1966, it is a ten-storey, H-shaped reinforced concrete block and was Harvard's first high-rise. The colour of its concrete earned it the nickname "gray elephant". Mark Rothko installed five large paintings in the penthouse dining room, where they hung from 1964 to 1979. Today it is a student centre that also holds university offices, health services and a row of restaurants. Extensive renovation added places to gather, relax and study, along with room for exhibitions, events and performances, and the building reopened in 2018.

Standing at 919 N. Michigan Avenue, Chicago's Palmolive Building is a 37-storey Art Deco tower by Holabird & Root, finished in 1929 as the home of the Colgate-Palmolive-Peet Company. In 1930 it gained a beacon named for aviator Charles Lindbergh, which turned through a full circle and was meant to guide planes safely to Midway Airport. Playboy Enterprises bought the leasehold in 1965, and as the Playboy Building it held the magazine's editorial and business offices until 1989, when they left for 680 N Lake Shore Drive. The city named it a Chicago Landmark in 2000. After a 2001 sale, the developer Draper and Kramer turned it into homes with Booth Hansen Architects, keeping the lowest two floors for upscale offices and shops. In 2003 it was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

Villa Fallet, in the Swiss town of La Chaux-de-Fonds, was the first house by Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, who later became known as Le Corbusier. In 1905, aged eighteen, he designed and built it with two other students under their teacher René Chapallaz, a strong influence on his earliest houses. The client was Louis Fallet, an engraver and a friend of Charles L'Eplattenier, another of his teachers. Set on a wooded hillside, it is a large chalet in the local alpine manner, with a steep roof and a façade carefully decorated with coloured geometric patterns of pine cones and triangular pine trees. Its style is the Style Sapin, the Swiss version of Art Nouveau. Its success led to two similar villas nearby, Jacquemet and Stotzer.

Clemens Holzmeister designed the present Großes Festspielhaus, or Large Festival House, in Salzburg in 1956 as a home for the Salzburg Festival. Herbert von Karajan, who also helped shape parts of the design, conducted Richard Strauss's Der Rosenkavalier at its opening on 26 July 1960. Along with offices and tunnels dug into the Mönchsberg, the building holds a hall of 2,179 seats that works for both staged and unstaged events and can be tuned down acoustically for piano and song recitals. The auditorium is square, and its 100-metre (330 ft) stage ranks among the world's widest. From the street, visitors pass through five bronze doors into the lobby, beneath a Latin motto by Thomas Michels saying that the Muse's holy house stands open to those stirred by song.

Bard College's Richard B. Fisher Center for the Performing Arts stands in Annandale-on-Hudson, a hamlet in New York's Hudson Valley, and presents orchestral, chamber and jazz music along with theatre, dance and opera. Frank Gehry designed the building, which covers 110,000 square feet (10,000 m²), cost $62 million, took three years and opened in April 2003. It holds two theatres, four rehearsal studios and professional support spaces. The 900-seat Sosnoff Theater has a pit for opera and acoustics by Yasuhisa Toyota, including a shell that turns it into a concert hall for chamber and symphonic music. The smaller LUMA Theater is a flexible 200-seat room used by Bard's theatre and dance programmes during term. Geothermal sources supply all heating and cooling, so in normal use the building burns no fossil fuel.

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed Westmount Square, an office and apartment complex in Westmount, Quebec, in the International Style. Work began in 1964, and it opened on 13 December 1967. It has two residential towers of 21 floors, each 69 metres (226 ft) high, along with Tower 1, a 22-floor office block 83 metres (272 ft) tall, and a two-floor office pavilion, once the Eastern Airlines Building and now the Tower 4 Pavilion. The towers sit on an underground shopping centre of thirty-five shops, linked by tunnel to Place Alexis Nihon, Dawson College and Atwater Metro station. The curtain-wall façades pair black anodized aluminium with smoked glass, following the model of the Lake Shore Drive Apartments in Chicago. Skylights added to the shopping concourse roof in 1990 drew criticism from architectural preservationists.

On Brasília's Praça dos Três Poderes, the Tancredo Neves Pantheon of the Fatherland and Freedom is a cenotaph honouring Brazil's national heroes. It was conceived amid the national shock after Tancredo Neves, the president-elect and the first civilian elected after two decades of military government, died in 1985. Unlike other national pantheons, it holds no tombs. Oscar Niemeyer designed it as a modernist building symbolising a dove. French President François Mitterrand laid the foundation stone on 15 October 1985, and the official opening came on 7 September 1986. Three floors give 2,105 square metres. The Red Hall holds Athos Bulcão's Mural of Freedom, and the third floor has stained glass by Marianne Peretti. Outside, an eternal flame atop a diagonal tower stands for the people's freedom and the country's independence. It was listed in 2007 with 34 other Niemeyer works.

The Belgian Henry van de Velde designed and built Villa Esche in Chemnitz-Helbersdorf in 1902–1903 and extended it in 1911. Made for the family of Herbert Esche, a textile entrepreneur, it is thought to be van de Velde's first German commission and so the start of modern architecture in Chemnitz. In the Art Nouveau sense it is a Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art, including furniture, textiles, everyday objects and even clothing. Van de Velde's wife, Maria Séthe, probably designed the small park. From 1945 it served in turn as the Soviet military commander's seat, a residence, a base for the Ministry for State Security and an educational institution, then stood empty after 1989. Restored in 1998–2001 by Werner Wendisch, partly with Karl-Heinz Barth, the villa now holds a Henry van de Velde Museum with parts of the original furnishings.

Langer Eugen ("Tall Eugene"), an office tower in Bonn's Gronau district, went up from 1966 to 1969. Egon Eiermann, a leading German architect of the time, received the contract for its design and artistic direction in March 1965. The name mocks the short Eugen Gerstenmaier, then President of the Bundestag and the project's driving force. Until the Bundestag left for Berlin in 1999 it was the main office building for members of the Bundestag; since 2006 it has housed several UN organisations. It rises 115 metres over 30 storeys, with three basement levels, on an all-steel frame, highly unusual in central Europe. That makes it Germany's tallest steel-framed building, and when finished it was briefly Germany's second-tallest building, after the Bayer-Hochhaus. Preservationists saw its façade, free of hierarchy, as a vivid example of democratic building in young West Germany.

PPG Place, designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee, is a group of six buildings on 5.5 acres over three city blocks in downtown Pittsburgh. It is named after PPG Industries, which began the project for its headquarters and fills half of the main building, One PPG Place, a 40-storey tower. A 14-storey building and four of six storeys complete the group, all in one glass design of 19,750 pieces, marked by 231 glass spires, the tallest 82 feet (25 m) high. The neo-Gothic style, with modern innovations, drew on London's Victoria Tower, the Allegheny County Courthouse by H. H. Richardson and the Cathedral of Learning by Charles Klauder. The glass reflects summer heat away and keeps infrared heat inside in winter, and heat from computers is recycled through the building. In winter the plaza becomes an ice rink.

On Inverness Terrace, within the Hallfield Estate in Westminster, London, Hallfield Primary School was designed by Denys Lasdun and built in 1953–1955. With its bare concrete, its angular forms and its more human scale, it gave the first clue to the mature style Lasdun went on to develop. The building is listed at grade II*. By the 1970s the original school had become overcrowded, and in 2005 fresh funding paid for two further buildings by Caruso St John, which won a RIBA Award in 2006.

Richard Neutra's Jardinette Apartments, now called the Marathon Apartments, is a four-storey block in Hollywood, Los Angeles, and was his first US commission. Neutra used reinforced concrete, whose long spans allowed continuous bands of windows, and the first design also put gardens on the roof. The main wing stretches east–west across the back of the plot, with a short wing at each end framing a shallow courtyard. Unlike other 1920s apartment blocks in the city, it had no ornament. It was meant to be the first of a series of Hollywood garden apartments, but its developer, Joseph H. Miller, went broke while it was being built, so the others never happened. MoMA's 1932 'Modern Architecture' show included it as one of few American examples, and it was listed on the National Register in 1986.

The Märkisches Museum, founded in 1874 to cover Berlin and the March of Brandenburg, sits at the northern edge of Köllnischer Park by the Spree. It was Ludwig Hoffmann's first big task after he became the city's Stadtbaurat (chief of construction) in 1896; plans were approved in 1897 and work ran from 1899 to 1907, or 1908 by another account. Hoffmann made it six different buildings around two courtyards that together echo Brandenburg brick architecture from Gothic to Renaissance, a 'historical collage' to suit the collections. Rooms suited their contents: low vaults and rough plaster for prehistory, a Gothic-style chapel for medieval altars, a bright upper room for rococo porcelain. Its 53-metre tower copies either the castle keep at Wittstock or Ratzeburg cathedral; sources differ. Closed for renovation in 2023, it should reopen by 2029.

Kollhoff Tower is a 25-storey skyscraper, 103 metres tall, on Potsdamer Platz in Berlin. It is named after Hans Kollhoff of Kollhoff und Timmermann Architekten and was completed in 1999, four years after work began. Built for DaimlerChrysler in an old New York brick style, it follows early 20th-century high-rise design, as does the same office's nearby Delbrück tower at the Beisheim Center. With the Bahntower to its north and Renzo Piano's Forum Tower to its south, it forms a cluster of high-rises in central Berlin. Shops fill the lowest floors and offices the rest. A top-level viewing platform opened on 15 April 2000, served by what is said to be Europe's fastest passenger lift, at 8.65 metres per second. In 2009 the clinker façade needed repairs, as water seeping in can freeze and loosen pieces.

The James A. Farley Building in New York City is a Beaux-Arts design by McKim, Mead & White, built from 1911 to 1914, with an annex added in 1932–35. Its four storeys are a steel frame wrapped in granite ashlar. Along Eighth Avenue, twenty Corinthian columns 53 feet (16 m) tall form a monumental front, meant to match the colonnade of the same firm's original Pennsylvania Station across the street. The entablature carries the inscription beginning 'Neither snow nor rain', a line from Herodotus' Histories. It became a city landmark in 1966 and was added to the National Register in 1973. Since 2021 the former main mail-sorting room has held Moynihan Train Hall by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, a $1.6 billion project whose 31,000 sq ft concourse lies under a 92-foot glass skylight, with a 320-seat waiting area.

Wolfgang Hänsch designed the Kulturpalast in Dresden in the GDR era; when it opened in 1969 it was the city's largest multi-purpose hall, used for concerts, dances and conferences. Early plans had called for a Socialist Classicist high-rise like Moscow's Seven Sisters, but what was built is plain International Style, unlike its neighbours on the Altmarkt, and is seen as a sister to Berlin's demolished Palast der Republik. A 'tilting parquet' let the original ballroom work as a 2,435-seat raked auditorium or a flat banquet hall. On the west wall, Gerhard Bondzin's 30 by 10.5 metre mural, The Way of the Red Flag, uses concrete panels coated in coloured glass. Closed in 2012, it reopened in April 2017 with a new concert hall by Gerkan, Marg and Partners; it now also holds Dresden's main city library and a cabaret stage.

The National Space Centre in Leicester is a museum and teaching resource on space science and astronomy. Nicholas Grimshaw, the practice behind the Eden Project, won the design competition in September 1996 against four other firms. The 7,360 m² scheme rests on a disused storm-water tank, reused as its foundations to save money. Upright rockets stand in a 42-metre tower with slender steel supports, clad in inflated ETFE pillows, the material of the Eden Project domes and about 1% of the weight of equivalent glass; it has become one of the city's best-known landmarks. The main building is a 7,200 m² box on a 14-metre steel grid, wrapped in perforated metal, its roof laid with three colours of gravel in a crab nebula pattern. It opened to the public on 30 June 2001.

Place Bonaventure in downtown Montreal combines offices, exhibition space and a hotel beside the city's Central Station. Built from 1964 to 1967 to designs by the firm ARCOP, it stands over 18 railway tracks leading into the station and covers 2 hectares; at 288,000 m² it was the world's second-largest commercial building when finished. Its Brutalist outer walls are ribbed concrete, cast on site and sand-blasted, while inside the walls are sand-blasted concrete or brick. The 23,000 m² Concordia Hall held its first trade show in 1966, before the upper floors were done. On top sits a 397-room hotel with a heated outdoor pool used all year and a 2.5-acre roof garden with trees and waterfalls. A CAD$60 million renovation in 1998 reworked it for large, continuous office floors, and it links to Montreal's underground city.

The Lowry stands at the tip of Pier 8 in Salford, with the Manchester Ship Canal on most sides. The idea of a major arts venue arose in 1988, early in the plans to regenerate Salford Quays; first called the Salford Quays Centre for the Performing Arts, it became the Lowry Project in 1994 and had raised £64 million by February 1996. The design is credited to James Stirling and Michael Wilford. Opened on 28 April 2000, it contains two theatres, the Lyric with 1,730 seats and the Quays with 466, along with studios and 1,610 m² of galleries. The centre is associated with L. S. Lowry and holds a collection of his work. In 2001 it received the Royal Fine Art Commission's Building of the Year Award.

The Mackintosh Building is the best-known part of the Glasgow School of Art. Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh designed it in phases between 1896 and 1909; one half was complete in 1899, the other in 1909. Francis Newbery, the school's director, gave Mackintosh the job while the school was growing fast. The building is called a pioneer of the British form of Art Nouveau, known as the Modern Style, and it helped make Mackintosh's name abroad. Critics rank it among Britain's finest buildings. A fire in May 2014 badly damaged it; restoration of the design, including its famous library, started in 2016 with original woods like longleaf pine and tulipwood. A second fire in June 2018 left only a burnt-out shell, and there are plans to rebuild it in keeping with Mackintosh's style.

The Institute of Contemporary Art moved in 2006 to a new home on Fan Pier in Boston's South Boston Seaport District, designed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro after the ICA won a 1999 competition for the site. It was among the firm's first completed buildings and its first in the United States, and Boston's first new art museum in more than a century. The 65,000 sq ft building holds galleries and a performance space. Its form recalls the gantry cranes on the nearby waterfront, and many critics praised its openness, the large outdoor staircase and the way it turns towards the harbour. It won the 2007 Harleston Parker Medal. Not every review agreed: critic Philip Nobel called it a 'botched box', faulting its circulation, its dull landward side and the shadow it casts on the harbourside walk.

The Everson Museum of Art in downtown Syracuse, New York, focuses on American art. It grew from a $1 million gift Helen Everson made to the city in 1941 to pay for a museum; ground was broken in 1965 and the building opened in 1968. I. M. Pei designed it, and it is seen as a work of art in itself. Pei intended a sculptural object set against the surrounding modern city rather than just a 'monumental container for art', and four cantilevered square volumes strengthen that reading. Its outer walls often serve as screens for projected films and images, watched by people gathered in the courtyard next door. Skateboarders have used the site since the mid-1980s, and some call it an 'East Coast skate mecca'.

Palazzo Piccolomini stands in the centre of Pienza, Italy, beside the cathedral. Built from 1459 to a design by Bernardo Rossellino, it counts among the earliest works of Renaissance architecture. Pope Pius II, born Enea Silvio Piccolomini, commissioned it as part of rebuilding Pienza as an ideal city; the town was once the village of Corsignano, his birthplace, and was renamed in his honour. Rossellino took his lead from the Palazzo Rucellai in Florence, a work by his master Leon Battista Alberti. The palace, also called the Pontifical, has a square plan over three floors and is built of rough-faced pale stone. A main entrance at ground level opens onto a rectangular central courtyard, with a loggia carried on stone columns, and a slender column splits every window in two.

The Museum of Military History (Heeresgeschichtliches Museum) is part of the Arsenal in Vienna, a group of brick buildings set out in a rectangle south of the Landstraßer Gürtel. The Arsenal as a whole is counted as Vienna's finest group of buildings in Romantic historicism, mixing Italian-medieval with Byzantine-Islamic forms. Its site was split into sectors, each overseen by one of six architects, among them Theophil von Hansen, Ludwig Förster, Eduard van der Nüll and August Sicard von Sicardsburg. The museum is one of Hansen's early works, still in the romantic manner he later left behind as the leading figure of Neo-Renaissance historicism, a style that came to be called Viennese. The museum took until 1891 to complete. Bombing in 1945 badly damaged the Arsenal, but after the war most of it was rebuilt as it had been.

The Palazzo dell'Arte in Milan's Parco Sempione is home to the Triennale di Milano, a museum devoted to art and design. Giovanni Muzio designed it, and it went up between 1931 and 1933, funded by the brothers Antonio, Andrea and Michele Bernocchi. It was the new venue for an exhibition that moved to Milan in 1933, when the show also became a triennial; Gio Ponti's Torre Branca was part of that setting. Muzio also designed the theatre inside, the Teatro dell'Arte. The Milan Triennial, an international show of art and design, was held here thirteen times from 1936 to 1996 and once more in 2016. The Triennale Design Museum, a permanent museum of Italian design, opened in 2007.

Opus Hong Kong is a 12-storey residential tower, 42.62 metres tall, finished in 2012 at 53 Stubbs Road in the Mid-Levels. Frank Gehry designed it with Ronald Lu and Partners for the developer Swire Properties, and it was his first housing project in Asia. The building holds just 12 homes of 560 to 640 m² each, two of them duplexes with their own pools. The 3,020 m² site also has underground parking, swimming pools, gyms, electric car charging and a system that reuses rainwater to water the grounds. In August 2012 one flat, filling the whole eighth floor at 580 m², sold for HK$470 million, making it the most expensive apartment in Hong Kong at that point.

The Tagblatt-Turm in Stuttgart is a 16-storey tower, 61 metres high. Ernst Otto Oßwald planned it in 1924, facing the Schocken department store, as Stuttgart's first high-rise and Germany's first in reinforced concrete; it was built between 1924 and 1928 from crushed stone and cement, one of the country's earliest high-rises. When finished it was second in height in the city only to the old city hall of 1905, and the tallest office building in Germany. Its modern look stirred controversy while it was going up, but it is now treated as a cultural and architectural landmark. The name comes from its first tenant, the local paper Stuttgarter Neues Tagblatt, whose editors and publisher were based there from 1928 to 1943. After a major renovation it became a cultural centre with several theatres in 2004, Kultur unterm Turm.

UTEC, the University of Engineering and Technology, has its Lima campus where the Barranco District begins, between Reducto Avenue, the Bajada de Armendáriz and the Paseo de la República. Its designers, Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara of the Irish practice Grafton Architects, won the UTEC competition and drew the scheme in 2011; Graña y Montero built it in 2015 with a construction budget of US$100 million. It sits on what was left of huaca La Viñita, Barranco's last pre-Columbian archaeological site, some 5,000 m² in size. The brutalist building won a Silver Lion at the 13th Venice Architecture Biennale and was among the works cited when Farrell and McNamara received the 2020 Pritzker Prize. Opinion is split: supporters call it a 'modern Machu Picchu', while critics attack its 'unfinished appearance' and liken it to buildings of Juan Velasco Alvarado's government.

The Supreme Federal Court Palace in Brasília houses Brazil's highest appeals court, which is also its constitutional court.
