Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and the engineer Joaquim Cardozo did the structural work. It stands on the Three Powers Plaza (Praça dos Três Poderes) with the Palácio do Planalto, the presidential palace, and the National Congress. Like Niemeyer's other Brasília buildings designed by 1960, among them the Congress, the Cathedral and the Palácio da Alvorada, it was experimental and shares design elements with them. Pillars along its sides lift the building slightly off the ground, which makes the whole look light, and Cardozo's calculations let its foundations stay thin, barely touching the ground. In front stands Alfredo Ceschiatti's statue A Justiça (Justice), carved in 1961. IPHAN declared it national heritage in 2007, the year Niemeyer turned 100.

The Palmach Museum in Ramat Aviv, Israel, honours the Palmach, the strike force of the Haganah, the underground defence group of the years before the state, which was later merged into the Israel Defense Forces. It opened in 2000 and marks the Palmach's part in founding the State of Israel. The Israeli architects Zvi Hecker and Rafi Segal designed it. Visitors move underground through a sequence of multimedia rooms, beginning with a memorial to the fallen. The plan zigzags at sharp angles around trees that were kept on the site, and the walls are faced with a local sandstone found while digging for the project. The design was shown at the Venice Biennale.

Museo Jumex, the main home of the Fundación Jumex Arte Contemporáneo and its collection, opened in November 2013 in the Polanco district of Mexico City, in a building by David Chipperfield. Zoning rules limited the space available, so Chipperfield moved the offices, shop and library into existing buildings next door and gave the museum itself almost entirely to exhibitions. The concrete structure stands on fourteen columns and is faced with travertine slabs from Xalapa in Veracruz, part of a design that responds to its setting and uses materials sourced in Mexico. Skylights on the roof, facing west, bring daylight into the upper galleries, while the lower floors have full-height windows framed in stainless steel. It belongs to the Plaza Carso mixed-use development, which includes a shopping mall, and faces the Museo Soumaya across the street.

Palacio Barolo is an office building at 1370 Avenida de Mayo, in the Monserrat district of Buenos Aires. Luis Barolo, an Italian immigrant who made his fortune in knitted fabrics, hired the Italian architect Mario Palanti to design it. Palanti admired Dante and shaped the building around the cosmology of the Divine Comedy. Its 22 floors fall into three parts: the basement and ground floor stand for hell, floors 1 to 14 for purgatory and 15 to 22 for heaven. It rises 100 metres, one for each canto, and nine vaulted arches spread from a central dome, standing for the nine circles of hell. On completion in 1923 no building in South America was taller, and it led the city until the Kavanagh Building of 1936. Its rooftop lighthouse was meant to welcome arrivals to the Río de la Plata.

The Rockefeller Archaeological Museum stands beside Herod's Gate in Jerusalem and holds a large collection of finds from digs in British-ruled Mandatory Palestine, mostly from the 1920s and 1930s. John D. Rockefeller Jr., the American philanthropist, agreed to give two million dollars towards it. Its architect, Austen Harrison, chief architect of the Mandate's Public Works Department, drew a white limestone building that blends eastern and western elements. Its foundation stone went down in June 1930, and it opened in January 1938, known as the Palestine Archaeological Museum until 1967. Over the entrance the British sculptor Eric Gill carved Asia meeting Africa; he also made ten reliefs of different cultures, a gargoyle fountain for the inner courtyard and stone signs in English, Hebrew and Arabic. The Dead Sea Scrolls were kept here from 1947 until 1967.

Yad Kennedy, a memorial to Kennedy, was paid for by American Jewish communities and built in 1966. It crowns the tallest of the Jerusalem hills, 825 metres high and 11 km from the city centre. David Resnick, an Israeli architect born in Brazil who later won the Israel Prize for architecture in 1995, designed it with Dov Feigin, an Israeli sculptor born in Ukraine. Because money came from groups in every state and in Washington, D.C., the idea of a column for each helped lead to the image of a tree trunk, a life felled in its prime. The 18-metre memorial is shaped like a cut stump, ringed by 51 concrete columns bearing state emblems and that of the capital, with slim glass strips between. Inside are a bronze relief of Kennedy and an eternal flame burning at the centre.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium, known as SVP Stadium, is in Ahmedabad's Navrangpura district, and India's first One Day International was played there. Sheth Chinubhai Chimanbhai, an industrialist then serving as mayor, hired Charles Correa to design the stadium and clubhouse, with Mahendra Raj as consulting structural engineer. Work began in 1959, but money ran short, and by 1966 only the roofed south pavilion was done; stands round the whole ground followed by the 1980s. It was the first building in India with a folded plate structure. The reinforced concrete cantilever roof over the pavilion, 20 metres wide and 326 feet long, was the world's longest span of its kind in 1963. Outside, geometric concrete frames leave open space under the seats. In 2020 the Getty Foundation gave it a grant, naming it among 13 significant twentieth-century buildings worldwide.

The Pakistan Monument on the western Shakarparian Hills in Islamabad serves as both national monument and heritage museum. It expresses the unity of the nation's people and honours those who sacrificed their own 'today' so that 'tomorrow' would be better. Arif Masoud's design was chosen from 21 entries and given approval on 10 July 2003. Its foundation stone went down on 25 May 2004, and President Pervez Musharraf opened it on 23 March 2007. The petals come from the muqarnas of Mughal architecture: four large granite petals stand for the Punjabi, Baloch, Sindhi and Pakhtun cultures, and three smaller ones for Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Kashmir and the minorities. They project as cantilevers, among Asia's largest. From the air the plan reads as the star and crescent of the national flag, and workers' handprints line the walls of Freedom Plaza.

Independence Memorial Hall stands in Independence Square in Colombo's Cinnamon Gardens. This national monument marks Sri Lanka's independence from British rule, when full governing power passed to an elected Ceylonese legislature on 4 February 1948, and occupies the spot where Prince Henry, Duke of Gloucester, opened the first parliament that day. Its design came from eight architects under Tom Neville Wynne-Jones, including Shirley de Alwis, Justin Samarasekera and F. H. Billimoria. The form follows the Magul Maduwa, royal audience hall of the Kingdom of Kandy, which was the island's last native kingdom. Until parliament moved to a new complex, it was the ceremonial assembly hall of the Senate and the House of Representatives; it now hosts religious events and the yearly national day. A statue of Don Stephen Senanayake, the first prime minister, stands at its head.

SOTA, the School of the Arts, is an independent specialist school in Singapore whose six-year course mixes arts training with academic study and ends in an International Baccalaureate diploma or a career-related programme. The 5.3-hectare campus sits at the foot of Mount Sophia in Bras Basah, its address 1 Zubir Said Drive. Credited to WOHA, the permanent campus cost S$145 million and was finished in 2009, and the school took up residence on 4 January 2010. At the 2010 World Architecture Festival it won the World Learning Building of the Year award, and in 2011 it received a RIBA International Award.

People's Park Complex is a tower of shops and flats on Park Road in Singapore's Outram area, beside Chinatown MRT station. Design Partnership, which William Lim co-founded in 1967, won the commission in its first year. At 31 storeys and 103 metres, it was Southeast Asia's first shopping centre of its type and a model for later retail in Singapore. The shopping centre was finished in October 1970 and the flats in 1973. The housing block has been called the nearest thing to the high-rise living Le Corbusier set out in his Marseille Unité d'Habitation; its 25 levels, nicknamed 'streets in the air', were meant for neighbours to meet. The mall holds Singapore's first 'city room', an idea of Japanese Metabolist architects: two interlocking multi-storey atriums holding many shops and kiosks. Its original finish was raw exposed concrete.

The Singapore Conference Hall is a five-storey modernist building by Lim Chong Keat, William Lim and Chan Voon Fee of Malayan Architects Co-Partnership, whose entry won a government competition in 1962. Finished in October 1965, it hosted conferences and exhibitions and housed the head office of the National Trades Union Congress. Concrete columns carry the cantilevered V-shaped roof and terraces, and the roof collects rain and drains it through a central downpipe. Although air-conditioned, the building also has natural ventilation worked into the design for the tropical climate. Walls and ceilings inside use local timbers such as merbau and mersawa to express local identity, and mosaic tiles in Malay mat patterns cover the walls. It houses the Singapore Chinese Orchestra in an 831-seat concert hall. No post-colonial building in Singapore had been gazetted as a national monument before it.

The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum is a large building at the centre of Ba Đình Square in Hanoi, where on 2 September 1945 Ho read out the Declaration of Independence. Building began on 2 September 1973 and the mausoleum was opened on 29 August 1975. The design is credited to Garol Isakovich. It draws on Lenin's Mausoleum in Moscow but adds Vietnamese features like its sloping roof. Grey granite clads the outside, while the inside uses polished grey, black and red stone. The structure measures 21.6 metres high and 41.2 metres wide, with two seven-step viewing platforms for parades. Ho's embalmed body rests in a dimly lit glass case in the cool central hall, under a military guard of honour. Nearly 250 species of plants and flowers from all over Vietnam grow in the gardens around it.

The Voortrekker Monument, a granite structure on a Pretoria hilltop, honours the Voortrekkers, who left the Cape Colony in 1835–1854. Gerard Moerdijk designed it, and Prime Minister D. F. Malan inaugurated it on 16 December 1949. Standing 62 metres high on a 40 by 40 metre base, it recalls European monuments such as the Dôme des Invalides and the Völkerschlachtdenkmal yet shows African influences. A gate leads into a laager of 64 granite ox-wagons, as many as at the Battle of Blood River. A vast inner space flanked by four arched windows of yellow Belgian glass holds the Historical Frieze, the world's biggest in marble. A round opening in the Hall of Heroes floor looks down on the Cenotaph; at noon each 16 December, sunlight through an oculus in the dome falls on its words 'Ons vir Jou, Suid-Afrika'.

Nasr City in Cairo is home to the Unknown Soldier Memorial, a monument in the shape of a pyramid. President Anwar Sadat ordered it in 1974 in honour of the Egyptians and Arabs who died in the October War of 1973, and it opened in October 1975. Its designer was Sami Rafi, an artist who taught at Cairo's Faculty of Fine Arts. The concrete form is a hollow pyramid, 25 metres high on a base 14.3 metres wide. Four pillars, 1.9 metres thick, bear 71 symbolic names, and in the middle of the base a solid basalt cube represents the soldier's tomb. When Sadat was assassinated in October 1981, the same site was chosen for his own grave.

MUAC, the Museo Universitario Arte Contemporáneo, is a large art museum on UNAM's main campus in Mexico City. It opened in November 2008 as Mexico's first public museum given over entirely to art of the 21st century. The architect, Teodoro González de León, also designed the COLMEX building and the Museo Rufino Tamayo, and worked with Abraham Zabludovsky on the National Auditorium. The museum belongs to the University Cultural Center, a vast group of auditoriums, galleries, libraries and research spaces. Its plain, sloping glass front stands apart from its neighbours, which were mostly designed in the 1970s, and its large, high-ceilinged halls can show many kinds of art. On the plaza in front rises La espiga, a carbon-steel sculpture by Rufino Tamayo more than 18 metres tall.

In central Mexico City, Museo Experimental El Eco now serves as a gallery of contemporary art. It began in 1952, when the businessman Daniel Mont asked the artist Mathias Goeritz for a place that would join his restaurant-bar business to the avant-garde mood of some cultural figures of the day, and break with convention. Goeritz, who designed it in 1952–53, thought of the building as a sculpture people could walk into. Its walls, ceilings, rooms, corridors and openings were arranged so that moving through them became an emotional act, an idea that ran against the functionalism then leading architecture. Goeritz first presented his Emotional Architecture Manifesto at its pre-inauguration in 1953. In 2004 the building was bought by the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, and after many months of work restoring its original state it reopened on 7 September 2005.

Caracas's Teresa Carreño Cultural Complex, known too as the Teresa Carreño Theatre, ranks as the most important theatre in the city and in Venezuela, with opera, ballet, plays, and both symphonic and popular concerts. In South America only Buenos Aires' Néstor Kirchner Cultural Centre is larger. Pedro Antonio Ríos Reyna proposed it in the 1970s as a home for the Venezuela Symphony Orchestra. Funding came in September 1970, and it was designed by Tomás Lugo, Jesús Sandoval and Dietrich Kunckel. It opened in two stages: its first hall, José Félix Ribas, in February 1976, with the Ríos Reyna Hall and everything else following on 19 April 1983. It covers a surface of 22,586 m2, and its completed area exceeds 80,000 m2. Huge columns and overlapping hexagonal roofs mark its design.

The SOMISA Building in Buenos Aires, whose official name is Teniente General Castiñeiras, served as head office of SOMISA (Sociedad Mixta Siderúrgica Argentina), a metallurgy company owned by the state. Mario Roberto Álvarez designed it in the modernist style, and it went up between 1966 and 1977. No building in Argentina before it had been made wholly from 3 mm steel sheet and welded throughout. It stands in Monserrat, on Julio Argentino Roca Avenue. When SOMISA was privatised in 1993, the national government acquired the building as headquarters for the newly formed office of the Cabinet chief, and today it is one of that office's two seats.

Praça das Artes, in central São Paulo, was created to bring artistic groups and training schools together in one well-equipped place. Extending the work of the Municipal Theater, it houses the theatre's artistic groups, the city's Dance School, the Municipal Music School and the Conservatory Hall. Marcelo Ferraz, Francisco Fanucci and Marcos Cartum designed it around the drama and music conservatory, mixing building and square, entered from Conselheiro Crispiniano Street, Avenida São João and the Anhangabaú Valley. Damaged buildings were expropriated: the conservatory was restored and absorbed, and the Cairo cinema kept its front. Work started in 2009 on 28,500 m2, the first module opened on 5 December 2012, and a second phase added an inner square onto the valley, a garden and an open-air bar. Icon Magazine's Icon Awards named it Building of the Year in 2013.

The Juscelino Kubitschek Bridge, usually called Ponte JK, is an arch bridge of steel and concrete crossing Brasília's Lake Paranoá. The architect Alexandre Chan designed it with Mário Vila Verde as structural engineer, and Chan wanted a landmark the community could enjoy, not simply a way over the water. Four pillars rest on the lakebed beneath the main span. Three asymmetrical steel arches, each 61 m (200 ft) tall, cross one another diagonally and carry the deck, which hangs from steel cables that switch from side to side, weaving into a twisted plane. The whole structure runs 1,200 m and cost US$56.8 million. It opened to traffic on 15 December 2002, and its outline soon became a Brasília landmark. At a 2003 meeting in Pittsburgh, the International Bridge Conference, Chan was given the Gustav Lindenthal Medal for this project.

The Schocken Library in Jerusalem was built to hold Salman Schocken's important collection of books. Schocken had commissioned Modernist buildings from the German Jewish architect Erich Mendelsohn, and after he moved from Germany to the Holy Land in 1934, Mendelsohn designed this library for him too. It was built close to his home, at today's 6 Balfour Street. The historic building now houses the Jewish Theological Seminary of America's Schocken Institute for Jewish Research. The institute keeps the Salman Schocken Library there, as well as other important archives and book collections, Jewish and otherwise.

On Bar-Ilan University's main campus in Ramat Gan, Israel, the Wohl Centre serves as a convention centre. Daniel Libeskind designed it with the Heder Partnership, a local firm, and it was his first building in Israel. Built from 2001 to 2005 on a fairly small budget, it covers about 3,900 m2 (42,000 sq ft). Three long rectangular bars form the base, and a 1,000-seat auditorium sits on top of them. The angular shape recalls an open book, which Libeskind said embodies how the dynamics of knowledge relate to the unifying role of faith. Windows shaped after Hebrew letters cut through the gold-coloured aluminium skin. It is noted for a stark exterior and an uncluttered interior. In 2006 it received a RIBA International Award, and in 2019 it was listed as a B-class conservation site.

KAFD Metro Station is an interchange in the al-Aqeeq neighbourhood of Riyadh, inside the King Abdullah Financial District, where the Yellow, Blue and Purple Lines of the Riyadh Metro meet on six tracks. Zaha Hadid Architects won the Royal Commission for Riyadh City's design competition for it in 2013, when it was due to be finished by 2017. The design takes its cues from mashrabiya screens and from the patterns desert winds leave in sand dunes. The station covers 8,150 m2. Building started in 2014, tunnelling for the Blue Line followed in July 2015, and by 2019 the bare frame of the exterior could be seen. It received LEED Gold certification in October 2024 and was completed and opened to the public in December 2024.

In Dallas's Victory Park, the Perot Museum of Nature and Science, named for Margot and Ross Perot, deals with natural history and science. Thom Mayne of Morphosis Architects shaped it as a large cube floating above a landscaped base. That base carries a rolling green roof of about 0.4 ha, of rock and drought-resistant native grasses, reflecting Texas's native landscape as a living system meant to evolve naturally. A 16 m escalator climbs inside a 46 m glass tube that juts diagonally out of the cube. Skylights light the atrium, and rainwater from the roof and car park meets 74% of non-potable water needs and all irrigation. It has six floors, about 14 storeys high; five are public and hold 11 permanent exhibit halls and 6 learning labs. Donations paid for it, with no debt or public money.

National Museum – Architecture in Oslo opened in 2008 at Bankplassen 3. The Architecture Museum behind it was founded in 1975 by the Norwegian Architects National Association and joined the National Museum on 1 July 2003. The National Museum holds Norway's most important architecture collection, more than 300,000 items from the 1830s to the present; models, drawings and photographs are shown in changing exhibitions. Three buildings are joined together on the site. The oldest and main one is the former Christiania branch of Norges Bank, the work of Christian H. Grosch, completed in 1830. A storage building by Henry Bucher dates from 1911. Set diagonally behind them is the Ulltveit-Moe Pavilion, Sverre Fehn's addition, dated 2002.

New Delhi's National Crafts Museum, whose official name is National Handicrafts and Handlooms Museum, is one of India's largest museums of crafts. It occupies a corner of Pragati Maidan, opposite the Purana Quila complex. Charles Correa designed the building between 1975 and 1990, setting a traditional architectural vocabulary within a modern design, and organised it around courtyards he called "the rooms open to the sky". More than 35,000 pieces cover painting, embroidery, textiles and work in clay, stone and wood. A 2 ha village complex, left over from a 1972 temporary exhibition on rural India, holds 15 structures representing homes, courtyards and shrines of various states. Each month folk artists come to paint its open corridor walls. In a 2015 renovation, Ganga Devi's painted walls were whitewashed and her murals lost.

Le Corbusier's Open Hand Monument stands in Sector 1 of Chandigarh's Capitol Complex, against the Shivalik hills of the Himalaya. A frequent theme in his architecture, the open hand meant peace and reconciliation to him. Here it is the emblem of the Government of Chandigarh. The largest of his many Open Hand sculptures, it rises 26 m (85 ft) over a 12.5 by 9 m trench. The vane, 14 m tall and weighing 50 tons, rests on a concrete platform and looks like a bird in flight. It was cast by hand from sheet metal in Nangal, at a workshop of the Bhakra Nangal Management Board, faced with polished steel and set on a ball-bearing steel shaft so the wind can turn it. Le Corbusier died in 1965; his dream project was only built twenty years later, in 1985.

The Shaheed Minar, or Martyr Tower, in Dhaka honours those killed in the 1952 Bengali language movement protests in then East Pakistan. The sculptors Hamidur Rahman and Novera Ahmed designed and built it; martial law delayed the work, and it was finished in 1963. A half circle of columns on a central dais stands for a mother with her fallen sons, with a red sun shining behind. The marble floor was meant to mirror the columns' moving shadows, and the basement held a 140 m2 (1,500 sq ft) fresco on the movement's history. The monument was wholly destroyed during Operation Searchlight in 1971, rebuilt after independence later that year, and expanded in 1983. Hurried repair left the column shorter, its head more bent than planned and its proportions altered. Each 21 February, Language Movement Day, events centre on it.

The Jim Thompson House in central Bangkok is a museum of the art collection of James Harrison Wilson Thompson, the American businessman and architect who designed and owned it. Begun in 1958 as a home that would also show his collection, it was built in 1959 on one rai, about 2,023 m2. It combines six traditional Thai-style houses, mainly of wood, plus old Thai structures collected nationwide in the 1950s and 60s. Most of these 19th-century houses were taken apart in Ayutthaya, brought by river and pieced together again. The biggest, a weaver's house now used as the living room, was brought from Bangkrua, across the Saen Saep canal, where his company's weavers then worked. When Thompson vanished in Malaysia in 1967, it passed to a foundation bearing his name, with Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn as its royal patron.

Phnom Penh's Independence Monument was built in 1958 to mark Cambodia winning independence from France in 1953. It rises 37 m from a roundabout in the city centre, where Sihanouk Boulevard crosses Norodom Boulevard. The Cambodian architect Vann Molyvann designed it, chosen for the task by Prince Norodom Sihanouk, who told him how it should look and asked for a blend of "the religious and the secular." Its form is a stupa shaped like a lotus, in the style found at Banteay Srei's temple and at other historic Khmer sites. At national celebrations the monument becomes the focus of activity: a royal or senior official often lights a ceremonial flame on the pedestal inside, and flowers are laid along the stairs.

Terminal 2 at Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru was designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill as a tribute to the city's name as the "Garden City", and Larsen & Toubro built it. Work on the first phase began in 2018 and was slowed by the COVID-19 pandemic. Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated it on 11 November 2022, and it began operating in January 2023. That first phase cost ₹5,000 crore (US$520 million), covers 255,000 m2 and adds room for 25 million passengers a year; a second phase, now being built, will add 20 million more. Arrivals are on the ground floor and departures on the floor above. Since 12 September 2023 the terminal has handled all of the airport's international flights, the first being Saudia flight SV867 from Jeddah.

The Kigali Convention Centre is in Kigali, Rwanda's capital and largest city. It stands on Highway KN5 beside the KG2 Roundabout, about 6 km (4 mi) west of Kigali International Airport. Three Rwandan corporate investors pooled resources in 2007 for the project and formed a company, Ultimate Concept Limited, that would develop and own it. Work began in 2009 to a design by Roland Dieterle, a German architect, and ended in 2016. Besides a conference centre seating 2,600, the complex holds the five-star Radisson Blu Hotel Kigali, whose 292 rooms are spread over six floors.

Turkey's Grand National Assembly meets in a large modern building in the Bakanlıklar district of Ankara, the third building to house the country's parliament. Its design was the work of Clemens Holzmeister (1886–1993), an architect and professor. The previous building, by Vedat Tek, served the parliament from 1924 to 1960. Holzmeister's building appeared on the back of Turkey's 50,000 lira banknotes between 1989 and 1999. During the attempted coup of 2016 it was struck from the air three times and visibly damaged, and it was renovated that summer.

Porto's Faculty of Architecture sees itself as heir to teaching it has shared with Fine Arts since 1779, and is tied to the Porto School. Its building, above the Douro on the Campo Alegre campus, was designed by Álvaro Siza, a former teacher there, and built in stages from the mid-1980s. First the Quinta da Póvoa estate was adapted and the Carlos Ramos Pavilion (1985–86) added: conceived as provisional, it is U-shaped around a half-open courtyard, placed to suit the existing trees. To the north, a long block, a semicircular volume and a prism hold offices, auditorium, gallery and library, screening the courtyard from bridge traffic. To the south, four detached four-storey studio towers point their narrow ends at the river; one tower was omitted so the courtyard opens to the Arrábida Bridge. Atria, galleries, ramps and stairs link everything.

James Stirling and James Gowan were commissioned for the University of Leicester's Engineering Building in 1957; the design dates from 1959 and it was built from 1960 to 1963, with Frank Newby as consulting structural engineer. Workshops fill a low hall with a rectangular plan, walled entirely in frosted glass. Joined to it, a tower faced with red tiles and glass holds an auditorium, offices and laboratories, with the water tank on top; the sloping auditorium floor shows outside as a sharp wedge. The roof geometry is turned 45 degrees to the plan, giving a jagged roof line, a diamond-patterned edge and a run of translucent prisms. Seen as Stirling's first move from brutalism towards postmodernism, it counts among the origins of postmodern architecture and belongs to the Red Trilogy. It is Grade II listed.

The Faculty of Architecture is one of the faculties that Altuğ and Behruz Çinici designed for the campus of Ankara's Middle East Technical University (METU). The pair won the METU campus competition in 1961, in 1962 shifted their office to Ankara and went on designing for the campus until 1980. Behruz Çinici said their approach to the campus set out to challenge the International Style, then dominant in architectural theory, teaching and culture. Instead of reshaping the land to fit a plan, their campus proposal grew out of many visits to the site and close study of its terrain. On the campus they worked with a 'piece construction' system and favoured durable, often uncoated materials over coatings that damage easily. Bare concrete techniques, which the two pioneered in Turkey, were first developed on this campus.

Musée Yves Saint Laurent Marrakech is a museum devoted to the fashion designer, on the street named after him, near the Majorelle Garden, his former Moroccan home. Pierre Bergé, his business and one-time life partner, said a museum in Morocco was natural, since even the colours and shapes of his clothes owed much to the country. Studio KO designed the 4,000 m2 building, and the Moroccan arm of Bouygues built it. Earth-coloured cubes and curves are wrapped in brickwork laid like lace, recalling woven fabric. The materials, terracotta, concrete and terrazzo, are coloured to merge with the setting, and the earth bricks were made locally from Moroccan soil. Inside are a hall for Jacques Majorelle, temporary exhibition rooms and a 130-seat auditorium. Opened on 19 October 2017, it was named best new public building at Wallpaper magazine's 2018 Design Awards.

In Le Raincy, near Paris, the Roman Catholic church of Notre-Dame du Raincy was built in 1922–23 to designs by Auguste and Gustave Perret. Parish priest Felix Nègre proposed it in 1918 to honour France's 1914 victory on the Marne. Concrete kept costs down and, rather than imitating stone, was used for what it is: standard parts, slim supports and thin membranes opened up by windows. The non-load-bearing outer walls are built of square precast panels, called claustra, cut with geometric openings that hold the glass, in a few repeated patterns. For economy, Marguerite Huré coloured clear glass with coatings to make the stained glass; blues by the door give way to warmer colours at the altar end. Inside, the columns are left plain and the concrete vaults are the main ornament. Listing as a historic monument followed in 1966.

The Palace of Justice in Chandigarh is the building of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, the court shared by Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh, a Union Territory. Le Corbusier, author of Chandigarh's master plan, was picked to carry out the court building as well. Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, backed the project with enthusiasm and followed its progress closely. The court moved to its present home in Chandigarh on 17 January 1955. In July 2016 the building was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with other works by Le Corbusier, in a listing of seventeen of his projects in seven countries titled The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement.

Tadao Ando's Rokko Housing stands at Rokko, just outside Kobe. It is a complex warren of atriums, shafts, terraces and balconies. Rokko Housing One dates from 1983 and Rokko Housing Two from 1993, and both designs illustrate issues of traditional architectural vocabulary: solid against void, open against closed, light against dark. Ando's engineering here was specific to the site, and the buildings came through the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake without damage. Together with the Church of the Light, the Rokko apartments brought Ando international recognition, and Ando was noticed by those who see a regional quality in concrete building.

Aldo Rossi and Gianni Braghieri are credited with this extension of San Cataldo Cemetery in Modena. Rossi won the design competition for the extension in 1971, and the win made him known internationally. In scale it is the largest of all his projects; work began in 1971 and it has still not been completed. Rossi called it a "city of the dead". The design shows the repetition typical of his postmodernist work, and it also shows the objection often raised against that work: that it puts "monumental collectivity" ahead of the individual.

Takasugi-an is a tea house by Terunobu Fujimori in Chino, Nagano Prefecture, built in 2003–04. Its name means, literally, "too high tea house". The room, four and a half tatami mats in size, is raised six metres off the ground on two load-bearing trees. These are chestnut trees, cut on a mountain nearby and moved to the site. Tea houses are usually entered by stooping low; here the guest climbs a ladder to reach the top instead. The hanging picture scroll (kakejiku) that would normally hint at the season gives way to a large window, which frames a view of the town of Fujimori's childhood.

Vidhan Bhavan in Bhopal is the home of the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly, the single-chamber legislature of the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh, which now has 230 members elected directly from single-seat constituencies. The large building is in the Arera Hill part of Bhopal, at the heart of the Capital Complex. Charles Correa designed it in 1967; it came after his first significant project, the Mahatma Gandhi Sangrahalaya in Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Ashram, 1958–63. The building won an Aga Khan Award for Architecture during the award's seventh cycle, in 1998.

Skogskyrkogården, the Woodland Cemetery, is in Gamla Enskede, south of central Stockholm. Designed by Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz, it traces architecture's shift from Nordic Classicism to a mature functionalism. After changes urged by the competition jury, work started in 1917 on gravel pits overgrown with pines; the first phase took three years; it opened in 1920. From the colonnaded entrance a long path forks: one way crosses pastoral land past a big pond and a tree-lined meditation hill, the other rises to a detached granite cross, the crematorium's abstract portico and the chapels of Faith, Hope and the Holy Cross. The architects designed everything down to the lamps, with sculptures by Carl Milles built in. Lewerentz's Resurrection Chapel is from 1925; Asplund's crematorium, his last work, opened in 1940, just before he died. UNESCO listed it in 1994.

The flower kiosk stands at Östra kyrkogården, the Eastern Cemetery in the Öster district of Malmö, Sweden. Sigurd Lewerentz designed the cemetery after winning its competition, and from 1917 to 1969 he was responsible for every major new building and change there. The kiosk, a flower shop from 1969, was his last building at the cemetery and the last of his career, and it has been widely praised. It is made of raw concrete, in a single, radically simplified form with carefully refined details. Visitors come from around the world to see the kiosk and the cemetery's architecture.

Jetwing Lighthouse, first named the Lighthouse Hotel, is a five-star hotel run by Jetwing Hotels in Galle, Sri Lanka, just north of Galle Fort on the coast. Herbert Cooray commissioned it in 1995, and it opened on 7 June 1997, among Geoffrey Bawa's last major works. Like the 17th-century Dutch fort, it overlooks the sea from a rocky headland. A small doorway opens to a walled court where a spiral stair climbs under a blue-tiled Moorish dome; its bronze and copper balustrade, by Laki Senanayake, depicts the Sinhalese fighting the Portuguese at the Battle of Randeniwela. In the dim lobby, sunlight pools on polished concrete and the room seems to reach the ocean. Bawa made natural boulders a focus, framing them from the dining room and open-air lounge. A 2013 wing added twenty rooms, two suites and a restaurant.

Potato Head Beach Club, credited to Andra Matin, opened in Seminyak in 2010 after a year of development. Its form recalls an amphitheatre, and it is built from thousands of wooden shutters that were recycled and reclaimed; it immediately became an architectural landmark. The Potato Head brand began in Jakarta, launched in 2009 as a restaurant and bar under the PTT Family hospitality group. Its founder, Ronald Akili, is an Indonesian entrepreneur and art collector based in Singapore. Also in 2010, work began on growing the beach club into a "desa" on the shore of Petitenget Beach. The wider resort complex holds a hotel, the beach club, places to eat and art installations, and the resort's architecture was a collaboration between OMA and Andra Matin.

This art centre stands in Harrania, a suburb of Cairo close to the Pyramids of Giza. Ramses Wissa Wassef, an architect, started it in 1951 with Sophie, his wife, who taught art, as a school and training centre for village children and young people; it is run as a cooperative. On land the couple bought in what was then countryside, workshops and homes were raised to his plans in traditional mud brick. He drew on the Nubian mud-brick buildings of the Aswan region, with their domes and vaults. Its artists weave tapestries straight from imagination onto the looms, never from set patterns. The centre received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1983; a museum extension came in 1989.

San Francisco's Federal Building, also named for Speaker Nancy Pelosi, is an 18-storey tower 234 ft (71.3 m) tall in South of Market. Thom Mayne of Morphosis set grey concrete walls against perforated metal panels and faceted wood ceilings. It was meant to use less than half the energy of an ordinary office tower; daylight lights 80 percent of it, and it was the first Federal Building certified under LEED. Dropping the usual HVAC system saved $11 million of a $144 million budget. Some elevators stop at every third floor, and people walk one level up or down. In one comparison it ranked lowest for employee satisfaction, at 13 percent. It won an AIA San Francisco Design Award in 2008.

The Hive, also known as the Learning Hub, is a multi-purpose teaching building at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, opened in 2015 within a campus redevelopment. Thomas Heatherwick designed it at a cost of S$45 million as 12 eight-storey towers that narrow towards the ground and gather around a public atrium. Instead of rectangular rooms and corridors, these tubular stacks hold 56 classrooms without corners, a plan meant to bring students and staff from different fields together. Concrete is the main material, with metal balcony stacks and screened stairs. Twelve silicone moulds pressed horizontal lines into the tower walls, and the reddish-brown stair and lift cores carry 700 drawings by British artist Sara Fanelli. Informally it is called the "dim sum basket building". It gained a Green Mark Platinum Award before completion and a 2015 WAN Concrete in Architecture shortlisting.

The Index is an 80-storey skyscraper in Dubai, 328 m (1,076 ft) high. Services fill floors 1 to 4 and offices 5 to 29; homes run from 31 to 77, with duplex penthouses on 73 and 75 and triplex penthouses from 77 to the top. A double-height sky lobby with a pool and gym divides work from living. The tower runs exactly east–west, so concrete cores at each end block the low, deep-reaching sun of morning and evening, leaving only the south face open to the high midday sun, where extensive shades cut solar gain. This cuts the need for air conditioning; even in high summer, without cooling, the interior should stay at or below 28 °C (82 °F). In 2011 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat named it Best Tall Building Middle East & Africa.

Marcel Breuer designed this 35,000-square-metre building when IBM moved its French laboratory for research and product development out of Paris. It sits in 23 hectares of rough country by La Gaude, overlooking Nice and its airport. IBM chose the site because the Riviera could attract France's best engineers, the airport, the country's second largest, was close by, and the move suited the government's aim of decentralising away from Paris. The façades are modular prefabricated concrete panels, a system Breuer later used on many institutional buildings and on the whole town of Flaine. At first, 700 people, mostly engineers, worked here; by 1987 the original B1 building held 1,500 engineers. B2 was added in 1969 and B3, which has a patio, in 1978. Here IBM engineers created the first business telephone systems in the world to be controlled by computer.

Jakob + MacFarlane's Orange Cube houses offices and a design showroom in La Confluence, in Lyon's 2nd arrondissement. The Paris-based firm won a 2005 competition for it, launched to raise interest in the industrial Confluence district, and the brief required the scheme to include negative space. Their response is an orange cube punched full of holes, nicknamed "La Mimolette" after a cheese of similar colour. Twenty-five perforated aluminium screens, thermo-lacquered and all produced locally, cover two façades. Two conical voids cut into the volume and pull in cool air; writing in Architectural Record, Jenna M. McKnight said they open a conversation with the river that nearly brings it indoors. Finished in 2011 for about €12 million, the building has 6,284 m² of interior space on a 29 m × 33 m footprint.

Frank Gehry designed the LUMA Tower for the LUMA Arles arts centre, for arts patron Maja Hoffmann, who founded the LUMA Foundation. Hoffmann and Gehry first put a scheme to the city in July 2008, but it was refused for its height; the third attempt was approved, in December 2012. The finished tower, 56 metres tall with 15,000 square metres of space, rises from a rotunda called "the Drum", 54 metres across and 16 to 18 metres high. Gehry said he set out to evoke the place, from Van Gogh's Starry Night to the rock clusters of the Camargue, with the drum echoing the round plan of the Roman amphitheatre. Inside are exhibition spaces, workshops, a library, a 150-seat auditorium and a café. It opened on 4 July 2021.

This museum in Menton, on the French Riviera, honours Jean Cocteau and incorporates the collection of Séverin Wunderman, a businessman and Cocteau admirer who gave the town almost 1,000 of the artist's works in 2005. The council launched an international competition in 2007, and in June 2008 French architect Rudy Ricciotti, who championed 'hedonist architecture' in the 1980s, was named the winner. The foundation stone was laid that December, the shell was finished in January 2011, and the museum opened the same year. Ricciotti drew on Cocteau's life and work, saying that here black and white act less as colours than as "an interplay of structural forces". The façade has been compared to "a fierce set of teeth" and to a spider, its jagged black pillars sprawling like legs. The museum covers 29,000 sq ft in seven parts.

This memorial marks the Ardeatine massacre of 24 March 1944, when German occupation troops in Rome killed 335 civilians and political prisoners, a reprisal for an attack on the SS Police Regiment Bozen in Via Rasella the day before. The Ardeatine Caves site was later declared a National Monument and Memorial Cemetery, open daily. A national competition produced the design, by five architects, Mario Fiorentino, Giuseppe Perugini, Nello Aprile, Cino Calcaprina and Aldo Cardelli, and two sculptors. Mirko Basaldella's bronze gate fuses the barbed wire of battlefields and concentration camps with the curling forms of a Tree of Life. At the entrance, Francesco Coccia's giant concrete statue shows three men standing as one, their faces turned to the forecourt, the old quarries and the burial slab. On every anniversary a state ceremony is held and 335 names are read out.

Also known as the Viadotto dell'Industria, the bridge over the Basento or simply the Musmeci Bridge, this crossing in Potenza, Basilicata, joins the city-centre exit of the Sicignano–Potenza motorway to the main roads serving the south of the city. Italian engineer Sergio Musmeci designed it in 1967, and it was built from 1971 to 1976 as a full expression of his ideas on architecture. Its whole structure is a single reinforced-concrete membrane, around 30 cm (1 ft) thick, moulded into four arches that run into each other. This sheet takes a "finger-like" form that carries the entire bridge and doubles as a footpath for pedestrians. No prefabricated parts went into its construction. In 2003 Italy's Ministry of Heritage and Culture listed it as a "monument of cultural interest".

Designed by Renzo Piano, the Genova San Giorgio Bridge is a motorway viaduct over the Polcevera river and the Sampierdarena and Cornigliano districts of Genoa. It replaced the Ponte Morandi, which partly fell on 14 August 2018 and was pulled down in June 2019. The new structure combines steel and concrete; it runs 1,067 metres with a width of about 31 metres and a height of 45 metres, and its 19 spans rest on 18 reinforced-concrete piers that all share one elliptical section. Robots inspect its underside and clean the windproof barriers and solar panels. A network of 240 fibre-optic sensors keeps track of deck movement, pier tilt, vibration and traffic, reporting live to the operator of that stretch of motorway. The bridge opened on 3 August 2020.

Kim Swoo-geun designed this multi-purpose stadium, whose profile follows the graceful curves of Joseon white porcelain. It was the main venue built for the 1986 Asian Games, the tenth, and for the 1988 Summer Olympics, and it anchors the Seoul Sports Complex in Songpa District, south of the Han River in the city's southeast. Planned first for the Asian Games, it became the centrepiece of the Olympic plans once Seoul won the right to host them in September 1981. It officially opened on 29 September 1984. Spectators sit on two tiers, 69,950 in all, beneath a roof that covers part of the stands. It is South Korea's largest stadium. At the Olympics it staged athletics, the football finals, the individual show-jumping final, and both the opening and the closing ceremony.

At the heart of Seoul, in Taepyeongno in Jung District, the city hall connects to City Hall Station, which serves Subway Lines 1 and 2. In front stand Seoul Plaza and the former city hall, a registered cultural asset that now houses the Seoul Metropolitan Library. A competition jury picked Yoo Kerl of iArc on 18 February 2008. The design draws partly on the eaves of traditional Korean homes. Planned as eco-friendly, it has a double-skin façade and is meant to draw over a quarter of its energy from photovoltaic, geothermal and solar thermal sources. Inside, a green wall of 70,000-plus plants of 14 species spreads over 1,516 m²; in 2013 Guinness World Records named it the world's largest vertical garden. The public was let in on 27 August 2012, and the city government moved in on 1 September.

Government Complex Sejong, credited to Haeahn Architecture, was built in Sejong, South Korea, to help form a new administrative city outside the capital region. Moving central government agencies there was meant to ease crowding around the metropolis, decentralise and spread development more evenly. The complex stands on a 213,000-square-metre plot and has seven storeys above one basement level. Across its roofs runs a garden whose design draws on Sunseongnori, a traditional Korean pastime; in 2016 Guinness World Records named it the world's largest garden, a 3.6 km route tying 15 buildings together. Inside, nothing separates departments or individual staff, and desks are grouped together whatever a person's rank.

Seonyudo Park in Seoul, by Seoahn Total Landscape (Jung Young-sun) and Joh Sung-yong, is an ecological park covering a small island of 0.11 km², where it meets the Yanghwa Bridge. Building that bridge between 1962 and 1965 made Seonyubong vanish entirely. From 1978 to 2000 the island held a water filtration plant serving south-western Seoul. After the plant shut in December 2000, the site was turned into a park, which opened to the public on 26 April 2002. Its water purification plant, made from the old works, now cleans water with aquatic plants and sends it on to other facilities in the park. In the Garden of Green Columns, the columns of the former reservoir have been kept standing, with ivy climbing them, as a trace of the reservoir that once held water.

Rem Koolhaas of OMA designed the Seoul National University Museum of Art. The project began in 1995, when Professor Jong-Sang Lee proposed a museum and the Samsung Cultural Foundation agreed to fund it. Work on the structure ran from 2004 to 2005, and the museum opened on 8 June 2006. Its outer walls are U-glass, through which the steel trusses of the frame show. The architect used the sloping site as part of the design: the building cantilevers from a concrete core, so it seems light, almost floating. The slope also serves the auditorium, which has ramped seating. The plan is divided into four areas: operations, education, exhibition and a library. The museum regularly shows student work as well as work by designers and artists from Korea and abroad.

The Galileo Galilei Planetarium, known locally as the Planetario, sits inside Palermo's Parque Tres de Febrero in Buenos Aires. The idea took shape in 1958, through an agreement between José Luis Peña, a Socialist member of the city council, and Dr. Aldo Cocca, the municipal Secretary of Culture. Building began in 1962 under architect Enrique Jan. It was inaugurated on 20 December 1966 but opened officially to the public only on 5 April 1968. It stands on the ground from which the Buenos Aires Cricket Club and the Buenos Aires Football Club were evicted in the late 1940s. The building has five floors and six staircases. Its main room, 20 metres across, seats 360 under a half-sphere dome lined with reflective aluminium, and the museum keeps a piece of Apollo 11 moon rock given by Richard Nixon.

Serra Dourada Stadium is a football ground in Goiânia, in the Brazilian state of Goiás, designed by Paulo Mendes da Rocha, the Brazilian architect and Pritzker Prize winner. It was completed in 1975 and opened on 9 March of that year. A crowd of 79,610 came to the opening match, which set the stadium's attendance record. The state government of Goiás owns the ground, and state matches make up most of its fixtures. Three local clubs, Vila Nova, Goiás Esporte Clube and Atlético Goianiense, have stadiums of their own for most league games, but they move to Serra Dourada for derbies and other big matches. In 1989 it served as one of the venues of the Copa América.

Cuba's National Art Schools, now the Instituto Superior de Arte, were designed by Ricardo Porro, Vittorio Garatti and Roberto Gottardi, and historians rank them among the Cuban Revolution's most outstanding architectural achievements. Fidel Castro and Che Guevara founded the schools in 1961 on a former country club site in Cubanacán, far western Havana. The design broke with the International Style of the day. With the US embargo making imported rebar and Portland cement expensive, the architects turned to local brick and terracotta tile, building with the Catalan vault for its potential for organic form. There were five schools: modern dance, plastic arts, dramatic arts, music and ballet. The music school snakes for 330 metres, following the land's contours toward the river. Work halted in July 1965, finished or not, and in November 2010 Cuba made the schools national monuments.

Zaha Hadid designed the Sheikh Zayed Bridge, which links the island of Abu Dhabi with the mainland and with Abu Dhabi International Airport. It honours Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan and was built between 1997 and 2010, becoming the island's third crossing to the mainland, after the Maqta and Mussafah bridges. Seen from the side, it reads as a wave, led by a main arch 235 metres long that rises 60 metres over the water. The whole crossing measures 842 metres and carries four traffic lanes plus walkways for people on foot. Both the form and the lighting, whose colours shift slowly, were meant to suggest movement. It was opened on 25 November 2010 by Sheikh Khalifa, the late President of the UAE.

Lusail Stadium, credited to Foster + Partners and Populous, is the largest stadium by capacity in Qatar and the Middle East, and belongs to the Qatar Football Association. It was one of eight venues built for the 2022 FIFA World Cup and hosted the final, Argentina against France, on 18 December 2022. Construction started on 11 April 2017, carried out jointly by HBK Contracting and China Railway Construction Corporation, and the Lusail Super Cup opened the ground on 9 September 2022. Solar power cools it, it is claimed to have a zero carbon footprint, and GSAS awarded it five stars for design and construction. After the tournament, seating was to drop from 88,966 to 40,000, and other parts were to become community space for shops, cafés, sport, learning and a health clinic. By December 2025 this had not happened.

Qatar University is a public research university and the only public university in Qatar. Its campus lies in Al Tarfa, a district at the northern edge of Doha, roughly 16 kilometres from the city centre. The institution started in 1973 as the College of Education, created by a decree of the Emir of Qatar. A College of Business & Economics was added in 1985, and these new colleges led to a major expansion of the campus, overseen by Kamal El Kafrawi. About 70% of the students are women, who have their own set of classrooms and facilities.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was designed by Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum (HOK). Planning and site selection for a replacement of the old airport began in 1974, and construction started in 1976. King Fahd opened the airport on 16 November 1983, and scheduled flights began on 5 December. Each of the four original terminals is a triangle in plan covering 47,500 square metres, with eight aero-bridges, and three linking buildings 168 metres long connect them. Parking holds 11,600 vehicles. The Royal Pavilion shares the triangular plan, under a roof of 33 arched sections peaking 30 metres above the ground, lit by glass walls. HOK also designed the airport's hexagonal mosque, covering 5,600 m². Separately, the Royal Mosque has stained glass by British artist Brian Clarke, considered the largest and most technically advanced such work of the modern period.

The Holiday Inn Beirut was designed by French architect André Wogenscky with Lebanese architect Maurice Hindié, and built from 1971 to 1974 by Lebanese developer Abdal Mohsin Kattan. The 26-storey tower had 400 rooms, a revolving restaurant on its top floor and a nightclub just below, in the mixed-use St. Charles City Center, with a cinema, offices, shops and a supermarket. Opening in 1974, during Beirut's boom years, it had just one normal year before the Lebanese Civil War started. From 25 October 1975 it was the focus of the Battle of the Hotels, months of fighting that killed more than 1,000 people. Scavengers then stripped it to its concrete frame. The Lebanese Army now controls it within a military zone, and its two half-owners disagree over renovating it as condos or replacing it with a new tower.

Rifat Chadirji's Monument to the Unknown Soldier went up in 1959 in Firdos Square, Baghdad. The Iraqi architect received the commission to honour the wars of independence waged against the monarchy the British had imposed. His arch was a modern reworking of the ancient arch of Ctesiphon. Design sketches found at Baghdad's Institute of Fine Arts reveal the image behind the form: a mother bending down to lift her martyred child. The structure has been described as simple, symbolic and modernist, and comparing it with the monument that later replaced it shows how Iraqi art of the period grew more abstract and sophisticated. The original arch was eventually removed to clear space for a statue of Saddam Hussein.

The Kazakhstan Central Concert Hall in Astana is by the Italian architect Manfredi Nicoletti. President Nursultan Nazarbayev opened it on 15 December 2009, the country's Independence Day. Its outline recalls the movement of a flower's petals. Outside, curved, leaning concrete walls, clad in glass panels painted blue on the back, shield the rooms within from Astana's harsh climate. Behind them, a foyer 30 metres tall and over 3,000 square metres in area is meant to work as an indoor public square at city scale, open all year. The main hall, with 3,500 seats, is among the largest of its kind. Acoustic curtains and a false ceiling called a black hole, which soaks up most reflected sound, let it stage classical and pop music, ballet and conferences. Two smaller rooms, of 400 and 200 seats, suit chamber music, films and meetings.

The Palace of the Republic in Almaty, by Nikolai Ripinsky, Leonid Ukhobotov and their team, stands on Abai Square, where Dostyq and Abai avenues meet. Built in 1970 under the name Lenin Palace of Culture, it opened during celebrations for the centenary of Lenin's birth. Its tent-like roof rests on eight concrete pillars, and since the outer walls stop short of it, the roof seems to float. A white chandelier hangs in the 13-metre-high main lobby, where national motifs appear in details such as the stair railings and marble floors. The stage is 48 metres wide and 18 deep; after a reconstruction the hall seats 2,567 instead of 3,000. In 1978 the Alma-Ata Declaration on primary health care was adopted here, and in 2008 the building was listed as a monument of republican significance.

The arched stage of the Tallinn Song Festival Grounds was built in 1959, ahead of the Estonian SSR's 20th anniversary, to a design by Henno Sepmann working with Alar Kotli and Endel Paalmann. The grounds, in Kadriorg, host the Estonian Song Festival, Laulupidu, every five years. Karl Burman's earlier stage on this spot, built for the 9th festival in 1928, held 15,000 performers. The new stage was planned for more than 15,000 singers, but it also works in reverse, with the show in front and the audience seated on the stage. The 15th festival, in 1960, took place on it. A 42-metre fire tower on its north side is used during festivals. In 1988 Estonians gathered here to sing patriotic hymns in what became the Singing Revolution, which led to the end of Soviet rule.

Lascaux IV, by Snøhetta with Duncan Lewis, is a life-size copy of the whole Lascaux cave. The real caves have been closed to visitors since 1963 because their condition was getting worse quickly, and several replicas now exist. An earlier one, Lascaux II, opened close by in 1983 so that people could still see the paintings without harming the originals; since 2016 a bigger and more faithful copy has been on show at Lascaux IV. It sits on the same hill above Montignac, 400 metres from the original site, within the Centre International de l'Art Pariétal, a centre for parietal (cave wall) art opened in December 2016. The museum brings digital technology, workshops and films into adjoining display rooms.

The Fondation Avicenne in Paris was built as the Maison de l'Iran, a residence for students in the Cité internationale universitaire de Paris. The architects Heydar Ghiai and Mohsen Foroughi first prepared a scheme that the Paris authorities would not approve. André Bloc then introduced them to the French architect Claude Parent, and the four of them finished a joint design in 1969. The residence was meant to give around 100 rooms to Iranian students. Its living floors hang from a macrostructure of three welded-steel frames roughly 38 metres high, and a large steel staircase outside was designed as a sculptural element in its own right. In 1972 the building passed to the Cité internationale and took the name Fondation Avicenne. In 2008 France listed it as a historic monument.

In February 1936 a fire left only the facade of Turin's Teatro Regio standing, closing it for 37 years; Carlo Mollino rebuilt it behind that front. A national competition sought an architect, but war and money troubles delayed the foundation stone until 25 September 1963, and work began only in September 1967. The house reopened on 10 April 1973 with Verdi's I vespri siciliani, staged by Maria Callas and Giuseppe Di Stefano. Its elliptical hall seats 1,750, with 37 boxes around the rim and an added acoustic shell. In the foyer Mollino turned Piranesi's Prisons into a curved, brutalist maze on four levels. Outside, custom-cut bricks form a relief of stars overlapping like fish scales. In its wider setting, the theatre belongs to Piazza Castello, and the Regio's facade counts among the Piedmontese buildings of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Erdene Zuu, at Kharkhorin in Mongolia's Övörkhangai Province, is probably the country's oldest surviving Buddhist monastery. It was founded in 1585 on the orders of Abtai Sain Khan, who led the Khalkha Mongols, after he met the 3rd Dalai Lama and Tibetan Buddhism became the state religion. Its builders reused stone from the nearby ruins of Karakorum, the 13th-century Mongol capital. Planners aimed for an outer wall with 108 stupas, like a Buddhist rosary, though probably never completed it. Its temples had painted walls and green-tiled roofs in the Chinese style. By 1792 it held 68 temples and around 15,000 lamas. In 1939 Choibalsan had it destroyed in a purge; three small temples and the stupa wall survived. After communism ended in 1990, lamas restored it for worship. It now lies within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape World Heritage Site.

Konstantin Melnikov designed the Kauchuk Factory Club, an avant-garde public building of 1927 to 1929 in Moscow's Khamovniki District, by Devichye Pole park. The Kauchuk rubber factory had moved here from Riga in 1915, under German threat, and later grew a great deal. A club fitted the 1920s national drive to replace religion with more suitable entertainment. Melnikov held that a club was no stern temple: workers should run there by choice, past home and pub. The bold outdoor stairs of his clubs came from 1920s codes requiring wide indoor stairs for fire escape; to save room inside, he joined the main halls to outside galleries, which the code did not cover. Preservationists had held off demolition as of March 2007, but the interiors have been lost to careless renovation and the windows replaced with badly sized frames.

The Kyiv Crematorium in Memory Park is seen as a landmark of neomodernist architecture, its farewell halls shaped like opened petals or portals. Avraam Miletsky designed it, and the park around it, with the monumental artists Ada Rybachuk and Volodymyr Melnychenko. Beside the crematorium, in the wider complex, the two artists worked from 1968 to 1981 on the Wall of Memory, making a retaining wall that held the park's soil into the site's centrepiece. The relief stretched 213 metres, stood 4.5 to 16 metres high and has been described as Europe's largest bas-relief. When it was nearly finished, Soviet authorities ordered it covered on ideological grounds, and in May 1982 tons of liquid concrete buried it, earning the name "Wall of Oblivion". In 2018 a fragment of about six square metres was cleared beside the path to the crematorium.

Completed in 1976, the Kuwait Water Towers are a group of 31 towers in Kuwait City. In 1965 the government asked the Swedish engineering firm VBB, known since 1997 as Sweco, to plan and carry out a modern water supply for the city. VBB raised five groups of towers in standard reinforced concrete, nicknamed "the mushroom towers" and designed by the firm's chief architect, Sune Lindström; each holds 3,000 cubic metres of water. The groups vary in number, height, colour and ornament, and each acts as a landmark for its own district. At a sixth site the Amir, Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmed, wanted something more spectacular, and the result was Kuwait Towers, a set of three, two of which also store water. Together with Kuwait Tower, the water towers won an Aga Khan Award in the 1980 cycle.

Šerefudin's White Mosque in Visoko was first built in 1477, then entirely reconstructed under the architect Zlatko Ugljen and finished in 1980. He kept the usual Bosnian plan, in which a courtyard opens onto a square prayer space under a cupola. But instead of the archetype's cupola, his roof is a quarter of a cupola, freely bent and pierced by five skylights. Five-panel windows stand for the Five Pillars of Islam while also lighting the interior. Walls and cupola are plastered concrete, with white mortar and pine inside, local travertine paving outside and iron tubes for the minarets. Inside and out it is painted white. It won the 1983 Aga Khan Award, whose jury praised its boldness and originality, and in 2007 Hungarian architects named it one of Europe's three best-designed places of worship.

Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS is a private research university in Malaysia, set up on 10 January 1997 and wholly owned by PETRONAS, Malaysia's multinational oil and gas company. Its campus spreads over 400 hectares in Seri Iskandar, a new township in the state of Perak. Foster and Partners designed the new academic complex. The master plan was finished in 2002, and the first phase of building in August 2004. Seen in plan, the complex forms a five-pointed star made of five semicircles. A "star concept" diagram, laying vision, site, programme and quality over one another, served as the template for zoning the facilities and starting the preliminary design. In 2007 the scheme won an Aga Khan Award for Architecture. Solar panels totalling 7.3 MWp have been fitted on the roof.

Majara Residence, whose Persian name means "Adventure", is a seaside holiday complex on Iran's Hormuz Island, in the Persian Gulf. Designed by Tehran's ZAV Architects and completed in 2020 as the island's first eco-tourism hotel, it won the Aga Khan Award in 2025. About 5 kilometres from the city of Hormuz, 200 domes of varied sizes, some linked, are grouped like a village. Of these, 130 contain 17 suites for up to 85 guests, and the rest hold galleries, restaurants, cafés, a prayer room and a shop. ZAV adapted Superadobe, stacked bags of on-site earth and sand that form a compression structure, to make wider, lower domes, and trained 50 unskilled locals as master builders. Earth's high thermal mass suits the dry climate. The domes are tinted yellow, red, blue and green, not the island's own ochre, for environmental reasons.

The Price Tower in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, is a 19-storey, 67-metre skyscraper, one of the few tall buildings by Frank Lloyd Wright, derived from a 1929 scheme for apartment blocks in New York City. Harold Price commissioned it in 1952 as a headquarters for the H. C. Price Company. Wright thought the site ideal: skyscrapers, he believed, belonged in the countryside, standing clear of the landscape. The plan sets parallelograms built from 30-60-90 triangles around a pinwheel-shaped core of four piers, from which the concrete floors cantilever. The facade combines embossed copper spandrels and louvres, tinted glass and poured stucco. Its roughly 3,900 m² of rentable space held three office quadrants and one of apartments, among the first skyscrapers to mix the two from the outset. It won the AIA Twenty-five Year Award in 1983 and is a National Historic Landmark.

Monterey Bay Aquarium, a nonprofit in Monterey, California, designed by EHDD, focuses on the marine habitats of its bay. It stands on the site of the defunct Hovden sardine cannery, which the team intended to rebuild rather than destroy; EHDD said demolition would be "a big disservice" to visitors and the community. Concrete sections stayed, the warehouse became offices, a seawater system replaced the pump house, and the building wraps around the old boiler house, kept as a static exhibit. Windows, plain cement walls, many roofs and exposed ducts echo the cannery and Cannery Row. Nearly half the aquarium stands over water up to 37 metres deep, so foundations went in at low tide, often at night. Opening on 20 October 1984, it was the largest public aquarium in the US and the first to show a living kelp forest.

Harry Weese designed the first group of stations for Washington's Metro, whose opening stretch began service on March 27, 1976: 4.6 miles (7.4 km) of the Red Line with five stations between Rhode Island Avenue and Farragut North. Underground, the stations are cathedral-like concrete arches washed in soft, indirect light, and the vaulted ceilings where lines cross have been said to stir an almost religious feeling. Weese devised a shared kit of parts that still guided new stations more than 25 years later, and the AIA cited his role when it named the system for its Twenty-five Year Award in January 2014. In the AIA's 2007 public survey, America's Favorite Architecture, the vaulted stations placed 106th of 150, the only brutalist design on the list. Massimo Vignelli proposed the name Metro and designed its signage.

Built from 1968 to 1971 as student rooms for The Queen's College, Oxford, the Florey Building completed James Stirling's 'Red Trilogy', after his Leicester engineering and Cambridge history buildings. It shares their red industrial brick and tile, factory glazing and sculptural forms. Eleven irregular A-shaped concrete frames, 7 m apart and linked on every floor by spine beams, carry the structure, faced in red ceramic tiles. The horseshoe plan, set back from the road, opens north: every room is glazed floor to ceiling towards the inner court and looks over the River Cherwell, while few windows face outward. It has 74 single rooms on four levels and double-height graduate rooms above. The provost Howard Florey commissioned it, and it bears his name. Listed Grade II in 2009 and raised to II* in 2018, it has stood empty since 2018–19.

Rudy Ricciotti's memorial occupies the Camp de Rivesaltes, a military camp built in 1938 near Perpignan used as an internment and transit camp during the Second World War. Between 11 August and 20 October 1942, 2,313 foreign Jews, 209 of them children, were sent from here through Drancy to Auschwitz and murdered. The last residents left in February 1977. After part of its archives turned up in a rubbish dump in 1997, more than a thousand people, among them Simone Veil, Claude Simon and Edgar Morin, signed a petition against its threatened demolition. In 2000 the site joined the state's supplementary list of historic monuments, and the department's General Council bought part of the land. Ricciotti won the competition in January 2006, with Robert Badinter as sponsor, and Prime Minister Manuel Valls inaugurated the site on 16 October 2015.

Designed by O'Donnell + Tuomey after a design competition run by RIBA Competitions, this student centre at the LSE opened in January 2014 as the school's first new campus building in more than four decades. It takes its name from Saw Swee Hock, a Singaporean statistician and philanthropist. Inside, it brings together the LSE Students' Union, the accommodation office and the careers service with a bar, an events space, a gym, a dance studio, a media centre, a learning café and a terrace on the roof. Its environmental performance earned a BREEAM 'Outstanding' rating. Among its prizes were a RIBA National Award and the London Building of the Year Award, and it reached the Stirling Prize shortlist. The project is dated 2009 to 2015, the year O'Donnell + Tuomey received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal.

Alsop and Störmer designed Peckham Library, a library and community building in south-east London, with AKT II as engineers. Its form is an upside-down capital L: the upper block rests on thin steel columns that lean at seemingly random angles, and the outside is covered in pre-patinated copper. The design lifts the footprint of a standard library into the air, leaving a public space underneath and moving the quiet reading areas away from the noise of the street. Of the building's five floors, the library service takes up the fourth. It opened to the public on 8 March 2000, and the culture secretary Chris Smith opened it officially on 15 May. That same year it won the Stirling Prize. More than half a million people visit it every year.

The artist Damien Hirst created Newport Street Gallery in London to show works from his own collection and to stage exhibitions that interest him. He announced the plan in March 2012, and it opened in October 2015 with a café, a shop and offices for his company. The building began in 1913 as a workshop making theatre scenery and carpentry. Its architect was John Woodward, then the London County Council's district surveyor for that part of the city, and it is listed at Grade II. Caruso St John redesigned it as a gallery, work praised for its 'virtuosity' that won the RIBA Stirling Prize in October 2016. Across 37,000 square feet (3,400 m²) on two levels there are six exhibition spaces, one of them with a ceiling 11 metres (36 ft) high.

The Everyman Theatre stands on Liverpool's Hope Street, at its northern end. The company was founded in 1964 inside Hope Hall, a dissenters' chapel of 1837 that later became a cinema, in a part of the city known for its bohemian, politically sharp character, and it soon became known for ground-breaking productions. In July 2011 the theatre shut so that it could be rebuilt from scratch, and the new building by Haworth Tompkins reopened in February 2014. That October the practice won RIBA's Stirling Prize, given for the year's best building in Britain, for the new Everyman.

Dominique Perrault won an international competition in 1992 for this sports complex in Berlin's Prenzlauer Berg, built for the city's unsuccessful bid for the 2000 Summer Olympics. His idea was an orchard of apple trees with two buildings sunk into the ground, one round and one rectangular, both covered in wire mesh that shimmers in the sun so they look more like sheets of water than buildings. The complex holds the Velodrom, an indoor cycling arena for up to 12,000 people that was also Berlin's biggest concert venue until Uber Arena opened in 2008, and a swimming pool. The arena's steel roof, 142 metres across, is the largest in Europe. The arena replaced the Werner-Seelenbinder-Halle, pulled down in 1993. Perrault received second prize in the German Award of Architecture for the velodrome and Olympic pool.

The Neurosciences Institute moved to San Diego in 1993 and, after temporary quarters, settled in 1995 into this three-building complex by Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects on the campus of The Scripps Research Institute, on Torrey Pines Mesa. The aim in choosing an architect was to realise a vision of a 'scientific monastery', where the brain could be studied creatively with few rules and unlimited chances to talk. Severud Associates engineered the structure. With the acoustician Cyril Harris, the architects shaped a 352-seat auditorium whose walls and ceiling are lined with faceted plaster panels that scatter sound so each seat hears the same; it became a favoured venue for music and performance in the area. The complex received an AIA Honor Award for Architecture in 1997. After the institute restructured in 2012, Scripps took over the buildings.

Moesgaard Museum, a regional museum of archaeology and ethnography in Denmark, stands east of Beder, a suburban village of Aarhus. Its large new building by Henning Larsen Architects, inaugurated in 2014, holds both the public galleries and the base for its academic work. A wide central staircase organises the building: changing exhibitions on world history and culture fill the upper floors, and the permanent displays on the history and culture of Denmark, Scandinavia and Europe sit below. Finds on show include the Grauballe Man, described as the best-preserved bog body in the world, and the large ritual weapon deposits from Illerup Ådal, evidence of Iron Age power struggles and war. The roof is covered in grass, and the 2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships ran over it. In 2015 the building received the International Architecture Award from The Chicago Athenaeum.

Caruso St John won The New Art Gallery Walsall after an international contest in 1995, and the commission brought the practice wider attention. Opened in January 2000, the gallery of modern and contemporary art in this West Midlands town took the place of Walsall's old gallery and of an arts centre the council had shut nearly ten years before. It cost £21 million in public money: £15.75 million came from the UK National Lottery, and more from City Challenge and the European Regional Development Fund. The five-storey building is faced in pale terracotta and has 5,000 m² (53,820 sq ft) of floor space; inside, concrete is used heavily alongside Douglas fir boarding 75 mm thick. Richard Wentworth and Catherine Yass designed the public square around it. In 2000 it was on the Stirling Prize shortlist.

The Glucksman, formerly the Lewis Glucksman Gallery, is an art museum at University College Cork, designed by the Irish practice O'Donnell & Tuomey with Arup Consulting Engineers. It stands near the main gate of a campus that adjoins Cork city centre. Three floors of galleries host themed temporary shows. President Mary McAleese opened it on 14 October 2004. In June 2005 the RIAI, Ireland's architects' institute, named it the country's best public building; its other prizes include a UK Civic Trust award and an RIBA award, and it was one of the last few in the running for the Stirling Prize in 2005. The 2009 Cork floods closed it, with other campus buildings, from November that year until January 2010. It is named after its benefactor, the Wall Street financier Lewis Glucksman, who chaired Lehman Brothers, Kuhn, Loeb.

Built to mark 25 years of Indian independence, the Hall of Nations at Pragati Maidan in New Delhi was designed by Raj Rewal, with Mahendra Raj as structural engineer. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi inaugurated it in 1972 for Asia 72, the India International Trade Fair. It has been called the world's first reinforced concrete space frame and, at the time, the largest in span. Four halls of different sizes made up the group, linked by ramps. When plans to demolish it for redevelopment came to light in November 2015, architects and museums such as MoMA protested, and the Centre Pompidou asked the Indian government to consider preserving the buildings as heritage. With cases still before the Delhi High Court, it was torn down overnight in April 2017, drawing criticism in India and abroad. Bharat Mandapam now occupies the site.

The Shri Ram Centre, a New Delhi theatre company and venue, sits on Safdar Hashmi Marg in the Mandi House area, close to Kamani Auditorium, the National School of Drama, Triveni Kala Sangam and Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra. Its Brutalist building went up between 1966 and 1969, designed by Shiv Nath Prasad with Mahendra Raj and helped by the theatre figure Ebrahim Alkazi, while the industrialist Vinay Bharat Ram of the Shriram Group oversaw the work. It opened in 1971: the first play, Sai Paranjpye's Hindi play Ek Tamasha Achchha Khasa, was staged on 26 February that year. Its main hall, Shankar Lal Murli Dhar Auditorium, seats 375 on two levels behind a proscenium, 300 in the stalls and 75 in the balcony. Prasad, an architect and planner known for Brutalist work, was nicknamed the 'Le Corbusier of India'.

Joseph Allen Stein designed both the India International Centre's main complex in New Delhi and its annex beside Lodhi Gardens. He also designed several other major institutions around it, so the area is popularly known as 'Steinabad'. Japan's Prince Akihito, visiting India on his honeymoon, laid the foundation stone in 1960, and S. Radhakrishnan, the second President of India, inaugurated the centre in 1962. Its own description calls it 'Triveni', Sanskrit for 'a structure of three', after its three main streams of activity.
