The Gandhi-King Plaza, honouring Martin Luther King Jr. and Mahatma Gandhi, was opened by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on 21 January 1970, and Karan Singh, the IIC's president, inaugurated the annex in 1996.

Masjid-e-Tooba, also called Gol Masjid ('Round Mosque'), stands in Karachi's Defence Housing Authority, Phase II, close to the main Korangi Road. The Pakistani architect Babar Hameed Chauhan designed it, with Zaheer Haider Naqvi as structural engineer. Work started in 1966 and took three years, ending in 1969. The prayer hall sits beneath one wide dome, 212 feet (65 m) across, with no columns or pillars inside, and the dome rests on a low wall that runs around it. The hall holds up to 5,000 worshippers, and a single minaret rises 120 feet (37 m). Of all mosques with one dome and no pillars in the central prayer hall, it is considered the largest.

The Teacher-Student Centre, known as TSC, stands on the University of Dhaka campus in Shahbagh, Dhaka. The university set it up in 1961 through its Division of Public Affairs, and the Pakistan Government and the Ford Foundation paid for its construction. Credited to Constantinos Doxiadis, the building is arranged around a court, and a second, butterfly-shaped roof spreads over the front of the main block to help keep it cool. Extensions added in the 1980s brought north–south cross-ventilation. Inside are dining, meeting and rehearsal rooms, libraries, rooms for art and music, stages, a multipurpose hall, game rooms and a film lab, which make it the social and cultural centre of the campus. Many important political meetings and debates took place here during the Bangladesh Liberation War.

In 2013 Kunlé Adeyemi of NLÉ proposed the Makoko Floating School as a prototype for Makoko, a Lagos waterfront community: a school floating beside the homes, clear of floods on land. Built mainly of wood, with bamboo and other local materials, it was a triangular A-frame with a play area of about 1,000 square feet. Classrooms on the second tier, partly enclosed by adjustable louvres, had a playground beneath and another open-air classroom on the roof. About 250 plastic barrels kept it afloat, and it used solar cells, rainwater collection and composting toilets. It won the 2013 AR+D emerging architecture award and was shortlisted for the Design Museum's Design of the Year 2014. Abandoned for safety reasons in March 2016, it collapsed in a storm that June. A prefabricated second version won a Silver Lion at the 2016 Venice Biennale.

The Royal Theatre of Rabat, previously called the Grand Theatre of Rabat, stands on the Bou Regreg river's left bank in Morocco's capital. Zaha Hadid designed it with Zaha Hadid Architects; it was among her last major projects, already under development when she died in 2016, and building went on until it was finished in 2021. Its composition takes cues from the river's winding course, from Arabic calligraphy, and from Islamic and Moroccan building traditions. The main auditorium seats 1,821, its faceted surfaces drawing on Moroccan muqarnas; a smaller theatre seats 170 or holds 250 standing, and an outdoor amphitheatre takes about 7,000. Reinforced concrete and steel form the structure, with glass fibre reinforced concrete (GRC) on parts of the skin so its complex geometry could be built. It opened on 22 April 2026 with an inaugural arts programme.

Carrières Centrales, a group of modernist housing estates designed in the 1950s by Georges Candilis, Shadrach Woods and Alexis Josic, lies in Casablanca's Hay Mohammadi district; Nid d'Abeille, one of its blocks, is credited to Candilis and Woods of ATBAT-Afrique. The estate was the first site to test an 8 x 8 metre model that was pioneering in collective housing. Shaped by the shared life of the slums and by Le Corbusier's Unité d'habitation, the mid-rise blocks offer strongly communal living over several levels, with countless balconies. Residents named the buildings Nid d'Abeille (honeycomb) and Sémiramis after their likeness to honeycombs and to the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. Both count among the first examples of vernacular modernism, which weighs local culture and climate alongside modernist principles. Many residents have since altered the blocks, most often by closing in the balconies.

Nasreddin Murat-Khan designed this cricket ground in Lahore, built in 1959 as the Lahore Stadium; Mian Abdul Khaliq and Company carried out the construction. On 19 March 1972, President Zulfikar Ali Bhutto renamed it after the Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. Ahead of the 1996 Cricket World Cup, Nayyar Ali Dada, a graduate of the National College of Arts, renovated it in 1995–96 with hand-laid red brick and arches, and plastic seats replaced the concrete benches. The area under the stands was enclosed for shops and offices, and the redesigned enclosures cut capacity from 65,250 to 27,000. On March 17, 1996 it staged the World Cup final, the first played in Pakistan. It also houses the Pakistan Cricket Board's headquarters.

Highpoint I is an apartment complex in Highgate, London, designed by the Tecton Group, which Berthold Lubetkin co-founded in 1932 with Francis Skinner, Denys Lasdun and five others. Tecton, which broke up in 1939, helped lead the arrival of continental modernism in Britain. Built in 1935, the block was an important experiment in tall housing. It was first meant for working-class tenants, yet it raised the standard of luxury for urban living. Tecton went on to design Highpoint II on the neighbouring plot, which was more luxurious still.

Built in 1934 at London Zoo in Regent's Park, this penguin enclosure by Berthold Lubetkin and the Tecton Group follows the International Modernist style. Experimental for its day, it was made wholly of reinforced concrete with a white cement render. Cantilevered spiral ramps interlock across a central elliptical pool, seemingly unsupported; there is also a glass-fronted diving area, nesting boxes at one end and an outer viewing gallery. The ramps relied on the idea that concrete slabs cast in one piece, with joints as strong as mid-span, could take any length and shape. It was listed Grade I in 1970. It housed the zoo's penguins for 70 years, closed in 2004 amid changing views on captivity and doubts over its fitness for penguins, was replaced by Penguin Beach, and after a spell unused became a water feature.

Near Cardross, Argyll and Bute, this former Roman Catholic seminary was designed by Gillespie, Kidd & Coia and is seen as their most significant work. A 1946 fire at the seminary's earlier home in Bearsden, a Glasgow suburb, made a new building necessary. Talks began in 1953, but plans were settled only in 1961, when building started. Firmly modernist and brutalist, with a large debt to Le Corbusier, it is widely ranked among Scotland's key modernist works; Docomomo International calls it of 'world significance', and it is one of just 42 Scottish post-war buildings listed at Category A. The seminary shut in February 1980; maintenance problems left the modern buildings unused after 1984, and vandalism followed. Since July 2020 the site has belonged to the Kilmahew Education Trust, which plans to conserve it and bring back its educational use.

The Royal Commonwealth Pool in St Leonard's, Edinburgh, is one of Scotland's principal pools. The council commissioned it in 1966, following a plan from Lord Provost Sir Herbert Brechin. Robert Matthew Johnson Marshall were the architects, with Ove Arup & Partners on the structure. Work ran from 1967 to October 1969, and the pool held the aquatic events of the 1970 British Commonwealth Games. The conservation body DoCoMoMo chose it in 1993 as one of sixty key post-war monuments in Scotland, and it is Category A listed. A refurbishment of about £37 million, led from August 2009 by S&P Architects (now Space&Place), added new 25-metre diving and teaching pools; expected by mid-2011, the pool reopened only in March 2012, and the architects won a 2012 Scottish Design Award for reuse of a listed building.

Built in Art Deco style in 1931–33 as the Warsaw base of the British Prudential Insurance Company, Marcin Weinfeld's Prudential House held offices below and luxury flats above. Wenczesław Poniż and Stefan Bryła designed its then-innovative steel frame. Rising 18 storeys and 66 m, it was interwar Poland's tallest building and, when new, Europe's fourth-tallest skyscraper; it stayed Warsaw's tallest until the Palace of Culture and Science (1955). In 1936 Janusz Groszkowski fitted a 27-metre antenna to the roof and started Europe's first television broadcasts there. In the Warsaw Uprising about 1,000 shells struck it, one a 2-tonne shell from a Karl-Gerät mortar, leaving only the bent steel frame standing. After the war Weinfeld turned it into a hotel. The Art Deco façade has since been restored, and it reopened in November 2018 as the five-star, 142-room Hotel Warszawa.

Standing on Laisvės alėja, Kaunas Central Post Office was once the headquarters of the postal service and is among the most notable buildings of the period when Kaunas was Lithuania's temporary capital. Feliksas Vizbaras (1880–1966), trained in Riga and one of the key architects who shaped Kaunas modernism, designed it, and it was completed in 1931. It joined functionalism with a national decorative style, and its many innovations made it a model of Kaunas modernism; like other particularly innovative projects, it has windows of curved glass. It is one of the notable examples of that style, several of which have received the European Heritage Label (2015) and UNESCO World Heritage status (2023).

Erik Bryggman's Resurrection Chapel stands in the Turku cemetery. Dated 1938 to 1941, it was finished in wartime and ranks, with his 1935 extension to the Åbo Akademi University library, as one of his two best-known works. Where the library follows a stricter Functionalism, the chapel is a mature synthesis of his architecture, turning towards organic forms and setting up a dialogue with the landscape around it. Bryggman's work is known for mixing Nordic, classical and modernist qualities. On the strength of this design, he was asked after the war to design many war memorials and cemetery chapels, the best known at Lappeenranta, Lohja and Honkanummi in Vantaa.

Alvar Aalto designed the Turun Sanomat Building in Turku in 1929–30, around the time of his Standard Apartment Building in the city (1928–29) and the Paimio Sanatorium (1929–32). Turun Sanomat, the newspaper whose name it carries, is published in Turku, leads the regional press of Southwest Finland and ranks third among Finnish morning papers by readership, after Helsingin Sanomat and Aamulehti. The building's advanced formal language, drawn from Le Corbusier, was one of several things behind Aalto's turn to modernism, alongside his travels in Europe and his trials with prefabricated concrete in the apartment building. The newspaper building and Paimio are fairly pure modernist works, yet both already held the seeds of his doubts about strict modernism and of a bolder, more synthetic approach.

A pulp mill opened at Sunila in Kotka in 1938, where a sawmill had stood, operated by Sunila Oy, an Ahlström subsidiary. Ahlström's chief executive, Harry Gullichsen, proposed Alvar and Aino Aalto as architects; the mill, housing and town plan are dated 1936–1939. Next to the mill, staff housing mainly by Aalto grew to more than 20 buildings, mostly low-rise flats, with terraced houses and the manager's detached house, Kantola, finished first. The housing went up from the mid-1930s to the mid-1950s. The homes stand in natural woodland, meant to aid residents' health, and follow the contours of the land. Sunila is the largest Aalto-designed ensemble ever built. Finland nominated it in 2025 among 13 Aalto sites, and the Aalto Works joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in July 2026. The plant still operates as Finland's oldest surviving sulfate pulp mill.

Pier Luigi Nervi and his son Antonio, also an architect, designed the Stadio Flaminio in 1957 and 1958. Built for the 1960 Summer Olympics on the former site of the Stadio Nazionale PNF, it opened in 1959 and later hosted the Olympic football final. It stands on the Via Flaminia, 3 km northwest of central Rome and 300 metres from Parco di Villa Glori. Football was its main use, but the interior also includes a covered pool and rooms for boxing, fencing, gymnastics, weightlifting and amateur wrestling. Holding 32,000, with 8,000 places under cover, it was the Six Nations' smallest ground. Left unused for years, it is now badly decayed. In July 2017 a Getty Foundation grant paid for work on a conservation plan, with the city, Sapienza University, the Pier Luigi Nervi Project Association and DO.CO.MO.MO. Italy involved.

Richard Neutra designed and built this International Style house in the Los Feliz district of Los Angeles between 1927 and 1929. The client, physician and naturopath Philip Lovell, championed natural living and stressed health-focused features: outdoor space for sunbathing, a roof solarium and rooms planned for maximum UV light. It is often called America's first steel-frame house and is also an early use of gunite, or sprayed concrete. It uses open-web steel joists and steel posts four inches square, set five feet apart. The cantilevers look free-standing but are carried by the roof structure, and the porches and balconies hang from roof level. Repeated factory-made windows reflect the architect's interest in industrial production. The three-storey house is entered from the top floor, across a terrace. In 1932 MoMA included it in the New York exhibition that defined the International Style.

Eero Saarinen designed this house in Columbus, Indiana, for the businessman J. Irwin Miller and his wife Xenia. Landscape architect Dan Kiley, interior designer Alexander Girard and Saarinen's associate Kevin Roche helped with parts of it. The house has one storey, six bedrooms and 6,838 square feet under a flat roof on a terrace. Sixteen free-standing cruciform steel columns, four by four, carry the ceiling and define nine bays. Four zones turn in a pinwheel around a central living room with a conversation pit, much like Palladio's Villa La Rotonda, where rooms also gather round a middle space. Skylights run unbroken around the eaves. Kiley's garden gives formal European symmetry a modernist twist, drawing on farm plots he saw from the air while flying to Columbus. The Indianapolis Museum of Art has owned this National Historic Landmark since 2009.

SOM designed this New York bank branch for the Manufacturers Trust Company. The chosen design, by Charles Evans Hughes III, had glass walls and a vault visible from outside; Gordon Bunshaft was then asked to revise it. Opened in 1954, it was the first bank branch in the US built in the International Style. The facade is mostly glass in aluminium mullions; from the street one sees the ground-floor vault door, designed by Henry Dreyfuss. Each second-floor pane, about 2.9 by 6.7 metres and 680 kg, was the largest yet made for a building. Concrete floor slabs on steel and concrete beams project past the columns, unsupported at the edges. Beside the west wall floats Bertoia's Golden Arbor, a 21-metre screen of 800 brass, copper and nickel panels. The facade became a city landmark in 1997, the interior in 2011.

Credited to Lúcio Costa, this tower in Brasília sends out radio and television signals and opened in 1967 at a height of 224 metres. At its foot is a triangular block of exposed concrete, 25 metres tall and wrapped in glass, which holds the Gems Museum. Three pillars meet in a V and pass into this block; their inner parts tie into the steel tower and form its base. The metal mast rises 192 metres in three stretches of 122, 45 and 24 metres. Since the tower stands at the centre of the capital and offers a good view, a lookout for 150 people was set 75 metres up. It is the fourth tallest structure in Brazil and one of the most visible from the Juscelino Kubitschek Bridge.

Morumbi, the football stadium in the São Paulo district of the same name, was designed by João Batista Vilanova Artigas. Its formal title is Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo, and for sponsorship it is now called MorumBIS. Part of the work was done by 1960, when it opened for up to 70,000 people. Finished in 1970, it then held 149,408. Renovations and changes to the permitted limit later brought that down, to 72,039 by 2006 and to 66,795 by 2012. Its biggest crowd, 138,032 people, came in 1977, when Corinthians beat Ponte Preta 2–1. No privately owned stadium in Brazil is larger. Morumbi counts as a monument of Brazilian modernism, and the city prefecture formally recognised it as a cultural building in 2018.

Rino Levi designed this São Paulo theatre together with Fa Pestalozzi and Roberto Cerqueira César. It was built between 1947 and 1950, a time of great enthusiasm, and belongs to a turn in Levi's practice towards theatres that also produced the Cine Ufa Palace. Inside, two concert halls are stacked one above the other: Sala Esther Mesquita, with 1,156 seats, and Sala Rubens Sverner, with 339. The opening concerts, on 8–9 March 1950, were led by Camargo Guarnieri and Heitor Villa-Lobos, two leading Brazilian composers and conductors, who directed the São Paulo Symphony Orchestra in their own music and began that year's concert season. The main hall, Esther Mesquita, was later wholly destroyed, while Di Cavalcanti's facade survived.

Mario Pani Darqui designed this tower, also called Torre Banobras or the Nonoalco Tlatelolco Tower, where Insurgentes Norte meets Ricardo Flores Magón, inside the Tlatelolco housing complex in Mexico City. It is 127 metres tall with 25 floors; finished in 1962, it was then second in height in Mexico only to the Torre Latinoamericana. The tower is a triangular prism with a reinforced concrete frame, and its materials are concrete, glass and aluminium. At its highest point sits a carillon of 47 bells by Petit & Fritsen, given to the city by the Belgian government and among the tallest in the world. The state bank Banobras had its headquarters here until the 1985 earthquake, when the building was abandoned. It stayed empty until 2011, when its offices were let to other companies, and it has been remodelled at least twice.

Carlos Raúl Villanueva meant the Covered Plaza to serve as the physical and cultural centre of the University City of Caracas, inspired by halls and central squares in Europe. Planned as an indoor-outdoor "open museum", it blends art into its surroundings and architecture into art. Pierced walls, gaps in the roof and linking ramps give the space a sense of flow. It ties together many buildings of the Central Complex, including the Aula Magna, the Paraninfo, the students' union, the rector's offices and the main library. Plaza and Aula Magna were inaugurated together on 2 March 1954. UNESCO names it, with the Aula Magna and its "Clouds" by Alexander Calder and the Olympic Stadium, among the campus's leading works of modern architecture and art, and it is considered one of Venezuela's key artistic and cultural works.

Parque Central mixes housing, shops and cultural spaces in El Conde, next to Paseo Vargas in central Caracas; Centro Simón Bolívar carried it out. Its eight residential blocks, each 127 metres and 44 storeys high with 317 flats, were finished in 1972. The two office towers, the Central Park Towers, went up between 1970 and 1983, each 225 metres and 59 storeys tall. From the west tower's completion in 1979 until Santiago's Gran Torre Costanera topped out in 2012, they were South America's tallest buildings and Latin America's until 2003, when Torre Mayor in Mexico City beat them by under a metre. The complex also holds museums, cinemas and a heliport. Shortly before midnight on 17 October 2004, a fire in the East Tower, home to government offices, affected floors 34 to 50.

Credited to Juan Antonio Scasso, the Estadio Centenario is a football stadium in the Parque Batlle neighbourhood of Montevideo, owned by the Montevideo Department. Its name, "Centenary Stadium", marks a hundred years of Uruguay's Constitution. It went up between 1929 and 1930 for the first FIFA World Cup, built by immigrant workers in a record nine months. The final of that tournament, Uruguay against Argentina, ended 4–2 to Uruguay. Four lanes separate the ground's four grandstands. A 2004 remodelling added a panoramic lift to the Torre de los Homenajes, and the stadium's museum keeps a large collection of objects recalling high points of Uruguayan and world football. On 18 July 1983 FIFA named it the first Historical Monument of World Football, and no other building anywhere has received that title.

Today called the Ministry of Health Building, this rationalist block stands where 9 de Julio Avenue crosses Belgrano Avenue, in the Monserrat district of Buenos Aires. The architect José Hortal first proposed it to Manuel Alvarado, then Minister of Public Works, while the design is credited to Belgrano Alberto Blanco. Construction ran from 1932 to 1935. The ministry's offices were its first occupants, which explains the name most people still use. The building came several years before 9 de Julio Avenue took its present form. Its north and south walls carry large steel portraits of Evita Perón, made in 2011 by the Argentine artist Alejandro Marmo, who works under the single name Marmo.

Philip Johnson and Richard Foster designed the New York State Pavilion for the New York World's Fair of 1964, with Lev Zetlin as structural engineer. It is made of three structures in reinforced concrete and steel. The elliptical Tent of Tomorrow measures 76 by 107 metres under a cable suspension roof, with a terrazzo road map of the state across its floor; jacks raised the roof to the column tops 0.76 metres at a time. The observation towers, the tallest 69 metres high, were a change to the first plans, made because Rockefeller wanted the fair's tallest structure. The drum-shaped concrete Theaterama has held the Queens Theatre since 1989. NYC Parks owns the pavilion, which is on the National Register of Historic Places. After long campaigns to save it, the tent was repainted in 2014, and rehabilitation began in 2019.

Michael Wilford completed No 1 Poultry after the death of James Stirling, for whom it was one of the final designs (1988–98). The office and retail building fills the tip of a City of London site where Poultry and Queen Victoria Street converge on Mansion House Street, near Bank junction. An alternative, a Mies van der Rohe tower in the manner of the Seagram Building, was dropped after a much-publicised dispute in the 1980s. Outside, pink and yellow limestone alternate in bands and voussoirs frame the arch at the apex; the courtyard atrium shows the vivid colour typical of Stirling. Bucklersbury Passage runs through it. The turret has drawn comparison with a submarine's conning tower. After users, neighbours and experts urged Historic England to protect it, it was listed Grade II*, then the youngest building in England at that grade.

Oscar Niemeyer designed this headquarters in Segrate for Arnoldo Mondadori Editore, a major Italian publisher, and construction ran from 1970 to 1975. The commission followed a 1965 visit by the company's president, Giorgio Mondadori, to Brasília's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, also by Niemeyer. Three parts rise from a man-made lake by Pietro Porcinai: a long five-storey glass box for offices and newsrooms and two smaller, curved, more organic buildings. The glass box, 38 by 200 metres, hangs entirely from concrete arches and floats 13 metres above the water, so light glass plays against heavy concrete. The arches keep an irregular, rippling rhythm, unlike the even bays in Brasília. When the first structural scheme proved unworkable, the engineer Bruno Contarini devised the suspension system. Bronze-tinted outer glass and clear inner glass, with an air gap between, limit heat gain.

Frank Gehry designed the Stata Center, also called Building 32, for MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts: 40,000 m² of academic space over a 27,000 m² underground garage. It first opened to occupants on 16 March 2004. The site once held Building 20, a temporary wartime structure put up in haste for the Radiation Laboratory and demolished in 1998. A wide ground-floor passage, the Charles M. Vest Student Street, runs the full length of the building. Above the fourth floor it splits into the Gates and Dreyfoos towers, with computer science, AI, linguistics and philosophy upstairs. One commentator saw brick, mirror-finish steel, brushed aluminium, bright paint and corrugated metal changing at every turn and read its improvised look as a metaphor for daring research. In 2007 MIT sued Gehry and the builders over leaks, cracked masonry, mould and drainage problems.

Tadao Ando, the Japanese modernist, designed this Buddhist shrine at Makomanai Takino Cemetery in Sapporo. Its Japanese name, Atama Daibutsu, means "Large Buddha's Head". The 13.5-metre Buddha statue was carved around 2000 and had stood on its own until Ando's design took it in. He wrapped it in a man-made hill: a rotunda planted with 150,000 lavender plants. As visitors walk up, only the head shows above the slope. They then pass through a tunnel and see the full figure only once they are inside the open rotunda. The shrine opened in December 2015.

Renzo Piano Building Workshop designed the Zentrum Paul Klee near Bern between 1999 and 2005, adding to a series of art museums by Piano in which each one differs sharply from the others. A main aim of the design was to shield Paul Klee's fragile drawings from sunlight. The work is shown in a row of galleries whose forms resemble the rolling hills of the Swiss countryside. Piano explained that the gallery shapes came from naval architecture: a ship's hull is shaped to meet the waves, and in the same way his building is shaped to meet the landscape around it.

Hong Kong International Airport, at Chek Lap Kok, was planned to replace Kai Tak, which dated from 1925. Building started in 1991 and the airport opened in 1998. The terminal's detailed design went to a consortium headed by Mott Connell, Mott MacDonald's Hong Kong office, with Foster and Partners as architects, BAA PLC for airport-specific design and Ove Arup for the roof structure. Terminal 1 covers 570,000 square metres. It was the largest passenger terminal anywhere when the airport opened and is still one of the biggest, after the likes of Dubai's and Beijing Capital's Terminal 3. Its mostly glass sides were made to break in high winds, letting pressure out so the terminal can survive a severe typhoon. For all its size it was designed for convenience, with its layout and signs, moving walkways and an automated people mover.

Milstein Hall, named for Paul Milstein, was designed by OMA's Rem Koolhaas and Shohei Shigematsu and stands directly behind Sibley at Cornell University in Ithaca. It is a prominent cantilevered building: its studio space reaches out over University Avenue. It also holds a stepped auditorium used for presentations and meetings, space for crits, galleries and a sunken garden, and it is LEED-certified. Students moved in during the autumn of 2011 while it was still unfinished, and the formal completion was set for the following spring. In 2013 the American Institute of Architects gave it a design Honor Award, one of 11 such awards to buildings across the US and Canada.

Finished in 1994, the European Court of Human Rights building in Strasbourg is credited to Richard Rogers Partnership with Claude Bucher. It stands in the European Quarter, on the eastern corner where the Ill and the Canal de la Marne au Rhin cross. The aim was a symbolic landmark that was not a monument, and, given the court's nature, a welcoming, open building rather than a fortress. The court and the commission each have a large round chamber, with offices in a "tail" behind. During design, office needs rose by half after the Eastern Bloc collapsed, so the plan was lengthened. Daylight and natural ventilation serve all but the entrance hall, which has energy-saving air conditioning. The Court Room seats 260. Council of Europe member states paid the 544 million French francs, and the city gave the site.

Jean Nouvel designed the Lucerne Culture and Congress Centre, which stands by the lake in the middle of the city. It brings together a concert hall, the Museum of Art Lucerne (Kunstmuseum Luzern), conference facilities and restaurants, and its roof measures 100 by 100 metres. The design paid close attention to acoustics, and the concert hall, whose acoustics are by Russell Johnson, is counted among the leading halls in the world. That hall opened first, on 18 August 1998; the complete centre was inaugurated in March 2000. It hosts cultural events on a regular basis and is the central venue of the yearly Lucerne Festival.

Opera Village Africa, or Operndorf Afrika, was begun by Christoph Schlingensief, a German artist, actor and director for film and theatre, as an arts education project in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso's capital. In 2008 he asked Diébédo Francis Kéré, a Burkina-born architect and development activist, to realise it. Kéré combines a traditional building style with ecological thinking and sustainable materials. Local people trained in construction put up the buildings, and Kéré cools them with building materials he developed himself. Sixteen buildings, including a primary school that admits 50 new pupils a year, opened in 2011. A hospital with primary care, maternity and dental units was begun in April 2012 and opened in 2014. At the centre of the grounds a Festspielhaus, meant as a meeting place for culture, is planned as the heart of the project.

Vulcania, billed as the "European Park of Volcanism", is a volcano-themed museum and educational amusement park at Saint-Ours-les-Roches in Auvergne, 15 km to the north-west of Clermont-Ferrand. The idea came from two French volcanologists, Maurice and Katia Krafft, who died at Mount Unzen in 1991. The project, credited to Hans Hollein, ran from 1997 to 2002, and the park officially opened in 2002. Three-quarters of the foundations lie below ground, which helped restore the land. Visitors descend a ramp to a 'metaphorical volcano', a cone faced with dark stone and lined with gold metal inside. There are also research and conference spaces, IMAX theatres, greenhouses showing fertility as a benefit of volcanism, and a restaurant overlooking the park. Building within the Chaîne des Puys drew strong opposition from conservationists.

The design of Preston Bus Station came from Building Design Partnership's Keith Ingham and Charles Wilson, working with E. H. Stazicker; Ove Arup & Partners were the engineers and John Laing the builder. Built in the Brutalist style in 1968–69, it had room until 2017 for 80 double-deckers, 40 on either side. People on foot originally entered by three subways, one running directly to the Guild Hall next door. A five-floor car park for 1,100 cars is part of the design. Arup curved the car park balconies because finishing a vertical wall acceptably cost too much; the curves add to its sculptural look and protect car bumpers. The Twentieth Century Society rates it among the UK's most significant Brutalist buildings. Listed Grade II in September 2013 after two failed attempts, it was refurbished and reopened in July 2018.

Quay Quarter Tower in Sydney began life as the AMP Centre, built in 1976. 3XN's winning design was revealed on 24 September 2014, and BVN joined as executive architect to develop it with 3XN. The 2018–2021 redevelopment kept the internal core, two-thirds of the columns, beams and slabs, and nearly all the internal walls. A new northern section was added in stages and joined to the old core and southern part, which was reclad to match. The tower now reaches 216 metres over 54 floors, with cantilevers, a wholly new interior layout and twice the floor area, and it reopened under its new name in early 2022. Described as the first upcycled skyscraper anywhere, it was made World Building of the Year at the 15th World Architecture Festival, and in 2023 CTBUH judged it the world's best new tall building.

Kurilpa Bridge runs from Tank Street in Brisbane's business district to Kurilpa Point on the South Brisbane side. Baulderstone built it, with Cox Rayner Architects and Arup Engineers in its design team. The bridge is a cable-stayed, multi-mast structure based on tensegrity, where balanced tension and compression parts make a light yet very strong whole; it is the largest hybrid tensegrity bridge anywhere. Its 470 metres include a 128-metre main span, assembled from 18 steel deck sections, 20 steel masts and 16 horizontal spars. A canopy shelters its full length. Depending on the lighting, solar power supplies 75 to 100 percent of its needs. Its name, meaning 'place for water rats', is the Aboriginal word for the area around South Brisbane and West End. It was World Transport Building of the Year at the 2011 World Architecture Festival.

Morphogenesis designed the Surat Diamond Bourse, a diamond trading centre in DREAM City, Surat, Gujarat. With 660,000 square metres of floor space, it overtook the Pentagon when Guinness World Records declared it the largest office building in the world on 22 August 2023. 4,200 offices, from 28 to 700 square metres, fill nine linked 15-storey towers. A central corridor joins the towers, leading to services as in an airport terminal, and nine Panchtattva courts between them act as green spaces. The central spine opens into vertical fins that draw light winds through by the Venturi effect, while staggered atria let warm air out by the stack effect. Natural lighting halves its energy use, earning an IGBC Platinum rating. Traders have been lukewarm, given its site on the city's edge and poor links compared with Mumbai's Bharat Diamond Bourse.

Mangera Yvars designed the Minaretein building for the Qatar Faculty of Islamic Studies on the Hamad Bin Khalifa University campus, and it was completed in 2013. Besides a mosque it holds teaching and staff space and a research centre. Five large columns, standing for the five pillars of Islam and each bearing a verse from the Qur'an, carry the building. The design draws on the Islamic idea of the kulliyya, which sees faith as the source of all knowledge, and explores an endless spiral in the plan and paths linking the teaching and learning spaces with the mosque. A four-storey ablution cascade under the mosque divides the two symbolically and helps keep the mosque cool. It was named Best Religious Building at the 2015 World Architecture Festival, and RIBA nominated it the next year for its first international prize.

Scale Lane Bridge is a black steel pedestrian swing bridge in Hull, shaped like an apostrophe. A rotating mechanism swings it open to let vessels on the River Hull through, and it was the world's first bridge that lets people stay on and ride it while it moves. Planning began in 2005; McDowell+Benedetti won the competition, with Alan Baxter Ltd as structural engineers. The cantilevered deck curves upward so small boats can pass under, and swings open for bigger ones. It weighs 1,000 tonnes, carries up to 1,000 people at a time and is 53 metres long, 35 of them cantilevered. Linking the Old Town with a former industrial district, it was meant to help regenerate the area. Text and sound by Nayan Kulkarni and lighting by Sutton Vane Associates signal its movement. It opened on 28 June 2013.

The Paula Fox Melanoma and Cancer Centre in Melbourne, Australia, is both a medical centre and a research institute. It includes spaces where cancer patients are treated as well as laboratories used for cancer research. Lyons Architecture shaped the outside of the building so that it looks like a skin graft. Work on site started on 20 June 2022, and the project was delivered by Kane Constructions. Building it was budgeted at A$152 million, with A$50 million coming from the state government and another A$50 million from the federal government. The centre had its official opening on 19 April 2024, performed by Jacinta Allan, the premier of Victoria, together with prime minister Anthony Albanese.

Lyons Israel Ellis designed Wyndham Court in 1966 for Southampton City Council, with E. D. Lyons leading the job, and it was finished in 1969 close to the Mayflower Theatre and Southampton Central station. It holds 184 homes, mostly two- and three-bedroom maisonettes, plus 13 shops and three cafes or restaurants. The structure is reinforced concrete, faced in white board-marked concrete chosen to sit well with the older civic buildings that dominate the centre. On its sloping site the block has six storeys at the north end and seven at the south. Its shape calls to mind the cruise ships that leave the nearby port, and English Heritage describes its uneven facades as "sculptural and expressive". The design won an Architectural Design Project award in 1966; in 1998, despite objections from the local press, it gained Grade II listing.

In 1961 the University of East Anglia's first vice-chancellor, Frank Thistlethwaite, asked Denys Lasdun, a New Brutalist, to design the permanent campus. Lasdun put teaching and research into one 460-metre concrete block following the site's contours, with a walkway beside it and roads below. On the walkway's south side, six linked residence blocks were built to read as one. These Norfolk Terrace halls, with four more in Suffolk Terrace, are known as the "Ziggurats"; Lasdun meant them to recall French vineyards or rocks jutting from a hillside. His work here, halls, library and teaching wall together, is regarded as one of the best 1960s brutalist university campuses. Bernard Feilden replaced him as consultant architect in 1968. The Ziggurats shut in 2023 in the crisis over reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete, with no repair date as of February 2025.

The J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, D.C., is the FBI's headquarters. The GSA hired Charles F. Murphy and Associates in June 1963 to help design it, with Stanislaw Z. Gladych as chief architect. The FBI asked for bomb-proof lower storeys and only a few, tightly guarded entrances elsewhere. It is eight storeys tall facing Pennsylvania Avenue and 11 facing E Street, and two wings link its two main blocks around an open-air, trapezoid-shaped courtyard. Its buff concrete, precast and cast in place, shows the marks of rough wooden formwork around deeply recessed, square windows of bronze-tinted glass. Gerald Ford dedicated it on 30 September 1975, the month work ended. Critics at the opening were divided between warm praise and sharp dislike; in later years it has drawn wide criticism for its looks and its effect on the city.

Wurster Hall at UC Berkeley was designed by three members of the college's own faculty, Joseph Esherick, Donald Olsen and Vernon DeMars, as a home for the new College of Environmental Design (CED), and it opened in 1964 at the southeast corner of the main campus. The college had been formed in 1959 under Dean William W. Wurster, who joined together four existing units: architecture, landscape architecture, city planning and decorative arts. The architecture school went back to 1903 and John Galen Howard, and the landscape school to 1913 and John William Gregg. In 2020 the building took the name Bauer Wurster Hall, once archive papers showed that its name had been intended to honour Catherine Bauer Wurster, the college's associate dean, as well as William Wurster, for their roles in founding CED.

St. Agnes in Berlin's Kreuzberg district was built in the 1960s as a Catholic church complex by Werner Düttmann, a German architect and city planner, and it is regarded as a prime example of Brutalism. In 2012 the gallery owner König signed a long-term lease on the complex, and the German architect Arno Brandlhuber turned it into exhibition space for his gallery. König Galerie opened there as its second location in May 2015. The conversion, commissioned by Johann and Lena König, received the Berlin Architectural Prize in 2016. The gallery is not the only user of the building today: other tenants share it, among them the art studio of New York University Berlin.

The Eastern City Gate in Belgrade, officially called Rudo, went up between 1973 and 1976. Architect Vera Ćirković designed the buildings with civil engineer Milutin Jerotijević, and Milica Jakšić prepared the urban design. The complex is three towers, each 85 metres high with 28 storeys and 190 flats. Every tower is triangular and stepped, and the three stand on a circle, so one always seems to sit between the other two. Like the Western City Gate, it is brutalist. Dragoljub Mićović, who oversaw the construction, named the towers after his hometown. The complex is seen as a symbol of the city and of Yugoslav Socialism. By 2013 pieces of concrete as heavy as 60 kg were dropping from the towers, and specialists from the University of Belgrade's civil engineering faculty said the facade was in "extremely bad shape".

Ruhr University Bochum was set up in 1962, the first new public university founded in Germany after the Second World War, and classes began in 1965. The design is credited to Hentrich, Petschnigg & Partner, and the overall planning and institute buildings are dated 1963 to 1972. Unlike many older German universities, all of its buildings stand together on one campus, south of Bochum. That campus is almost wholly brutalist and is formed by 14 high-rise blocks that are close to identical. On high, rolling ground beside the Ruhr valley, at a green belt's edge, the blocks respond to the site: their roofs seem to meet one shared skyline, while their true heights change with each block's position on the land. PCB contamination means that some of the first buildings from the 1960s will be rebuilt instead of refurbished.

The Queensland Art Gallery in Brisbane was completed in 1982, the year the first stage of Robin Gibson's Queensland Cultural Centre opened on South Bank. Its 4,700 square metres of display space are split up by walls and barriers placed on purpose to steer and turn visitors as they move through. The Watermall is the main element for finding your way: it divides the quiet galleries from the more active areas for administration, public programmes and education. Shifts in ceiling height and floor level, colour and textured surfaces add variety and set the order of the display areas. Light-coloured, low-maintenance materials such as cement suit Brisbane's subtropical, almost Mediterranean climate. In 2004 the state chapter of the Australian Institute of Architects gave it the 25 Year Award, now named after Gibson, and in 2015 it became a State Heritage Place.

The Golden Mile Complex, since renamed the Golden Mile, is a high-rise on Singapore's Beach Road mixing homes and businesses. Gan Eng Oon, William Lim and Tay Kheng Soon of Design Partnership, now DP Architects, designed it; the linear city ideas of Le Corbusier and Arturo Soria y Mata influenced the design. Completed in 1973 for S$18 million, its 16-storey, 89-metre block was an early example in Singapore of combining many uses in one development. Offices and a mall fill the lower floors, lit by staggered atria. Above, terraces step back, giving upper flats views of sea and sky, and every flat has a balcony. The thin sloping slab aids ventilation and shades a lofty shared concourse. Fumihiko Maki called it a "collective form", and on 22 October 2021 the national development minister announced its gazetting as a conserved building.

The Joseph Regenstein Library in Chicago is named after Joseph Regenstein, an industrialist and philanthropist, and holds one of the world's largest collections of books. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill of Chicago designed it, with senior architect Walter Netsch in charge, on land that was once Stagg Field. The university broke ground in 1968, and the library opened in 1970, for a total of $20,750,000. Its walls are grooved limestone, which looks like concrete from far away, and it is known for its brutalist design. Five floors stand above ground, with two basements below. Each floor has a big central reading room with desks, rooms for group study, lockers and reference shelves. The stacks sit apart on the west side, so they can be kept cooler for the sake of the books, while 220 faculty studies line the east side.

The Andrews Building, made up of the Science and Humanities wings, is the oldest building on the University of Toronto's Scarborough campus. Built in 1964 close to Highland Creek, it was one of John Andrews's first large commissions, at age 29, and at the time it was among the world's biggest mostly concrete buildings. Andrews laid it out as "indoor streets" so students could move about without facing the winter cold. A central atrium, the Meeting Place, joins the two wings under a big coffered concrete skylight, and outside a stepped concrete peak climbs from the sloping walls to three large chimneys. Lectures recorded at the St. George campus were meant to be shown here on television. Andrews disliked the word brutalist, calling the college "a very human building". Time put it on its cover on 13 January 1967.

Miami Marine Stadium, finished in 1963 on land the Matheson family gave the City of Miami for water sports, is the first US stadium built for powerboat racing. Its architect, Hilario Candela, was 28 and newly arrived from Cuba; his firm's work with his distant relative Félix Candela on a Bacardí warehouse in Mexico, and internships with Max Borges Jr., architect of Havana's Tropicana Club, shaped his approach. All in concrete, its folded plate roof cantilevers from eight slanting columns anchored through the grandstand and joined by a long beam. The columns stand well back to keep views of the water clear, and a gap in the seats reveals their height. After Hurricane Andrew it was declared unsafe and abandoned in 1992. It was named a National Treasure in 2012 and joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2018.

Arthur Erickson designed University Hall for the University of Lethbridge in Canada, and it sits in the coulees that rise above the Oldman River. On 18 May 1968, once the university's first convocation was over, more than 500 students, teachers and local people marched in support of placing the university in west Lethbridge, and soon afterwards the government chose that site. With University Hall complete in 1971, the university moved to west Lethbridge permanently, and enrolment rose past 1,200 students. The building was one of four chosen for a Canadian postage stamp marking the centenary of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada.

The National Arts Centre in Ottawa, a performing arts venue on the Rideau Canal, was one of several projects launched by Lester B. Pearson's government for Canada's 1967 centenary. Built for C$46 million, it opened on 31 May 1969. Fred Lebensold based the brutalist design on the triangle and the hexagon, and the structure is reinforced concrete. The outer walls and many inner ones are faced with precast panels showing crushed brown Laurentian granite. The roof of the base forms a terraced public garden that links to the Mackenzie King Bridge, and the three main halls rise from it as hexagons clad in brown panels of varied texture. Inside, hexagons recur in ceilings, lights and floors. It was named a National Historic Site in 2006, and it reopened after renovation on 1 July 2017, for Canada's 150th anniversary.

The memorial at Majdanek, in Lublin, was put up in 1969 where the Nazi extermination camp once stood, marking 25 years since the camp's liberation, and is dedicated to victims of the Holocaust. The design is credited to Wiktor Tołkin and Janusz Dembek; Tołkin, a Polish sculptor and architect, also designed the symbolic tombstone at Stutthof. It is laid out in three parts: a symbolic gate called the Pylon, 11 metres high and 35 metres wide, at the camp's entrance; a road; and, at the far end, the Mausoleum. About 1,300 cubic metres of topsoil mixed with human ashes and pieces of bone were gathered and formed into a large mound, which was later made into the Mausoleum.

The National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto, known as MoMAK, is a national institution in Japan that collects and preserves twentieth-century art and related reference material, from Japan and from elsewhere in the world. It gives special weight to artists and movements from Kyoto and the Kansai region of western Japan, such as the Japanese-style painting of the Kyoto School. The present building, by Fumihiko Maki, replaced an older one that was taken down. It opened to visitors on 26 October 1986 with a total floor area of 9,761.99 square metres, of which 2,604.94 square metres is given over to exhibitions.

Opened in 1836, the main line station at London Bridge is the oldest in London's fare zone 1 and among the oldest in the world. Between 2009 and 2017 Grimshaw Architects thoroughly redeveloped it: all platforms were renewed, two large street-level entrances were added, and the concourses and shops were reworked. A 1970s footbridge for changing platforms gave way to an interchange concourse under the tracks, reached by lifts, stairs and escalators. A big street-level concourse with ticket office, shops and waiting areas links the platforms, opening onto St Thomas Street and Tooley Street. Through platforms rose from six to nine, all fit for 12-car trains. Prince William opened it officially on 9 May 2018; the project was valued at about £1 billion. It won a World Architecture Festival transport award and made the Stirling Prize shortlist in July 2019.

Built for the 70th anniversary of the insurer Nippon Life, the Nissay Theatre sits inside the Nissay Hibiya Building in Tokyo, designed by Togo Murano. Finished in 1963, the theatre opened with the Deutsche Oper Berlin giving the first Japanese performance of Beethoven's opera Fidelio. The auditorium has 1,330 seats, and inside it the walls and ceilings curve throughout, leaving no straight lines at all. Some 20,000 pearl oyster shells cover the ceiling. Since the opening night the stage has hosted many kinds of performance, from kabuki and opera to musicals and shows for families.

Shinjuku Park Tower, designed by Kenzo Tange and finished in 1994, is the second-tallest building in Shinjuku, Tokyo. It stands where a gas storage facility once was, and Tokyo Gas Urban Development, part of Tokyo Gas, owns and runs it. The single building is made of three linked blocks: the S tower reaches 235 metres and 52 storeys, the C tower 209 metres and 47, and the N tower 182 metres and 41. Shops fill floors 1 to 8 and offices floors 9 to 37, while the Park Hyatt Tokyo hotel takes floors 39 to 52, with a pool overlooking the city. The hotel was the main setting of Sofia Coppola's film Lost in Translation. On site, Tokyo Gas runs a centre that heats and cools the Nishi-Shinjuku high-rise district and powers the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building next door.

Toyota Stadium, in the city of Toyota in Aichi Prefecture, Japan, has its design credited to Kisho Kurokawa; the project is dated 1997 to 2001 and the stadium was built in 2001. It was made for football only, which gives matches a true football atmosphere, and the J1 League club Nagoya Grampus often plays its home games there. Because it lies outside Nagoya, though, it does little to bring together fans in the club's named home city. The stadium has a retractable roof that folds up much like an accordion, but it has stayed open since 2015 because closing it would add maintenance costs. The ground also hosted matches at the 2019 Rugby World Cup, the first Rugby World Cup held in Asia.

The NOA Building is a 15-storey landmark in Tokyo's Azabu district, in Minato, facing both Sakurada Street and Gaien-Higashi Street. Yoshitsuru Nagao, whose real estate company was founded in 1969, gave the design to the Japanese architect Seiichi Shirai. The tower stands 61.75 metres high, with 15 floors above ground and two below. Its base is clad in red brick to a height of about 8 metres, and above it rises an elliptical cylinder with almost no windows, apart from a single full-height one on the eighth or ninth floor. The building is known for its wide use of brick and for its large entrance. Among its tenants is the Embassy of Fiji.

Takanawa Gateway Station in Tokyo was designed by Kengo Kuma and is run by JR East, the East Japan Railway Company. Construction started on 10 February 2017. The station opened on 14 March 2020, just ten days before the COVID-19 pandemic forced the summer Olympics to be postponed to 2021. No station on the Yamanote or Keihin–Tōhoku lines is newer, and it is the only Yamanote Line station opened this century. It sits over the existing Tamachi Depot, and 13 hectares of depot land were redeveloped for new uses. There are four tracks and two island platforms. From each platform, three escalators and two lifts, one carrying 24 people and one carrying 18, lead up to the paid side of the second-floor concourse.

The Kasumigaseki Building, a 36-storey tower in Kasumigaseki, Chiyoda, Tokyo, was completed in 1968 and is widely seen as Japan's first modern office skyscraper. Tall buildings had not gone up in the country before because the Building Standard Law fixed a strict height limit of 31 metres until 1963, when a limit on floor area ratio took its place. The design is credited to Yamashita Sekkei with Mitsui Fudosan, and the building was built by Kajima Construction, which also backed the film Chōkōsō no Akebono, whose main subject is the tower. Its owner is the Kasumi Kaikan, an association of the former kazoku high nobility. For years people in Japan used the building as a yardstick for describing very large volumes, a habit that lasted until the Tokyo Dome indoor stadium was built.

The Nippon Budokan, usually just the Budokan, stands in Tokyo's Chiyoda ward and was first built as the judo venue for the Tokyo Olympics of 1964. Its design is credited to Mamoru Yamada. The eight-sided hall rises 42 metres and holds 14,471 people: 2,946 on the arena floor, 3,199 on the first floor, 7,846 on the second floor and 480 standing. Martial arts contests remain its main use, yet it has also become famous worldwide as a place to hear live music. In 1966 the Beatles became the first rock band to perform there, giving five half-hour concerts from 30 June to 2 July. Some objected, believing that a western pop act would defile a hall built for the martial arts.

Kyoto Tower is the city's tallest structure, with an observation deck 100 metres up and a spire reaching 131 metres. Mamoru Yamada designed it with advice from the Kyoto University engineer Makoto Tanahashi, so that it could resist both earthquakes and typhoons. Rather than a metal lattice like Tokyo Tower's, its inner structure is a stack of steel rings, wrapped in light steel sheets 12 to 22 mm thick that were welded together and painted white to suggest a Japanese candle. The 800-ton tower rests entirely on a nine-storey base, holding a hotel and shops, that supplies its first 30.8 metres. Work started in 1963 where Kyoto's central post office had stood and ended late in 1964. There was public opposition, over the ¥380 million cost and because many thought the needle-like spire too modern for the ancient capital.

Kirjatalo, meaning 'Book House', is a commercial building by Alvar Aalto at the corner of Pohjoisesplanadi and Keskuskatu in central Helsinki. Its best-known occupant is probably the flagship shop of the Academic Bookstore. In 1961 the retailer Stockmann, which owned the plot and has its main department store across the street, held a competition for a new mixed-use building there, and Aalto won it. Aalto was also the architect of the nearby Rautatalo, and Kirjatalo's copper-clad outside and central atrium were made to match that building's. Skylights reaching down from the roof bring daylight into the atrium, which is ringed by the mezzanines of the upper floors. Those floors were first meant for offices but the bookshop has since taken them over. Café Aalto, opened in 1986, is on the first floor.

Filmhuset, the "House of Film", stands in Gärdet, in the Östermalm district of Stockholm. Peter Celsing designed it in a Brutalist style, and it was built between 1968 and 1971. He shaped the building to look like a camera, and its exposed concrete facade resembles strips of film. Inside is a large archive of books and magazines about film. A major renovation in 2008 created open-plan offices. The Stockholm City Museum has given the building a "code blue" listing, its highest grade for the cultural and historical value of buildings.

The Henie Onstad Kunstsenter, an art museum at Høvikodden in the Norwegian municipality of Bærum, sits on a headland pushing out into the Oslofjord about 10 kilometres southwest of Oslo. It was founded in 1968 by the figure skater Sonja Henie, a world and Olympic champion, and her husband Niels Onstad, a shipping magnate and art collector. In 1964 the couple launched a design competition, which two Norwegian architects, Jon Eikvar and Svein-Erik Engebretsen, won with what was their first commission. Completed in 1968, the centre was planned to fit the fjord-side landscape and uses glass, stone, copper and natural concrete. A later wing by the same pair joins the main building as an organic extension. The building now covers about 9,500 square metres, 3,500 of them for exhibitions, and a park with 30 sculptures surrounds it.

Sanomatalo is a building for shops and offices in the centre of Helsinki. To its south lie Postitalo and the city's central railway station, and to its north the Helsinki Music Centre. It was designed by Jan Söderlund, a professor, together with the architect Antti-Matti Siikala, and completed in 1999. It has twelve floors, three of them underground. As the city's first "glassy" building, it drew protests from environmentalists who feared its glass walls could kill birds, and there were further protests because two extra floors were added against the zoning plan. The top floors hold open-plan offices used by Helsingin Sanomat, Ilta-Sanomat, Radio Rock and others. The two lowest floors are given to shops and exhibitions, including an R-kioski branch.

The Sibelius Hall in Lahti, Finland, is a concert hall named after the composer Jean Sibelius, and it was completed in 2000. Its architects were Kimmo Lintula and Hannu Tikka, and it is made of glulam. Lahti's cultural ambitions show in particular in this building, which serves as a large congress centre as well as a concert venue. Artec Consultants of New York engineered the acoustics, which are counted among the building's strongest qualities. The hall seats 1,250 people. It is the home of the Lahti Symphony Orchestra, one of the best-known orchestras in Finland, which plays both classical and popular music and puts particular focus on the works of Sibelius.

Stockholm City Hall occupies the eastern point of Kungsholmen, on Riddarfjärden's north shore, facing Riddarholmen and Södermalm. After a further competition against the architect Westman, Ragnar Östberg was given the City Hall, while Westman got the Court House; Östberg then reworked his design using parts of Westman's, the tower among them. Built between 1911 and 1923, it used nearly eight million red bricks. In this National Romantic work, the waterside site set the central theme: the meeting of city and water seen across Stockholm. Heavy, plain northern European brick is mixed with Venetian Gothic touches, such as turrets with golden stars, ornate balconies, wooden masts and statues. The arcaded Blue Hall, which has no blue decoration, hosts the Nobel Prize banquet. A 106-metre tower topped by the Three Crowns rises at the southeast corner, reached by lift or 365 steps.

The Helsinki Olympic Stadium, about 2.3 kilometres from the city centre in Töölö, is the largest stadium in Finland. Yrjö Lindegren and Toivo Jäntti designed it in the functionalist style, and Architectural Digest has featured it among the finest Olympic buildings. Construction ran from 1934 to 1938, ahead of the 1940 Summer Olympics, which had been moved from Tokyo to Helsinki and were then cancelled because of the Second World War. The stadium hosted the 1952 Games instead, when temporary additions to the upper tier of three stands lifted its capacity above 70,000; today it holds 36,251. Its 72.71-metre tower matches the length of Matti Järvinen's gold-medal javelin throw at the 1932 Olympics. A renovation roofed every stand with canopies, renewed the field and track, and added restaurants and indoor sports space, and the stadium reopened in September 2020.

The Sveriges Riksbank building, headquarters of the Bank of Sweden, stands on Brunkebergstorg in Stockholm next to Peter Celsing's Kulturhuset on Sergels torg, and was among the last buildings he designed. Its design is ruled by cubes, squares, spheres and circles, every one of them chosen to suggest stability. The facade is made of thick slabs of dark granite, roughly hewn. This draws on the Renaissance habit of rusticated stone to express solidity, and more directly on its use for banks in the neo-Renaissance buildings of the 19th century. Since 1907 the bank had occupied a semicircular building on Helgeandsholmen, and it moved into Celsing's building in 1976.

Hornbækhus in Copenhagen is a perimeter block designed by Kay Fisker when he was young and still fairly inexperienced. Roughly 200 metres long and 80 metres wide, it contains 290 apartments, and it is counted among the best examples of the very large Danish blocks known as storkarréer ("Grand Blocks"), or the "kilometre style". Blocks of this kind went up during the 1920s to ease a growing shortage of homes, and their repetitive design was chosen to hold down building costs. On the street side the walls are red brick; on the yard side they are yellow-flamed brick. A modilioned cornice tops both faces, and red tiles cover the pitched roof. The central garden is the work of Gudmund Nyeland Brandt. In 1983 the block was entered on the Danish registry of protected buildings and places.

The Nordic House in Tórshavn is a cultural institution promoting Nordic and Faroese culture. Ola Steen of Norway and Kolbrún Ragnarsdóttir of Iceland won the 1977 Nordic competition for its design, which attracted 158 architects. True to folklore, they shaped it like a hill of elves, and it opened in 1983. Dragon-like steel struts brace its 2,000 m² turf roof against the strain of frequent hurricane winds. All rooms get daylight except the 800 m² hall, whose movable west wall lets it open onto the lobby and amphitheatre. A tall cast concrete wall in that hall is the bearing element: everything rests on it or relates to it. The steel span reaching out from it leaves room in the lobby for snakelike stairs and a ramp. Norwegian slate from Gudbrandsdal lines the lobby and ramps; the floors are Swedish pine.

St. Hallvard's Church and Monastery stands on Enerhaugen in Oslo, not far from the former medieval St. Hallvard's Cathedral, and serves the largest current Catholic parish in Norway. Lund & Slaatto, the practice of Kjell Lund and Nils Slaatto, arranged it in three parts: the monastery, the parish offices and the church, all wrapped around a circular nave. Seen from outside, the three-level building is square, severe and inward-looking; at its centre, the round church is packed inside the square. Brick and concrete are left exposed inside and out. The church's ceiling hangs downward, so the room is lowest at the point where a church would usually be highest. On completion in 1966 it drew wide interest among academics and won several architecture awards, and in 1975 it received the Houen Foundation Award.

Standing at Vester Vedsted, near Ribe in Denmark, the Wadden Sea Centre is both museum and visitor centre for the Wadden Sea, an intertidal zone of the North Sea that UNESCO lists as a World Heritage Site. Opened in February 2017, it aims to build public awareness of the sea and the marshlands that surround it. The Danish architect Dorte Mandrup designed the building, and in its opening year a committee of leading Danish architects named it Danish Building of the Year. It also received the City of Esbjerg's City-Fund Award in 2017. Inside, two rooms are given over entirely to birds, with videos, interactive games built around bird calls, and artworks showing the different birds found along the Wadden Sea.

Taipei's National Dr. Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall commemorates Sun Yat-sen, the National Father of the Republic of China. Architect Wang Da-hong's plan won a public contest and was then adjusted to stress Chinese architectural traits; the main construction ended on 16 May 1972. The building covers 29,464 m² on an open site of 115,000 m² in Chung-shan Park, where gardens, historical decorative walls and spaces for exhibitions and shows surround Lake Cui, or Emerald Pond. Exhibits trace Sun's life and the revolution under his leadership, and the hall also holds a performance hall, about 1,000 m² of exhibition space, a multimedia theatre, lecture halls and a library of over 300,000 books. It is also a public centre for social, educational and cultural life, and every year its auditorium hosts Taiwan's highest film honours, the Golden Horse Awards.

The north building of Shanghai's Peace Hotel was completed in 1929 as Sassoon House, home of the Cathay Hotel. Palmer and Turner designed it with a reinforced concrete structure, and building began in 1926. It was Victor Sassoon's first high-rise: at 77 m to the top of its tower it stood fifty feet over any other building on the Bund, and it was among the Far East's first tall buildings. Sassoon once lived in the tenth-floor penthouse. Art Deco is followed consistently, outside and in. Most walls are faced in granite, with terracotta on the ninth floor and roof. The east front, facing the Huangpu River, rises to a steep pyramid roof about 10 m tall, its copper now corroded light green. A three-year renovation from 2007 led to its reopening in 2010 under the name Fairmont Peace Hotel Shanghai.

The Xiqu Centre sits in Tsim Sha Tsui as part of the West Kowloon Cultural District, and it was the first building finished under the district's plan. Work started on 24 September 2013 and ended in 2018, at a cost of HK$2.7 billion, and the public was let in from 20 January 2019. The design is credited to Revery Architecture and Ronald Lu and Partners. The centre is among the projects designed and built by the Revery team under Venelin Kokalov, who has led that team since 2016. In 2019 the building won a Green Building Merit Award for completed institutional buildings from the Hong Kong Green Building Council, and the Grand Award at the DFA Design for Asia Awards.

On the southwestern point of Tsim Sha Tsui, the Hong Kong Cultural Centre is a public venue for many kinds of performance. Its site once held the Kowloon station of the Kowloon–Canton Railway, and demolishing that historic station when work finally started caused great controversy. The design came from José Lei, at the time chief architect of the Public Works Department. Neighbours include the Star Ferry pier to the west, the Space Museum and Museum of Art to the east, and the historic Clock Tower between centre and pier. Charles, Prince of Wales, and Princess Diana opened it officially on 8 November 1989. Oak of high quality lines the oval, two-tier Concert Hall, which has 2,019 seats and an acoustic canopy and curtains that can be adjusted. Its organ of 8,000 pipes, built by Austria's Rieger Orgelbau, is Asia's largest.

MADE IN Architects, a Spanish team set up for this competition under Manuel Monteserín, designed the Kaohsiung Music Center in 2011. The design aims for a varied landscape, each building answering its own use and setting. There is an outdoor amphitheatre for 10,000, a concert hall for 6,000, six live houses called the "Whales", five restaurants linked by a raised walkway, two towers of offices, museum spaces and rehearsal rooms, and an exhibition centre, joined by parks and promenades. Locals now use the team's nicknames, such as "Dolphins". Above the live houses, walkable green roofs form low hills looking over harbour and sea, and at the exhibition centre hexagonal structures shade an open platform for markets, dance and theatre. Over a thousand trees planted at the Love River's mouth make a park. It officially opened on 31 October 2021.

Nung Chan Monastery, in Taipei's Beitou District, takes its name, meaning 'Farming Ch'an', from its first residents, who grew their own food while devoting themselves to Ch'an practice. Dongchu, a scholar monk and a disciple of the Chinese Buddhist master Taixu, formally founded it in 1975. The original complex was almost levelled in 2004, until the city government of Taipei listed one of its original farmhouses as a heritage property. In 2012 the architect Kris Yao reconstructed the monastery, which also goes by the name Water-Moon Monastery.

In Taipei's Nangang District, the Taipei Music Center, whose Chinese name means 'Taipei Popular Music Center', serves as a venue for performing arts and culture. Its facilities include a concert hall seating 5,000, a cultural hall and spaces for creative production. On July 24, 2008, city officials said they would hold an international design competition for it, alongside plans for the Taipei Performing Arts Center. The winner, named in 2012, was Reiser + Umemoto, RUR Architecture, a New York firm led jointly by the American architect Jesse A. Reiser and the Japanese architect Nanako Umemoto. Building work started on 19 June 2013. The center opened its doors on September 5, 2020, and soon after, on October 3, staged the 31st Golden Melody Awards.

The Shanghai Museum, a public museum of ancient Chinese art run by the city, stands on People's Square in Shanghai's Huangpu District. Its present building, by the local architect Xing Tonghe, was begun in August 1993 and opened to wide praise on October 12, 1996. Its form takes after a ding, an ancient bronze cooking vessel, and the Da Ke ding displayed inside is said to have been the specific model. A round top sits on a square base, standing for the old Chinese idea of a 'round sky, square earth'. The building rises 29.5 metres over five floors and covers 39,200 m² in all. Ma Chengyuan, director from 1985 to 1999, is said to have done much to secure a large, purpose-built home. The collection exceeds 120,000 pieces, from bronzes, ceramics and jades to calligraphy, paintings, coins and furniture.

Tianjin Binhai New Area Library, nicknamed "The Eye", is one of five central attractions of the Binhai Cultural Center. MVRDV of Rotterdam designed it with the Tianjin Urban Planning and Design Institute, a group of local architects. Over five levels and 33,700 m², full-height terraced shelves can take 1.2 million books, and a glowing sphere at the centre holds a 110-seat auditorium. From the park, the sphere looks like an iris through an eye-shaped opening. The local government's tight schedule took the project from early drawings to opening in three years, in October 2017. That rush, and a conflict with the approved plans, mean the main atrium cannot store books: rooms reaching the upper shelves were never built, and printed spines filled the shelf backs for opening-day photos. About 10,000 visitors a day came in the first week.

Tao Zhu Yin Yuan, also called Agora Garden, is a residential tower in Taipei's Xinyi Special District, designed by the Belgian architect Vincent Callebaut and finished in 2018. It reaches 93.2 m with 21 floors above ground and four basement levels, giving 42,335 m² of floor space. Its form twists like the double helix of DNA, turning 90 degrees from bottom to top, with each floor set 4.5 degrees round from the one below. About 20,000 trees and shrubs cover the building, meant to soak up some 130 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and so cut Taipei's carbon footprint. It holds a LEED Gold label and a Diamond rating from the Low Carbon Building Alliance.

Wah Fu Estate is a public housing estate beside Waterfall Bay, Pok Fu Lam, in Hong Kong's Southern District. It was designed by Dr. Donald Liao, a former director of housing, and built from 1967 on a new town concept. The estate is split into Wah Fu (I) and Wah Fu (II), and its 18 residential blocks were finished between 1967 and 1978. The estate uses the 'Twin Tower Block' design: like the Z-plan castles of Scotland, each pairs two towers with a hollow plan ringed by internal galleries. The estate was renovated in 2003. In the 2014 Policy Address, Hong Kong's chief executive announced that it will be redeveloped, with the new estate built nearby.

Zhongshan Hall stands on Yanping South Road in Taipei's Ximending neighbourhood and was originally the Taipei (Taihoku) City Public Auditorium. Work ran from 23 November 1932 to 26 November 1936 under Ide Kaoru, chief engineer in Taiwan for the Japanese government, at a total cost of 980,000 yen, with 94,500 workers taking part. Its four-storey steel frame was designed to resist fire, severe earthquakes and typhoons. The building was first clad in light green tile so that bombers overhead would find it harder to see, and its windows carry classical ornament in a Spanish Islamic style. On 25 October 1945 the auditorium hosted the surrender ceremony for the Taiwan District of the China warzone. The government named it a historic site in 1992, and it still serves daily for concerts and cultural events.

The Shanghai Oriental Art Center, or SHOAC, off Century Avenue in Pudong, is among Shanghai's leading venues for performance and culture. The French architect Paul Andreu designed it with the Huadong Architectural Design & Research Institute. From above, five linked hemispherical halls, or 'petals', take the shape of a butterfly orchid. Laminated glass with perforated metal sheets makes up most of the facades, and at night the ceiling changes colour to suit the performances inside. Dark granite floors and layered glass screen walls are meant to give a softly diffused effect, like a forest floor. The Concert Hall seats 1,953 and has a computer-controlled lifting stage and a Rieger organ from Austria; the 333-seat Performance Hall follows the semicircular Roman theatre. The building first opened with a concert on New Year's Eve 2004, and officially on July 1, 2005.

The College of Social Sciences at National Taiwan University, designed by the Japanese architect Toyo Ito, is among the recent additions that brought contemporary architecture into the university's historic campus plan. Its library, the Koo Chen-Fu Memorial Library, is named after Koo Chen-fu, a former Political Science student, in recognition of his donation. The design centres on the first-floor reading room, where books sit on open shelves. Floor-to-ceiling glass closes the library on three sides, and inside, 88 columns set out irregularly carry a tree-like roof pierced by skylights of many shapes, meant to create a forest of knowledge. Curved bamboo bookshelves are intended to make the reading room look like a grove. The library officially opened inside the new School of Social Sciences building.

Prime Tower, by Gigon/Guyer, stands close to Hardbrücke station in the Industriequartier of Zurich, on land where an industrial facility once stood. Built from 2008 to 2011, it rises 126 metres and was Switzerland's tallest building until the Roche Tower in Basel, at 178 metres, was finished in 2015. Its 36 floors provide 39,500 m² of office space, and the 35th holds a restaurant. The weight of the floors is carried by a central core and columns, which also keep the structure steady. The tower cost CHF 355 million to develop and forms a complex with two neighbouring buildings, Cubus and Diagonal. It is one of several major projects the practice has completed in this formerly industrial part of the city, known as Zürich West.

Kirchner Museum Davos is devoted to the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, who spent the years 1918 to 1938 in Davos and made many of his works there. It was the first major commission carried out by Annette Gigon and Mike Guyer, architects based in Zürich. Their building, a gift from Roman Norbert Ketterer, administrator of Kirchner's estate, opened on September 4, 1992. Answering the climate, light and flat-roofed architecture of Davos, but above all the meeting of visitors and art, they made four cubes as exhibition halls. A branching foyer with wide windows joins them, a place for reflection that looks out on the alpine landscape that inspired Kirchner. Glass covers the whole facade, opaque panels alternating with clear, and broken glass covers the roof, called the fifth facade. The museum won the Velux Foundation's Daylight Award in 2012.

Bremerhaven's German Maritime Museum exists to collect, record, study and show documents and objects from Germany's history at sea. Hans Scharoun planned its main building, one of several important works completed only after his death in Berlin in 1972. Walter Scheel, then president of Germany, opened it on 5 September 1975, though scientific work had begun in 1971. The museum also includes ships in Bremerhaven's Old Harbour, among them the windjammer Seute Deern. Set between the Old Harbour and the Weser dike, the building and the eight vessels of the fleet were protected together as one heritage ensemble by Bremen in 2005. For the museum's 25th anniversary in 2000, it unveiled the Hansekogge, a ship from around 1380 found in the Weser in 1962, after long conservation in a basin of preservative. The buildings were restored in 2024.

The Kunstmuseum Basel holds the world's oldest public art collection and is widely regarded as Switzerland's most important art museum. The contest for its new building drew star names, five of them Pritzker Prize laureates: Jean Nouvel, Tadao Ando, Rafael Moneo, Zaha Hadid and Peter Zumthor. The winner was a young local practice, Christ & Gantenbein. Their design is an angled block clad in concrete bricks, kept to the height of the original museum and linked to it by an underpass. Finished in April 2016 with money from the Laurenz Foundation (Laurenz-Stiftung) and the Canton of Basel-Stadt, the extension adds 2,750 m² of galleries, bringing the total close to 10,000 m². Art from the 15th century to 1950 now hangs in the original building, while later work is shown in the new one.

Museum Brandhorst, in Munich's Kunstareal beside the Pinakothek der Moderne, opened on 21 May 2009. It shows around 200 works from the modern art collection of Udo and Anette Brandhorst, heirs of the Henkel trust. When Anette died in 1999, Udo gave their collection to Bavaria, provided the state built a fitting home for it, and Bavaria met the $67 million building cost. Sauerbruch Hutton designed a long rectangular building of two storeys. Its facade is made of 36,000 vertical ceramic louvres, glazed in 23 different colours. Stairs link three exhibition areas inside, and apart from the Media Suite every gallery has white walls and Danish oak floorboards. One room, an irregular octagon, was made for the twelve-part painting known as the Lepanto cycle. The project also started the architects' work with glazed ceramic as a facade material.

GSW Headquarters in Berlin-Kreuzberg, called Rocket-Tower since 2017, began with a limited competition in 1991 to enlarge the offices of GSW, the largest social housing association in Berlin.
