Sauerbruch Hutton won first prize and the commission, and the building went up from 1995 to 1999. Their design sets a second tower, close in height, beside an existing 1950s office tower. The new slab is thin and gently curved, concave to the west and convex to the east. Its facades have two skins; on the west, a one-metre-deep convection facade works with the 'flying roof' to ventilate the offices naturally, keeping them comfortable and cutting energy use by 40%. A computer turns the aluminium louvres of each window, coloured red, pink and orange, in response to the sun. It was nominated for the Stirling Prize and the EU's contemporary architecture prize.

Kunstmuseum Bonn, also called the Bonn Museum of Modern Art, was founded in 1947 and belongs to the city's 'Museum Mile'. Its present building opened in 1992, designed by Axel Schultes of the BJSS firm together with Jürgen Pleuser, and cost about DM 100 million. It offers around 4,000 m² for exhibitions and has three entrances, meant to stand for openness. The design of its staircase has been described as "precise geometry, cut like jewellery". The collection centres on three areas: Rhenish Expressionism, of which it holds the world's largest collection; post-war German art, above all from the 1960s into the early 1990s; and post-war prints from around the world.

Kaufhaus Tyrol stands in a pedestrian stretch of Maria-Theresien-Straße in central Innsbruck. The Jewish families Bauer and Schwarz opened the original store in 1908 as Tyrol's first department store. René Benko bought it in 2004, demolished it in 2005 and put up a new store that opened in 2010; its place in the historic centre made it controversial. The English architect David Chipperfield designed the new building with Dieter Mathoi of Innsbruck. Rather than copy historic buildings, the facade was meant to bridge old and new. A glass dome lets daylight in, and a system called Thermische Bauteilaktivierung handles heating, ventilation and air conditioning, cutting energy use and cost. With 55 shops, it is Innsbruck's largest department store. A RIBA European Award came in 2011, the same year it reached the Mies van der Rohe Award shortlist.

The Lentos Art Museum, a modern art museum in Linz, sits right on the bank of the Danube, with the Nibelungen Bridge on one side and the Brucknerhaus on the other. It succeeded the city's earlier New Gallery, the Neue Galerie. The decision to build was taken in 1998, and the museum, designed by the Zurich firm Weber & Hofer, opened in May 2003. The building runs 130 metres in length and has about 8,000 m² of floor space, and its clear glass facade glows when lit at night. Its holdings include around 1,500 paintings, sculptures and objects, some 850 photographs and more than 10,000 works on paper. Among the photographs are important contributions to artistic photography by Man Ray and Alexander Rodtschenko.

In Vienna's 15th district, Wiener Stadthalle serves as both an indoor arena for many uses and a convention centre. Roland Rainer, an Austrian architect, was responsible for the original halls, built in the 1950s and since enlarged. Six connected halls now make up the complex: A and B are gymnasiums that can also take conferences or lectures, C is an indoor ice rink, D is an indoor arena used mainly for concerts or sport, E is a small multi-purpose hall, and F is an arena hall suited to more intimate concerts. The main hall, the largest indoor arena in Austria, holds up to about 16,083 people. The structure measures 98 by 110 metres, with a ridge 26.6 metres high. Solar panels were later fitted to the roof of Hall D, and the square in front, Roland-Rainer-Platz, carries the architect's name.

Werkraum Haus, in the centre of Andelsbuch, was planned by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, and the member firms of the Werkraum Bregenzerwald built it. That association brings together craftsmen of the Bregenz Forest; founded in 1999, it aims to link and support the area's craft, design and technology businesses. Open to the public, the house is where their craftsmanship is presented, where building culture is promoted together with architects, and where design skills and the quality of craft are raised, ideally with young people involved. In 2023 the house displayed 40 of Zumthor's architectural models, some never before seen in public.

Torres de Colón are two office towers in Madrid's Plaza de Colón district, designed by the Spanish architect Antonio Lamela and built between 1968 and 1976. With the engineer Fernández Casado, Lamela used the project to bring 'suspended architecture' to Spain. Unlike a conventional tower, each sends its loads up to a cap at the top, then down a central core of concrete to the foundations, and the towers were built from the top down, floor by floor. Floors are fully open, free of pillars and beams, for flexible layouts. The structure is reinforced concrete with high-strength post-tensioning. When built, the towers held the world record for the number of slabs suspended using pre-stressed concrete: 21. A 2020 to 2024 renovation, presented by Mutua Madrileña, replaced the plug-shaped Art Deco crown with a four-storey structure over both towers.

Run by Patrimonio Nacional, Madrid's Royal Collections Gallery (first called the Royal Collections Museum) keeps and shows paintings, tapestries, carriages and more from the Spanish royal collection. Its new building rises above the Campo del Moro gardens, beside the Royal Palace and the Almudena Cathedral. Emilio Tuñón and Luis Moreno Mansilla won the 2002 ideas contest, and building started in 2006, slowed when remains of a 9th-century Muslim settlement were found there. Huge blocks of Gris Quintana granite face the main front, hollowed out behind to clad the reinforced concrete structure. The building was finished in 2016, but a caretaker government could not sign the extra contract for the interior, and the doors finally opened on 28 June 2023. Over 600,000 people came in its first year. In 2017 it won the Spanish Architecture Award and a FAD Award.

Atlético Madrid's home ground since 2017, the Metropolitano Stadium stands in the Rosas neighbourhood of Madrid's San Blas-Canillejas district and now officially carries the sponsor's name Riyadh Air Metropolitano. Its story starts earlier: work on a stadium here began in 1990 to a design by Cruz y Ortiz, a single tier of 20,000 seats nicknamed La Peineta because its outline recalled a traditional hair comb. That venue was later rebuilt, and the new ground, credited to Cruz y Ortiz, opened on 16 September 2017 with a La Liga match against Málaga, reopening with 68,456 seats. The club borrowed the Metropolitano name from the arena where it played between 1923 and 1966. The rebuilt ground was the world's first 100% LED stadium, and on 1 June 2019 it staged the UEFA Champions League Final, in which Liverpool beat Tottenham Hotspur 2–0.

Designed by Harry Seidler, Grosvenor Place is a 44-floor office tower, 180 metres tall, on George Street where the south-eastern corner of The Rocks meets the northern end of Sydney's CBD. Its plan is made of two crescents around an elliptical core, placed and turned so the floors look out over Sydney Harbour, the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House. Every floor is open and free of columns, spanning 2,000 square metres. A concrete core works with steel beams, and the outside is clad in prefabricated granite. Two low heritage buildings on Grosvenor Street belong to the complex, with a diagonal footpath between them and the tower. The lobby holds Pillars & Cones by the American minimalist Frank Stella. The tower took the RAIA's Lustig & Moar National Prize in 1989 and the Sulman Award in 1991.

Finished in 1991 to a design by Harry Seidler, QV1 is a modernist skyscraper of 40 storeys in Perth, Western Australia. At 163 metres it ranks fourth in height in the city, and its name comes from the Latin phrase Quo vadis, 'where are you going?'. To soften its impact as seen from Parliament House, the tower shows only a narrow side that way. Seidler also asked for passive design to cut energy costs, met with tinted double glazing and sun shades, both horizontal and vertical, beside the windows. A concrete core 21.5 metres square resists wind, while perimeter columns 7.3 metres apart leave every floor clear inside. At the St Georges Terrace entrance, stone-clad hyperboloid supports carry two perimeter columns that end at the third floor. The tower won the 2019 Richard Roach Jewell Award for Enduring Architecture.

Australian architect Robin Boyd, of the firm Romberg & Boyd, designed Featherston House in Ivanhoe, Victoria, in 1967, and it was finished in 1969. It stands on a slope beside suburban parkland. Its owners, the Featherstons, were open to new ideas, and Boyd had the freedom to try a different scheme built around living in a garden. A garden sits at ground level, platforms reach out from a central chimney, and fully glazed windows face the bush, and the house echoes a tree house, an approach then seen as radical. A roof of translucent cellular polycarbonate lets soft light into the space below all day, and a glass wall on the south side adds more light and views to the trees of the park. Three flaps in the platform can pull air from a 'cool room' to ventilate the house.

Brisbane's Queen Elizabeth II Courts of Law, also known as the city's Supreme and District Court, were finished in 2012 on George Street; the design is credited to Architectus with Guymer Bailey Architects. The building was made for the Supreme Court and District Court of Queensland, which share it, and with the Magistrates Court next door it forms a legal precinct covering a whole city block. It ranks among Australia's largest court buildings, with 39 courtrooms, a big ceremonial court, the Queensland Court of Appeal, 23 criminal and 14 civil courts, a library, rooms for 68 judges and basement cells. Witnesses, victims of crime and the public get enhanced facilities. In the Supreme Court foyer, the Sir Harry Gibbs Legal Heritage Centre is a museum of Queensland's legal history. The name honours Queen Elizabeth II and marks her Diamond Jubilee.

Sean Godsell Architects, working with Peddle Thorp Architects, designed the RMIT Design Hub, finished in May 2012 for the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology on the old Carlton & United Breweries site. Two buildings sit either side of a central forecourt: one for research and archives, the other for exhibitions and work space. The façade is a second skin of sandblasted glass discs on a steel cylindrical frame, inspired by the brewing trade the site once housed. A computer turns each cell with rotational motors to suit Melbourne's daily weather, managing sun and access, and the façade and building systems are ready for the shade cells to be replaced by solar cells as that technology improves. Inside, galvanized steel walkway grating lines the walls, reflecting RMIT's character as an industrial college. The project won the 2013 Victorian Architecture Medal.

Designed by the firm Lyons, RMIT's Swanston Academic Building stands on Swanston Street in Melbourne, across from Building 8, designed by Peter Corrigan, and ARM's Storey Hall. It went up between September 2010 and September 2012 and offers 35,000 square metres over 11 storeys, counting the basement, with six large lecture theatres for students. The aim was for the building to 'wear the cloak of the city': a survey of Melbourne's main colours set the palette of its multicoloured façade, meant to reflect its surroundings. That outer layer is made of external panels and triangular pieces, each side shaded to a different degree according to the way it faces. On every level, student 'portals' connect what happens inside with the cityscape around the building.

In 1989 Athfield Architects were asked to design a new central library for Wellington, known in Māori as Te Matapihi ki te Ao Nui. Ian Athfield had toured American libraries and liked the idea of the library as an 'information supermarket' serving the widest public with the most information. Toward Civic Square, a curved glass wall three storeys high held window seats and desks. A colonnade of columns shaped as metal nikau palms climbed by ramp from Victoria Street to the square. It is said to have been Australasia's first public library with a café inside, though for security the café kept its own entrances. Heritage New Zealand lists it in Category 1, calling it an excellent example of late twentieth-century library design and postmodern architecture. Closed suddenly in 2019 over earthquake risk, it reopened in March 2026 after restructuring.

Provided by the city council, Palmerston North City Library is this New Zealand city's main public library. New Zealand architect Ian Athfield designed its present home, a restored and extended building on The Square in the city centre, an award-winning building that opened in 1996. It is the sixth place the library has occupied over the years, and four branches elsewhere in the city work alongside it. The library brands itself as the city's 'Living Room', with a stated aim to inspire people to explore the world's pathways, given in Māori as Te Ara Whanui o Te Ao. From this central building it offers people both recreation and learning.

The Melbourne Recital Centre opened in 2009 as part of a Southbank complex, shared with the Melbourne Theatre Company's Southbank Theatre and designed by Ashton Raggatt McDougall; Arup advised on acoustics and theatre. After Hamer Hall, it is the city's second-largest hall for classical music. It has two auditoria: a smaller Salon and the Elisabeth Murdoch Hall, named after Dame Elisabeth Murdoch, a 'modified shoe box' seating 1,000 on two levels. To shut out the cars and trams of Southbank Boulevard, the hall is wrapped in 250 mm of concrete resting on 38 steel springs. Hoop Pine plywood lines the inside to give ideal bass for cello and low brass, while the room's shape, size and timber aim at 1.6 to 1.8 seconds of reverberation. In 2009 the complex won the Victorian Architecture Medal and two more state awards.

Set in the Carlton Gardens, the Melbourne Museum covers natural and cultural history and was designed in a post-modernist manner by Denton Corker Marshall. Built under the Kennett government of 1992–1999, it was opened on 21 October 2000 by Steve Bracks, then Premier of Victoria. The design works both as a single building and as separate parts woven into the gardens. It lines up on an axis with the neighbouring Italianate Royal Exhibition Building and refers to it, as well as to the city-centre towers. Two very long, high, sloping canopies, or blades, dominate, rising from the entrance opposite the Exhibition Building's north door to lead people in from the street. A blade section of roof rises to 35 metres, enclosing a small rainforest, and the centrepiece houses the Forest Gallery, which portrays the temperate forests of eastern Victoria.

On reclaimed land by Civic Square, the Michael Fowler Centre combines a concert hall with a convention centre and is central Wellington's top concert venue. It was commissioned in 1975 as the New Town Hall, when the first plan was to demolish the Wellington Town Hall. Warren and Mahoney's Miles Warren and Maurice Mahoney designed it, advised on acoustics by A. Harold Marshall, a University of Auckland researcher. Delayed, it was opened by the Duke of Wellington in September 1983, at a final cost of $17.5 million. Outside, stainless steel cladding and concrete panels meet a raised glass passage for circulation, and the main auditorium uses wooden reflectors. New Zealand's Institute of Architects honoured it for Enduring Architecture in 2010. Rated earthquake prone in 2023, it faced three options the next year, demolition and remediation among them.

Auckland's Sky Tower is for telecommunications and sightseeing. It went up as part of the Skycity casino precinct, and the Skycity Entertainment Group's brief asked for a tower that would draw tourists and also be a telecommunications facility it could market. The architect was Gordon Moller, of the firm Craig Craig Moller. Building took two years and nine months, and it opened on 3 August 1997, and from 1996 to 2022 no freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere stood taller. Its 12-metre-wide shaft of high-performance reinforced concrete rests on eight 'legs' over 16 piles sunk more than 15 metres into sandstone. The observation decks wear aluminium and blue-green reflective glass. Designed for winds above 200 km/h, it can sway up to a metre in extreme gusts. It has won a national award from New Zealand's Institute of Architects.

Designed by Denton Corker Marshall, the Governor Phillip Tower complex was completed in 1994 on a raised site in the north-east of Sydney's CBD, and was seen then as setting new standards of design and finish for the city's offices. Its site includes that of the first Government House, among Australia's oldest and most important European heritage places. The archaeological remains were conserved and built into the Museum of Sydney, while the state government moved floor space from the foundations' area to the land just south. Zinc-plated transfer beams lift the tower 10 floors above the street, over a sandstone-clad podium shared with Governor Macquarie Tower, maximising views from every level. Grey granite and glass give a costly, finely detailed facade, and the steel blades of the roof are nicknamed the milk-crate. Critics fault its overbearing scale at street level.

Tūranga, the public library in central Christchurch, New Zealand, opened on 12 October 2018. It took over from the old Christchurch Central Library nearby, shut since the day of the 2011 earthquake, and was one of 17 anchor projects in the city's 2012 recovery plan, known as the Blueprint. Two firms shared the design: Architectus from New Zealand and the Danish practice Schmidt Hammer Lassen. The building stands in the north-eastern quadrant of Cathedral Square, facing Gloucester and Colombo Streets, and takes its cue from the golden light reflected on the Port Hills, a key part of the cityscape. A third larger than its predecessor, it is the biggest library in the South Island and third in the country, after Auckland's and Wellington's. Te Ngāi Tūāhuriri rūnanga gave the name, which refers to Whitireia, the Māori name for Cathedral Square.

University House is the oldest residential college at the Australian National University in Canberra. Planned from 1947 and designed by Brian Lewis, it had its foundation stone laid in 1949, and in 1950, while it was going up, it was decided it should also hold modern art. Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, opened it on 16 February 1954 for faculty, staff and postgraduate students. At first it was meant to follow the Oxbridge college model, with students expected at regular seminars and a formal daily dinner in the hall with the faculty. Leonard French decorated that hall: his Regeneration (1972) decorates the western, rostrum end, and the ten paintings of his series The Journey (1974) hang there too. The university, the national architects' institute and the Australian government list it as heritage. It reopened in August 2026 after extensive repairs.

Started in 1955 for the head office of Imperial Chemical Industries' Australian arm, later spun off as the independent company Orica, ICI House (now Orica House) rises 19 storeys on Nicholson Street, East Melbourne. On completion in 1958 it was Australia's tallest building, breaking Melbourne's long-held 132-foot height limit, and the country's first International Style skyscraper. The architect, Osborn McCutcheon of Bates Smart McCutcheon, closely followed the best American corporate glass towers of the day, among them the UN Secretariat. In post-war Melbourne it stood for progress, modernity and business power, and heralded the high-rise offices that reshaped Australia's cities. Soon after it was built, coloured glass panes shattered, dropping onto the street below, a result of impurities and summer heat. In 2005 it was the first office building of the post-war era added to the Australian National Heritage List.

Built between 1955 and 1957 to a design by Rudder, Littlemore & Rudder, Qantas House, also called No. 1 Chifley Square, is a heritage-listed office building on Hunter Street, Sydney. It was the first planned world headquarters of Qantas Empire Airways, then Australia's only, state-owned international airline, and Prime Minister Robert Menzies opened it on 28 October 1957. Its curved, segmented front follows Chifley Square, keeping to the semicircle drawn for the square's north side in 1908. That face is a 46-metre-high curtain wall, double glazed in green, with enamelled blue-green steel spandrels, and its aerofoil-shaped aluminium mullions express the airline's outward-looking image as air travel grew. Off-centre service cores leave room for a rear light well that brings daylight deep inside. In 1959 the Royal Institute of British Architects named it the Commonwealth's best new building.

Rising 297.3 metres in Melbourne's Southbank, Eureka Tower was designed by the local firm Fender Katsalidis Architects and built by Grocon. The plaza was completed in June 2006 and the tower opened officially on 11 October that year. Measured by roof height or by its highest lived-in floor, it was then the world's tallest residential building. The name recalls the Eureka Stockade, an 1854 revolt during the Victorian gold rush, and the design tells that story: the gold crown stands for the gold rush, a red stripe for the blood shed in the uprising, and the blue glass over most of the building, with its white lines, for the stockade's flag. Windows on the top ten floors are plated with 24-carat gold. To damp swaying caused by wind, pumps keep moving water between two tanks that each hold 300,000 litres.

Rialto Towers stands at 525 Collins Street, on the western side of Melbourne's central business district. Gerard de Preu and Partners designed it with Perrott Lyon Mathieson, and it was built from 1982, opening in October 1986. Two joined towers make up the complex: the taller rises 251 metres over 55 floors and three basements, the North Tower 185 metres over 43 floors. On completion it overtook Sydney's MLC Centre as Australia's tallest building and was the Southern Hemisphere's tallest office building, keeping the national title until 101 Collins Street passed it in 1991. Its main feature is a vast curtain wall of reinforced, blue-tinted mirror glass whose colour changes through the day, from a deep blue to bright gold at sunset. From 1994 until the last day of 2009 it offered Melbourne's first public observation deck in a skyscraper.

Known simply as Te Uru, and earlier as Lopdell House Gallery, this contemporary art gallery in Titirangi serves West Auckland. It opened in 1986 inside Lopdell House and closed in 2012 for a building project. The new purpose-built gallery, the work of Julie Stout of the firm Mitchell & Stout Architects, opened on 1 November 2014. Critics greeted it warmly, and in 2015 it took Auckland Architecture Awards for public building and heritage, plus a national award for public buildings. Its name comes from Te Hau a Uru, a Māori phrase for the west wind, recalling the air currents for which this part of West Auckland is known; it was chosen together with the local iwi, Te Kawerau ā Maki. Every year it hosts the Portage Ceramic Awards, the country's top prize for ceramics.

Still often called Centrepoint Tower, and also called the Sydney Tower Eye or Westfield Tower, Sydney Tower serves for observation and telecommunications and is the city's tallest structure. It climbs 309 metres above the CBD from a Market Street site between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets, on top of the Westfield Sydney shopping centre. Australian architect Donald Crone designed it. Plans were first unveiled in March 1968; the office building was started in 1970 and the tower itself in 1975, and visitors were first allowed up on 25 September 1981. Up to 960 people fit in the golden turret near its top, and the lifts slow to half or a quarter of full speed when the wind requires. It is the second-tallest observation tower in the Southern Hemisphere, and Engineers Australia has honoured it with an Engineering Heritage Plaque.

Known as Spencer Street station until 2005, Southern Cross is a major Melbourne railway station, in Docklands on Spencer Street at the CBD's western edge. It is the terminus for V/Line regional trains, The Overland service to Adelaide and the XPT to Sydney. The original station opened in 1859 as a dead-end terminus with a single main platform. Between October 2002 and late 2006 the Civic Nexus consortium rebuilt it, to a design by Grimshaw Architects with Jackson Architecture; most transport facilities were ready for the 2006 Commonwealth Games. An undulating, wave-shaped roof defines the design, alongside a new Collins Street entrance and concourse and a coach interchange. It won the Lubetkin Prize from the Royal Institute of British Architects. Local architects have criticised its poor links to nearby streets and how it tapers off into a boxy shopping centre.

The University of Warsaw Library, known as BUW, opened its new building on 15 December 1999 to a design by the architects Marek Budzyński and Zbigniew Badowski; Pope John Paul II had blessed it on 11 June that year. Its roof carries a public botanical garden of one hectare, laid out by landscape architect Irena Bajerska and one of Europe's largest roof gardens. The upper garden is split into four parts: Golden to the north, Silver to the east, Crimson to the south and Green to the west. Along Dobra Street the main facade bears large blocks of classical writing in several scripts, among them Old Polish lines by Jan Kochanowski, Greek by Plato and Hebrew from the Book of Ezekiel. Inside stands a traditional Japanese tea pavilion, a chashitsu, a 2004 gift from Kyoei Steel that hosts tea events.

Legiobanka, the Bank of the Czechoslovak Legions, was a cooperative bank set up in Irkutsk in 1919 to look after the Czechoslovak Legion's finances. In 1923 it moved into a new Prague head office that Josef Gočár had designed in 1921. After his cubist phase, Gočár turned in the early 1920s to Rondocubism, a 'national' style, and this building represents that Czechoslovak strand of art deco so fully that the style is sometimes named after it. Four works by the sculptor Jan Štursa show the Legion in battle on the Italian, Eastern, Russian Far East and Western fronts, and above them Otto Gutfreund's frieze shows the Legions coming home. The bank ČSOB bought it in 1990 and renovated it in 1991–1994. Since a theatre inside was revived as the Archa Theatre in 1994, it is also called the Archa Palace.

Now the Fairmont Golden Prague, the former InterContinental Prague is a Brutalist luxury hotel by the Vltava, where Pařížská Street ends to the north. Czech architect Karel Filsak designed it, and it was built between 1968 and 1974 as a project of the state travel agency ČEDOK with Intercontinental Hotels Corporation, becoming Czechoslovakia's first international five-star hotel, which officially opened on 7 December 1974. Building, interiors and art were conceived as one: sculptor Zbyněk Sekal designed the ceramic façade elements, and glass artists Stanislav Libenský and Jaroslava Brychtová added architectural glass. From 2021 to 2025 a reconstruction led by Marek Tichý of TaK Architects aimed to recover parts of Filsak's design hidden by later alterations, restoring its exposed concrete, ceramic façade and post-war art. It reopened on 15 April 2025 with 320 rooms, suites and residences.

Le Havre's Hôtel de Ville took the place of a stone Châteauesque town hall designed by Charles Brunet-Debaine and finished in 1857, which British bombing wiped out in September 1944. Auguste Perret designed its modern replacement, begun in reinforced concrete in 1953. When Perret died in February 1954, Jacques Tournant steered the design to its official opening on 14 July 1958. A main block 143 metres long, for exhibitions and receptions, turns 15 symmetrical bays south to the square, with tall first-floor windows below smaller second-floor ones, all framed by columns under a long entablature. An 18-storey office tower, 70 metres high, marks the west end. Some councillors wanted the old hall back, and critics called the tower American, not French. The building became a monument historique in 2017; Perret's rebuilt city joined UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2005.

Tour Montparnasse, formally Tour Maine-Montparnasse, is an office skyscraper of 59 floors, 210 metres tall, built from 1969 to 1973 to designs by Eugène Beaudouin, Urbain Cassan and Louis de Hoÿm de Marien. It was France's tallest skyscraper until Tour First at La Défense overtook it in 2011, and it remains the tallest building within Paris. It stands on 56 reinforced concrete pillars 70 metres deep, and because planning put it just above a Métro line at Montparnasse–Bienvenüe, a concrete shield protects the Métro structures instead of using them as supports. Only perimeter offices have windows. Many Parisians have criticised its plain, massive, monolithic look as out of place, and two years after its completion Paris responded by banning buildings over seven storeys in the city centre. In 2017 Nouvelle AOM won a competition to redesign the façade.

The national stadium, Stade de France, stands in Saint-Denis, north of Paris; its 81,338 seats make it France's largest. It was built for the 1998 World Cup and named at the suggestion of Michel Platini, the organising committee's head; with only 31 months allowed, work began on 2 May 1995. A France–Spain friendly opened it on 28 January 1998, and on 12 July the hosts beat Brazil 3–0 there in the final. The design, credited to Michel Macary, Aymeric Zublena, Michel Regembal and Claude Constantini, draws on Pan Am's Worldport at New York's JFK airport. It was designed to shelter 80,000 spectators without covering the pitch, and tinted glass at the centre passes the blue and green light the grass needs. To uncover the athletics track, rear sections drop 7.1 metres and inner sections retract 15 metres into the gap.

The Palais de Chaillot is perched on Chaillot Hill, in the Trocadéro area of Paris's 16th arrondissement. It was made for the 1937 Exposition Internationale by partly demolishing and partly rebuilding the Palais du Trocadéro of 1878. Its architects, Jacques Carlu, Louis-Hippolyte Boileau and Léon Azéma, worked in a classicising 'moderne' style. Two separate wings bend in a broad arc: they are the old palace's wings, fronted by new, taller sections. The old central hall and towers came down, leaving only the basement, and a wide esplanade built on top opens a clear view across toward the Eiffel Tower and further. Quotations by Paul Valéry adorn the buildings, along with sculpture groups at attic level by Alfred Bottiau, Raymond Delamarre and Carlo Sarrabezolles. Here, on 10 December 1948, the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Station F, a business incubator for start-ups in Paris's 13th arrondissement, close to the national library's François Mitterrand site, fills a former rail freight depot known as the Halle Freyssinet, which gives it its 'F'. The hall was built in 1927–1929 for the Gare d'Austerlitz to a design by Eugène Freyssinet, a French structural engineer who pioneered prestressed concrete. Architects Wilmotte & Associates remodelled it extensively for small start-ups, and President Emmanuel Macron formally opened the 34,000-square-metre site in June 2017. Called the world's largest start-up facility, it houses up to 1,000 young businesses as well as corporate partners such as Facebook, Microsoft and Naver, with 3,000 desks, private meeting rooms, a 370-seat auditorium and dining open to the public. It also holds La Felicità, from the Big Mamma group, which at 4,500 square metres is Europe's largest restaurant.

Once provisionally named Bercy-Tolbiac, the Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir carries only people on foot and bicycles across the Seine between the Pont de Bercy and the Pont de Tolbiac, linking Paris's 12th and 13th arrondissements. Opened on 13 July 2006 as the city's 37th bridge over the river, it was the first of them named after a woman. It runs 304 metres with a clear span of 190 metres, and its five crossings leap the river with no supports in the water. The steel central span, which Dietmar Feichtinger's firm called the peltinée, is a 650-tonne lens, 106 metres long and 12 metres wide, shaped to reduce shear. Midway, the lens shelters people from rain. Built by the Eiffel company in Alsace, the span came by canal, sea and river and was lifted into place in two hours in January 2006.

Le Grand Bleu, as Marseille's Hôtel du Département is known, houses the Bouches-du-Rhône Conseil Général and its council chambers. Will Alsop and Jan Störmer designed this regional government seat; the scheme won an international competition, beating Foster + Partners in the final round. In the Saint-Just district north of the centre, the High-Tech building was meant to unite scattered offices on one site: two administrative blocks joined by an atrium, with a separate debating chamber, the 'Deliberatif', set against them. X-shaped concrete pilotis, cast in place, mark the building. Built in 26 months and opened in 1994, it is the largest twentieth-century public building in provincial France. Artist Brian Clarke conceived the facade as a 'skin of art': blue glass, coloured by a ceramic glazing technique he devised. Its colour, near Yves Klein blue, took the architects longest to settle.

This factory in Saint-Dié-des-Vosges is the one industrial building Le Corbusier designed. Design studies started in January 1947, building work in early April 1948, and the structure was finished in 1951; the factory went into use in 1952, once Charlotte Perriand and Jean Prouvé had furnished its interior. Raised on stilts and made of reinforced concrete, it was completed ahead of the Unité in Marseille and was the first building designed with the Modulor. Vladimir Bodiansky and André Wogenscky, close collaborators of the architect, used it to test a full-size sunshade hung on the facade, meant to cut direct light on the workstations and protect delicately coloured fabrics. Le Corbusier saw its roof terrace as a key social space for its users. In 2016 it joined UNESCO's World Heritage List with sixteen other works by him.

Built between 1937 and 1946 on the Plateau d'Assy, in the commune of Passy in Haute-Savoie, this Roman Catholic church looks out towards Mont Blanc. Maurice Novarina, then a young architect, won the 1937 competition and worked with Édouard Malot on a design in Taveyannaz sandstone, a local stone often used for Savoie chalets. The pointed roof is shaped to carry heavy snow, and the twenty-eight-metre bell tower was designed with local tectonic movement in mind. Inside, a rectangular nave between two aisles recalls a Roman chapel, and a semicircular choir with an ambulatory stands over the crypt. Fernand Léger, Henri Matisse, Marc Chagall, Georges Braque, Germaine Richier and other artists added work ranging from mosaic and tapestry to stained glass. The church became a monument historique in June 2004.

The Garabit Viaduct takes a single railway line across the gorge of the Truyère near Ruynes-en-Margeride, in the mountains of the Massif Central. Gustave Eiffel was handed the job without the usual competitive tender, his company having already bridged the Douro at Porto with the Maria Pia Bridge (1875–1877); Maurice Koechlin did the structural engineering. Work ran from 1882 to 1884, and it opened in November 1885. A parabolic arch spanning 165 m carries the line 124 m above the river; when finished it was the longest arch anywhere in the world. The whole crossing runs 565 m and weighs 3,587 tonnes. Passing trains make it deflect by about 8 mm, the same figure Eiffel had calculated.

Le CentQuatre, French for "104", stands on rue d'Aubervilliers in Paris's 19th arrondissement. Its first architects were Édouard Delebarre de Bay and Godon, working under Victor Baltard, then the city's chief architect, and the building was opened in 1874, two years after work began. Glass and brick fill a cast-iron frame, in the industrial manner of the period's big stations and exhibition halls. Two vast covered halls, loading bays, stables and cellars ran for more than 270 m, over an area equal to the Place de la République. For upwards of 120 years Paris's undertakers worked here, over 1,000 people organising 150 funeral processions a day. Listed in 1997, the site was converted by Atelier Novembre, chosen by tender in 2003, and reopened as a cultural centre on 11 October 2008; events and exhibitions now fill the former basement stables.

In the late 1920s the council of Boulogne-Billancourt, led by mayor André Morizet, decided on a larger town hall at the heart of the town, choosing an old quarry site where Rue Gallieni meets Rue Paul-Bert. Tony Garnier and Jacques Debat-Ponsan designed it in the Art Deco style, in reinforced concrete. Work began in December 1931, and Morizet opened the building on 15 December 1934. Two rectangular blocks stand one behind the other, the rear one taller and wider. The front block presents a symmetrical 19-bay facade, its central bay reached by a few steps that lead to a deep-set doorway under a curved canopy. The rear block holds the main room, the Grand Hall des Guichets, 65 m long and 28 m wide. The building was listed as a monument historique in 1975.

Villa Arson occupies 23,000 m2 on a hill in Saint Barthélemy, a neighbourhood in the north of Nice. In 1965 the city gave the school the Arson family's old house, and Michel Marot designed its enlargement into an international school of fine art, completed in 1970. From the hillside the site looks across the city to the coast of the French Riviera, and the design makes the most of that view, of planting and of daylight, using many courtyards, terraces and gardens. A national centre for contemporary art was set up in 1971, and in 1972 Jacques Duhamel, then Minister of Cultural Affairs, opened the school and the centre together as "la Villa Arson". Today it serves as an art museum, a school and a research institution for contemporary art.

No railway station in Italy is busier than Roma Termini, and only four in Europe are; it handles about 150 million passengers a year and 850 trains a day. Two teams chosen in a 1947 competition designed it: Leo Calini and Eugenio Montuori; and Massimo Castellazzi, Vasco Fadigati, Achille Pintonello and Annibale Vitellozzi. It opened in 1950. Full-height glass walls front the great hall, whose concrete roof, a flattened and segmented arch, reworks a Roman bath's barrel vault in modern form and runs into a cantilevered canopy over the entrance drive. Anodized aluminium panels along the glass, by the Hungarian-Italian artist Amerigo Tot, evoke a train's sound and speed. Behind, a longer travertine-clad block holds a 10-storey hotel. Side structures from Angiolo Mazzoni's design are still part of the station.

Enrico Del Debbio designed the Stadio dei Marmi in the 1920s as a training ground for students of the neighbouring Fascist Academy of Physical Education, today home to CONI, the Italian Olympic Committee. It opened in 1932 near Monte Mario, on the tenth anniversary of the March on Rome, under Benito Mussolini's rule, and was built to celebrate Fascist achievements and the party's youth movement. Sixty Carrara marble athletes, each 4 m tall and given by Italy's provinces, ring the stadium. Twenty-four sculptors picked by contest made them, taking Greek and Roman works such as the Doryphoros of Polykleitos and Myron's Discobolus as models; the figures stand out against the stadium's plain white marble architecture. Del Debbio spoke of a complex of "severe monumentality". The stadium later hosted some field hockey preliminaries of the 1960 Summer Olympics.

Piero Portaluppi, an important Rationalist architect in Milan, designed this single-family house on via Mozart, built between 1932 and 1935. It was meant to be elegant yet comfortable and modern in style and services, with a lift, a dumbwaiter, intercoms, telephones and a heated pool. The pool, set in a large garden with a tennis court, was the city's second and the first on private land. From 1938, for twenty years, the family had the architect Tomaso Buzzi remodel the exterior and later some rooms' furnishings in a manner drawn from 18th-century art, softer and more ornate than Portaluppi's minimalism. Bequeathed to FAI, the Italian Environmental Fund, the house opened to the public in May 2008 after more than three years of work costing about six million euros. In 2009 Luca Guadagnino filmed I Am Love there.

Torre Galfa stands in Milan's Centro Direzionale district, north of the city centre. Melchiorre Bega designed it in 1956 and it was finished in 1959. Its name joins the two streets it faces, Via Galvani and Via Fara. Rising 109 m over 31 floors, with two more below ground, it ranks as Milan's eleventh-tallest skyscraper. The design draws mainly on the International Style: a rectangular tower above two wider lower floors, its reinforced concrete frame almost hidden behind glass and aluminium curtain walls. Built for the Sarom company, it was sold in the mid-1970s to a bank, Popolare di Milano, which made it a headquarters and service centre. In May 2012 a group occupied it to create an artists' space, Macao. Refurbishment by Studio BG&K began in 2016, planned as a mix of homes, a hotel and commercial uses.

Lingotto, on Via Nizza in Turin, was built as a car factory for Fiat. Work began in 1916 and ended in 1923, to a design by the young Giacomo Matté-Trucco, with G A Porcheddu's company as builder. Its five floors worked unusually: raw materials entered at ground level, and cars were assembled on a line climbing through the building, emerging on the roof onto a 1.5 km test track with spiral concrete ramps at either end. At the time no car factory in the world was bigger, and Le Corbusier called it "a guideline for town planning". Superseded by Fiat's bigger Mirafiori plant, it closed in 1982. Renzo Piano won the competition to convert it, and it now holds concert halls, a theatre, a convention centre, shops, a hotel and Fiat's administrative headquarters. Visitors can still see the rooftop track.

The Palazzo della Farnesina stands in the Foro Italico area of Rome, between Monte Mario and the River Tiber, on land once called the Farnese Gardens after Pope Paul III, born Alessandro Farnese. Enrico Del Debbio, Arnaldo Foschini and Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo designed the nine-storey building in 1935 as headquarters for Italy's National Fascist Party. Work stopped in 1943 and through the Second World War, and it was finished in 1959, changed only slightly from the original design. It then brought the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, until then spread over 13 offices, under one roof, and the ministry is still there. Faced in travertine, it has over 1,300 rooms and is 169 m wide and 51 m tall, with a total area of 120,000 m2. In size it compares with the Caserta Palace and ranks among Italy's largest buildings.

The Palazzo del Cinema on the Lido di Venezia is home to the Venice Film Festival and also hosts congresses. The first festival screenings were held in August 1932 at the Hotel Excelsior, out on its terrace, and their success soon demanded a proper venue. The engineer Luigi Quagliata designed one along modernist lines, built in 1936–37 and opened on 10 August 1937 for the festival's fifth edition, with a plain hall and a cinema seating a thousand, today's Great Hall. The plan set three rationalist buildings in symmetry: the Casino in the middle, the cinema to its left and a twin on the right for an ice rink, never built because of the Second World War. In 1952 Quagliata was asked to enlarge the palazzo, but only the forepart and an open-air arena were built.

Conte Giovanni Querini, the last of the Venetian Querini Stampalia family, asked for this cultural foundation to be set up, and it was founded in 1869. Its home is the Palazzo Querini Stampalia in the Castello sestiere, a short way south of Santa Maria Formosa. The palazzo holds an archive, a library, living quarters and the Pinacoteca Querini Stampalia, with its paintings and furnishings. From 1961 to 1963 the architect Carlo Scarpa reworked the ground floor of the historic building, designing spaces and elements both indoors and outdoors, as well as the garden; Giuseppe Mazzariol directed the foundation when this was finished. Researchers may use the foundation, and its library is the only one in the city that opens on Sundays; it is thought to be among the loveliest public libraries in Venice.

The Stadio Olimpico stands within the Foro Italico in northwestern Rome. Seating more than 70,000, it is the city's biggest sports venue and the second biggest in Italy, after San Siro in Milan. Building began in 1928 with Enrico Del Debbio, Luigi Moretti enlarged it in 1937, and Annibale Vitellozzi joined the project in 1951. Rebuilding ended in 1952 at a cost of 3.4 billion lire: a 33,500 m2 concrete structure clad in travertine, its pitch sunk so the stadium would not dominate the Foro Italico skyline and would sit well with its neighbours. President Luigi Einaudi opened it on 17 May 1953 as the Stadio dei Centomila, named for the 100,000 it was expected to hold. For the 1990 World Cup it was rebuilt under a Teflon and fibreglass roof hung from 88 steel cables between two steel rings.

Venice's Ponte della Costituzione, or Constitution Bridge, was the fourth to cross the Grand Canal, joining Santa Lucia railway station on the north side to Piazzale Roma, where buses and cars arrive, on the south. Santiago Calatrava was chosen in November 1999. He proposed a broad arched truss, 180 m in radius, made elsewhere and set in place wholly from the water; a central arch, a pair of side arches and two lower ones are tied by cross girders. In July 2007, amid public and political protest, a barge brought it into position. The steps alternate pietra d'Istria, a traditional Venetian stone, with glass lit from below. Critics cited the lack of wheelchair access, doubted the need for it and disliked its minimalist style. As people kept falling, the city chose in 2022 to swap all the glass for trachyte.

Roma Tiburtina, the second-largest station in Rome after Termini, first opened in 1866. The architect Paolo Desideri designed its redevelopment, while the Gemmo Railway Division ran the design and construction phases. The new station is a large bridge over the tracks that joins the Nomentano and Pietralata districts: a closed, glazed box 240 m long and 50 m wide, lifted 9 m above the ground. Inside, eight separate rooms hang from the roof, which helps shield them from the noise and vibration of trains passing below. Twenty-nine escalators and 52 lifts link them to the platforms at ground level. Construction used about 13,400 tonnes of steel and 95,000 m3 of concrete. After three years of work it opened on 28 November 2011, its cost having nearly doubled from the first estimate to around €330 million.

The Grattacielo Intesa Sanpaolo in Turin is the headquarters of the Intesa Sanpaolo banking group. After disputes over its height and its effect on the skyline, work began in December 2008; on completion in December 2014 the first 50 bank staff moved in. Only the Mole Antonelliana and the Piedmont Region Headquarters stand taller in the city. Besides offices for over 2,000 staff it has public spaces: a 364-seat hall at the base, hung from transfer trusses four floors up, and at the top a greenhouse with the Piano35 restaurant, a garden and a viewing terrace. Renzo Piano called it a "bioclimatic building", naturally ventilated and cooled, with photovoltaic panels on the south facade meant to supply much of its power. It is Europe's only LEED Platinum high-rise, and topped ArchDaily's 2016 readers' vote for offices.

Zaha Hadid Architects won the contract for this station near Naples in 2003, and Zaha Hadid presented the scheme that November, with opening then planned for 2009; it was inaugurated in June 2017. It was always conceived as a bridge over the four tracks, four levels and up to 25 m high, holding a 20,000 m2 concourse with space for 10,000 m2 more. Setting the concourse right above the platforms shortens walks and favours neither end's community. Outside, large glass panels form winding shapes said to evoke a moving train. Against earthquakes, the building is split into zones no longer than 50 m that can move on their own. The glazed roof cuts glare with shading and acoustic baffles, and vents let out surplus heat. The curved structure is mostly concrete, shaped with prefabricated steel units and CNC-milled temporary moulds.

Museion takes its name from the Greek word for a temple of the muses. Founded in 1985, it collects modern and contemporary art for Bolzano, in the South Tyrol region of Italy. Its new home in the centre of the city, by the architects KSV Krüger Schuberth Vandreike, opened to the public on 24 May 2008. The main building is a rectangular block 54 m long, 25 m high and 23 m wide, with see-through front and rear facades, and it serves as a link, both physical and symbolic, between the two parts of the city. The museum's 4,500 works, by international and local artists, are shown in a rotation built around themes. Its library, which focuses on modern and contemporary art, keeps 25,000 volumes, 50 art journal subscriptions and 400 DVDs.

Kensal House stands where Ladbroke Grove ends to the north, in Kensal Green, London: two curved blocks holding 68 housing association flats, finished in 1937. The Gas Light and Coke Company commissioned and paid for the scheme, which housed 380 people. No earlier modernist block in the UK had been designed for working-class tenants, and many saw it then as a prototype for modern living. The architect Maxwell Fry designed it, and a committee of five architects plus Elizabeth Denby, a social reformer and his colleague on the Peckham Pioneer Health Centre, developed it. Fry spoke of an "urban village". A community centre, shared laundry, canteen and nursery school were included. Unusually, there was no electricity: fires, cookers, water heaters and even irons ran on gas or coke. It has been Grade II* listed since 1981.

King's Cross, in Camden at the edge of central London, ranks among the UK's busiest stations and starts the East Coast Main Line north to Yorkshire, the North East and Scotland. Lewis Cubitt did the detailed design; his brother was Thomas Cubitt, architect of Belgravia. Two great arched train sheds stand behind a brick south front, echoing their arches, with a 34 m clock tower. When it opened on 14 October 1852 it was England's largest station. A £500 million restoration plan, announced in 2005, set out to reglaze the original shed roof and replace a 1972 front extension with an open plaza. West of the station, a semicircular departures concourse by John McAslan opened in March 2012; its Arup-engineered roof has a 54 m radius and over 2,000 triangular panels, half glass.

Pallant House Gallery in Chichester, West Sussex, keeps one of the world's best collections of British art from the 20th century. Its heart is a Queen Anne townhouse of 1712, listed at Grade I, built for Henry "Lisbon" Peckham, a wine merchant, and his wife Elizabeth. Council offices from 1919, it was restored in 1979 and became a gallery in 1982. Sir Colin Wilson and Long & Kentish designed a new wing, opened in June 2006: a frankly modern block beside the old house and joined to it. It took the 2007 Gulbenkian Prize, whose judges praised how old and new play off each other. Thought to be the first UK gallery heated and cooled geothermally, it pumps water through 69 pipes reaching 35 m down, roughly halving its carbon emissions.

The Whitworth, a University of Manchester gallery in Whitworth Park, holds more than 60,000 items. J.W. Beaumont designed the original Grade II listed building, built from 1895 to 1900 in a free Jacobean style: two storeys over a basement, in red brick banded and trimmed with matching terracotta, under green slate roofs. The architects MUMA led a refurbishment, and an extension in glass, brick and stainless steel followed, its two wings reaching from the rear into the park, linked by a glazed promenade. After complications delayed a reopening planned for 2014, the extension opened on 14 February 2015, doubling the public space. The work won a RIBA National Award that year and was then shortlisted for the Stirling Prize. Over 440,000 people visited in its first year, and the Art Fund named it Museum of the Year in 2015.

Completed in 1848 at Kew, the Royal Botanic Gardens in London, the Palm House grows palms and other plants from the tropics and subtropics. In 1844 Sir William J. Hooker, Kew's director since 1841, asked Decimus Burton for early sketches as part of a plan to lift the garden's image. The iron-maker Richard Turner built it. Turner's first plans were Gothic, which Burton at first opposed, and the final design follows Burton's preferred Neoclassical style. No greenhouse had been built at this scale before, and no earlier building had used wrought iron structurally on such a scale. An upper walkway rises among the larger plants, which include the world's oldest pot plant. Kew said in 2025 that the house would close in 2027 for a five-year, £50 million renovation to make it carbon neutral.

Brighton's Royal Pavilion, a Grade I listed former royal home, grew in three stages from 1787 as a retreat by the sea for George, Prince of Wales, later Prince Regent (1811) and then King George IV (1820). In 1787 he had Henry Holland, designer of Carlton House, enlarge the existing building. From 1815 to 1822 John Nash remodelled and greatly extended it, and what stands today is his: Mughal-inspired bulbous domes, minarets topped with chhatris, and cusped arches. The tented roofs over the music room and banqueting room use laminated timber joined with iron connectors, a system Nash had worked out with William Nixon, his assistant, in 1814, so they need no central columns. Frederick Crace and the decorative painter Robert Jones did most of the interiors, drawing heavily on Chinese and Indian fashion.

The Spire of Dublin, also called the Monument of Light, is a slender stainless steel needle rising 120 m from O'Connell Street, the city's main thoroughfare, where Nelson's Pillar once stood. A committee led by the Lord Mayor, Joe Doyle, ran an international open competition in 1998 and chose it from 205 entries. Its designer, Ian Ritchie of Ian Ritchie Architects, wanted a simplicity that would bridge art and technology. Its eight hollow steel cones, the longest 20 m, went up on 21 January 2003, tapering from 3 m wide to 15 cm. Inside the fifth section, two tuned mass dampers by Arup check its sway. A pattern at the base draws on a rock core from the site and the DNA double helix. At dusk, LEDs shine through 11,884 holes in its top 10 m.

The Golden Lane Estate is council housing at the City of London's northern edge, built in the 1950s on a site bombed in the Second World War. Chamberlin, Powell and Bon became a partnership when Geoffry Powell was named winner of the design competition on 26 February 1952. Housing 200 people per acre was dense, yet 60% of the site is open space, by building taller than was usual in 1951. The first phase opened in 1957, and further land allowed three more buildings, Crescent House among them. Red and blue panels face the maisonette blocks, yellow the tower. At the centre, the 16-storey Great Arthur House was briefly Britain's tallest residential building. The architects openly acknowledged Le Corbusier's influence. The estate is Grade II listed, with Crescent House at Grade II* for its importance as post-war housing.

St Pancras International, on Euston Road in Camden, is a major London terminus, served by Eurostar trains from Belgium, France and the Netherlands. William Henry Barlow designed the station, whose single-span roof stands on wrought iron pillars; 210 m long, 73 m wide and 30 m high, no enclosed space in the world was larger at the time. The roof's middle half is glazed. Land here was valuable, so the lower level went to freight, mainly beer from Burton, and the undercroft was laid out like a beer warehouse, its module a barrel's length. After the station opened on 1 October 1868, George Gilbert Scott's ornate red-brick Gothic Midland Grand Hotel was built across its front. In the 1960s John Betjeman, later Poet Laureate, led a winning campaign against closure and demolition; Grade I listing followed in 1967.

Named after David Livingstone, this high-rise belongs to the John Anderson Campus of the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow. It went up from 1962 to 1964 as Alec House, an office block for commercial tenants, through a partnership of Glasgow Corporation, a developer and the former Royal College of Science and Technology. Its reinforced concrete frame used methods advanced for the time, wrapped in a curtain wall of opaque dark green glass panels set between orange metal uprights. Its four high-speed Otis lifts could respond to the flow of people at set times of day. It rises from a three-level concrete podium shared with the McCance Building and a car park. Arguably International Style, it contrasts with the Brutalist buildings attached to it. Standing on the Rottenrow drumlin, it can be seen far across the East End.

The Scottish Storytelling Centre stands on the High Street, on Edinburgh's Royal Mile, and is said to be the first modern building anywhere made specifically for telling stories live. Malcolm Fraser Architects designed it to replace the Netherbow Arts Centre, which had in turn taken the place of the Moray-Knox Church after that was demolished in the 1960s. The new building incorporates John Knox House. Patricia Ferguson MSP, then the Scottish Executive's Minister for Culture, formally opened the centre on 1 June 2006. It received a RIBA Award in 2007, and in 2017 the Sunday Herald Culture Awards nominated it for Best Performing Arts Venue.

Swansea Civic Centre, once called County Hall, is the main administrative centre of Swansea Council. It stands about 800 m southwest of the city centre on the seafront, looking over Swansea Bay, and holds the council chamber and offices along with a café, the main library, exhibition space and archives. Unhappy sharing facilities with Swansea Council, county leaders chose a site once used as a railway goods yard for the Mumbles Railway. C. W. Quick, of the county architects department of West Glamorgan, designed the Brutalist building, which opened in July 1982. Continuous bands of glazing run between deep panels of washed calcined flint. It took its present name in March 2008. Plans announced in 2016 would see it demolished for a city beach, and in 2021 the Twentieth Century Society listed it among its ten buildings most at risk.

The Peace Bridge takes walkers and cyclists over the Foyle in Derry, Northern Ireland, and opened on 25 June 2011. Its curving path links the Guildhall in the city centre with Ebrington Square and St. Columb's Park in the Waterside area, and it also spans the railway near Waterside station. AECOM, whose work includes the Sutong Yangtze River Bridge, designed it with Wilkinson Eyre Architects, designers of the Gateshead Millennium Bridge. The asymmetric deck, 235 m long and 4 m wide, rests on two sloping pillars and stands for the two communities coming together. By easing movement between the mostly unionist Waterside, east of the river, and the mostly nationalist Cityside, on the west, it aims to improve relations. Funding totalling £14 million came from two government departments, matched by the SEUPB Peace III programme.

Tate St Ives in Cornwall shows modern British artists connected with the area. It replaced a former gasworks above Porthmeor Beach, bought in 1988, when Eldred Evans and David Shalev were asked to design a gallery that echoed the gasworks. Work began in 1991, funded by European regional development money, the Henry Moore Foundation and public donations, and ended in 1993 with a central rotunda facing the beach. It opened that June as the Tate's second regional gallery, after Tate Liverpool, and drew over 120,000 visitors by the end of the year. BAM Construct UK later built a 1,200 m2 extension by Jamie Fobert, with the original architect involved in work on the old building. In July 2018 it was named the Art Fund's Museum of the Year, and that month it reached the Stirling Prize shortlist.

Glasgow Tower, once known as the Millennium Tower, rises 127 m on the south bank of the Clyde within the Glasgow Science Centre. No building in Glasgow or Scotland has been taller since it was finished in 2001, and Guinness lists it as the tallest freestanding structure that can turn a full 360 degrees. The architect Richard Horden designed it in 1992, when it was first proposed for St Enoch Square, with Buro Happold as engineering designers; after commissioning, the Glasgow architects BDP took the project over. Shaped like an aircraft wing stood on end, it is turned into the wind by four 6 kW motors, so the split airflow presses equally on both sides. Rather than being fixed to its foundations, it turns on two dozen rubber-sprung roller bearings. Thrust bearing faults closed it from 2002 to 2004.

St Albert's is the Roman Catholic chaplaincy of the University of Edinburgh, and it began in 1931, when the Dominicans moved into its house. That house, now category A listed, was designed in 1766 and built by 1779, as part of the building of George Square. A new chapel was added in the garden and opened in July 2012; no new Dominican chapel had been built in Scotland since the Reformation. Stuart Allan of the practice Simpson & Brown designed it for 150 people, with a clear window behind the altar that looks straight out to the garden. In 2013 the chapel was honoured by the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland, the Scottish Civic Trust and the RIBA, which gave it an award for architectural excellence.

Terminal 5 serves Heathrow, London's main airport, and its main building is the UK's biggest free-standing structure. Planning studies began in February 1988, and in 1989 the Richard Rogers Partnership was chosen to design it; the aviation architects Pascall+Watson did the production design, with Arup and Mott MacDonald as structural engineers. Richard Rogers likened it to the Centre Pompidou for its flexibility. It took £4 billion and nearly 20 years, including Britain's longest public inquiry. The terminal is 396 m long, 176 m wide and 40 m high, its four storeys under one undulating single-span steel roof, with glass walls leaning 6.5 degrees off vertical. Ordinary cranes would have cut into the airport's radar field, so the roof was assembled on the ground and jacked up on eight purpose-built towers. Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 14 March 2008.

Saïd Business School is the University of Oxford's business school, part of its Social Sciences Division. It was founded in 1996, when Wafic Saïd, a Syrian-born businessman, offered the university a donation. Its home is on Park End Street, across from Oxford railway station, on land once taken up by the old Rewley Road station, and Edward Jones and Sir Jeremy Dixon designed the building. At its opening on 5 November 2001, students protested, troubled by the controversy around the gift; Saïd had been tied to the Al-Yamamah arms deal the UK signed. In 2002 Nelson Mandela came at Saïd's invitation to open a lecture theatre that bears his name. A later gift from Saïd paid for the Thatcher Business Education Centre on the same site.

The Weston Library began as the New Bodleian, built because by the 1920s the Bodleian Library had run short of space. Work started in 1937 at Broad Street's northeast corner, facing the Clarendon Building, to a design by the architect Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, and was finished in 1940. Its ziggurat form was new for the time, with 60% of the bookstack underground. A tunnel beneath Broad Street, with a footway and a book conveyor, links it to the Old Bodleian. The building closed on 29 July 2011 and was rebuilt behind its original facade to a concept by WilkinsonEyre, to store rare and fragile material better and serve readers and visitors well. It reopened to readers as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

Completed in 2007, the Manchester Civil Justice Centre brings together the city's county court, its family court, the probate registry, the High Court's district registry and Court Service offices. It was the first major court complex in Britain since George Edmund Street's Royal Courts of Justice, finished in London in 1882. Denton Corker Marshall, an Australian practice, won the competition in August 2002 with engineers Mott MacDonald. Drawing on Expressionist architecture and on Futurism's dynamic lines, the 17-storey, 80 m building ends in cantilevered "fingers" over its lower floors, which earned it the nickname "filing cabinet". Its west side faces the River Irwell with a hanging glass wall 60 m square, described as Europe's largest. Its long, slim plan allows cross-ventilation and daylight in most areas. It made the Stirling Prize shortlist.

The Royal Liver Building stands at the Pier Head in Liverpool, one of the city's Three Graces on the waterfront alongside the Cunard Building and the Port of Liverpool Building. Built for Royal Liver Assurance, it opened in 1911, three years after its foundation stone was laid. Walter Aubrey Thomas designed it in the Edwardian Baroque style, Edmund Nuttall Limited built it, and L. G. Mouchel & Partners advised on the structure. An early reinforced concrete building, its radical design struck some as "impossible to build". Two clock towers crown its ten storeys, each carrying a copper Liver bird 5.5 m tall designed by Carl Bernard Bartels. The clock faces, 7.6 m across, are bigger than those of the Great Westminster Clock, and no electronically driven clocks in the UK are larger. It is Grade I listed.

Philip Webb, an architect, and William Morris, a designer, worked out Red House together in 1859 as Morris's family home; it was finished in 1860. It was Webb's first independent commission, and Morris never built another house. Built on Morris's ideals of craft and artisan skill, it is an early instance of what was later called the Arts and Crafts movement. The plan is an L of two storeys under a steep red-tiled roof. Windows were placed to suit each room, not to make the outside symmetrical, so many types sit side by side, from tall casements to bull's-eye windows. There is no applied ornament; arches over windows and other decoration come from construction itself. Morris wanted house and garden designed as one; rose trellises split the garden into four squares. It was listed at Grade I in 1950.

Dynamic Earth, first named Our Dynamic Earth, is a not-for-profit science centre in Holyrood, Edinburgh, next to the Scottish Parliament and below Salisbury Crags; no interactive attraction in Scotland is larger. James Hutton, the Scottish geologist, lived and worked nearby in the 18th century, and the site itself was most recently a gasworks and part of the former Holyrood Brewery. Michael Hopkins and Partners designed the building: a membrane, held up by steel masts, over a steel frame. The design keeps the wall that once enclosed the Abbey Brewery's ale stores. The exhibition cost about £34 million to design and build, and was the first major millennium attraction in the UK to open; Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1999. Awards followed from the Civic Trust (2000) and the RIBA (2001).

Queen's Cross Church in Glasgow, once a Church of Scotland parish church, is the only church by Charles Rennie Mackintosh ever built, hence its other name, the Mackintosh Church. In 1896 St Matthew's Free Church asked Honeyman and Keppie, an established Glasgow practice, for a church and hall in growing Springbank, and John Honeyman gave the job to Mackintosh, then a young trainee. The corner plot was awkward, hemmed in by tenements and a big warehouse, and the Free Church wanted a simple design. Its memorial stone was laid in June 1898, with the first service in September 1899. Instead of a tall spire the church is squat, more like a Norman castle; its south-west tower follows one Mackintosh saw at Merriot in Somerset in 1895. A barrel vault lined in timber spans the full forty-foot width of the nave.

The Pierhead Building in Cardiff dates from 1897. Its designer, William Frame, was an English architect, and it took the place of the Bute Dock Company's headquarters, lost to fire in 1892. Until William Burges, his mentor, died in 1881, Frame had worked alongside him rebuilding Cardiff Castle and Castell Coch. The company's coat of arms on the facade bears its Welsh motto, meaning "by water and fire", the two elements of the steam power that transformed Wales. A French-Gothic Renaissance theme brings six-sided chimneys, gargoyles, carved friezes and an ornate clock tower whose clock is nicknamed the "Big Ben of Wales". The outside is faced in glazed terracotta. Its features, and its role as Cardiff, its docks and industrial Wales grew, earned it Grade I listing. It is now part of the Senedd estate.

Before it moved to Stranmillis in 1929, the Ulster Museum was known as Belfast’s Municipal Museum and Art Gallery; James Cumming Wynne designed its new home there. Francis Pym won a 1964 competition for a large extension, built by McLaughlin & Harvey Ltd and opened in 1972, the only work of his ever completed. Magazines published it, and until it was altered it was Northern Ireland’s most important Brutalist example. David Evans praised the “almost barbaric power” of its huge cubic projections and cantilevers, likening them to a mastodon brooding over the botanic gardens’ conifers. A later redevelopment drew fire from many architectural figures and the Twentieth Century Society, mainly for changing that Brutalist character and dismantling the spiral of rooms in Pym’s wing. The museum reopened in October 2009, exactly eighty years after it first opened.

Knock Basilica, in full the Basilica of Our Lady, Queen of Ireland, is a Roman Catholic church in Knock, a small town in County Mayo, Ireland. Architect Daithi Hanly, working with Louis J Brennan and Brian Brennan, gave it a modern design in concrete, and it was completed in 1976. Monsignor James Horan, Knock’s parish priest from 1967 until he died in 1986, supervised the building work. A decree of Pope John Paul II, Abunde Constat Quam, made the shrine a Minor Basilica on 17 July 1979. Holding roughly 10,000 people, the church serves Tuam’s Roman Catholic archdiocese. It shares the Knock Shrine grounds with four other churches, among them the Apparition Church, where Catholic belief holds that Mary, Joseph and John the Evangelist appeared on the evening of 21 August 1879.

Lys Kernow (Court of Cornwall), on Treyew Road in Truro, is the headquarters of Cornwall Council; from 1966 to 2009 it was called New County Hall. Francis Kenneth Hicklin, then Duchy Architect, designed the Brutalist building with his successor, Alan Groves, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 14 July 1966. Its three concrete-framed storeys formed a square of roughly 50 bays a side, with a window on each floor between concrete slabs. The council chamber was on the first floor and cantilevered out to the east. Sir Geoffrey Jellicoe landscaped the central courtyard, where Barbara Hepworth’s “Rock form, Porthcurno” was unveiled at the opening. A refurbishment by the St Ives designers Poynton Bradbury Wynter Cole was completed in 2013. The building is Grade II listed.

At Eltham Palace the medieval great hall of a one-time royal residence meets an Art Deco house added in the 1930s. In 1933 Stephen Courtauld and Virginia, his wife, leased the site for 99 years and engaged Seely & Paget to restore the great hall and attach a modern home. The architects gave the hall a minstrels’ gallery and took inspiration for the house from Christopher Wren’s buildings at Hampton Court Palace and at Trinity College, Cambridge. Rolf Engströmer, a Swedish designer, made the entrance hall, lit by a glazed dome over blackbean veneer and figurative marquetry, while Piero Malacrida de Saint-August, an Italian designer, did the dining and drawing rooms and Virginia’s circular bedroom. The hall’s hammerbeam roof is England’s third-largest of its type. English Heritage took over management in 1995 and finished major repairs in 1999.

Hornsey Town Hall stands in Hatherley Gardens, Crouch End, and was the first major Modernist building put up in the UK. Reginald Uren, an architect born in New Zealand, designed it for the borough of Hornsey, with Hilversum Town Hall as a visible influence, and his design won a bronze medal from the Royal Institute of British Architects. Gee, Walker & Slater Ltd were the builders, and it opened on 4 November 1935. Its symmetrical seven-bay front looks onto a small courtyard, closed on the right by a six-bay wing. Wide steps lead to three doorways under a canopy, a wrought-iron balcony fronts the central three of seven tall first-floor windows, and a tall flagpole tower rises at the courtyard’s corner. Listed in 1981 as one of the earliest 1930s buildings to be protected, it is now Grade II*.

Shell plc’s global headquarters, the Shell Centre, sits by County Hall on the Thames’s South Bank and now serves as the London Eye’s backdrop. Sir Howard Robertson designed it, and Sir Robert McAlpine built it from 1957 to 1962. Its tower climbs 107 metres (351 ft) over 27 storeys, one of them a mezzanine, and was the first office tower in London to top the Victoria Tower of the Palace of Westminster. Modern Movement critics condemned the Portland stone cladding and individual bronze-framed windows, and the complex has generally been judged dull. Yet that conservative facing has aged better than most concrete, aggregate or curtain-wall fronts of its era. The lavish first interiors drew on a British team, many of them veterans of the Festival of Britain, and on Ernesto Nathan Rogers, who had worked on Milan’s Torre Velasca.

Newcastle Civic Centre, a municipal building in the city’s Haymarket area, was designed by George Kenyon for Newcastle City Council. It replaced a Victorian Town Hall that had stood in St Nicholas Square. Sir Robert McAlpine started work in May 1960, and on 30 November of that year Gladys Robson, the Lord Mayor, laid the foundation stone. Built in 1967, it was given its formal opening on 14 November 1968 by Norway’s King Olav V. Rising 200 feet (61 m), it shares eighth place among Newcastle’s tallest buildings and is Grade II* listed. Modern sculpture is a notable feature: David Wynne made the River God Tyne and Swans in Flight, and John Robert Murray McCheyne the seahorses crowning the tower. The Customer Service Centre, once the cashiers’ reception of the old rates hall, holds two of Victor Pasmore’s abstract murals.

The Palace of Westminster, where the UK Parliament meets, is largely the replacement built after a second, bigger fire wrecked most of the old palace in 1834. The eleventh-century Westminster Hall was spared and absorbed into the new building. Charles Barry won the design competition and picked Gothic Revival, a style he had little experience with, so he leaned heavily on Augustus Pugin for the details. Work began in 1840 and lasted 30 years, slowed by delays and cost overruns, and both Barry and Pugin, his assistant, died while it went on. Known for its ornate decoration, the palace helped Gothic Revival spread elsewhere. Its Elizabeth Tower, home of the bell nicknamed Big Ben, is a landmark of London and the UK. The palace became Grade I listed in 1970 and joined a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

Bath’s Royal Crescent is a sweeping curve of 30 terraced houses, designed by John Wood, the Younger, and built from 1767 to 1774. Grade I listed, it counts among the greatest Georgian architecture in the United Kingdom. Its facade stretches 500 feet (150 m), with 114 Ionic columns at first-floor level under a Palladian-style entablature. No crescent of terraced houses had been built before it, and its view across the parkland opposite makes it an instance of “rus in urbe”, country in the city. The original buyers each purchased a length of frontage and had their own architect build behind it to suit them, so two apparent houses are sometimes one. From the road at the back this shows in varied roof heights and windows, while the front stays uniform and symmetrical.

London Stadium, once known as the Olympic Stadium, is an outdoor, multi-purpose venue at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, London. It was built to stage athletics and the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2012 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. On 13 October 2006 LOCOG, the Games’ organising committee, chose Sir Robert McAlpine and Populous for exclusive negotiations on the design-and-build contract. The track-and-field arena is dug into soft clay and ringed by 25,000 permanent seats built with concrete “rakers”, while a demountable upper tier of steel and precast concrete rose above this bowl for 55,000 more. Its roughly 10,700 tons of steel are just under a quarter of what Beijing’s 2008 Olympic Stadium used, and its compression truss reused surplus North Sea gas pipes. Nominated for the 2012 Stirling Prize, it was remodelled in 2013–2015 to 66,000 seats.

Belfast Waterfront, a multi-purpose venue for conferences and entertainment in Northern Ireland, was designed by the local firm Robinson McIlwaine, with practice partner Peter McGuckin as project architect. Planning started in 1989, and the hall was completed in 1997 at a cost of £32 million. The circular main auditorium, seating 2,241, takes Hans Scharoun’s Berlin Philharmonic Hall as its model, yet its stalls seating can be moved to open out a larger arena. Copper covers the dome so that it will weather to green, in time matching the dome of Belfast City Hall and the city centre’s other Victorian buildings. The Ulster Orchestra gives concerts there, and it is a key venue of the Belfast Festival at Queen’s.

Beside the River Clyde, on its south bank, Glasgow Science Centre was opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 5 July 2001. Three main buildings make it up: an IMAX cinema, the Glasgow Tower and the Science Mall. Building Design Partnership were the centre’s architects, but the tower’s original design came from Richard Horden, with Buro Happold as engineers, and it was meant to be the world’s tallest tower able to rotate freely. Each building has its own metal cladding: aluminium for the tower, stainless steel for the Science Mall and titanium for the IMAX. When finished, the Science Mall, first clad in titanium, was with the IMAX Britain’s only titanium-skinned building. Its crescent shape represents a ship’s canted hull, a reference to the nearby “canting basin”, where boats had marine growth cleared from their hulls.

Tower Bridge in London was built from 1886 to 1894 to designs by Horace Jones, with John Wolfe Barry as engineer, helped by Henry Marc Brunel. It was meant to serve the 39% of Londoners living east of London Bridge while keeping the Pool of London open to shipping.
