Barry teamed up with Jones in 1885, and his idea of a “level soffit” for the upper bridge let the present design go ahead. Unusually, it mixes three types: suspension spans link each shore to the piers, the opening centre is a pair of bascules, and the high walkways were cantilevers until their 1960 conversion to suspension. Its two towers rise 213 feet (65 m). Portland stone and Cornish granite clad their steel frames, protecting the steel and helping the bridge suit the Tower of London. It is Grade I listed.

Wolfson is a graduate college of Oxford University, in north Oxford on the River Cherwell, strong in areas such as global health, economics, environmental studies and the humanities. Sir Isaiah Berlin, a historian and philosopher, helped found it in 1965 and served as its first president. Powell and Moya Architects designed the main building, completed in 1974; few Oxford colleges have a main building as modern. It is arranged around three quadrangles: the central Berlin Quad, named after him; the Tree Quad, built around trees already growing there; and the River Quad, where the Cherwell was diverted to make a punt harbour. Both the main building and the footbridge over the river were Grade II listed in June 2011. There is no high table, all members share one common room, and gowns come out only on special occasions.

Louis Kahn designed this building for Rochester’s First Unitarian Church, a congregation of the Unitarian Universalist Association; it was completed in 1962, and Kahn added a major extension in 1969. He drew a square to stand for the sanctuary and ringed it with concentric circles for an ambulatory, a corridor and the church school. The outside is marked by deeply folded brick walls, made by a sequence of thin, two-storey light hoods that shade the windows from direct sun. Light towers at each corner of the sanctuary’s intricate ceiling bring in indirect daylight. Kahn’s roof layout was kept but reworked as a folded plate of prestressed concrete held only at its edges, removing the heavy beams he had planned. In 1982 the Pulitzer Prize-winning critic Paul Goldberger counted it among the century’s most significant works of religious architecture.

Harbor Towers are two 40-storey residential towers on the Boston waterfront, standing between the Rowes Wharf development and the New England Aquarium. They were designed by Henry N. Cobb, the architect also behind Boston’s John Hancock Tower, and went up in 1971 within a major effort to revive the city’s run-down waterfront. Three towers were planned, but only two were built, along with a parking garage. Tower I is 400 ft (121.9 m) tall and Tower II 396 ft (120.7 m). Apartments are arranged in a pinwheel around a central core, and the structure is reinforced concrete cast in place; against the flat facade, the concrete balconies look like a giant zipper. Designed as affordable rental housing, the flats were turned into condominiums in the 1980s. David von Schlegell’s 1964 stainless steel sculpture Untitled Landscape stands at the base.

Standing on the campus of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, the Murray D. Lincoln Campus Center is a concrete high-rise designed by Marcel Breuer, who also designed its attached parking garage, in the Modernist and Brutalist styles. It is named for Murray D. Lincoln, a cooperative movement leader who helped found the company that became Nationwide Insurance, and who co-founded CARE and was its first president. The centre stands beside the Student Union, with passageways reaching it from the Union and from the garage’s main level. Hotel UMass, formerly The Campus Center Hotel, fills floors three to seven with 116 rooms, and the lower level holds a large auditorium and several conference rooms.

Louis Kahn’s Richards Medical Research Laboratories, on the University of Pennsylvania campus in Philadelphia, are regarded as a breakthrough in his career. He was commissioned in 1957, and the building was completed in 1960. Three laboratory towers cluster in a pinwheel around a fourth, central tower for stairs, lifts, mechanical systems and research animals. Every lab floor, eight per tower, measures 45 feet (14 m) square and has no stairs, lifts or internal columns. The frames are prestressed concrete parts made off-site and craned into place, while brick-faced shafts of cast-in-place concrete are the most prominent part of the exterior. The design is described as Kahn’s first clear statement of “servant” and “served” spaces, an idea that influenced younger architects, Richard Rogers above all, whose buildings, such as Lloyd’s of London and the Centre Georges Pompidou, put service areas fully outside.

The Douglas and Charlotte Grant House in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, is a Usonian-style home by Frank Lloyd Wright on a 40-acre (16 ha) site. It went up from 1949 to 1951, though some work carried on until about 1960, and the owners quarried its limestone on the property themselves. Typical of Wright, it is woven into its site and opens to the outdoors, with window walls, horizontal bands of windows, natural light and ventilation, and natural materials. Its mass and proportions stress the horizontal under a flat roof, a carport takes the place of a garage, and the slab-on-grade floor has radiant heating set into it. Inside are an open plan, ceilings of varied heights, built-in furniture and three large fireplaces with a central hearth. In 1988 it was added to the US National Register of Historic Places.

Louis Sullivan, the Chicago architect, designed eight banks, and the Home Building Association Bank in Newark, Ohio, at 1 North Third Street, is one of them. Construction took place in 1914, and the bank opened on August 25, 1915, under the name The Home Building Association Company, though people commonly called it “The Old Home”. Given a narrow lot, Sullivan made the building bigger by taking it up two storeys, which was unusual among his banks. Its walls are covered in gray-green terra cotta slabs framed with his typical Sullivanesque borders, and its ornament included a winged lion much like the lions found at Cedar Rapids, Grinnell and Sidney. Listed on the US National Register of Historic Places in 1973, it had its facades restored between May 2019 and 2021.

Marcel Breuer’s Hubert H. Humphrey Building, at first named the South Portal Building, holds the headquarters of the US Department of Health and Human Services on Independence Avenue in Southwest Washington, D.C. Completed in 1977 in the Brutalist style, it was among the last designs by Breuer, who retired from practice in 1976. Its site shaped the design: it sits above a sewage line and the Third Street highway tunnel, next to air ducts. Its lowest two floors are recessed under the upper storeys, which hang from steel trusses overhead, as in the Armstrong Rubber Building, an earlier Breuer design in Connecticut. The facade combines travertine with precast and cast-in-place concrete, and sloping concrete brises soleil over the windows limit sunlight. Southwest Washington gained nine Brutalist federal buildings in the century’s third quarter, and this is one of them.

Kips Bay Towers is a condominium complex of 1,118 units in two buildings in Manhattan’s Kips Bay, New York City. I.M. Pei and S. J. Kessler designed it in the Brutalist style, with James Ingo Freed involved, and it was finished in 1965. Webb & Knapp developed it as Kips Bay Plaza, with middle-income rental flats that became condominiums in the mid-1980s. With fewer blocks and a large open space between them, Pei hoped to “take the project-itis out of” the scheme, a nod to public housing, often simply called “the projects”. The concrete facades, cast on site, are part of each building’s frame and work as a Vierendeel truss, the first use of the window-truss-wall idea Pei developed with the structural engineer August Komendant. Set 14.5 inches (370 mm) back, the round-cornered windows are shaded by the facade.

Founded in 1919, Munson is a regional fine arts centre in Utica, New York; its formal name is the Munson-Williams-Proctor Arts Institute. Philip Johnson designed its International-style building, completed in 1960, and a model was displayed at the 1958 Brussels World’s Fair, inside the United States Pavilion. The building, a 60,000 sq ft square, rests on eight external piers of ferro-concrete, two per side, and these outer structural parts are faced in bronze and “black” granite from Canada. The windowless cube sits over office areas with windows, recessed in a dry moat, which makes it seem to float. Inside, a skylight lights a two-storey central court, the Edward Wales Root Sculpture Court. The building was added to the US National Register of Historic Places in 2010.

North Shore Congregation Israel, a Reform Jewish congregation, has its synagogue at 1185 Sheridan Road in Glencoe, Illinois, on Chicago’s North Shore. The 1964 building is the work of Minoru Yamasaki, a modernist architect based in Detroit, and one of two notable synagogues he designed, the other being Temple Beth El (1973) in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan. Yamasaki shaped it as a row of arching fan vaults. Between the concrete shells, coloured glass fills the upper gaps and clear glass the lower ones, at eye level. He describes it as “a confluence of daylight and solids”. The lakefront site of 19 acres (7.7 ha) once held a 1911 mansion designed by the Chicago architect David Adler. In 2018, marking the Illinois Bicentennial, the Illinois branch of the American Institute of Architects named it among the Illinois 200 Great Places.

H. H. Richardson, the American architect, designed Oakes Ames Memorial Hall, and Frederick Law Olmsted landscaped it. It stands on Main Street in North Easton, a village of Easton, Massachusetts, next to the Ames Free Library, another Richardson work. Built in 1879–81, it was the gift of Congressman Oakes Ames’s children to the town. The main front, 96 feet (29 m) long and 51 feet (16 m) deep, has an arcade of five massive arches under a row of windows, with an octagonal tower at its right corner. Below is pinkish-grey granite from North Easton itself, trimmed in brownstone; above is brick, topped by a steep red-tiled roof. The upstairs hall is 59 by 47 feet (18 by 14 m). In 1885 American architects named ten buildings as the best, and this was one of the five by Richardson.

In 1966 the Italian company Olivetti asked Louis Kahn to design a plant in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, to make its Underwood typewriters; it was finished in 1970. The brief demanded a factory floor as open as possible, so machines could be quickly rearranged for changing markets. Kahn designed it in concrete, relying on the structural engineer August Komendant, his preferred collaborator. The building is 72 prestressed concrete units locked together in an 8x9 grid. Each unit’s dish is a prismatic shell, 15 cm (6 in) thick, spanning 18 m (60 ft) and lifted 9 m (30 ft) over the floor. Clipped outer corners leave a gap where four units meet, and a translucent skylight there lets daylight in. Renzo Piano, then a young Italian architect, spent several months with Kahn, in effect as an intern, mostly on the roofing system.

Finished in 1958, the headquarters of the Reynolds Metals Company is an International Style complex in a designed landscape in Henrico County, close to Richmond, Virginia. Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill designed its low-rise Executive Office Building with Charles F. Gillette, a landscape architect from Richmond. The complex has been called a prototype for modern suburban offices. To show off the firm’s goods, aluminium went in wherever possible: mostly in the outer cladding, but even in furnishings, down to carpets and curtains containing aluminium fibres. Its three storeys rest on a raised podium, and an interior courtyard brings light inside. Deep fixed overhangs shade the south windows, while bright blue adjustable aluminium louvres control the sun on the east and west. In 2000 it was added to the US National Register of Historic Places.

Edward Durell Stone designed the Richard H. Mandel House in Bedford Hills, Westchester County, New York, and it was built in the International style between 1933 and 1935. Its Z-shaped plan looks out over the Croton Reservoir. The two-storey house combines a steel frame with concrete block and stucco, and a partial basement is set into the sloping ground. Its features include a flat roof, smooth, even walls with no applied ornament, and an asymmetrical, horizontal composition with projecting balconies and broad runs of ribbon windows. Donald Deskey designed its interiors and furnishings. In 1996 it was added to the US National Register of Historic Places.

River City is a mixed-use complex by the Chicago River in the city’s South Loop, designed by Bertrand Goldberg and completed in 1986; it shares elements with his Marina City. Two serpentine residential towers, 7 to 14 storeys high, are built of reinforced concrete “shells” poured in place and hold 449 homes. They stand on a four-storey post-and-beam “plinth” with about 225,000 sq ft (20,900 m²) of shops and offices, underground parking and a 70-slip marina kept ice-free by bubblers. The plinth’s roof carries Skyline Park, a private landscaped acre for residents, and River Road, a skylit atrium ten storeys tall between the towers. As first planned, the complex was to house up to 30,000 families, the peak of Goldberg’s utopian idea of a self-contained city. Preservationists objected when River Road’s raw concrete was painted white.

Philip Johnson designed this guest house on the south side of 52nd Street, between Second and Third Avenues in New York, and it was completed in 1950; it is the only private residence he designed in the city. He was hired in 1948 to design it for the philanthropist Blanchette Rockefeller, wife of John D. Rockefeller III, who wanted a separate building for her modern art collection because her husband did not care for modern art. The symmetrical two-storey front is brick at street level and glass above, the upper storey formed by six translucent glass panels divided by four steel bars. Inside, the layout follows the unbuilt “court house” designs that Ludwig Mies van der Rohe drew in the 1930s. In 2000 the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission made it an official landmark.

Built in 1971, Brown University’s Sciences Library in Providence, Rhode Island, known as “SciLi” (said “sigh-lie”), is a Brutalist tower. In the late 1960s Brown wanted to expand quickly but had little land, so it chose to build the library high. The firm Warner Burns Toan & Lunde designed it, with most of the work by Danforth Toan and M. Rosaria Piomelli. Its 180 feet (55 m) tie it for 16th place among Providence’s tallest buildings, and it ranks among four notable Brutalist buildings at Brown. McKenzie Woodward, an architectural historian, condemned the tower for overwhelming its surroundings and likened it, from too many distant viewpoints, to a Panelák of the Soviet era. In 2006 the basement and the two lowest floors were heavily renovated and became the Friedman Study Center.

Seventeenth Church of Christ, Scientist, a 1968 Christian Science church, stands in Chicago’s Loop, on East Wacker Drive at Wabash Avenue. Its architect, the Chicago-based Harry Weese, is best known for the Washington Metro and remembered for shaping Chicago’s skyline and how the city thought about its lakefront and historic buildings. It is a circular concrete building. The amphitheatre has no ordinary windows; instead, a skylight crowning the oculus at the centre of the conical roof brings in outside light. People cross a bridge over a sunken garden to get in, and Weese said the garden was there for the windowless Sunday School underneath, which gets daylight through it. In the semicircular auditorium, which holds 764, every seat lies within 54 feet of the Readers’ Platform, the focus of all Christian Science auditoriums.

Quincy’s Thomas Crane Public Library, in Massachusetts, is known for its Richardsonian Romanesque design. The Crane family funded it in memory of Thomas Crane, a rich stone contractor who had started out in the Quincy quarries. Henry Hobson Richardson designed the first building (1882). It then grew in three stages: an ell for book stacks and stained glass, designed in Richardson’s manner by William Martin Aiken (1908); a major expansion by Paul A. and Carroll Coletti (1939), with stone carvings by the Quincy sculptor Joseph Coletti; and an addition by the Boston architects Childs, Bertman, and Tseckares (2001) that doubled its size. Richardson counted it among his most successful civic works, and Harper’s Weekly praised it as the country’s finest village library. Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect, designed the grounds. It was made a National Historic Landmark in 1987.

Charles M. Goodman, a local architect, designed the sanctuary of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Arlington in 1964 as a Brutalist building in precast concrete. Of the three churches he designed, it is the only one in Virginia. Founded in 1948, the congregation was the first Unitarian church in the suburbs of Washington, D.C. Goodman’s plan also had an adjoining wing, left unbuilt at the time because of the budget. An overhanging flat roof and corrugated panels, all concrete, define the outside. Its 62-foot (19 m) square meeting room has a polished reinforced concrete floor in a large grid, with daylight supplemented by patterned rows of ceiling lights. Two later additions match the original and complete Goodman’s plan for more educational, administrative and social space. The building was listed on the US and Virginia historic registers in 2014.

The US Tax Court Building, the court’s headquarters, stands on Second Street NW in Washington, D.C.’s Judiciary Square area. Victor A. Lundy was chosen as architect in 1965, and a year later the GSA approved his idea of a landscaped plaza, heavy masses at each end and a cantilevered courtroom block in the middle. Its dedication, on November 22, 1974, marked fifty years since the Revenue Act created the court. It reads as a cube broken into four parts: the courtroom block pushed out at the front, office blocks to the sides and rear. The 4,000-ton courtroom block projects over the entrance, carried by six slender columns, compression and post-tensioned bridges and steel cables concealed in the walls. Inside, a clerestory roof lights the four-storey Hall of Justice. The design took a GSA Honor Award in 1972.

The Van Allen Building, a former department store, stands on a street corner in Clinton, Iowa. John Delbert Van Allen commissioned the four-storey store from Louis Sullivan, and it was built in 1913–14; today it holds flats and commercial space. Its steel frame recalls his high-rises, and the arrangement of its facade scales down the one he used on his earlier Carson Pirie Scott Store in Chicago. As the building is short and wide, Sullivan stressed the horizontal with spandrel panels and wide windows. Above the shopfronts, the brick upper storeys carry terracotta ornament. Unlike his earlier buildings, this one has some ornament that is purely decorative, and its interior plan helped shape the facade. It was named a National Historic Landmark in 1976, largely as one of the best-kept survivors of Sullivan’s later work.

One of three libraries at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, the W. E. B. Du Bois Library was designed by Edward Durell Stone, who followed a Boston library consultant’s advice that growing student demand called for a building of almost 310,000 square feet. It opened in 1973 and was officially dedicated in 1974. At 28 storeys and about 88 m (286 ft), it is the world’s third-tallest library, after Jakarta’s National Library of Indonesia and the Shanghai Library, and is considered the tallest academic research library. Floors come in threes: two stack floors for related subjects and a carrel floor for the matching departments and librarians. Bricks spalling from the facade led the then chancellor, Henry Koffler, to close it in September 1979, and in 1983 the state legislature gave $2.5 million to begin repairing the brick veneer.

The W. R. Grace Building, a 50-storey Manhattan skyscraper 630 feet (190 m) tall, looks out over Bryant Park and the main branch of the New York Public Library. Gordon Bunshaft was its principal designer, and it was completed in 1972. One notable feature is the concave vertical slope of its two street facades, on 42nd and 43rd Streets, though only the 42nd Street side has an entrance. The building reuses Bunshaft’s original, rejected facade design for the Solow Building, another of his works. White travertine covers the exterior, contrasting with the black windows so the tower looks brighter than its neighbours, and a garage below holds 185 vehicles. Since it opened it has drawn criticism for its place on the skyline, its unusual shape and the space its plaza takes up.

Six buildings in Washington’s Foggy Bottom make up the Watergate complex, which combines cooperative flats, a hotel and offices. Built from 1963 to 1971, it had Luigi Moretti (University of Rome) as chief architect and Milton Fischer, of the D.C. firm Corning, Moore, Elmore and Fischer, as associate. It was the District’s first mixed-use development, meant to recast the area as a place for business and homes instead of industry, and planned as a self-sufficient “city within a city”. Its curving forms made it one of the first big US projects in which computers did significant design work, and they give flats good views of the Potomac. It became one of Washington’s most sought-after addresses, favoured by members of Congress and executive-branch appointees. In October 2005 the whole development was added to the US National Register of Historic Places.

Named for Andrew Smith Hallidie, a pioneer of San Francisco’s cable cars, the Hallidie Building is a seven-storey office block at 130 Sutter Street in the city’s Financial District, designed by Willis Polk and opened in 1918. It is best known for its glazed front, symmetrical fire escapes and decorative ironwork. It has one of the first glass curtain walls in the United States, an early sign of the modern skyscraper, though Louis Curtiss’s Boley Clothing Company building of 1909, in Kansas City, Missouri, came first. The Crystal Palace may have inspired Polk; any other source is unclear. When a bank was weighing a much taller replacement in 1971, San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors declared it a historic monument. After the city judged its sheet-metal friezes, cornices, balconies and fire escapes unsafe, a two-year restoration followed, ending in April 2013.

Irving Gill designed Horatio West Court, which went up in 1919 in Santa Monica, California, as an early case of attached homes that share access for walkers and cars. Six little buildings share a narrow 60-foot lot that a full-length driveway divides symmetrically: two units sit either side of it, and two rear garages have small flats on top. Every building is a two-storey, flat-roofed cube, slightly inflected, with a small entrance porch and a walled terrace. The arched entries and little patio courts reveal Gill’s affinity for Mission Revival, but the buildings are squarely Modern Movement work. Richard Neutra photographed it extensively, as he did Gill’s Dodge House, and published the photographs in his 1930 book Amerika: Neues Bauen in der Welt. In 1977 it became the first Santa Monica building on the US National Register of Historic Places.

The Hyatt Regency, a hotel in San Francisco’s financial district, sits at Market Street’s foot, by The Embarcadero, and belongs to the Embarcadero Center, developed by John Portman, Trammell Crow and David Rockefeller. Portman, its architect, has said that watching Things to Come, the 1935 science fiction film, suggested the design to him. Guinness lists the atrium, as of 2024, as the world’s largest hotel lobby: 107 m long, 49 m wide and 52 m (15 storeys) high. Eclipse, a big modernist sculpture by Charles O Perry, sits inside it. John King, architecture critic of the San Francisco Chronicle, has called the 1973 building a “temple of hermetic urbanism” whose sci-fi style had grown “dated” by 2016 while staying “visually dazzling”. The 1974 film The Towering Inferno used the atrium as its Glass Tower lobby.

Richard Neutra and Robert Alexander designed the Los Angeles County Hall of Records, an International Style high-rise at the north end of the Civic Center downtown. Plans first had two separate buildings, one for records and one for staff, but the architects combined them. The plan is a T: the north side has only odd-numbered floors, with double-height ceilings and tall windows, while the records block to the south has a floor every 8 feet. To save energy, big aluminium louvres run the full height of the south face; originally they pivoted with the sun during the day to admit more indirect light. Malcolm Leland, known too for ModulArt work, designed the grilles and screens beside the escalators up to the third floor. The American Institute of Architects nominated the building for the R. S. Reynolds Memorial Award of 1964.

Seating 739 around a thrust stage, the Mark Taper Forum stands in the Los Angeles Music Center on Bunker Hill. Welton Becket and Associates designed the whole Music Center, the West Coast’s counterpart to Lincoln Center, in the New Formalism style, which stressed geometric shapes. The Taper, which opened in 1967, was designed by Becket without knowing who would use it. Perfectly circular, it is counted among his best works; Jacques Overhoff’s lacy precast relief wraps the outside of its decorated drum, and Tony Duquette made the lobby’s curving abalone wall. The stage thrusts into a classical semicircular amphitheatre, making the bond between audience and performer especially intimate. In July 2007 a $30-million renovation began under the Los Angeles firm Rios Clementi Hale Studios; it updated almost everything that was not concrete without changing the round shape.

Known as the PDC, the Pacific Design Center is a multi-use facility of 1,600,000 sq ft (150,000 m²) for the design community in West Hollywood, California. Its architect was César Pelli, from Argentina, working at Gruen Associates, and Norma Merrick Sklarek, also an architect, contributed to the design. The 14-acre campus opened in 1975 with Center Blue, 750,000 sq ft, Pelli’s first landmark building; locals call it the “Blue Whale” for its great size beside its neighbours and its vivid blue glass cladding. Center Green followed in 1988 with 450,000 sq ft, and the final phase, Center Red, added 400,000 sq ft. Its 100 showrooms show and sell 2,200 lines of interior products to professional interior designers, architects, decorators, dealers and facility managers.

Parker Center, first named the Police Administration Building, or the Police Facilities Building, held the Los Angeles Police Department’s headquarters from 1955 to October 2009. Ground was broken on December 30, 1952. The architects were Welton Becket & Associates, with J.E. Stanton as associated architect; Maynard Woodard directed the design and Francis Runcy was project architect. Its eight storeys were reinforced concrete, with louvres over aluminium sash windows, and Gladding, McBean ceramic tile covered the west front. The building gathered police facilities that had been spread across the Civic Center. Two notable artworks were commissioned: Bernard Rosenthal’s large modernist bronze The American Family at the entrance, and Joseph Young’s lobby mosaic of Los Angeles landmarks. Dragnet featured it from the 1955 television series’ fifth season on. Demolition above ground ended on July 15, 2019.

John Lautner designed the Pearlman Mountain Cabin, a cottage in Idyllwild, in 1957. The Pearlmans’ lot was thought to be full of problems: rocky throughout, it sloped by as much as 40%. Lautner’s answer was a circular platform built over a boulder, with the cabin itself a cylinder whose flat roof overhangs a ring of tree trunks that hold it up. Apart from those trunks, the outer wall is entirely glass, the windows zigzagging along a rough semicircle; their large size and unusual placement blur inside and outside for the viewer. Because Agnes Pearlman was a gifted pianist, the roof and facade were designed to give the interior good acoustics. The US National Register of Historic Places lists it as “character-defining” for organic architecture.

Los Angeles International Airport's Theme Building first welcomed the public in 1961. The contract for its design went to Charles Luckman, his former partner William Pereira, and Welton Becket, who was based in Los Angeles; the work is credited too as a collaboration with Paul Williams. Luckman had been carrying the idea since 1953. In its first form it was to be much bigger, chiefly a glass dome holding the main ticket hall and terminals of LAX. A $50 million revamp of the entire airport had begun in April 1960. A revolving restaurant was planned to give diners a 360-degree view, but the turning mechanism soon cost too much to maintain, and the restaurant stopped moving.

This former Enco filling station in Palm Springs, California, was designed by Albert Frey and Robson C. Chambers and built in 1965; the firm Clark, Frey and Chambers is also credited with it. It sits at the bottom of Tramway Road, the only road up to the base of the aerial tramway, which gives the station its name. The idea was that it would be the first building in Palm Springs seen by visitors arriving from the north on California State Route 111. Its wedge-shaped canopy cantilevers outward; a historic marker on the building calls the form a hyperbolic paraboloid. It is regarded as a prime example of modernist design. Since 2003 the Palm Springs Bureau of Tourism has run it as the Palm Springs Visitor Center, and in 2015 it joined the US National Register of Historic Places.

Lloyd Wright, whose father was Frank Lloyd Wright, drew up Wayfarers Chapel, "The Glass Church", in the late 1940s; it was built from 1949 to 1951 for $25,000. The 100-seat chapel stood on a bluff over the Pacific in Rancho Palos Verdes as a memorial to Emanuel Swedenborg, an 18th-century scientist and theosopher, and was linked to the Swedenborgian Church. Breaking with the habit of masonry, Wright made it an indoor/outdoor structure almost wholly of glass, so that the landscape around it would define the sacred space. In 2005 it entered the US National Register of Historic Places, and in 2023 it became a National Historic Landmark. Extreme earth movement damaged it, and in 2024 it was dismantled and stored. The prospective new location is the Battery Barnes military site, roughly 1 mile (1.6 km) west of the original one.

E. Stewart Williams designed this Palm Springs house in 1955 for Leon and Thea Koerner, a couple based in Vancouver. It is a fine case of the homes Williams produced from 1947 through the 1960s. The house sits on one level under a shed roof, with deep overhangs and broad areas of glass. Sliding glass doors help the rooms flow out to the open air, so that indoors and outdoors run into each other. Eckbo, Royston and Williams laid out the landscaping around it. In 2016 the house was added to the US National Register of Historic Places.

Reunion Tower is an observation tower in Dallas, 561 ft (171 m) high, designed by the firm Welton Becket & Associates. Known locally as "The Ball", it was finished on February 2, 1978, together with the Hyatt Regency Dallas at Reunion, within an urban renewal scheme that also restored the historic Union Station. Its structure rests on four shafts of concrete poured in place. A cylindrical shaft at the centre carries the stairs and mechanical plant, while three rectangular shafts holding the elevators rise beside it. On top sit three floors, each circular in plan, wrapped in an open-air sphere: a geodesic dome made of aluminum struts. It is one of the most recognisable landmarks in Dallas.

The Tacoma Dome, a multi-purpose indoor arena, sits south of Downtown Tacoma, Washington, next to Tacoma Dome Station and Interstate 5. Jim McGranahan and Lyn Messenger, both local architects, won an international competition to design it, and it cost $44 million to build. Its opening on April 21, 1983 drew 25,000 people. The dome measures 530 feet (160 m) across and 152 feet (46 m) high, and seats 20,722 for basketball, or up to 21,000 in all. When it opened it was, by volume, the biggest wooden-domed arena in the world. The roof alone weighs 650 t (1.44 million pounds), and some of its planks were cut from timber felled after Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980. Unlike most arenas this size, it has little fixed seating, to keep the seating and the shape of the playing field flexible.

Tempe's city hall in Arizona takes the shape of an upside-down pyramid. Michael Goodwin, Kemper Goodwin and Rolf Osland designed it, and it was built between 1969 and 1971. Michael Goodwin's first proposal, a large concrete block much like Boston City Hall, was turned down by the city council. In the design that went ahead, each floor is bigger than the one below: the ground floor has just 2,025 square feet of reception space, the second floor 5,625 and the third 10,000. This inverted form helps the building stay cooler in summer and warmer in winter. The council chambers lie in a basement level that is partly sunk into the ground, and separate fire stair towers stand on either side. The building was finished in 1971 and opened on October 2 of that year.

Built in 1956 in Albuquerque, New Mexico, the Solar Building was the first commercial building in the world heated mainly by the sun. Stanley & Wright were its architects, and it was made for the engineering firm Bridgers & Paxton, who designed its heating system. It is a single-storey International Style building in two main parts. In section it forms an irregular four-sided shape: the roof tilts at 20 degrees and the south wall at 30, giving the solar collectors high exposure to the south. Its active system used 56 solar thermal collectors covering 800 square feet (74 m2). Of the $58,500 total cost, about $15,000 went on heating and cooling, roughly twice the price of an ordinary system. New Mexico's state register listed it in 1985; the national one followed in 1989, a mere 33 years after construction.

Philip Johnson and John Burgee, noted architects from New York, designed the Fort Worth Water Gardens, built in 1974; the Amon G. Carter Foundation dedicated them to the city. The park fills 1.7 hectares (4.3 acres) beside the convention center, between Houston and Commerce Streets. Three pools form its focal points. Cypress trees and tall walls ring the Quiet Pool, where thin sheets of water slide almost vertically down the walls into a sunken blue basin. The Active Pool, the main attraction, drops water 38 feet (11 m) over terraces and steps into a little pool below. Before the park reopened on March 4, 2007, modifications made the main pool shallower, cutting its depth from 2.7 m (9 ft) to 0.61 m (2 ft).

In 1997 Raymond Nasher bought land in downtown Dallas, opposite the Dallas Museum of Art, and brought in Renzo Piano to design a museum for the sculpture collection of Patsy and Raymond Nasher, which spans modern and contemporary work. The Nasher Sculpture Center opened in 2003 on a 9,700 m2 (2.4-acre) site in the Dallas Arts District; the Nasher Foundation paid the full $70 million for design and building. Piano planned the roof to let suitable indirect sunlight into the galleries, following the sun's arc. For the 8,100 m2 Garden, which drops in terraces toward the auditorium to make an open-air theater, he worked with Peter Walker, a landscape architect at PWP Landscape Architecture. The Beck Group was the builder and associate architect. The glass of the nearby Museum Tower has reflected unwanted glare into the center.

The Dee and Charles Wyly Theatre in Dallas was designed by REX | OMA, with Joshua Prince-Ramus as partner in charge and Rem Koolhaas, a winner of the Pritzker Prize. Dedicated on October 12, 2009, it is one of the four venues of the AT&T Performing Arts Center. Its facility is organised vertically, or "stacked", a layout that rethinks the traditional form of a theatre. The building rises twelve stories with 80,300 square feet of space, seating around 600 depending on how the stage is set up. Vertical rods of extruded anodized aluminum line all four outer walls, meant to suggest the folds of a stage curtain. It is the venue for the Dallas Theater Center, the Dallas Black Dance Theatre and the Anita N. Martinez Ballet Folklorico. In 2011 the AIA gave it a National Honor Award.

Zimmer Gunsul Frasca Architects (ZGF) designed the Oregon Convention Center in Portland, the largest in the state with almost 93,000 m2 (1 million sq ft). Finished in 1989, it opened in 1990 in the Lloyd District, east of the Willamette River, and was enlarged in 2003 with ZGF again among the designers. Its twin spire towers are what most people know it for: they bring daylight into the interior. The building also holds the largest Foucault pendulum in the world. A solar array of 6,500 panels supplies around a quarter of the electricity it uses, the second biggest on any convention center in the United States. Inside and around it is a large public art collection, with works by more than two dozen artists, mostly from the Pacific Northwest.

The Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, once called the Pasadena Art Institute and then the Pasadena Art Museum, gained a new building, completed in 1969. Two Pasadena architects of the firm Ladd & Kelsey, Thornton Ladd and John Kelsey, designed it. Its curving outer walls are clad in 115,000 glazed tiles in varied deep browns, with an undulating surface, made by the ceramic artisan Edith Heath. The museum stands on Colorado Boulevard, on the Rose Parade route, so these brown walls appear behind television coverage of the event. In 1995 a $5 million renovation began with Frank Gehry, long a trustee of the museum. It produced medium-sized, more intimate galleries with raised ceilings and better lighting, more room for changing shows, a whole floor for Asian art, and renewed access to the gardens.

Jacobs Medical Center, a teaching hospital run by UC San Diego Health at UC San Diego, was designed by CannonDesign. It began as a plan for a simple extension of the hospital but grew into a ten-story facility for quaternary care. Ground was broken on April 9, 2012, and the inpatient tower opened in November 2016, with Kitchell Contractors, Inc. as general contractor. The finished tower holds 245 beds in 509,500 sq ft and cost over $940 million. It is organised into three specialty pavilions. The hospital looks out to the Pacific Ocean, La Jolla, the Torrey Pines Mesa and UC San Diego.

MacMillan Bloedel, a forestry company, built this 27-storey Vancouver tower as its head office. Erickson/Massey Architects designed it, with Arthur Erickson as partner in charge of design; he conceived it in 1965. Construction started in October 1966, and the official opening came on 13 December 1968. It is among Erickson's earliest works and an outstanding Canadian example of brutalism. The plan is two parallel towers, set off from each other and joined by a mechanical core. Concrete outer walls carry the load, which leaves each floor free of columns; they taper from 10 ft thick at ground level to 1 ft at the top. The windows, 7 feet square, are single panes of glass set into the concrete. Erickson called it "a Doric building in its starkness and simplicity." In 1970 it won the Massey Medal for Architecture.

In Ottawa's Lower Town, at 125 Sussex Drive, the Lester B. Pearson Building now serves as headquarters for Global Affairs Canada. Webb Zerafa Menkes, an architecture firm from Toronto, designed it, and its style has been described as late modern, influenced by Brutalism. Queen Elizabeth II officially opened the building on 1 August 1973. The complex is made up of four "towers" between 4 and 10 storeys high, three of them linked to one another from the first floor up to the fifth. In 2013 Canada's Department of Public Works and Government Services made it a Federal Heritage Building, citing its ties to history as well as the value of its architecture and environment.

Roy Thomson Hall in Toronto was designed by Arthur Erickson, assisted by the Toronto firm Mathers and Haldenby. Built between 1972 and 1982, it opened in 1982 as a circular building with a curving, sloping skin of glass. Erickson drew on his travels in Japan and on his relationship with the Aboriginal peoples of North America. He described the grey structure as a container that people would fill with their own decorations. Itzhak Perlman advised the architects on the access needs of disabled performers and guests. The hall seats 2,630 and has a pipe organ by Gabriel Kney, a Canadian organ builder from London, Ontario. After years of musicians' complaints about its acoustics, it was renovated over six months in 2002. Its resident companies include the Toronto Symphony Orchestra and the Toronto Mendelssohn Choir.

Montreal's Grande Bibliothèque is a public library downtown whose holdings form part of Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec, Québec's national library. A pet project of Lucien Bouchard, a former Québec premier, it was designed by Patkau Architects of Vancouver with Croft-Pelletier/Gilles Guité of Quebec City. The $90.6 million, 33,000 m2 building was begun in 2001 where the Palais du commerce had stood. Its five storeys are wrapped in U-shaped glass plates, a type new to North America, laid horizontally on copper uprights running the full height. Inside, walls of wooden slats mark off spaces several storeys tall, admitting indirect daylight or blocking it as the collection requires; the slats are Québec-grown yellow birch, the province's official tree. The library credits part of its success to a direct underground link to Berri–UQAM station; in 2011 it drew 2.7 million visitors.

Our Lady of Victory Church in Inuvik, the "Igloo Church", took two years to build and was consecrated and opened in 1960. Brother Maurice Larocque, a Catholic missionary in the Arctic and former carpenter with no formal architectural training, designed it, sketching it on two plywood sheets now prominently displayed upstairs. The round form, painted like an igloo, was chosen to reduce harm from frost heave. Unlike every other major building in Inuvik, it does not stand on pilings: its 23-metre timber frame, "a dome within a dome" carried by wooden arches, rests on a concrete basement, a bowl-shaped slab and a metre of gravel above the permafrost. Its wood came from Fort Smith, nearly 2,000 km away, floated down the Mackenzie River. Aluminum scales in diamond shapes clad the roof, which has a 6.1-metre cupola at its centre.

Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava designed the Peace Bridge for people walking and cycling over the Bow River in Calgary; it opened on March 24, 2012. The city built it to link Downtown Calgary with Sunnyside. It had to avoid piers in the water, to limit its ecological footprint, and keep its height down because of the nearby City/Bow River Heliport. Where Calatrava's earlier designs were typically asymmetric and anchored by high masts, this is a helical tube of 850 tonnes of steel, built with a glass roof and coloured red and white like the flags of Canada and Calgary rather than his usual white. Made in Spain, it was moved across the river in November 2011. To cut the cost of replacing its glass, the city consulted Calatrava and decided on steel cables instead, to be completed in fall 2023.

The Monument to the Revolution in Mexico City's Plaza de la República started out as another project. Porfirio Díaz appointed Émile Bénard, a French architect, to design a neoclassical building for the deputies and senators, meant to show Mexico as an advanced nation. It had an iron frame, and instead of local stone its front was to be faced in marble from Italy and granite from Norway. The Mexican Revolution stopped the work, leaving the shell unfinished for twenty-five years. Under President Lázaro Cárdenas, Carlos Obregón Santacilia, a Mexican architect, proposed converting the abandoned dome to honour the revolution's heroes. The new structure, mixing Mexican socialist realism with Art Deco, was finished in 1938. At 67 m (220 ft), no triumphal arch in the world is taller, and it is also a mausoleum for leading revolutionary figures.

The Torre del Reformador (Tower of the Reformer) rises 71.85 metres (236 ft) in Guatemala City's Zone 9, a steel framework whose basic shape recalls the Eiffel Tower. It marks 100 years since Justo Rufino Barrios was born; he was a President of Guatemala who brought in several reforms. The United States Steel Products Company fabricated it in the United States from galvanized iron, costing Q49,775.60, and the engineer Arturo Bickford, then the city's mayor, assembled it. General Jorge Ubico Castañeda inaugurated it on 19 July 1935 under its first name, the Commemorative Tower of 19 July. A bell first crowned the top; in 1986 a beacon replaced it. Electric lights first lit the tower on 26 September 1958, funded by Cervecería Centro Americana, a brewery.

Hotel Nacional de Cuba stands on Taganana Hill, on Havana's Vedado seafront, overlooking city and sea. The New York firm McKim, Mead and White designed it, New York's National City Bank financed it, and the US engineers Purdy and Henderson built it in fourteen months. Its Spanish eclectic style mixes Art Deco with Sevillian, Roman and Moorish touches. The frame is steel, while much of the paving, columns, wall facings and ground-floor details are coral stone. Two Greek crosses set out the plan, so most rooms look toward the ocean. It opened on December 30, 1930, when Cuba drew many travellers from the US, and in October 1933 it saw a bloody siege. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, anti-aircraft guns were set up at the Santa Clara Battery site, and tunnels dug under the property are open to guided tours.

Havana's Gran Teatro is the home of the Cuban National Ballet. It went up in 1914 on the site of the older Teatro Tacón, designed by Paul Belau, a Belgian architect who also drew the Presidential Palace, and built by the US firm Purdy and Henderson, Engineers. They kept the old theatre and added the Centro Gallego, an extension in Baroque Revival style, that enlarged the hall's support spaces and brought in an elaborate circulation system. The Teatro Tacón was given new stone facing to match. Havana's Galician immigrants paid for the project as a community and social centre. Giuseppe Moretti and Geneva Mercer made four white marble sculptures representing charity, education, music and theater. Its main hall today, the García Lorca Auditorium, seats 1,500 and also serves other dance companies and musical performances.

Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal is the largest church in Canada and a National Historic Site. Saint André Bessette founded it in 1904, honouring his patron saint, and its building took six decades, many architects and thousands of workers. From 1914 to 1916 Dalbé Viau and Alphonse Venne built the crypt church, seating 1,000, which still stands at the top of the long stairs as the basilica's base. Their roof and dome were later redesigned entirely, with a far larger dome modelled on Florence Cathedral's, finished in 1941 after four years. The outer dome spans 39 m and rises 97 m above the nave floor; the inner one, 26 m and 60 m. A Renaissance Revival front contrasts with an Art Deco interior. Rising over 30 metres above the summit of Mount Royal, it is Montreal's highest building.

Edward James Lennox, a leading Toronto architect, designed Old City Hall in Richardsonian Romanesque, a version of the Romanesque Revival. Building it took over a decade and cost upward of $2.5 million; when finished in 1899 it was North America's largest civic building. It is built of sandstone from the valley of the Credit River, grey stone from near Orangeville, Ontario, and brown stone from New Brunswick. The plan is a vast square around an inner courtyard, and the clock tower on the front is set off centre to end the vista along Bay Street. Lennox had the stonemasons "sign" his name in corbels beneath the upper eaves all around: "EJ LENNOX ARCHITECT AD 1898". City Council sat here from 1899 to 1966, and provincial courts used it until 2023. It has been a National Historic Site since 1984.

The William G. Davis Building is the largest and oldest building on the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus. It formed part of the first plans for Erindale College, and the project passed to Raymond Moriyama, who drew a new design, among his earliest major commissions. His approved scheme put all academic facilities in one central building, a single mega-structure above the Credit River valley, so that the rest of the campus could keep its natural state. Built mainly of exposed concrete on the river's west bank, north of Wilson Pond, it was called the South Building when completed in 1973, and it is still the campus's largest academic space. In 2010 it was renamed after William G. Davis, who had been Ontario's premier and its education minister.

Mario Pani, the Mexican architect and urbanist, designed the Plaza de las Tres Culturas, the main square of Mexico City's Tlatelolco neighbourhood, completed in 1966. Its name, "Three Cultures", reflects three periods of Mexican history visible in the buildings around it: the pre-Columbian era, Spanish colonial rule and the independent nation. Within the square lie the archaeological remains of Tlatelolco, once a city-state. Beside it stands the College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, the oldest higher-learning school of European origin in the Americas, which the friar Juan de Torquemada built in 1536; a huge housing complex of 1964 lines another side. On 2 October 1968 the Tlatelolco massacre took place in the square, and the area's quality of life fell afterwards.

The National Theatre of Panama stands in the old part of Panama City, beside the Plaza Bolívar and the church of San Francisco. Act 52 of 1904 ordered its construction, and it opened on October 1, 1908. Its designer, the Italian architect Genaro Ruggieri, gave it the style of an Italian operetta theatre. The neoclassical manner he brought became the "official architecture" of that era, seen also in the National Institute, the Municipal Palace, the Palace of Justice and the Presidential Palace. The theatre forms part of a building laid out as a cross. Its main curtain, its ceiling painting and its foyer date from 1907, and the frescos on the ceiling are the work of the noted Panamanian artist Robert Lewis.

The Groninger Museum shows modern and contemporary art by local, national and international artists in Groningen, in the Netherlands. Its postmodern home, completed in 1994, sits in a canal facing Groningen railway station, and a bridge to the station forms part of a walking and cycling route into the city centre. Three main pavilions were each designed by a different hand: Philippe Starck made a silver cylinder, Alessandro Mendini a yellow tower, and Coop Himmelb(l)au a deconstructivist space in pale blue. Their bright, futuristic look echoes the Italian postmodern work of the Memphis Group. The American artist Frank Stella was first asked to design one of the pavilions, but his plan proved too costly because he wanted it built entirely of Teflon. It also appears among the "1001 Buildings You Must See Before You Die".

Het Nieuwe Instituut, or New Institute, works as a Rotterdam cultural centre for architecture, design and digital culture. Its building, a Jo Coenen project of 1988 to 1993, stands at Museumpark 25 in the city centre, beside Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen. Queen Beatrix opened it in 1993. Three bodies were put together in it: the Virtueel Platform, the Premsela Dutch Platform for Design and Fashion, and the Netherlands Architecture Institute. It keeps the national collection for urban planning and architecture in the Netherlands, and its archive runs to more than 18 kilometres, including many Dutch architects' personal collections. There are also exhibition spaces, a study centre, a shop and a cafe. The building also contains a pond, a small park and the Sonneveld House, a leading example of the Nieuwe Zakelijkheid style.

The Timmerhuis in Rotterdam joins two eras: post-war reconstruction architecture by J.R.A. Koops, the city's municipal architect, and a contemporary addition by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA). Koops's building went up from 1950 to 1953, among the first larger buildings raised in the empty centre of Rotterdam after the bombing. Its gabled roofs and chimneys look traditional, yet it was seen as progressive for its concrete frame, adaptable ventilation and self-service lifts. It became a municipal heritage monument in 2000 and has been thoroughly restored. OMA's extension consists of two towers whose apartment floors step back to make roof terraces. Between them, a ground-floor atrium carries a public walkway, the Halvemaanpassage, linking Haagseveer with Rodezand. The new complex opened on December 11, 2015, and holds offices, 91 apartments, underground parking and Museum Rotterdam.

The Royal Palace of Amsterdam began as the city's new town hall in the mid-1600s. Jacob van Campen, its main architect, took charge of the project in 1648, and it rests on 13,659 wooden piles. Cornelis de Graeff, the burgomaster of Amsterdam, opened the new town hall on 29 July 1655. Its yellowish sandstone has grown much darker over time, and a 6-metre statue of Atlas bearing the Globe stands astride the back of the building. Only in 1808, when the Netherlands was under Napoleon Bonaparte, did it become a royal palace, and because it was planned as a town hall it has no grand entrance, unlike most royal palaces. An Act of Parliament places it among the three Dutch palaces at the monarch's disposal. A renovation from 2005 to June 2009 included the removal of asbestos.

The Europa building, in the European Quarter of Brussels, houses both the European Council and the Council of the European Union. In 2005 a team led by Philippe Samyn and Partners, with Studio Valle Progettazioni and the engineers Buro Happold, won the design competition. Their scheme removed a 1960s extension and joined the two restored wings of the original L-shaped 1920s building with a large atrium formed as a glass cube. The listed Art Deco front of that older building now meets Samyn's contemporary design. Its defining feature is a lantern-shaped structure several storeys high holding the main meeting rooms; both councils use an image of it as their emblem. Recycled wooden frames, solar panels and a double skin feature, and the painter Georges Meurant added colourful grid patterns throughout. After design changes, it was completed in December 2016.

The Flagey Building, also called the Radio House, stands in Ixelles, Brussels, and holds the Flagey cultural centre. It began with a competition for a home for Belgium's first national broadcaster, the National Institute of Radio Broadcasting. Joseph Diongre won, chosen by a jury that included Victor Horta and Henry van de Velde. Completed in 1938 in Streamline Moderne, a style of Art Deco found internationally, it looks somewhat like a ship, which earned it the nickname "paquebot", or "Packet Boat". At its core, two acoustic towers held the twelve recording studios of the original plan. Parts of the building are listed. After a major renovation by a team of architects that included Storme Van Ranst, it reopened in 2002. Its Studio 4, home to the Brussels Philharmonic, ranks among the concert halls with the finest acoustics in the world.

Commissioned by King Leopold II and built from 1874 to 1905, the Royal Greenhouses of Laeken lie in the Royal Domain, joined to the palace by the orangery. Alphonse Balat drew the original design; after he died in 1895, Leopold called in Henri Maquet and Charles Girault. The complex is a group of domed buildings in iron and glass, linked by galleries with glass roofs and by flower-lined corridors hundreds of metres long. Its centrepiece, the domed Winter Garden, is a round take on the Palm House at Kew. Others include the Congo Greenhouse and the domed "Iron Church", first meant as the royal chapel. Iron and glass pushed Balat away from his classical approach, and he added decoration based on plants and flowers. This was an early step toward Art Nouveau, which Victor Horta, once his apprentice, carried further.

M Leuven, known simply as M, shows art in Leuven's inner city, in Belgium. Before it officially opened in 2009, the building was renovated to plans by the Belgian architect Stéphane Beel. His design sets historic parts beside sleek new architecture, all arranged around a courtyard, and the museum covers 13,500 square metres in total. Its main exhibition space is the former private home of Leopold Vander Kelen, once the city's mayor, in the historic centre, to which the collection was moved. The collection holds about 46,000 works: late-Gothic sculpture and painting, 16th-century local artists like Josse van der Baren and Jan Rombouts the Elder, and 19th-century work by Flemish masters such as George Minne, Jef Lambeaux and Constantin Meunier.

Leuven's Town Hall faces St. Peter's Church across the Grote Markt, the city's main square. Built from 1439 to 1469 in Brabantine late Gothic, it is famed for its lace-like carving. Sulpitius van Vorst, the first architect, died shortly after the rear wings were started; Jan Keldermans II took over briefly, and his death in 1445 halted the first phase. Work resumed in 1448 under Matheus de Layens. The early plans, inspired by Brussels' Town Hall, put a belfry at one corner, but de Layens changed this to today's symmetrical turrets. Three storeys of pointed windows face the square, under a gallery parapet and a steep roof with four tiers of dormers. Its 236 statues, set in original niches, date from after 1850. A World War II bomb that fell in front caused more damage, repaired only by 1983.

The museum at Tervuren was first put up to present the Congo Free State of King Leopold II at the 1897 International Exposition. Work on a new building started in 1904. Charles Girault, a French architect, designed it in a neoclassical "palace" manner that recalls the Paris Petit Palais, with wide gardens reaching into the Tervuren Forest, part of the Sonian Forest. The building measures 125 metres by 75. King Albert I, who succeeded Leopold, opened it in 1910, a year after Leopold's death, as the Museum of the Belgian Congo. For its later renewal, the Belgian Buildings Agency gave the plan to Stéphane Beel Architects (TV SBA). A reception pavilion, added in 2016 and set between the Palace of Africa and the management building, is now the way in. The museum reopened as the AfricaMuseum on 9 December 2018.

Luxembourg City's main venue for ballet, opera and drama is the Grand Théâtre. The winning designer was Alain Bourbonnais (1925–1988), an architect from Paris. Building started in autumn 1959; the festive inauguration followed on 15 April 1964, when it bore the name Théâtre Municipal de la Ville de Luxembourg. It has two auditoriums: a main house of 943 seats and a studio for up to 400 that can be divided. In 2002–2003 its stage technology and facilities were brought up to European standards, while the original 1960s building kept its distinctive design. It sits on the north-east corner of Rond-Point Schumann, between the Red Bridge and the Glacis. It hosted the Eurovision Song Contest twice, in 1973 and 1984.

Eye Filmmuseum combines a film archive, a museum and a cinema in Amsterdam, keeping and showing Dutch films as well as films from abroad that were shown in the Netherlands. In 2009 the Nederlands Filmmuseum merged with the Filmbank, the Netherlands Institute for Film Education and Holland Film, and plans were announced to move to the north side of the city's waterfront. Delugan Meissl Associated Architects designed the new building, which stands in the Overhoeks neighbourhood. Queen Beatrix officially opened it on 4 April 2012; by then the institution was called the Eye Film Institute Netherlands. Inside are two exhibition galleries and four cinemas: one with 300 seats, two with 127 seats each, and a small fourth room of roughly 67 seats.

Gustave Strauven, who started out as an assistant designer to Victor Horta, designed the Saint-Cyr House in Brussels, built from 1901 to 1903 in the Art Nouveau style. It was the home of George Léonard de Saint-Cyr, a painter and decorator, and is seen as Strauven's most important building. The house is just 4 m (13 ft) wide, yet elaborate architectural inventions give it great height. Polychrome brick covers the whole front, with a great deal of wrought iron carrying geometric motifs and decorative balustrades on every floor. The ironwork imitates plants, and ornament fills every bit of space, earning the house the label Art Nouveau-Baroque. It was protected as a historic monument on 8 August 1988 and has had several owners. Once badly run down, it had been restored by March 2013 by the architect Francis Metzger.

The Swiss-Belgian architect Michel Polak designed Villa Empain for Baron Louis Empain, whose father was the industrialist Édouard Empain, and it was built in Brussels between 1930 and 1934 in the Art Deco style. Planned as a luxurious private home, it wraps around a large enclosed courtyard, its swimming pool at the far end. The façades are polished granite, and costly stone facings came from around the world, alongside marble and bronze. The project drew great interest in Belgium, where prestigious Art Deco houses were comparatively rare; it is counted among the city's best Art Deco buildings. RTL used it from 1980 to 1993, and it stood empty after 1995. Restored in 2009–2010 by the architect Francis Metzger, it reopened as a cultural centre and museum, and the work won a Europa Nostra Award in 2011.

Jan Wils designed Amsterdam's Olympic Stadium as the main venue for the 1928 Summer Olympics, and the design itself took the gold medal in that year's Olympic architecture competition. A fine example of the Amsterdamse School, it suits the surrounding district designed by H.P. Berlage. From January 1926 the site was raised with 750,000 cubic metres of sand. Beside it rises the Marathon tower, a tall tower in which the flame burned for the first time ever. After Rotterdam opened its rival De Kuip stadium in 1937, Amsterdam added a second ring, lifting capacity to 64,000. The city announced plans in 1987 to pull the stadium down, but listing as a national monument saved it. Renovation from 1996 returned it to its 1928 form, removing the 1937 ring, cutting capacity to 22,288 and making it fit for athletics again.

The Central Library, also called OBA Oosterdok, is the largest branch of Amsterdam's public library. First opened on the Prinsengracht in 1977, it moved in 2007 to the Oosterdokseiland, a short way east of Centraal station. Jo Coenen, formerly the Netherlands' state architect (Rijksbouwmeester), designed the new building, which cost €80 million. Its 28,500 m2 of floor space is spread over 10 floors, with 1,200 seats, 600 of them at computers linked to the internet; 200 people work there. Arup created the lighting to form "a landscape with different zones", along with a fresh-air system that cools the building by drawing in cold outside air. On the seventh floor a restaurant opens onto a terrace facing south. The building also holds the Gerard Reve Museum, the Library Museum, an exhibition room and an auditorium, plus parking for 2,000 bicycles.

Bratislava's Kamzík TV Tower, a television transmitter 196 metres (643 ft) tall, stands in the Koliba area of the Slovak capital. Built in 1975 to replace an earlier transmitter, it was designed by five architects: Ján Privitzer, Milan Jurica, Juraj Kozák, Jakub Tomašák and Stanislav Májek. It rises from Kamzík hill in the Little Carpathians, at an altitude of 437 m (1,434 ft), inside the Bratislava Forest Park, looking out over much of the city. From its public observation deck, on a clear day, visitors can see the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. The restaurant has three parts: an observation cafe bar; Brasseria, a second restaurant, on one floor; and, a floor lower, the main restaurant, whose rotating tables give a full 360-degree view.

Puskás Aréna is the home ground of Hungary's national football team, set in Zugló, the 14th district of Budapest. It stands where the old Ferenc Puskás Stadium stood until its demolition was finished in October 2016. Building work began in 2017 and was done before the close of 2019. The Hungarian architect György Skardelli, who had already designed the László Papp Budapest Sports Arena close by, drew the original plans. In 2014 the stadium's first designs won Stadiumdb.com's vote for best design, which praised the idea of a raised running track looking down on the pitch, with views of the city skyline. Every spectator is seated, and there are places for 67,215. Hungary played Uruguay to open the arena on 15 November 2019, and on 30 May 2026 it staged the UEFA Champions League final between Paris Saint-Germain and Arsenal.

Tallinn TV Tower was built to give the sailing regatta of the 1980 Moscow Summer Olympics better telecommunications. Its architects were David Baziladze and Juri Sinis, and its engineers Vladimir Obydov and Yevgeny Ignatov. At 313 m, it is Tallinn's tallest non-building structure: a 190-metre concrete shaft topped by a 124-metre metal mast. The shaft rose using a sliding mould, as a stack of 50 cm-thick concrete rings weighing 17,000 tonnes, out of roughly 20,000 tonnes in all. The observation deck, 38 m wide and 170 m up on the 21st floor, was first planned with a part that turned. The cornerstone went down in September 1975; the first broadcast followed in 1979 and the official opening on 11 July 1980. After KOKO Arhitektid redesigned its interior, the tower reopened on 5 April 2012.

The Grand Hotel Prishtina stands on Mother Theresa Boulevard in the centre of Pristina, Kosovo's capital. It was conceived alongside the city's socialist-era urban development. The design went to Bashkim Fehmiu, who was the first Albanian architect to study at the Faculty of Architecture of the University of Belgrade, who worked on it with two Serbian architects, Miša Jevremović and Dragan Kovačević. Work started in 1974 and ended in 1978. The hotel rises 13 floors and has a total area of more than 32,000 m2. Its interior was curated by Matej Rodiqi, an artist from Kosovo, and the floors from the 3rd to the 9th have held exhibitions by more than 30 artists, both from Kosovo and from abroad.

Zetra Olympic Hall, also called the Juan Antonio Samaranch Olympic Hall, is an indoor arena in Sarajevo used for many kinds of events. It was built for the 1984 Winter Olympics held in the city. Work started in June 1981, and Samaranch, who then led the International Olympic Committee, opened the complex on 14 February 1982. One description called it an "ultramodern, angular edifice", and its roof was clad in copper. During the Bosnian War, on 25 May 1992, Serb forces shelled and bombed the arena and set it on fire, leaving heavy damage. Its wooden seats were taken to make coffins for civilians who died in the fighting. The original plans were never found, yet rebuilding began in September 1997 with help from SFOR and was finished in 1999.

Stari Most spans the river Neretva and joins the two halves of Mostar, a city named after the mostari, keepers who guarded the bridge in Ottoman times. Suleiman the Magnificent ordered it in 1557, and its designer, Mimar Hayruddin, had trained under the architect Mimar Sinan. On completion it was the widest arch people had ever built. The hump-backed span is 30 metres long and 4 metres wide and rises 24 m above the water. Rather than foundations, it rests on limestone abutments tied into wing walls on the cliffs. Slobodan Praljak, commander of the Croat Defence Council, ordered its destruction, and shelling by Bosnian Croat forces brought it down on 9 November 1993. Rebuilt with the original methods and materials from 7 June 2001, it reopened on 23 July 2004, at an estimated cost of 15.5 million US dollars.

The Kadinjača Memorial remembers the Battle of Kadinjača, fought on 29 November 1941 during the Second World War, and the end of the Republic of Užice. It grew in stages between 1952 and 1979. The first part, from 1952, is a pyramid-shaped obelisk that serves as a crypt for members of the Workers' battalion who died in the battle. The complex took its present form in 1979, when it was greatly enlarged to a project by the sculptor Miodrag Živković and the architect Aleksandar Đokić. Josip Broz Tito, President of the SFRJ, opened the whole memorial on 23 September 1979. The same year it was named a Monument of Culture of Exceptional Importance, and it is protected by the Republic of Serbia. Its exhibition holds over three hundred objects and original documents, most of them linked to the Workers Battalion.

Seimas Palace houses the Seimas, Lithuania's parliament, though it was first planned as the seat of the Supreme Soviet of the Lithuanian SSR. The chosen site, on Gediminas Avenue, had been the Youth Football Stadium. The twin brothers Algimantas and Vytautas Nasvytis were picked to design the project and oversee it, and they settled on a square plan for the main building. The finished complex has three wings. The main, or first, wing contains the Parliament Hall, where laws are passed. In the old hall, on 11 March 1990, Lithuania re-established its independence and adopted the declaration of its break from the Soviet Union. A new Parliament Hall was formally opened on 10 September 2007.

This Second World War memorial in Podgarić, in Croatia's Berek municipality, is a sculpture by Dušan Džamonja honouring the people of Moslavina in that war. Its full name is the Monument to the Revolution of the People of Moslavina. Džamonja took the Greek goddess of victory, Nike, as his starting point and set the work deep into the landscape. At its centre a metal structure stands for a stylised sun, and two wings of unequal shape spread from it on either side. The whole piece is about 10 m tall and 20 m long. Josip Broz Tito, the president of Yugoslavia, dedicated it in 1967.

Known in Varna as the Russian Monument, this memorial crowns Turna Tepe hill in the city's north. It grew from a design competition in autumn 1973, won by the architect Kamen Goranov with the sculptors Evgeni Barumov and Alyosha Kafedzhiyski; work began in November 1974. Two large concrete wings open out from a central axis, a shape often read as a bird in flight facing the Black Sea and the Soviet Union beyond. Standing 23 metres tall and 48 metres across, it is the biggest monument in the region. The hill was planted as a park, climbed by the 301-step "Staircase of Victory". It opened on 13 November 1978. Unmaintained by the state since 1989, it has fallen into disrepair: thieves have stripped most of its bronze lettering, and its inner rooms have been shut since about 2019.

The Telephone Palace is an Art Deco office block on Bucharest's Calea Victoriei. It grew out of a loan the Romanian government took from J.P. Morgan & Co., a deal that gave ITT a 20-year telephone monopoly; ITT then formed SART, the Romanian Telephone Company, to modernise the network and build this palace. Edmond Van Saanen Algi, a Romanian architect of Dutch origin, designed it for SART. Built over about 20 months in 1931–1933 on a steel frame from the Reșița works, it was the street's first major modernist building, and King Carol II attended its opening in 1934. At 52.5 metres it stayed the city's tallest building until 1956. Enlarged in 1940 and 1946, it outlasted Allied bombing in 1944 and four earthquakes. A later rebuilding designed by Proiect Bucuresti strengthened the structure and copied the original façade.

The Palace of Culture in Iași rebuilt and enlarged the old Princely Palace of Moldavia, within the grounds of the medieval Princely Court, keeping that palace's foundations and first two floors. Where the earlier building was neoclassical, I. D. Berindei chose a flamboyant Neo-Gothic style, though he built it with modern methods, swapping stone blocks for lighter, cheaper materials. Work began in 1906–1907 and stalled in the First World War, when the shell housed troops, public institutions and military hospitals. It was finished on 11 October 1925, and King Ferdinand I opened it a year later. The entrance is a keep-like tower with battlements and an eagle on top, the centrepiece of the design. It served as the Administrative and Justice Palace until 1955, then passed to four museums. Restoration began in 2008; the main works ended in April 2016.

This bridge crosses the Drina River at Višegrad, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mehmed Paša Sokolović, a Grand Vizier who held power at the top of the Ottoman Empire under three sultans, commissioned it as a tribute to his home region and a sign of trade and prosperity. Mimar Sinan, the Ottoman court architect, designed it, and it was built between 1571 and 1577. It runs 179.5 metres over 11 stone arches, each spanning 11 to 15 metres, with a right-angled ramp on the west bank. Three arches were destroyed in the First World War and five damaged in the Second, all later restored. It was listed as a national monument in 2003 and as UNESCO World Heritage in 2007. Ivo Andrić, a Nobel Prize–winning Yugoslav writer, made it widely known in his 1945 book The Bridge on the Drina.

Peleș Castle sits in the Carpathian Mountains near Sinaia, Romania, on an old road between Transylvania and Wallachia. King Carol I wanted a hunting preserve and summer retreat here; the foundations were laid on 22 August 1873. He rejected the first three designs as costly copies of other Western European palaces. The German architect Johannes Schultz won with a fresher idea: a grand alpine castle drawing on several European styles, mostly Italian elegance and German taste along Renaissance lines. The result blends Neo-Renaissance and Gothic Revival, much like Bavaria's Neuschwanstein, while the courtyard's painted murals and timber framing show Saxon influence. It was inaugurated in 1883, but work continued: from 1893 the Czech architect Karel Liman added the towers, the central one 66 metres tall. It was the first castle anywhere fully powered by locally made electricity.

Miklós Ybl, a central name in 19th-century Hungarian architecture, designed this Budapest house, first called the Hungarian Royal Opera House. Budapest and Emperor Franz Joseph I paid for it; work began in 1875 and it opened on 27 September 1884. Its style is neo-Renaissance with Baroque touches, and the decoration of its symmetrical front takes music as its theme. The horseshoe auditorium seats 1,261; engineers from several countries tested it in the 1970s and ranked its acoustics third in Europe, behind Milan's La Scala and the Palais Garnier. A bronze chandelier of 3,050 kg lights Károly Lotz's fresco of the Greek gods on Olympus. The stage had the latest technology of its day, a revolving floor and metal hydraulics. Restored and given new stage machinery, it reopened in March 2022 with a three-day festival.

The Grand Hotel International was first planned for the military and only later opened to the public as a luxury hotel. After the site was chosen in 1951, the architect František Jeřábek and the army drew up a new, more complex design that added the luxury hotel. Construction ran from 1952 to 1956, and the interiors were decorated by 1957. Built in the socialist realist style and modelled on Moscow's Seven Sisters, the 88-metre building is the largest Stalinist building in Prague and a protected Czech cultural monument. A central tower rises between two matching wings. Marble columns, a painted stucco ceiling and wall art give the entrance hall and main stair a palatial feel, and the hotel's largest tapestry, Praga Regina Musicae, hangs there, showing Prague with the former Stalin monument at its centre. Much original art survives.

Prague's biggest railway station opened in 1871, named Franz Josef Station after the Austrian emperor. The present building and hall, designed by the Czech architect Josef Fanta, rose between 1901 and 1909 on the site of an older Neo-Renaissance station that was taken down. No Art Nouveau monument in the country is larger. The 150-metre building, with two towers, holds a coffer-ceilinged hall, a restaurant and offices, with 22 doors opening onto a platform paved in mosaic; this earned it the nickname "castle station". Sculptures of Czech cities by Stanislav Sucharda and Ladislav Šaloun decorate its dome. In 1905–1906 Jaroslav Marjanko and Rudolf Kornfeld roofed the tracks with an arched steel hall of two naves, spanning 2 × 33.3 m, 18 m tall and 233 m long. It has been a listed cultural monument since 31 December 1976.

Known as the Blue Mosque, this mosque in Shah Alam is Malaysia's largest and the second largest in Southeast Asia by capacity. Its design, credited to Baharuddin Abu Kassim, joins Malay and Modernist styles, with Malay and Islamic architectural elements in the finishes. Work ran from 1982 to 11 March 1988. A blue and silver dome sets it apart, and a minaret stands at each of the four corners. The dome, 51.2 m wide and 106.7 m above the ground, is among the largest religious domes anywhere. It is built of aluminium and clad outside in triangular steel panels of baked vitreous enamel, decorated with a rosette of Qur'anic verses. Blue stained glass dims the light, giving the interior a calm blue glow. The mosque holds 12,600 worshippers and on clear days can be seen from parts of Kuala Lumpur.

The Palace of Justice in Putrajaya houses Malaysia's two highest courts, the Federal Court and the Court of Appeal. Both moved here from Kuala Lumpur's Sultan Abdul Samad Building in 2003, when the complex was completed. aQidea Architects got the commission after finishing the nearby Prime Minister's Office, and its principal architect, AR Ahmad Rozi Abd Wahab, personally shaped the layout and concept. Its theme was "order", seen in neatly arranged plans. The design borrows from Classical Islamic work such as the Taj Mahal, Moorish buildings such as the Sultan Abdul Samad Building, and Western Palladian classicism. Rooms gather round a large central rotunda that guides new arrivals and looks up to the floors above. Separate passages keep judges, witnesses, the public and the accused apart from arrival to courtroom. The five-storey building cost RM362 million on a 3.3-hectare site.

Stadium Merdeka in Kuala Lumpur is where the Federation of Malaya formally declared independence on 31 August 1957. The American architect Stanley Edward Jewkes designed it on the instructions of Tunku Abdul Rahman, Malaysia's first Prime Minister, and it was built in less than a year, from September 1956 to August 1957. It is an earthed amphitheatre, sunk partly into the ground. With little money, builders used mostly local materials and avoided imports such as structural steel. A concrete shell roof covers the grandstand, chosen because it was affordable as well as beautiful. On completion the stadium held two world records, for the largest cantilevered shell roofs and for the tallest prestressed floodlight towers, which rise 120 feet.
