Now a national heritage building, it won a UNESCO heritage conservation award in 2008.

Sala Chalermkrung opened in 1933 as a Modernist cinema on Bangkok's Charoengkrung Road; today it stages classical Thai dance. King Prajadhipok paid for it as part of the 1932 celebrations of Bangkok's 150th anniversary, hence its name, meaning "Pavilion to Celebrate the City". He picked as architect Mom Chao Samaichaloem Kridakorn, then Chief Master Builder in the Department of Outer Palace. That was daring: Kridakorn was a recent Beaux-Arts graduate, and such posts had always gone to Europeans. Neon letters spelling its Thai name across the top of the front were Asia's largest, and its air-conditioning was new to many Siamese. Besides the 1,500-seat main hall there were a 350-seat hall, rooms for royal screenings, dance rooms and a dining room. Later, to favour traditional theatre, the stage was widened and given a hydraulic lift, cutting seating to 600.

Ho Chi Minh City Hall fills a downtown block in the Saigon ward, its front looking onto Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard. The French broke ground in 1898, once a canal was covered to make Charner Boulevard, with 1.5 million francs approved. The hard job took 11 years; the governors-general of French Indochina opened the building in 1909 to mark 50 years of French presence in the city. Under the architect Fernand Gardès, it followed the Paris town hall and recalls the belfries of northern France: a tall pointed tower between two matching attic towers and long, lower side wings. Renaissance, Baroque and Beaux-Arts ideas meet in its Rococo ornament, Corinthian columns, domed entrances and Art Nouveau doors of iron, with three figures of Marianne in the pediments. The wings gained another storey in the 1940s. It is a national heritage site.

The Saigon Opera House is one of Vietnam's French colonial opera houses, like those in Hanoi and Haiphong. Its character comes from the architect Félix Olivier; Ernest Guichard and Eugène Ferret, also architects, supervised the work. Work on the new theatre began in 1898 on the site of an older one and was complete by 1 January 1900. Its style follows the Flamboyant manner of France's Third Republic, and the front is shaped like the Petit Palais, built in France that same year. Its main floor and two balconies once held 1,800. In 1943 statues, carvings and other ornament were stripped off the front to make it look more up to date. From 1956 to 1967 the theatre, then seating 500, housed the single-chamber National Assembly. For Saigon's 300th anniversary in 1998, the front was restored.

The Hanoi Opera House anchors August Revolution Square at the top of Tràng Tiền street. The French colonial administration built it as the city's Municipal Theatre, one of three opera houses in French Indochina with those of Haiphong and Saigon. Work ran from June 1901 to December 1911. The French architect Broyer and Victorin Harlay, Chief Inspector of Public Buildings, conceived the design, and another French architect, François Lagisquet, completed it with Harlay. Modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris but smaller, it is Neoclassical with French Renaissance touches, built in materials better suited to local conditions. The theatre had 870 seats. In September 1945 the Viet Minh leadership proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam's independence from its balcony. A two-year restoration from 1995 employed 100 workers, overseen by Hồ Thiệu Trị, the French-Vietnamese architect who drew up the plan.

The Vietnam Museum of Ethnology in Hanoi presents the 54 ethnic groups that Vietnam officially recognises. Its grounds cover 43,799 square metres in Cầu Giấy District, some 8 km out of the centre. Ha Duc Linh, an architect from the Tày ethnic group, shaped the exhibition building like a Đông Sơn drum, while its interior architecture is by Véronique Dollfus, a French architect. Construction took from 1987 to 1995, and the public was let in on 12 November 1997. A second exhibition building, kite-shaped and covering the ethnology of Southeast Asia, opened in 2013. The holdings run to more than 15,000 objects, some 42,000 photographs, 2,190 slides and several hundred audio and video tapes.

Hotel Indonesia, in Central Jakarta, was among the first five-star hotels in Southeast Asia and is still one of the city's main landmarks. Sukarno, the country's first president, had it built for the 1962 Asian Games to show the world a modern Indonesia. The Danish architect Abel Sorensen designed it with his wife, Wendy Becker, on a site of 25,082 m2. It opened on 16 July 1962, run by InterContinental until 1974. Its two wings, the 16-storey Ramayana and the eight-storey Ganesha, include a presidential suite and four suites for diplomats. Jakarta's governor declared it a national cultural heritage site on 29 March 1993. After closing in 2004 for a complete overhaul, it returned in May 2009 as the Hotel Indonesia Kempinski, owned by Djarum and managed by Kempinski Hotels.

Gedung Sate stands in Bandung, in Indonesia's West Java province. The Dutch architect J. Gerber designed it to house the Dutch East Indies Department of Government Industries, blending a neoclassical scheme with native Indonesian features, among them Hindu-Buddhist elements. It was finished in 1924. Its popular name means "satay building", because the central pinnacle looks like a skewer of satay, the Indonesian dish. The six spheres on that pinnacle stand for the six million guilders it cost to build. Today the building is the office of West Java's governor and also a museum.

The Savoy Homann is a four-star hotel with a long history, on Asia Afrika Street in Bandung, Indonesia, built to replace the 19th-century Homann Hotel. Its Dutch architect, Albert Aalbers, gave it a curved, streamlined Art Deco form, and it is counted as a fine example of the colonial Art Deco architecture of the East Indies. Its ocean-wave facade has an upright tower at its centre. Aalbers drew on the work of Frank Lloyd Wright and Le Corbusier. The hotel has historic furniture. When Bandung hosted the first Asian–African Conference in 1955, the Savoy Homann hosted its VVIP guests and became part of the Historical Walk. It now has three wings, called Tower, Garden and Millennium, with 185 guest rooms in all.

Jakarta Cathedral is the seat of the city's Catholic Archbishop. The present church went up between 1891 and 1901, when it was consecrated, in the neo-Gothic style then usual for churches. Pastor Antonius Dijkmans, SJ, was its appointed architect; Marius Hulswit simplified the design so that builders without practical training could raise it, and added cast-iron spires for that reason. The cross-shaped plan ends in an eastern apse. It runs 60 metres from narthex to apse, and 10 metres wide plus 5 metres for each aisle. The two tallest of its three main spires, 60 metres high, flank the entrance. Its thick brick walls are plastered and patterned to pass for stone. Iron and wood stand in for the stone usual in neo-Gothic work because they are lighter, which matters in a land prone to earthquakes.

The Manila Central Post Office is the city's main post office and the headquarters of the national postal corporation, PHLPost. It sits on the Pasig River because the Burnham Plan for Manila saw the river as a handy mail route. The first building, by Juan M. Arellano with Tomás Mapúa and Ralph Doane, is thought of as Arellano's greatest work, a neoclassical design meant to convey order and balance. Sixteen Ionic columns rise above the front steps of the large rectangular block. A set-back attic storey crowns the main body, which two semicircular wings flank and brace. Rebuilt in 1946, it kept most of its design. The national museum declared it an Important Cultural Property in 2018, making it eligible for public funds. Late on 21 May 2023 a fire spread from the basement through the building, causing severe damage.

The Manila Hotel, credited to William E. Parsons, is a historic five-star hotel on Manila Bay. It opened on 4 July 1912, American Independence Day. It occupies 35,000 square metres of reclaimed land on Bonifacio Drive, at the northwestern tip of Rizal Park. The first design was H-shaped, its airy rooms in two wings facing the harbour, the Luneta and Intramuros. The top floor was a viewing deck, used among other things to watch the American navy steam in. From 1935 to 1941 General Douglas MacArthur lived in the penthouse while Military Advisor to the Philippine Commonwealth. A 1975 tower behind the original five-storey block raised the room count to 570; Leandro Locsin and Ildefonso Santos, both National Artists for Architecture, led the work with the interior designer Patricia Keller. The spartan, simplified Mission-style interiors gave way to richer furnishings.

This Manila building holds the University of Santo Tomas's administration and its faculties of Civil Law and Pharmacy, its College of Science and a museum. Designed by the priest Roque Ruaño, it was the first Philippine building made to withstand earthquakes. He took cues from the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo by Frank Lloyd Wright, and the design may have been refined after the Great Kantō earthquake of 1 September 1923 flattened Tokyo and Yokohama. Building began in 1924, and the first classes were held on 2 July 1927. The block, 86 metres by 74, encloses two courtyards. Its most important feature is that it is actually 40 separate structures, each independent of the others. From 4 January 1942, during the Japanese occupation in the Second World War, the campus became an internment camp for Americans and other foreigners.

Manila Cathedral, a minor basilica dedicated to the Immaculate Conception, is the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Manila. The first church here dates from 1581; the present one, completed in 1958, is the eighth rebuilding. Cardinal Rufino Santos oversaw the rebuilding, supervised by the Kapampangan architect Fernando Ocampo. Fernando Quiroga Palacios, Archbishop of Santiago de Compostela, laid its first cornerstone as Pope Pius XII's legate on 8 December 1954, and the church was consecrated on 7 December 1958. Its plan is a Latin cross. Its Neo-Romanesque northwest front copies the previous cathedral's, with saints carved in Roman travertine. Most of its 134 modern stained glass windows were designed and made by the Filipino artist Galo Ocampo in 1964. Its 6,446-pipe organ is Southeast Asia's largest. After the 2012 Negros earthquake it closed for repairs and seismic strengthening.

The Singapore Indoor Stadium is an arena in Kallang, a short walk from the Singapore National Stadium, and the two together form part of The Kallang. The Japanese architect Kenzo Tange designed it with Raglan Squire & Partners, giving it a cone-shaped roof over an arena free of columns. Work started on the first day of 1985, and the building cost S$90 million. It was finished on 1 March 1987 and opened to the public on 1 July 1988, and Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew formally opened it at an inaugural ceremony on 31 December 1989. Depending on the layout it holds up to 15,000 people, or 12,000 when everyone is seated. On 7 March 2024, the culture minister, Edwin Tong, announced plans to replace it with a new indoor arena.

Ipoh railway station, in the centre of Perak's capital, is the state's main terminal. Work on a second station and hotel began in 1914, but material shortages and rising labour costs during the First World War delayed completion until 1917. Its designer, Arthur Benison Hubback, was a British architectural assistant to the Director of Public Works, credited with many public buildings across British Malaya. Unlike Kuala Lumpur's station, Ipoh's exterior is mainly Western, in a late-Edwardian Baroque with a lightly rusticated base, open pointed and arched pediments, many engaged columns and a large dome over the carriage porch. Deep open loggias on both floors are a vernacular element; the lower one runs the full 183-metre front. Small chhatris over the corner columns add an Indo-Saracenic note. Locals call it the Taj Mahal of Ipoh, and it holds the Majestic Hotel.

Jakarta Kota Station stands in Kota Tua, the historic core of Jakarta. The earlier station shut in 1923 and was rebuilt in 1926–1929, while Batavia North station took all trains. The design, drawn in 1927–1928, came from three architects of the Batavia firm AIA: Asselbergs, Frans Johan Louwrens Ghijsels and Hes. Company staff opened it at a private ceremony on 8 October 1929. It is described as Ghijsels' greatest work in the Het Indische Bouwen manner, which joins modern Western Art Deco structure and methods with local traditional forms. A barrel-vaulted roof covers the entrance and hall, with bands of openings below upright lunettes. Rough brown ceramic lines the hall walls, and greenish-yellow plaster covers the outside base. Floors are yellow teak and grey wood, with waffle teak on the platforms. It was designated cultural heritage in 1993.

Wat Rong Khun, widely called the White Temple, is a private contemporary art work in the form of a Buddhist temple, in Chiang Rai province, Thailand. Chalermchai Kositpipat, a national artist from the area, chose to rebuild the temple entirely with his own money; he designed and built it, welcoming visitors from 1997. Work continues and is not expected to end until 2070. Structurally it is a plain concrete frame with a wooden roof. From afar it seems made of glittering porcelain; up close the shine proves to be whitewash with clear mirror chips. The main hall, or ubosot, is approached across a bridge over a small lake, past hundreds of reaching hands that represent unchecked desire. All white and studded with mirror glass, it borrows from classic Thai architecture in its three-tiered roof and its many Nāga serpents.

The Inland Steel Building, a 332-foot (101 m) tower on West Monroe Street in Chicago, was built from 1956 to 1958 as the head office of the Inland Steel Company. Bruce Graham and Walter Netsch of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it in the International Style, and it was among the first Loop towers built after the Second World War. It comes in two parts: a 19-storey office block on the Dearborn corner, and a 25-storey service tower to the east holding every stair, lift and duct. Columns on the outside carry all the weight, leaving most floors free of inner columns. Its curtain wall pairs green-tinted glass with stainless steel spandrels, columns and mullions. The architects weighed black steel for the outer columns but rejected it as too like Mies van der Rohe's towers.

The John C. Kluczynski Federal Building is a 45-storey tower by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, finished in 1974 as the final piece of Chicago's new Federal Center. It is one of three Mies buildings grouped around Federal Center Plaza, joined by a post office and the Dirksen federal courthouse. The steel-framed tower holds 1,200,000 square feet. Its skin is bronze-tinted glass in bright aluminium frames, with black-painted steel panels below each window and projecting steel I-beams, also black, as mullions. The two-storey lobby is set back behind a ring of columns. The whole complex follows a 28-foot grid, so the joints in the plaza's granite paving run on into the lobbies and up the walls, binding the three together. On 24 October 1974, Alexander Calder's Flamingo, a red steel sculpture 53 feet tall, was unveiled on the plaza.

The Reliance Building stands in Chicago's Loop. John Root of the firm Burnham and Root designed its basement and ground floor in 1890; Charles B. Atwood finished the rest in 1895. It was the first skyscraper with large plate glass windows over most of its surface, a feature that grew dominant in the 20th century. Atwood clad it in white glazed terra-cotta, a material later linked closely to him through his work for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The steel frame of the top ten floors rose in fifteen days, from 16 July to 1 August 1895. It has been called "proto-Modernist" because its front lacks the ranked order of a classical facade, and its stacked bay windows and terra-cotta skin make it look remarkably light. It directly foreshadowed the all-glass Friedrichstrasse tower Mies van der Rohe proposed in 1921.

The Richard J. Daley Center is a Chicago tower of courtrooms and offices for Cook County's courts and State's Attorney, plus city and county offices. Jacques Brownson of C. F. Murphy Associates led the design, with Loebl, Schlossman, Bennett & Dart and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill as associates, in the International Style of the Second Chicago School. Finished in 1965, it was Chicago's tallest building until the John Hancock Center passed it four years later. It reaches 648 feet with only 31 storeys, 30 of them above a double-height lobby, making it the world's tallest flat-roofed building under 40 storeys. It is built with Cor-Ten, a steel meant to rust, which strengthens the structure and gives the tower its red-brown colour. Its granite plaza, used for gatherings, protests and events, holds the Chicago Picasso, the artist's gift to the city.

The Rookery, in Chicago's Loop, was completed in 1888 by the partners Daniel Burnham and John Wellborn Root, who once had their offices here. Twelve storeys and 181 feet tall, it is thought to be Chicago's oldest standing high-rise. It joined new methods, such as fireproofing, lifts and plate glass, with brick fronts and rich ornament. Masonry bearing walls work with cast and wrought iron framing, a step from masonry toward steel that the critic Paul Goldberger sees as leading to early skyscraper frames. Root devised a grillage foundation of iron rails and beams laid crosswise in concrete, carrying the great weight without heavy foundation stones. A white terracotta light court under a 5,000-pane skylight brings daylight to inner offices. In 1905 Frank Lloyd Wright reworked the lobby in his Prairie style, his only work in the Loop.

Paul Rudolph's addition to Sarasota High School, built in 1958–1959, stands beside the 60,000-square-foot Collegiate Gothic school that M. Leo Elliott designed in 1926. Begun in 1958 to extend the old building, the wing covers 20,000 square feet. Riverview High, just finished, was a steel design; Rudolph made this one different, as a composition of folded concrete planes. He worked out a system of horizontal plates and upright piers to suit Sarasota's climate, lining the classrooms along an open-air spine so that air could flow through them. In 1962 the design won Rudolph an AIA Award of Merit. After 50 years of classes, the wing became the campus's "front door" and its administrative offices. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2012.

Graycliff is a summer estate on a bluff above Lake Erie, looking toward downtown Buffalo and the Ontario shore. Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in 1926, and it was built between 1926 and 1931. It was his second complex for the Martins, after their city home, the Martin House Complex, and ranks among the largest and most ambitious summer estates of his career. It is one of only five Wright designs built from 1925 to 1935, and his only stone building between Taliesin and Fallingwater. Its three buildings sit in an 8.5-acre landscape, all of stone gathered at the lake's edge, ochre stucco and red cedar shingle roofs. The largest, the Isabelle R. Martin House, sets a glass-walled central pavilion between two stone-faced wings, so visitors can look straight through it to the lake, a bold idea for 1926.

In August 1936 the journalist Herbert Jacobs asked Frank Lloyd Wright to design him a home for $5,000 or less, and Wright had first plans ready within two months. Finished in 1937 in Madison, it is sometimes called Wright's first Usonian house. The single-storey, L-shaped home covers 1,550 square feet on ground falling toward Lake Wingra. The plan turns from the street to partly wrap a rear garden. Toward the street it shows brick and board-and-batten walls; toward the garden it opens up with large windows and glass doors. It rests on a concrete slab with heating set into the floor, under flat roofs at three levels with projecting eaves. Its board-and-batten walls, underfloor heating and modular floor grid were later widely used. In 2019 it became part of a World Heritage Site of Wright's work.

The journalist Loren Pope and his wife Charlotte commissioned this house in 1939; it was one of Frank Lloyd Wright's first Usonian designs. It was finished in 1941 in Falls Church, Virginia. Mindful of their budget, Wright shrank the plan from 1,800 to 1,200 square feet and dropped a planned workshop. It has the core Usonian traits: an L-shaped plan, a flat roof, natural materials, cantilevers (notably the carport) and close ties between indoors and out. The house has one storey on two levels that follow the slope, and three brick pillars carry the roof. Brick and wood are unpainted, treated with clear wax. Owned by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, it has been moved twice, the second time in 1995, just 30 feet, at a cost of $500,000, and stands at Woodlawn Plantation in Alexandria.

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the Chicago architect, designed this savings and loan office in Des Moines, completed in 1962. It was one of the earliest modernist steel-and-glass buildings downtown and is described as one of the city's best-known pieces of mid-century modern design. Mies first meant to hang the roof from two long trusses, as in his work for Chicago's Illinois Institute of Technology. He gave that up for a simpler, more direct answer: a steel frame filled with glass, set on a base of granite and travertine. The building has three storeys and stands 40.25 feet tall. In 1992 the philanthropist Ed Ochylski bought it as a gift for the Diocese of Des Moines, which moved its headquarters there. A $10 million renovation ran in 2016–2017, and in 2017 it joined the National Register of Historic Places.

The National Farmers' Bank in Owatonna, Minnesota, is a bank building by Louis Sullivan, with ornament by George Elmslie. The bank's officers sought him out partly because they felt ordinary bank designs of the day would not fit their needs. Built in 1908, it was the first of Louis Sullivan's series of small bank designs. Red brick walls with bands of green terra cotta wrap the building, and two large arches open onto the streets. Inside, Louis J. Millet designed two stained-glass windows and Oskar Gross painted a mural, while Elmslie drew four huge cast-iron electroliers that the Winslow Brothers Company cast. A 1940 remodelling destroyed much of the interior, but later campaigns, the last running from 1976 to 1981, restored it. It became a National Historic Landmark on 7 January 1976.

Finished in 1922 on North Lincoln Avenue in Chicago, this commercial building is counted as the last of Louis Sullivan's 126 buildings, though he did not design all of it. The client chose a neighbour, the architect William Presto, for the building itself; Presto, once a draftsman for Sullivan, then asked his old employer to draw the front. Sullivan covered that whole facade in green terra cotta, setting geometric shapes and curving, plant-like forms around a carefully framed picture window, an outgrowth of his belief in organic architecture. The store sold pianos and sheet music and was an early seller of radios. Chicago made the facade a landmark in 1977. Pooja and Peter Vukosavich bought the building in 2005, restored the terra cotta and turned the main floor into offices for their design agency.

Rising 17 storeys in Baltimore, Maryland, this federal office block went up between 1963 and 1967 as one piece of Charles Center, a large urban renewal scheme planned and carried out from 1955 to 1975. Its design, credited to Fisher, Nes, Campbell and Associates, follows the International Style: a frame of steel and reinforced concrete faced with granite panels from Minnesota. The building measures 480 by 223 feet and holds more than 725,000 gross square feet. Several federal agencies have offices inside, among them the Federal Highway Administration and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. A federal law, Public Law 91-653, gave it its present name in January 1971 in honour of George Hyde Fallon, a congressman who lived from 1902 to 1980. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2023.

Marcel Breuer designed this Brutalist federal complex in Columbia, South Carolina, with his partner Herbert Beckhard, and it was completed in 1979. For twenty-five years it held the federal district court for South Carolina. A tall office tower stands beside a long, low courthouse of three storeys and a landscaped plaza, an arrangement found in many Modern-era federal buildings, and a tunnel joins the two. The plain tower is defined by repeated windows under peaked hoods, or brise soleils, which block direct sun and keep rooms cooler in summer; Breuer repeated the same window on the courthouse to unify the group. A steel frame carries precast concrete panels and dark grey Cold Spring granite. A reflecting pool sits in the sunken courtyard, softened by grass, shrubs and trees. The building is named for Senator Strom Thurmond.

Until 2012 this was Istanbul's main terminal for trains serving the Anatolian side of Turkey. In 1904 Haydarpaşa became the northern end of both the Baghdad and Hejaz railways, and rising traffic called for a bigger building. The Anatolian Railway hired the German architects Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu, who chose a Neo-classical design; construction started in 1906. A steam hammer drove 1,100 timber piles, each 21 metres long, into the soft shore, and German and Italian stonemasons made the outside decoration. Completed on reclaimed land in August 1909, the terminal opened that 4 November, the birthday of Mehmed V. In 2010 a fire, caused by carelessness during restoration, destroyed the roof and the fourth floor. The original timber roof trusses, with their baroque influence, were later rebuilt, and the stone fronts were cleaned of salt from the nearby sea.

Emperor Justinian I commissioned two Byzantine Greek scholars, Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles, to design this cathedral in Constantinople, built from 532 to 537. Neither was trained as an architect, but as scientists they could organise thousands of workers and rare materials, among them stone from Egypt, Syria and Libya and columns from temples in Rome. Because earlier churches here had burned, the new one used baked brick and mortar, tied in places with iron, and no wood. The plan joins the long body of a Roman basilica to a central dome raised on a drum, and Isidore, author of a commentary On Vaulting, is thought to have done much of the dome work. Earthquakes often cracked it; part of the dome fell in 558. Isidore's nephew, Isidore the Younger, later repaired it and added the dome's ribs.

First called the Istanbul Sports and Exhibition Hall, this complex stands in Istanbul's Harbiye neighbourhood. Its project was drawn up by the Italian architect Paolo Vietti-Violi together with Şinasi Şahingiray and Fazıl Aysu, both Turkish. Ground was broken in January 1948 before Lütfi Kırdar, then both mayor and governor of the city, and the hall opened on 3 June 1949 with the European Wrestling Championships. Up to 7,000 spectators watched boxing, ice hockey and even circus shows in its main hall, and for many years no other indoor hall for sport and exhibitions existed in Turkey. In 1996 it was turned into a convention centre for the UN's Habitat II conference and given Kırdar's name. A nine-level underground extension of 120,000 square metres was added for the IMF and World Bank meetings of 2009.

At 435 metres, Milad Tower in Tehran is the tallest tower in Iran and ranks sixth among telecommunication towers worldwide. The Iranian architect Mohammad Reza Hafezi led its design. Construction took 11 years and ended in 2007, and the tower opened in October 2008 under the slogan "Heaven is near". It has five parts: foundation, a lobby or transition structure, shaft, head and antenna mast. The concrete shaft climbs about 315 metres, and the steel head weighs some 25,000 tonnes and holds 12 floors, among them an art gallery, a revolving restaurant, open and closed viewing decks and a sky dome. The octagonal base refers to traditional Iranian architecture. Planners studied 21 sites in the city before shortlisting four. The tower belongs to Tehran's International Trade and Convention Center, with a hotel, a convention centre and an IT park.

This tomb complex in Tus, in Iran's Razavi Khorasan province, honours the Persian poet Ferdowsi. Built in the early 1930s, it draws mainly on Achaemenid architecture to display Iran's long cultural history, and it resembles the tomb of Cyrus the Great. An earlier dome-shaped scheme is credited to Haj Hossein Lurzadeh; the cubical design standing today is credited mainly to Karim Taherzadeh. On a white marble base, a broad chamber forms the lower part, holding Ferdowsi's body at its centre, and above it rises a cube ringed by four pillars and decorated with text and scenes from the epic Shahnameh. Column details with a box and a two-horned bull closely copy those of Persepolis. A large Char-bagh, the Persian four-part garden, surrounds it, and inside, deep friezes of three-dimensional figures show scenes from the Shahnameh.

Commonly known as Saadieh, this mausoleum complex in Shiraz, in Iran's Fars province, honours the Persian poet Saadi, who was buried at a khanqah on the same site at the end of his life. The present building dates from 1950 to 1952. Its architect, Mohsen Foroughi, drew on the Chehel Sotoun and blended old and new elements. Eight brown stone pillars line the front, while the main structure is of white stone and tiles, with a travertine facade and marble inside. Two terraces meet at a right angle, with the tomb where they join. From outside the building reads as a cube; inside it becomes an octagon with marble walls and an azure arch, under a blue dome. A fish pond lies to the left of the tomb. Iran entered the complex on its National Heritage List in 1975.

This Beirut museum of modern and contemporary art occupies a villa that Nicolas Ibrahim Sursock, a Lebanese aristocrat, built in 1912 and left in his will to become a museum. With its Venetian and Ottoman influences, the house is an example of Lebanese architecture and one of the few villas of its time left in the city. The museum opened in 1961 with a show of contemporary Lebanese artists. The French architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte and the Lebanese architect Jacques Abou Khaled later designed an extension of four floors below the garden, costing US$12 million. It grew the museum from 1,500 to 8,500 square metres, adding galleries, a research library, an auditorium, a restoration workshop and a restaurant, and the museum reopened in October 2015. The explosion of 4 August 2020 caused serious damage, and 57 artworks had to be restored.

Often called the Blue Mosque, this Sunni mosque in downtown Beirut stands beside Saint George's Maronite Cathedral and rises 72 metres. The site once held a 19th-century zawiya named for Sheikh Abu Nasr al-Yafi. After the Lebanese Civil War, a donation from Rafic Hariri, the former prime minister, led to the foundation being laid in November 2002. During construction, archaeologists found part of the Roman city's main east-west street, the Decumanus Maximus, with its paving and columns. Azmi Fakhoury designed the mosque in a manner close to Ottoman Turkish architecture, with space for up to 6,400 worshippers and five domes clad in light blue tiles. It was inaugurated in 2008. The Beirut explosions of 4 August 2020 caused heavy damage, shattering its chandeliers and windows.

This complex on Jerusalem's King George Street is the headquarters of the Zionist movement's national institutions. A 1927 competition drew 37 entries. The brief set a limit of two storeys and asked for one building in three sections, for the Zionist Executive, the Jewish National Fund and Keren Hayesod. Yohanan Ratner's chosen design wraps around a large forecourt, giving it formal presence, blocking street noise and letting the low front hold its own. His International Style building has local touches: outer elements that echo the Tower of David, and windows recalling the narrow slits of the Old City walls. Money was short, so building went in stages: the first floor was dedicated in 1930, the second in 1936. A 1948 bombing devastated the building; it also hosted the Knesset's opening sessions and Chaim Weizmann's inauguration as Israel's first president.

The Great Synagogue stands at 56 King George Street in Jerusalem and serves an Orthodox Jewish congregation. When its earlier premises grew too small for the worshippers who came, a new and much larger building was planned. Its chief funder was Sir Isaac Wolfson, a British Jewish philanthropist, and his family dedicated the synagogue to the six million Jews killed in the Holocaust and to fallen soldiers of the Israel Defense Forces. The German-born architect Alexander Friedman modelled its style on the Jewish Temple. The building was inaugurated on Tu B'Av in 1982, and its sanctuary has seats for 850 men and 550 women.

This public research university lies beside the Red Sea at Thuwal in Saudi Arabia, and its core campus covers more than 36 square kilometres: 16.4 on land and 19.6 of marine sanctuary offshore. The architecture firm HOK (Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum) drew up the master plan, which used wind towers and solar panels, while separate advisers planned the academic structure and four research institutes. Ground was broken in October 2007. The campus was the first project in Saudi Arabia to earn LEED certification and is the largest LEED Platinum campus anywhere. In 2010 the American Institute of Architects' Committee on the Environment named it one of its Top Ten Green Projects, and the library won an AIA/ALA Library Building Award in 2011. When it opened, KAUST became the country's first mixed-gender university campus.

Officially the Alexander Spendiaryan National Academic Opera and Ballet Theatre, this building in Yerevan is known to residents simply as "Opera". The architect Alexander Tamanian designed it. Ground was broken on 28 November 1930 to mark ten years of Soviet Armenia, and the theatre opened officially on 20 January 1933 with Almast, an opera by the composer Alexander Spendiaryan, whose name it bears. Work went on for two more decades: the theatre hall was finished in 1939 to Tamanian's design, with his son supervising, and the whole building was not complete until 1953. It holds two halls; following several rounds of renovation, the Aram Khachaturian Concert Hall seats 1,300 and the opera and ballet theatre about 1,070. The theatre gained its national academic status in 1956.

Several of Azerbaijan's state ministries work from this building in central Baku. Its main front sits on Neftchiler Avenue facing Baku Boulevard, while the back looks onto busy Uzeyir Hajibeyov Street. The story began in 1934, when the Soviet authorities called a tender for a Baku Soviet Palace, the name the building carried before it became Government House. Lev Rudnev and Vladimir Munts, with K. Tkachenko taking part, won the competition. Their design was altered somewhat and built between 1936 and 1952, sized for 5,500 people. The project also produced Lenin Square, today Azadliq Square, laid out in front of the building. The Azerbaijani government carried out a renovation from 2006 to 2010.

At 8 Rustaveli Avenue in Tbilisi, near the foot of Mount Mtatsminda, this complex was built as the House of Government of Soviet Georgia. It took the place of the demolished 19th-century Alexander Nevsky Cathedral and its churchyard, where Georgian cadets killed in the Bolshevik invasion of 1921 were buried. Viktor Kokorin and Giorgi Lezhava designed the upper building, put up from 1933 to 1938; with Vladimer Nasaridze they added the lower one along the avenue from 1946 to 1953. A courtyard with stairs and fountains joins the two. Both draw heavily on traditional Georgian architecture, and the avenue front is a monumental arcade under heavy eaves. Light reinforced concrete is faced with tufa, granite and other materials. Badly damaged in the coup of 1991–92, the complex was restored and housed Georgia's parliament from 1997 to 2012.

Today the Presidium of Azerbaijan's Academy of Sciences, this building stands on Istiglaliyyat Street in Baku. It was built from 1908 to 1913 for a charity society, paid for by the millionaire Musa Naghiyev in memory of his late son Ismayil, after whom it is named. The Polish architect Józef Płoszko designed it in the Venetian Gothic style; it was the first project of his own in the 30 years he spent in Baku. After it opened, its white stone assembly hall held conferences of the Muslim Charity Society, meetings of Muslim women and the city's intellectuals, and congresses of clergy. Fire and fighting damaged the palace during the March Days of 1918. In 1923 it was rebuilt under an architect named Dubov, and the inscriptions on its front and side facades were taken off.

Rising 28 floors and 105 metres in São Paulo, the Martinelli Building was Brazil's first skyscraper. Giuseppe Martinelli, an Italian-born businessman, planned it in 1922; the design is credited to Vilmos (William) Fillinger. Building work ran from 1924 to 1929. On opening it was the tallest building anywhere in Latin America, and no concrete-framed building in the world was larger. Between 1975 and 1979, under Mayor Olavo Setúbal, it was completely remodelled. Its tenants today include municipal housing and planning departments, the companies Emurb and Cohab-SP, and the head office of the São Paulo banks' association, with shops at street level.

This stadium in Belo Horizonte belongs to the state of Minas Gerais, is used by the club Cruzeiro and seats 66,658. Its architects were Eduardo Mendes Guimarães Júnior and Caspar Garreto; Arthur Eugênio Jermann, an engineer, did the structural design, and Gil César Moreira de Abreu ran the building work. Some 5,000 people worked on it between 1963 and the opening on 5 September 1965. Engineers studied the Maracanã to avoid its structural weak points. A major challenge was the superstructure, a near-ellipse 275 by 217 metres, built with ordinary equipment. To test it, the team built a "mini-Mineirão", a trial section of stands and roof called sector 15. Local industry could not supply long enough steel bars, so workers welded them together on site. The stadium hosted games at the 2013 Confederations Cup and the 2014 World Cup.

Officially the Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho, this football ground in Rio de Janeiro is owned by the state government and run by the Flamengo and Fluminense clubs. The city opened a competition to design and build it in 1947, and the contract went to a group including Waldir Ramos, Raphael Galvão and Antônio Dias Carneiro. It opened for the 1950 World Cup, and on 16 July Uruguay beat Brazil 2–1 in the deciding game before 173,850 people, a record that still stands. It overtook Hampden Park as the world's largest stadium, yet was fully completed only in 1965. A rebuild began in 2010 ahead of the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics: a mostly single-tier bowl for 78,639 replaced the old two-tier one, and a coated fibreglass membrane took over from the concrete roof, now sheltering 95 percent of seats.

This opera house in Manaus follows a project by a Lisbon engineering and architecture office, the Gabinete Português de Engenharia e Arquitectura. Building work was set to begin by 1884, led by the Italian architect Celestial Sacardim. The style is generally called Renaissance Revival, and many materials travelled a long way: roof tiles came from Alsace, steel walls from Glasgow, and Carrara marble from Italy for stairs, statues and columns. Its dome is clad in 36,000 decorated ceramic tiles in the colours of Brazil's flag. The theatre was inaugurated on 31 December 1896, and its first performance, Amilcare Ponchielli's opera La Gioconda, was given on 7 January 1897. The auditorium seats 701. In July 2026 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site jointly with the Teatro da Paz.

Known simply as "Vila", this performing arts centre in Salvador, Bahia, was built in 1964 on Avenida Sete, on the west side of the Passeio Público, a public promenade from the 19th century. The Bahia state government gave the land in 1961. The architect Silvio Robatto (1935–2008) designed it in a Modern style that sets it sharply apart from the many Neoclassical buildings of the promenade and from the Palácio da Aclamação. The seating can be rearranged for different kinds of show and holds up to 350 people. In the 1960s the theatre was a centre of the counterculture movement Tropicália and of cultural resistance to Brazil's military dictatorship, which lasted from 1964 to 1985. The building was renovated on a large scale in 1998.

São Paulo's large public market, known as the Mercadão, stands near the Tamanduateí River on the old Várzea do Carmo floodplain, now mostly Dom Pedro II Park. Francisco Ramos de Azevedo designed it, and it opened on 25 January 1933 to sell fruit, vegetables, grain, meat, spices and other food, both wholesale and retail. Its facade is by Felisberto Ranzini (1882–1976), an Italian-Brazilian from Ramos de Azevedo's office, who combined Ionic and Doric columns. The heavy columns leave room for wide areas of glass that bring in plenty of daylight. Instead of religious scenes, its 72 stained-glass windows, set in 32 panels by Conrado Sorgenicht Filho and his firm, show food production around São Paulo. Shops fill the main floor of the 12,600 square metre market. A new 2,000 square metre mezzanine with eight restaurants was finished by 2004.

Known until 1992 as the Brasília Convention Center, this complex was then renamed in honour of Ulysses Guimarães. Sérgio Bernardes designed it in 1973; it opened on 12 March 1979 and was refurbished in 2005. It belongs to the Cultural Diffusion Sector on the city's Monumental Axis, which it shares with a planetarium and a choro music club. The centre is split into west, south and north wings. The part that was Bernardes's original building has 2,000 square metres of open space at ground level and four auditoriums. A further wing, air-conditioned and covering 10,200 square metres, is used for exhibitions and trade fairs. The north wing contains the Master Auditorium, which takes more than 3,000 people, along with 13 modular rooms, dressing rooms and rooms for the press and VIP guests.

This stadium in São Paulo's Pacaembu neighbourhood belongs to the city; its design is credited to the Escritório Técnico Ramos de Azevedo, Severo e Villares. It opened on 27 April 1940 before Brazil's president, Getúlio Vargas, the interventor Adhemar de Barros and the mayor, Prestes Maia. It once held 40,199 spectators around a pitch 104 by 70 metres, and six matches of the 1950 World Cup were played here. In 1998 the state heritage council, CONDEPHAAT, protected it for its Art Deco style, typical of its time. A museum of 6,900 square metres, built for R$32.5 million, lies beneath the stands. After a 40-month renovation the stadium reopened on 27 January 2025; the biggest change was the loss of the south stand, replaced by a five-storey building.

This opera house in Rio de Janeiro's Centro district was conceived by Francisco de Oliveira Passos, the son of the then mayor, Francisco Pereira Passos, with help from Albert Guilbert. Its eclectic design follows Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra, and names of classic European and Brazilian artists are inscribed on its outer walls. Construction began in 1905 on 1,180 timber poles driven into groundwater. Leading Brazilian artists, among them Eliseu Visconti, decorated it, while European craftsmen made the stained glass and mosaics. With 280 workers on two shifts it took four and a half years, a record, and President Nilo Peçanha opened it on 14 July 1909 with 1,739 seats. As the city grew, the hall was enlarged in 1934 to 2,205 seats in just three months, and later changes brought it to 2,361.

On Praça da República in Belém, capital of the Brazilian state of Pará, this theatre went up along neoclassical lines during the Amazon rubber boom. The engineer José Tibúrcio Pereira Magalhães planned it, with some changes from the Public Constructions office. Building lasted from 1869 to 1874, but the public was let in only after an official inquiry into the builders. Domenico de Angelis, an Italian who also decorated Manaus's Teatro Amazonas, planned the decoration and painted Greek gods on the auditorium ceiling. The front lost some columns over the main entrance over the years, but its lines are unchanged. A big renovation in the 1990s, under governor Almir Gabriel, brought back the original colours. Brazil's heritage institute IPHAN protected it in 1963, and UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2026.

Luz Station serves commuter and intercity trains in São Paulo's Bom Retiro district. It was built from 1895 to 1901 to a design by Charles Henry Driver, a British architect, as headquarters for the São Paulo Railway, a London company that laid the state's first line, linking the port of Santos with Jundiaí. Its materials came from Britain: Walter Macfarlane & Co.'s Saracen Foundry in Glasgow made the station, assembled it there, then took it apart and shipped it to São Paulo to be rebuilt. For years its clock tower dominated the skyline, and for a time the city set its clocks by it. Since 2006 it has housed a museum of the Portuguese language, where a fire broke out in December 2015, devastating the main building and killing a firefighter.

Benedictine monks from Bahia founded this abbey in Rio de Janeiro in 1590, and its Mannerist church is counted among the main examples of Portuguese colonial architecture in the city and in Brazil. Francisco Frias de Mesquita, a Portuguese military engineer, drew the plans and in 1617 oversaw building, in the Mannerist manner then in fashion in Portugal. Enslaved Africans did the labour. The church was started in 1633 under Abbot Francisco da Magdalena, with completion planned for 1671, and during building another architect changed the plan to give it three naves. Its front has a central block with three entrance arches and a triangular gable between two towers with pyramid spires. Inside, gold leaf covers the church. A convent by José Fernandes Pinto Alpoim, also a military engineer, completed the annex in 1755.

This large memorial in Rosario stands near the bank of the Paraná River. Across the water, on an island, Manuel Belgrano, who created Argentina's flag, first raised it on 27 February 1812, and the complex opened on 20 June 1957, the anniversary of his death. The architects Alejandro Bustillo and Ángel Guido designed it in 1944. It covers some 10,000 square metres, is built mostly of stone from the Andes and carries work by the sculptors José Fioravanti, Alfredo Bigatti and Eduardo Barnes. It has three parts: a 70-metre tower honouring the May Revolution of 1810, with Belgrano's crypt at its foot; a Civic Courtyard that stands for the organising of the state and hosts big outdoor shows; and a Triumphal Propylaeum for the nation after the 1853 Constitution, above a room showing the flags of every American nation.

This cultural centre in the La Boca neighbourhood of Buenos Aires fills a former power station, the Don Pedro de Mendoza plant. The design is credited to the Italian architect Giovanni Chiogna, working for the Italo-Argentine Electricity Company (CIAE); it was built from 1912 to 1916. For about 80 years it supplied the city with power, until the service was nationalised in the 1990s; then it was abandoned and decayed. The city government converted it and reopened it in May 2012 with a symphonic auditorium for 1,200. Its Italianate style is described as late Gothic or early Renaissance, and the clock tower is visible from afar, above all from the freeway that now runs over the site. Battlements, gargoyles, round arches, bare brick and plaster imitating stone recur across Chiogna's CIAE work. The old generator halls keep their iron trusses.

Uruguay's General Assembly meets in this palace in Montevideo's Aguada neighbourhood. A competition picked the project of the Italian architect Vittorio Meano, then building Argentina's National Congress in Buenos Aires, but he died suddenly and never learned of his win. The design is credited to Meano and another Italian, Gaetano Moretti, and the interior is lined with marble. Built from 1904 to 1925, the palace opened on 25 August 1925, a hundred years after Uruguay's Declaration of Independence. In an eclectic Greco-Roman style, its facades, walls, vaults and columns are faced with Uruguayan marbles. The main front lines up with Libertador Avenue. At its heart, the Hall of the Lost Steps, modelled on Renaissance cathedrals, has two vaults and a skylight and divides the two legislative chambers. It was declared a National Historic Monument in 1975.

This is the main bus terminal of Buenos Aires, two blocks to the north of the Retiro railway station in the district of the same name. Mayor Osvaldo Cacciatore's city government commissioned it in 1980, and it opened in 1983. Its architects were Fernando Serra, Jorge Valera and Raúl Petrucci. The building is almost 400 metres long and has 75 gates, and five raised walkways connect it to the car park. Coaches leave from here for every part of Argentina, for the neighbouring countries of Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay, and for Lima in Peru. Since 1993 the station has been operated privately, by Teba S.A.

Also called Torre Interama, this 200-metre observation tower rises in the Villa Soldati area of Buenos Aires. The Austrian firm Waagner-Biro designed and made it, and it was erected from 1980 to May 1981 to serve an amusement park, the Parque de la Ciudad. When Interama S.A., the company developing the park, went bankrupt, delivery of the tower's parts was held up, and the public could not go up until 9 July 1985. Viewing decks sit at 120, 124 and 176 metres, and from the top one the coast of Uruguay can be seen. The tower shut in 2003. The city named it a Cultural Landmark on 22 November 2010, and after renovation it reopened on 26 November 2011.

The Supreme Court and lower courts sit in this Buenos Aires palace. The French architect Norbert Maillart designed the original building, but the Baring financial crisis of 1890 stalled the start of work for almost two decades. Construction began in 1905, and President José Figueroa Alcorta opened a first section in 1910 during the centenary of the May Revolution. Around 1925 the growing courts needed more room, so the plan changed: an extra floor replaced the mansard meant to crown the building. The palace, in a monumental eclectic neoclassical style with 60,100 square metres of floors, was not complete until 1942. Its fronts are faced in imitation Paris stone, and Virginio Colombo came from Milan to design their many ornaments, then stayed to become a leading local figure of art nouveau. It became a National Historic Monument in 1999.

This hotel and casino stands on the Rambla of Montevideo, at the heart of the early 20th-century plan for the Carrasco district by two French landscape designers, Charles Thays and Edouard André. Building started in 1912 under Gastón Mallet and the Swiss architect Jacques Dunant, but the First World War stopped work for nine years. The city then bought the land and the large unfinished shell, completed it and opened it on 29 January 1921. Its eclectic, historicist style leans on neoclassical and baroque models and takes its cue from Europe's palace hotels. It quickly became a byword for luxury, and its famous guests included Albert Einstein in 1925 and Federico García Lorca in 1934. Declared national heritage in 1975, it closed in 1997; restoration ran from 2009 to 2013.

This museum in Santiago remembers the victims of human rights abuses under the military dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet, from 1973 to 1990. President Michelle Bachelet announced it in a speech to Congress on 21 May 2007 and, a month later, a public competition for its design. That August the winner was announced: a group of Brazilian architects from Estudio América, an office in São Paulo. Bachelet, who had herself been tortured under the dictatorship, laid the first stone on 10 December 2008 and opened the museum on 11 January 2010, as part of Chile's bicentennial. It holds instruments of torture, prisoners' letters home from detention centres, press cuttings and survivors' testimony. Across the entrance runs Estadio Chile, the last poem by the folk singer Víctor Jara, written shortly before he died in that stadium during the 1973 coup.

On the shore of Lake Llanquihue in Frutillar, in Chile's Los Lagos Region, this theatre and concert hall was built to give the Semanas Musicales de Frutillar a new cultural home once fire had destroyed the Hotel Frutillar in 1996. The architects Gerardo Köster and Gustavo Greene started construction on 27 January 1998. In 2008 a second team, from the firm Amercanda, joined to bring in materials with better acoustics. The 10,000 square metre building holds a concert hall for 1,178, an amphitheatre for 270, and foyers, exhibition areas, rehearsal rooms and conference halls. Twelve years after work began it opened, on 6 November 2010, at a cost of US$20 million, and became at once one of the biggest concert venues Chile had opened since the 1950s.

This former railway station sits beside the Mapocho River in Santiago, at the corner of Presidente Balmaceda and Bandera streets. Its design and building began in 1905 under Emilio Jecquier, a Chilean architect working from France, as one of several works marking a century of Chile's independence. The hall is 280 metres long and 17 metres high: a masonry base carries a steel vault made by Haine Saint Pierre, a Belgian firm, first glazed and now covered in copper. It was inaugurated in May 1912 and opened to the public in 1913. It was declared a National Monument in 1976 and has been a cultural centre since 1994. Its remodelling, led by a team including Montserrat Palmer and Teodoro Fernández, set out to change the 10,000 square metres as little as possible.

Home of Chile's National Opera, the Teatro Municipal is Santiago's leading theatre and opera house. Claudio Brunet des Baines gave it a French Neoclassical exterior, but after his death in 1855 the work was overseen by Lucien Hénault and his assistant Manuel Aldunate, helped by Charles Garnier, architect of the Paris Opéra. It opened on 17 September 1857 with Verdi's Ernani, and seated 1,800 under a teardrop crystal chandelier. On 8 December 1870, after a performance by the opera singer Carlotta Patti, fire all but destroyed it; it was rebuilt to Hénault's design by July 1873. An earthquake in 1906 took most of the interior, and another serious fire struck in 1927. After these rebuilds the main hall held fewer people, 1,500, but its interior grew richer. It became a National Monument in 1974.

La Moneda, the Palace of the Mint, is the seat of Chile's president in Santiago and was the city's mint in colonial times. The Italian architect Joaquín Toesca designed it; work began in 1784 and it opened in 1805, though Toesca died in 1799 and the military engineer Agustín Cavallero took over. Materials came from far and wide, from Valdivia's oak and cypress to metalwork from Vizcaya in Spain. Twenty kinds of brick were fired locally for walls over a metre thick. The style is pure neoclassical with Roman Doric touches. Behind the main front on Moneda street, rooms line two axes around three courtyards, the last of which hosts presidential ceremonies. Air Force rockets and cannon fire hit the palace in the coup of 11 September 1973; repairs ended in 1981, leaving some bullet marks visible.

This public building in Medellín's La Candelaria commune hosts concerts, talks and art exhibitions for the department of Antioquia. The Belgian architect Agustín Goovaerts designed it in the Gothic Revival style, and it was built between 1925 and 1937. Its metal frame was shipped from Belgium in 1928 and put together the way New York skyscrapers were: nuts and bolts were heated until they glowed, so that they tightened and made the structure strong without welding. Three architects, Gerardo Mejía, Gustavo Restrepo and Gustavo Aristizabal, were later hired to complete the building; they built the north facade and brought back some of the original decoration. Inside are four floors around a central courtyard, with a lookout on the roof, and the large dome doubles as an auditorium and film projection room. It was made a national monument in 1982.

Both chambers of Colombia's Congress meet in the National Capitol, which stands on Plaza de Bolívar in the centre of Bogotá. Work started in 1848 and was not completed until 1926. The building was designed by Thomas Reed, who lived from 1817 to 1878. A Danish architect, he was born on Saint Croix when the island was a Danish territory, studied in England and Germany, and came to the Republic of New Granada in 1847. President Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera engaged him for the capitol. In 1938 the painter Ignacio Gómez Jaramillo made two murals for the building. A fresco in its elliptical chamber, showing Simón Bolívar leaving the Congress of Cúcuta when Gran Colombia was created, is regarded as the country's most important fresco.

The Centro Financiero Confinanzas, an unfinished Caracas skyscraper, took its popular name, Torre de David, from David Brillembourg, its main investor, who died of cancer in 1993. The design is credited to Enrique Gómez and Associates. Work began in 1990 and stopped in 1994 because of the Venezuelan banking crisis. One of the complex's six buildings, Torre A, rises 171 m, or 45 storeys, with a heliport, and twelve levels serve as parking. The building lacks lifts, wired electricity, running water and windows, and in many places walls. In October 2007, during a housing shortage, more than 200 families moved in as squatters, led by former convicts; all had been rehoused by June 2015. Urban Think Tank's documentary Torre David took a Golden Lion at the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2012.

Home to Venezuela's National Assembly, the Capitolio in Caracas rose between 1872 and 1877 for President Antonio Guzmán Blanco, near Plaza Bolívar where a convent once stood. The design was by the architect Luciano Urdaneta Vargas. Cast iron forms part of the structure. Two rectangular blocks, joined by two lower sections, wrap a courtyard with a fountain in a small railed garden. A gilded oval dome tops the white building; over the elliptical Oval Room, Martín Tovar y Tovar painted the Battle of Carabobo, a key fight in the war against Spanish rule. The symmetrical façade centres on a portico; the middle one of its three columned portals carries two caryatids for Justice and Freedom. It became a National Historic Monument on 22 August 1997.

India's Supreme Court has sat in this New Delhi building since 1958. Its architect, Ganesh Bhikaji Deolalikar, was the first Indian to head the Central Public Works Department, and he designed it in the Indo-British style. The plan takes the form of the scales of justice: a central wing with a wing to each side, a shape chosen to suit a triangular site, with the main block standing on 17 acres (6.9 ha). At the centre is the court of the chief justice, the biggest of the courtrooms, with two court halls to either side, under a dome that rises 27.6 m (91 ft) and beside a broad verandah lined with columns. Fifteen courtrooms are spread through the building. The complex gained two more wings in 1979, and these were enlarged in 1994.

The Government of India built this New Delhi stadium for the 1982 Asian Games, and two German firms, the architects Gerkan, Marg and Partners and the structural engineers Schlaich Bergermann Partner, later redesigned it. Renovation started in 2007, with close to 4,000 workers on site in double shifts, and the heavily remodelled stadium opened on 27 July 2010. Seating fell to 60,254, down from 78,000. The new roof, by Schlaich Bergermann Partner, is coated in Teflon and covers 53,800 square metres; it cost ₹308 crore, about US$67 million. Taiyo Membrane Corporation supplied and fitted its PTFE glass-fibre fabric, which forms one of the biggest membrane roofs anywhere. The roof and its supports took 8,500 tonnes of steel. A stadium by the same company in Foshan, China, the Century Lotus Stadium, shares a similar design.

Virasat-e-Khalsa, or the Khalsa Heritage Complex, is a museum complex of Sikhism in Anandpur Sahib, Punjab, near Takht Kesgarh Sahib. Moshe Safdie designed it, mixing traditional Sikh architectural elements with modernism, and it opened on 25 November 2011 across more than a hundred acres. The buildings are cast-in-place concrete, with some beams and columns left bare and much of the structure meant to be faced in a honey-coloured local stone. Stainless steel covers the double-curved roofs, which catch the sky, while dams in the ravine form pools that mirror the complex at night. Safdie modelled the turrets on the old forts of Punjab; a cluster of five recalls the region's fortress architecture and stands out against the cliffs. The galleries are also gathered in fives, reflecting the Five Virtues central to Sikhism. A smaller western part holds a 400-seat auditorium.

Raj Mandir stands on Bhagwan Das Road in Jaipur, close to M.I. Road. W. M. Namjoshi designed it in Art Moderne, the style also known as Streamline Moderne or late Art Deco, and gave it an auditorium shaped like a meringue. The first show, on 1 June 1976, was the film Charas, screened as a charity fundraiser by Manav Hitkari Sangh. Many Hindi film premieres have followed, and the cinema is now a popular emblem of Jaipur. It was the Jaipur-based Golcha/Surana family's final cinema and the last of 34 cinema halls by Namjoshi, who designed them across India between 1938 and 1976. Nine stars on the outside stand for the nine gems of the Navaratna style, a nod to the owners' jewellery house. It has been granted the status of Asia's largest single-screen theatre.

Empress Bega Begum, Humayun's chief consort, commissioned this tomb in 1558 and paid its whole cost of 1.5 million rupees. She chose its Persian designers herself: Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son, Sayyid Muhammad. Built from 1565 to 1572 in Delhi, it was the subcontinent's first garden-tomb, at the heart of a 30-acre Persian-style charbagh. Its model was Gur-e Amir in Samarkand, the tomb of Humayun's ancestor Timur. Its rubble and red sandstone are faced in white marble, also used for the jaali screens and main dome. Rising 47 m, it was the first building in India with a Persian double dome on a tall drum. Inside a plain exterior, eight two-storey vaulted rooms ring a domed central chamber. It set the pattern for Mughal royal tombs up to the Taj Mahal, and became a World Heritage Site in 1993.

Achyut Kanvinde designed and built this temple complex in Delhi, on Hare Krishna Hills in the East of Kailash area, a short way from Nehru Place. In 1993 he agreed to take on the commission without a fee, working for the followers of Srila Prabhupada. The finished complex is one of the biggest of its kind in India. The complex also includes a 375-seat auditorium that hosts both cultural and religious gatherings. On 5 April 1998 the temple was inaugurated by Atal Bihari Vajpayee, then Prime Minister of India, with Sahib Singh Verma, a former Chief Minister of Delhi, also present.

This Orthodox church, which also goes by the names Parumala Seminary and Parumala Pally, stands in Parumala, in the Pathanamthitta district of Kerala, and serves the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church as both a pilgrimage centre and a mausoleum. It holds the tomb of Gregorios of Parumala, the first Christian saint from India to be canonised, who died on 2 November 1902, aged 54. Charles Correa designed the church, which holds more than 2,000 worshippers. Its plan is a circle 39 m across on the inside, cut into three parts by two straight chords, each 16 m long.

The Dr. B. R. Ambedkar Telangana Secretariat in Hyderabad houses the administrative offices of the Government of Telangana's staff. Demolition of the old secretariat on the site began in early July 2020 to make way for a new, modern complex. Two architects from Chennai, Ponni Concessao and Oscar Concessao, designed it, and Shapoorji Pallonji and Company built it to the norms of the Green Building Council. The design follows the Indo-Saracenic style and blends in Indo-Islamic features, notably domes. Beside the building stands a statue of B. R. Ambedkar, 125 ft tall.

Sir Cowasji Jehangir founded this Mumbai gallery after Homi J. Bhabha and K. K. Hebbar urged him to, and it is dedicated to the memory of his late son, Jehangir. It stands in Kala Ghoda, South Mumbai, just behind the city's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya and a short way from the Gateway of India. B. G. Kher, who was Chief Minister of Bombay State at the time, opened it on 21 January 1952. The design is credited to Durga Bajpai, and the building was among the city's early concrete structures. Since it combines a gallery with an auditorium, the building turns inward; it has four exhibition halls. Its play with concrete shows in the large, wave-like cantilevered entrance that reaches out to the street, while relief stone cladding gives texture to an otherwise plain façade.

Nehru Centre in Mumbai promotes the ideas and teachings of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, through education and cultural programmes. Conceived in 1972, with Indira Gandhi laying its foundation stone, it was finished in 1985 on six acres in Worli for ₹9 crore, as a "living memorial" to Nehru. The architect I. M. Kadri centred it on a cylindrical tower that grows out of a rising, planted slope, a form meant to show Nehru's picture of India moving from farming to industry. A latticed jaali wraps the tower, its pattern drawn from the rose motif often linked with Nehru. Across roughly 322,000 sq ft, the centre holds a 1,000-seat auditorium, a planetarium commissioned in 1977, an art gallery, a library and research facilities, laid out in open-plan spaces with castellated beams to suit exhibitions and cultural events.

This arch on Mumbai's waterfront marks the landing of King George V in December 1911, when he came to be crowned Emperor of India; no British monarch had visited India before him. Its foundation stone dates from March 1913, but George Wittet's final design was approved only in 1914, and work ended in 1924. Its Indo-Saracenic style draws on 16th-century Gujarati architecture, and the façade recalls Gujarati mosques such as Ahmedabad's Jama Mosque. In plan it is an octopylon, set on eight piers. The arch rises 26 m, under a central dome 15 m across, and is built of local yellow basalt and reinforced concrete. For lack of funds the approach road was never built, so the Gateway sits askew to the road reaching it. In February 1948 the last departing British troops marched through it to a 21-gun salute.

Named after Rabindranath Tagore, Ravindra Bharathi is an auditorium in Hyderabad, Telangana. The Government of Andhra Pradesh built it over more than a year, during the celebrations for the centenary of Tagore's birth, and Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, a former President of India, opened it on 11 May 1961 to serve the region's cultural life. Its designer, Mohammad Fayazuddin, had studied at the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London. Covering 1,919 m2 (2,295 square yards) at plinth level, the building seats 1,104. It spreads over three floors: the main hall comfortably takes 1,000 people, and two smaller halls seat 150 and 112. The stage measures 105 feet in width, 48 feet in depth and 38 feet in height.

Known also as UWC Mahindra, this international boarding school for pre-university students lies 40 km west of Pune. The campus sits on a hill among rural communities, looking across the Mula river valley close to Mulshi Dam. Nelson Mandela and Queen Noor of Jordan opened it on 28 November 1997. The architect Christopher Charles Benninger designed the campus, which has a residential and an academic part; he used local materials, honouring Indian architecture with wadas, stepped levels and lotus ponds. On the residential side, each wada is a shared cluster for 40 to 60 students and four to six teachers and their families; students live eight to a house, around common courtyards. In 2000 Business Week listed the college among the world's ten super structures, and Benninger's work has been noted as one of India's first examples of critical regionalism.

Ranga Shankara is a theatre in J.P. Nagar, in south Bangalore, run by the Sanket Trust. Arundathi Nag conceived it in memory of her late husband, Shankar Nag, an actor in Kannada cinema. The cost of around ₹3 crore came from donations, from ₹5 given by ordinary theatre lovers to large amounts from industrialists, and a shortage of funds held back construction until 2001. The architect Sharukh Mistry designed the complex, which opened its doors on 28 October 2004. The air-conditioned auditorium seats 320 around a thrust stage of 1,575 sq ft, with four green rooms and modern sound, lighting and technical equipment. Stage and hall are shaped so that the acoustics need no artificial amplification. The theatre stages at least one play a day, six days a week, closing on Mondays.

Opened on 15 December 2011, this Colombo theatre is a centre for the performing arts in Sri Lanka. Kahawita De Silva & Associates drew its architecture from the Nelum Pokuna, or lotus pond, of 12th-century Polonnaruwa, turning a historic landscape feature into a modern national monument to the country's arts. Its floors add up to 14,000 square metres. There are two permanent theatres, the 1,288-seat main auditorium and an open-air theatre, and the front steps can become a further outdoor venue. In the main hall, a moving stage of 690 square metres comes with an orchestra pit that can rise to stage level and drop again. A library and training facilities complete the centre. Of the project's estimated cost of LKR 3,080 million, China's government provided LKR 2,430 million.

At Rayerbazar, in the Mohammadpur area of Dhaka, this monument remembers the intellectuals killed in the Bangladesh Liberation War. From 22 entries, the jury chose the proposal of the architects Farid Uddin Ahmed and Md Jami-al-Shafi, and building took about three years, from 1996 to 1999. Its main element is a curved brick wall about 115.8 m long, 17.7 m high and 0.9 m thick, standing for the brickfield of Rayer Bazar where the bodies were found. Both ends of the wall are broken, to express grief and sorrow. A square opening on its south-west side lets the eye pass through to the sky beyond and brings the wall down in scale. Before the wall lies a pool of still water, and from it rises a column of black granite, another sign of grief.

Khwaja Nazimuddin, A. K. Fazlul Huq and Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, three prominent leaders of the Pakistan Movement from Bengal, are buried in this Dhaka mausoleum. It stands in Suhrawardy Udyan in Shahbagh, opposite Doel Square and near the University of Dhaka. S. A. Zahiruddin and Masud Ahmad designed it in a style that interprets Islamic arches. Over the three graves rises a structure in the form of a hyperbolic paraboloid. The tombs themselves lie underground, and replicas of the three graves are set below the monument. Work was finally completed in 1986, while Hussain Muhammad Ershad was president.

Khan Jahan Ali, governor of the Sundarbans, built this mosque in Bagerhat, in Bangladesh's Khulna Division, between 1442 and 1459. Part of Bagerhat's Mosque City, which UNESCO lists as a World Heritage Site, it is the biggest mosque in the country from the time of the Bengal Sultanate (1352–1576). It served for prayer and also as a madrasa and assembly hall. Despite the name, sixty columns carry 81 domes: 77 low ones in seven rows of eleven, plus one at each corner. The brick walls are unusually thick and tapered in the Tughlaq manner, and the hut-like roofline looks ahead to later styles. The oblong plan is 45.26 by 30.89 m outside and 37.57 by 23.22 m inside. The western wall has eleven mihrabs inside; ten are blind, and the central one projects on the exterior.

Hatirjheel, Bengali for Lake of Elephant, is a Dhaka lakefront wrapped in roads and bridges meant to ease traffic. The idea dates from 1995, to improve movement around Dhaka while protecting one of its main natural basins for holding rainwater, with drainage channels between the old and new city. The government launched it in 2008. Its team was led by the architect Iqbal Habib of VITTI Sthapati Brindo, working with Ehsan Khan and Ishtiaque Zahir. Across 302 acres it added an 8.8 km expressway, 9.8 km of service roads, bridges, overpasses and viaducts, at a revised cost of US$180 million; there is also an amphitheatre for 2,000. Opened in 2013, it is now a favourite place for residents to relax, but poor sewage infrastructure has left the water badly polluted, and it has failed as a rainwater store.

NESPAK (National Engineering Services Pakistan) and Nayyar Ali Dada & Associates designed this convention centre together. It sits in Lahore's Johar Town, at the corner where Abdul Haque Road meets Shahrah Nazaria-e-Pakistan. Pakistan's provincial and federal governments set it up jointly on a 400-kanal plot that the Lahore Development Authority leased to them in 2004 for 40 years. The aim was to give local exporters one central place to show their goods and to brief foreign trade delegations and buyers, all under a single roof. Building started in 2007 and finished in 2010. At the height of the COVID-19 crisis in 2020, a temporary field hospital was put up at the centre for overflow patients whom Lahore's hospitals, in the city and around it, had no room for.

The Karachi Chamber of Commerce & Industry has its headquarters in this heritage building in the centre of Karachi, often shortened to the KCCI Building. Mahatma Gandhi laid its foundation stone on 8 July 1934, when it was meant to house the Karachi Indian Merchants' Association. Ahmed Hussain Agha designed it in Anglo-Mughal, a Mughal-revival style in vogue during the 1920s, and its strong debt to Mughal architecture sets it apart from the city's earlier civic buildings. It is built of sandstone, and part of the material came from Jaipur, now in India's Rajasthan state. The outside looks much as it was first designed, while the inside has been altered a great deal over the years. It gained protection as a heritage site on 7 September 1995.

Ahmed Hussain Agha designed this palace, built in 1927 in Clifton, a wealthy seaside suburb of Karachi, as the summer house of Shivratan Mohatta, a Hindu Marwari businessman who came from present-day Rajasthan. It follows Rajasthan's tradition of stone palaces, pairing pink Jodhpur stone with yellow stone from nearby Gizri. Covering 1,720 m2, it has a façade worked with windows, stone brackets, spandrels, balustrades with floral motifs and nine domes, each ringed by peacock motifs. Blue windows face the garden at the front; arched stained-glass ones light the rear. Grand rooms for entertaining fill the ground floor, with private spaces and a shaded terrace above. Octagonal towers mark the corners; the two by the entrance hold spiral stairs to the roof. The Government of Sindh bought it in 1995 to become a museum of Pakistan's arts, which opened in 1999.

Built to be Karachi's town hall, Frere Hall is used today for exhibitions and as a library. Henry Saint Clair Wilkins won the commission over eleven other candidates. Work ran from August 1863 to October 1865, and the building was still not quite complete when it was inaugurated. Its style is Venetian Gothic, mixed with British and local elements, and it has pointed arches, flying buttresses, quatrefoils and ribbed vaults. Most of it is local limestone of a yellow tone, while its stone details are white oolite from the nearby town of Bholari. In one corner an octagonal tower rises to an iron cage, and the roof is coated in Muntz metal. In the 1980s the Pakistani artist Sadequain painted the hall's ceilings, leaving one mural unfinished when he died in 1987.

Rising 84 metres over 27 floors, Nyayo House stands where Uhuru Highway crosses Kenyatta Avenue in Nairobi. It holds government departments, immigration among them, and is the headquarters of Nairobi Province. Planning began in 1973, when the tower was to be called Nairobi House. The Ministry of Public Works and Ngotho Architects planned it, Laxmanbhai Construction built it, and work ran from 1979, a year after Daniel arap Moi became president of Kenya, to 1983. The building is best known for the detention cells in its basement, often called the "Nyayo House torture chambers", where Special Branch officers beat many opponents of Moi's government. The Special Branch later took a new name: the National Security Intelligence Service.

Both houses of Namibia's Parliament, the National Assembly and the National Council, meet in the Tintenpalast in Windhoek. The German architect Gottlieb Redecker designed it, giving the front a Neoclassical façade, and the firm Sander & Kock built it from regional materials in 1912 and 1913, as offices for the German colonial government. Forced labour was used on the project: Herero and Nama people who had survived the genocide against them and been held in concentration camps. The building opened on 12 April 1913, and its name, German for Ink Palace, refers to how much ink the staff inside got through. After Namibia won independence in 1990, the National Assembly moved in. It lies a little north of Robert Mugabe Avenue, within the Parliament Gardens, which Windhoek's residents enjoy.

Maputo's neoclassical city hall stands at the head of Independence Square, which was called Praça Mouzinho de Albuquerque until 1975. A design competition in 1938 was won by Carlos César dos Santos, a Portuguese-Brazilian architect. Building started in 1941 under Francisco dos Santos Pinto Teixeira, who had just become mayor, and ended in 1947. Santos gave the building a trapezoidal plan and set it on a hill, which made it the natural focus of what is now Samora Machel Avenue, the street joining the square to the Baixa, the city's downtown. The 65-metre façade follows Beaux-Arts rules throughout. Money was short, so the city used artificial stone in place of cut natural stone. In 2011 the building joined Maputo's list of cultural monuments.

Maputo's cathedral stands on Independence Square, beside the Hotel Rovuma and the City Hall. Its designer, Marcial Simões de Freitas e Costa, was a Portuguese civil engineer and at the time a railway director, and he gave his work free of charge to the Lourenço Marques archdiocese. The foundation stone went down on 28 June 1936; it sits in the narthex, bearing an inscription by D. Rafael Maria da Asunção, who was bishop of Mozambique and Cape Verde. The building was finished in 1944. Freitas took his cue from the plain style and materials of European churches of his day, and the cathedral was built in the end of concrete and cement. Among his models were Auguste Perret's Notre-Dame du Raincy (1921–1923) and Pardal Monteiro's Fátima church in Lisbon (1934–1938).

This Ethiopian Orthodox cathedral in Addis Ababa is known for its octagonal form.
