The Italian engineer Sebastiano Castagna designed and built it in 1911, on the ruins of a church dating from the 15th century. Empress Zewditu was crowned here in 1917 and Emperor Haile Selassie in 1930, and the cathedral became a place of pilgrimage for Rastafarians. In 1937 the Italian Fascist authorities set it on fire. A year later, an Italian tourist publication praised it as a fine example of a European reading of Ethiopian church design. Haile Selassie had it restored after the liberation of 1941.

Munyonyo lies about 13 km by road south of Kampala's central business district. It was here that King Mwanga took his fateful decision to begin killing Christians, and the Roman Catholic shrine on the site is dedicated to the Ugandan Martyrs; its design is credited to Robert Sseremba. Archbishop Michael A. Blume, the Pope's envoy to Uganda, and Cardinal Emmanuel Wamala broke ground on 3 May 2015 for a redevelopment that includes a new church, a museum, offices and the sites where the saints were martyred. Visiting Africa that year, Pope Francis blessed the cornerstone on 27 November. The church was finished in 2016, and Cardinal Fernando Filoni consecrated the shrine on 28 October 2017. In July 2019 the Holy See raised the church to the rank of Minor Basilica.

The Italian architect Raffaele Contigiani designed this Brutalist hotel for Habib Bourguiba's government, and building began in 1970. It sits at the eastern end of Avenue Habib Bourguiba, near the Lake of Tunis. The hotel rests on 190 reinforced concrete piles driven as deep as 60 m, and its exposed concrete (béton brut) wraps a steel frame. The result is one long ten-storey block; cantilevered stairs jut out at both ends, so the building forms an upside-down pyramid, its top floor twice the length of its ground floor, with most of the 416 bedrooms high up. Breaking with Arab and European traditions alike, it came to stand for modernism in the city and remains a key Brutalist work in North Africa; some liken it to the Star Wars sandcrawler. Privatised in the 1990s, it decayed and closed in 2000.

On a hill on the Nile's west bank at Aswan stands the tomb of Aga Khan III, commissioned by his wife, Begum Om Habibeh Aga Khan, and built from 1956 to 1960. Egypt was chosen as the former seat of power of the Fatimids, a Shia Ismaili dynasty, and Aga Khan IV, who died in 2025, rests here too. It overlooks the couple's winter villa by Hassan Fathy; Aga Khan III's will asked for burial near it. Farid Shafi'e, a close student of Fatimid buildings, based the design on the Masjid al-Juyushi of 1085, which shares its rectangular plan, high walls, central dome and smaller domes. Its pink limestone walls carry crenellated parapets and one arched entrance, on the west. Inside, Quranic inscriptions cover the Carrara marble tomb; the interior has been closed to visitors since 1997.

Also called Soccer City or the Calabash, the FNB Stadium hosts football and rugby in Johannesburg's Nasrec, bordering Soweto. Built in 1987, it was upgraded as the 2010 World Cup's main football venue, to a design by HOK Sport, now Populous, and Boogertman + Partners based on the calabash, an African pot. Its cladding is a mosaic of fire and earth colours, with a ring of lights at the base hinting at flames under the pot. The upgrade made it Africa's largest stadium, adding a longer upper tier that raised capacity to 88,958, and an encircling roof. No seat is over 100 m from the pitch or has a blocked view. Ten black vertical lines divide the stands; nine line up with the other 2010 stadiums. Nelson Mandela gave his first Johannesburg speech here after leaving prison in 1990.

Gqeberha, in South Africa's Eastern Cape, gained this football and rugby stadium for the 2010 FIFA World Cup, when it hosted several matches, among them the third-place play-off. It was one of three coastal venues built for the tournament and the first of the five new stadiums to start construction. Overlooking the South End Lake in the heart of the city, it cost R2 billion, about US$159 million. Architectural Design Associates and Dominic Bonnesse Architects led the architecture. About 40 m tall, it has six levels on the west and five on the other sides. White petal shapes in the roof make it look like a flower, hence its nickname, The Protea. It seats 46,000, plus 4,000 temporary World Cup seats, coloured from pale orange to deep red and scattered seemingly at random so the stands always look full.

Pretoria's railway station lies between Salvokop and the city's central business district, in a building of 1910 by Sir Herbert Baker, the first public building he designed. The city's first station had been built in 1892 by NZASM, the Netherlands-South African Railway Company, at the western end of its line to the port of Delagoa Bay, now Maputo. In 1910, just before the Union of South Africa was formed, the Transvaal Colony's government chose to spend its surplus money on a new Pretoria station instead of handing it over to the incoming national government. Almost the whole roof was later destroyed, though the structure itself survived. A restoration costing 18 million rand ran from June 2001 to February 2002.

Fumihiko Maki designed this art museum, which opened in 1983 in Ibusuki, Kagoshima Prefecture, within the grounds of a resort hotel. Its collection holds works by Western painters alongside works by Fujishima Takeji and Kuroda Seiki. Next door, the Iwasaki Yoshie Craft Gallery opened in 1998, founded through a bequest from Iwasaki Yoshie, who was married to the businessman Iwasaki Yohachirō, the museum's founder. Pictures of the museum by the photographer Osamu Murai appear on the slipcase and inner sleeves of Kankyō Ongaku: Japanese Ambient, Environmental & New Age Music 1980-1990, a box set of ambient music.

Run by Japan's health, labour and welfare ministry, the National Showa Memorial Museum stands in the Chiyoda ward of Tokyo, close to Kudanshita Station and to Kitanomaru Park's north entrance. Its planned name was War Victims Peace Commemoration Prayer Hall. Its opening on 27 March 1999 came partly in answer to strong lobbying from the Japan War-Bereaved Families Association, which has its headquarters next door in Kudan Hall. Kiyonori Kikutake, a leading Japanese architect and a founding member of the Metabolist group, designed the building.

This Hiroshima church honours the victims of war and of the city's atomic bomb. Construction began in 1950 under Father Enomiya-Lassalle, who had been exposed to the bomb, and the church opened four years later. Japanese architects, Kenzo Tange and Kunio Maekawa among them, sent in 177 designs, but none won outright, and Togo Murano, a juror, designed it. Its massing owes a debt to Auguste Perret, while a round dome above the sanctuary and a small cylindrical chapel to each side of the main body recall Byzantine work. The concrete post-and-beam frame and the window shapes in the tower call to mind traditional Japanese building. Its infill bricks, made of earth holding ash from the bomb, were laid rough side out to throw shadows across the façade. Japan named it an Important Cultural Property in 2006.

This public library in Kanazawa, in Japan's Ishikawa Prefecture, was finished in 2011 to a design by the Japanese architects Kazumi Kudo and Hiroshi Horiba. Coelacanth K&H, the firm behind the design, calls the building a "simple space", a box 45 metres on each side and 12 metres high. Around 6,000 small round glass blocks pierce its concrete surface, set out on a triangular pattern so that together they form an ornamental grid. Inside, the space is described as a single calm room that recalls a forest, full of soft light and an open feeling close to being outdoors. The building area is given as 2,311.9 square metres and the total floor area as 5,641.9 square metres. Kudo and Horiba received a Japan Institute of Architects Prize for the library in 2013.

Also called the Haruki Murakami Library, this building at Waseda University in Shinjuku, Tokyo, combines academic rooms, a library and museum exhibition space. The Japanese architect Kengo Kuma designed it as a rebuilding and renovation of the campus's old Building 4, a project that took three years from 2018. The novelist Murakami chose to give the university thousands of books, vinyl records and archival materials for its archives. Kuma wanted a lively setting where anyone, Murakami included, could talk over coffee about his writing and where literature is heading, rather than a formal room for silent study. The library holds more than 3,000 of his novels in various editions and translations into over 50 languages, and a public listening room on the second floor lets visitors play records. It opened to the public on 1 October 2021.

Kisho Kurokawa designed this government building in Naha, Okinawa, which opened in 1990 and ranks among the tallest buildings in the city. It serves as the centre of Japanese government work for the whole of Okinawa Prefecture. Building it cost close to 22 billion yen, or about 200 million US dollars. The building rises 14 floors above ground and reaches two levels below it, and among the spaces it holds are a city hall and a government information centre. At the top, an observation deck gives visitors a wide panorama over Naha.

Arata Isozaki, an architect from Oita Prefecture, designed the building of this railway station in the Yufuin neighbourhood of Yufu, Japan, and it was completed in 1990. The design takes its cue from a chapel. Outside, the walls are timber painted black; at the centre is an open concourse 12 metres high, with a waiting room beside it that also works as an event hall. Big, heavy glass doors can close the concourse off from the platform to keep the wind out, and hot spring water feeds the waiting room's underfloor heating. The station, operated by JR Kyushu on the Kyudai Main Line, sits 99.1 km from the line's start at Kurume. It includes a staffed Midori no Madoguchi ticket office and a tourist information centre for Yufuin Onsen.

This hall in Hibiya Park, Chiyoda, Tokyo, was the first full-scale concert hall in Japan. Kōichi Satō designed it after taking first place in a design competition, and it was completed on 19 October 1929. It shares a complex with the Shisei Kaikan (Municipal Research Building), with a basement, six floors above ground and a four-storey tower. The entrance faces the park, and the second floor was planned as a balcony joined to the park's gardens. Brownish scratch tiles clad it in a Neo-Gothic manner. As an early steel-frame reinforced concrete building, it is seen as historically important in architectural engineering, and lessons from the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake led to more than 2,000 pine piles strengthening its ground. Seismic problems have kept it closed for renovation since 2016; reopening is expected in 2029, a hundred years after it opened.

This church at 44 Yamate-cho in Naka-ku is the seat of Yokohama's Roman Catholic bishop, and people nearby usually call it Yamate Catholic Church. Its story starts in 1862, just after a long ban on Christianity was lifted, when the Paris Foreign Missions Society built a church in Yokohama's foreign settlement. In 1906 the church moved to the present site, into a brick building with two bell towers that the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake wiped out entirely. Jan Josef Švagr, a Czech architect who had settled in Japan that same year and went on to design many buildings there, drew the replacement in a Neo-Gothic manner, and it was finished in 1933. Four years later, in 1937, the new Diocese of Yokohama was created and the church became its cathedral.

As mother church to both the Anglican Church of Korea and the Diocese of Seoul, this building stands beside Deoksugung, the British Embassy, the city council and Seoul City Hall. The English architect Arthur Stansfield Dixon supplied the design, and work began in 1922, but a lack of money stopped building in 1926 with roughly half the planned church in place. Romanesque Revival forms and mosaic murals are what the cathedral is best known for. The Seoul Metropolitan Government listed it in 1978 as Tangible Cultural Property No. 35, and in 1987 it became a key location in the June 10th Protest. Expansion began in 1991: the city first turned the plans down, then approved them after the original drawings, lost during the Second World War or the Korean War, were found again in the British Museum archives.

Guangzhou's public library moved into this new building in Zhujiang New Town, designed by Nikken Sekkei, which opened in full on 23 June 2013. It stands on Flower City Square beside the Pearl River, and its position follows the new central axis of the city. The design idea was "Beautiful Books": the stepped, stacked "books" on the outside stand for layers of history and culture overlapping. Seen from east to west, the north and south towers together recall the Chinese character "之". The building also draws on the arcade, a typical architectural device, and carries elements of Lingnan art. With a gross area of 100,000 square metres, it holds a collection of 8.43 million items and gives readers 4,000 seats and 500 computers.

Wuhan, the capital of Hubei Province in China, has three main passenger stations, and this is one of them. A team of AREP, the Fourth Survey and Design Institute of China, MaP3 and SNCF-IGOA designed it after winning a two-stage competition in 2005. They took the yellow crane, Wuhan's city symbol, as their starting point: the roof is meant to suggest the bird's wings and follows a sine curve. The building is split into nine separate parts, standing for nine provinces of China, with a central passage running through. The main arch spans 116 metres (381 ft), and the top of the building is 58 metres (190 ft) above the ground. Building work ran from September 2006 to December 2009, leaving a station of 20 tracks served by 11 platforms.

Together with AsiaWorld–Expo, this is one of Hong Kong's two main convention and exhibition venues, in Wan Chai North on Hong Kong Island. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it with Wong & Ouyang (HK) Ltd, and Larry Oltmanns led the design as SOM's Design Partner. The first building went up in 1988 on reclaimed land off Gloucester Road; its glass curtain wall, facing Victoria Harbour on three sides, was then the largest in the world. A second phase followed between 1994 and 1997 on an artificial island, under a roof likened to a bird, or by some critics to a turtle. New World Development paid for construction, and two hotels and an apartment building sit on top. The 1997 handover ceremony, which ended British colonial rule, took place here.

Hong Kong's largest library heads the Hong Kong Public Libraries system and serves as the territory's national library. Ho Chiu-fan, a senior government architect, designed it. The choice was close. In August 1997 the Provisional Urban Council voted between the original design and a rival one by Rocco Yim Sen-kee, which architects praised as far better. The vote tied at 21 each, and the council's chairman used a second vote to keep the original. The 12-storey building faces Victoria Harbour and has 33,800 square metres of floor area. Over the front facade, an arched doorway stands for a Gate to Knowledge, built from a circle for the sky, a square for the land and a triangle for knowledge building up. Power and data lines reach every corner for digital services. It opened on 17 May 2001.

Daniel Libeskind designed this academic building in Hong Kong together with the firm Leigh and Orange Ltd, on a project that ran from 2002 to 2011, the year it was completed. It stands on City University's campus and bears the name of Run Run Shaw; the Shaw Foundation paid for it with a gift of HK$100 million. It is home to the School of Creative Media and to an applied computing and interactive media centre, along with the university's departments of English, computer science, and media and communication. The design won several awards, but it also drew sharp criticism: writing in the Architectural Review, the critic William JR Curtis dismissed it as "a pile-up of Libeskindian clichés without sense, form or meaning".

Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed this building in Beijing for the China Poly Group Corporation, and it was completed in 2007. Besides the company's headquarters, it holds offices, shops, restaurants and the Poly Museum. There are three parts: an L-shaped office block, a glazed atrium 21 storeys tall, and a suspended volume called the "lantern", named for its likeness to a pleated Chinese lantern. Its glass cable-net wall, 90 metres high and 60 metres wide, is the largest of its kind, four times the size of the one at New York's Time Warner Center. Its counterweight is the eight-storey lantern itself, hung from four parallel strand cables with no columns below: in effect one building hanging from another. On the south and west sides, a travertine fin-wall and sun shades keep out direct summer sun without blocking views.

From 1923 to 1955 this six-floor building on the Bund, also called the Municipal Government Building, was the Shanghai base of HSBC (The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation); SPD Bank occupies it now. Built from 1921 to 1923, it was designed by the British firm Palmer & Turner. With 23,415 square metres of floor space, it was then the biggest bank building in the Far East and second in the world only to the Bank of Scotland's in Edinburgh. The strictly neoclassical exterior is split in three both ways. At the centre is a dome whose base carries a triangular form modelled on Greek temples, above six Ionic columns spanning the second to fourth storeys. Behind the granite is a brick-filled steel lattice. Four trading hall columns are each cut from one marble block. Renovations in 1997 uncovered its mosaics.

On Huqiu Road near the Bund, this museum occupies the old home of the Royal Asiatic Society, an Art Deco design by the British firm Palmer and Turner, begun in 1932 and completed in 1933. To blend Western architecture into the city, the firm added traditional Chinese ornament, arriving at a hybrid style. Part of the story of cultural and academic exchange between China and Europe, its five storeys held a museum, a library and a lecture hall, and at their busiest drew over 7,000 visits a month. In 2007 David Chipperfield, a British architect who had earlier directed planning for Berlin's Museum Island, took charge of its restoration in a minimalist style. He kept the main facade true to the 1932 design; the biggest change is a skylight joining the top three floors. The museum has no permanent collection.

Ma Yansong and his colleagues at MAD Architects designed this science museum on the west coast of Haikou, in Hainan, China, and it was completed in 2025. The silver building takes the form of a spiral around a wide open core. Its outer skin is made of 843 panels of fibre-reinforced polymer, and three concrete core tubes carry the structure. The building has a total area of 45,528 square metres, holding a planetarium, a large-screen cinema and other exhibitions. Outside, the grounds include a covered plaza and a reflecting pool.

Known in English by several names, including Ximen Red House, this historic theatre stands in Ximending, in Taipei's Wanhua District. The Japanese architect Kondo Juro designed it, and it was built in 1908, during Japanese rule, as a market, with a department store on the ground floor. From 1945 it served as a theatre and was home to a Peking Opera troupe. Its style mixes Western forms with Meiji-era Japanese patterns, which reflects Kondo's training at Tokyo Imperial University, where he learned about Western architecture. The complex is made up of an octagonal block called the Octagon Building, a cross-shaped building and the square beside them. It was listed as a Class III Historical Site in 1997, and in 2016 the Octagon Building had its biggest renovation in a century.

Shenzhen Cultural Center brings together the city's concert hall and its library in the Futian district of Shenzhen, in Guangdong, China. The Japanese architect Arata Isozaki designed it, and the project ran from 1998 to 2007. The concert hall, which opened in 2007, has a vineyard layout with 1,800 seats. It sits beside the library and close to the Shenzhen civic center and the Children's Palace station on subway line 3. Along with the Nanshan cultural center, it is one of Shenzhen's two principal places to hear concerts. The Belt and Road International Music Festival was launched at the hall in 2019.

Built purely for viewing, with no offices or flats, this group of five round steel towers in Beijing was begun in 2011 and completed in 2014. Cui Kai and Li Cundong of CARDEG (Chinese Architecture Design and Research Group) won with their design; their colleague Zhao Wenbin designed the landscape around the base. All five rise from a gentle planted mound, the tallest reaching 258 metres with the other four around it, tied to it by big diagonal members. Each widens at its flat top into an observation deck. Four smaller round floors set below the largest one are meant to recall the Olympic rings, and the design drew on blades of grass, though some have compared it to "huge nails". The solid steel skin breaks into latticework for views out from the glass behind.

Shanghai Library East is a branch of the city's main library in Pudong, and it opened in September 2022 as one of the biggest new libraries in China. The firm Schmidt Hammer Lassen, founded by Danish architects, designed it with input from local artists, making abstract reference to taihu stones, which Jin dynasty scholars looked to for inspiration. Unlike the main library, the East branch has an open plan that gives most of its space over to the local community, while still holding 4.8 million books. Its design has collected a number of awards at local and national level, and in 2026 it was one of the buildings given the RIBA International Award for Excellence.

This pair of performance buildings in Taipei, completed in 1987, was designed overall by Yang Cho-cheng with the firm Architects and Engineers Associates. The two face each other across a square, one on its north side and one on its south, with the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall at the east end, and they were among the earliest major modern performing arts venues in Asia. Though modern in use, they take up traditional elements of Chinese palace architecture. Germany's G+H Company and the Dutch firm Philips led the design of the interior equipment, stage lighting and acoustics. The Concert Hall seats 2,022 and the smaller Recital Hall 354; its Flentrop Orgelbouw pipe organ was the largest in Asia when installed in 1987. In the theatre, the Proscenium Arch Theater seats 1,498, and the Experimental Theater is a flexible black box.

Louis Sullivan designed this 12-storey store at the corner of State and Madison in Chicago for the retailer Schlesinger & Mayer, and it opened in stages from 1899 to 1907. Among its former names is the Carson Pirie Scott Building, and it was the last large commercial building of Sullivan's career. The two main fronts meet at a rounded corner holding the entrance. Piers split each front into bays of wide Chicago windows; ornamental cast iron wraps the bottom two floors, and white terracotta bands frame the windows above. Columns of cast iron and steel carry terracotta floors over caissons and piles, leaving open floors between columns to give the most selling space. D. H. Burnham & Company built additions in 1906–1907, as did Holabird & Root in 1961. It is a Chicago Landmark and a National Historic Landmark.

Still widely called the Sears Tower, this 110-storey skyscraper in Chicago's Loop stands 1,451 feet (442.3 m) high. The architect Bruce Graham and the engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan, both of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, designed it, and when it opened in 1973 it was the tallest building in the world, a record it kept for nearly 25 years. Their scheme bundles nine square "tubes" into a three-by-three grid. Each tube is a column-free unit 75 feet (23 m) square, and seven of them stop at different heights, with setbacks at the 50th, 66th and 90th floors. This gave Sears the big lower floors and left more ordinary office space higher up to let. The walls are black glass and anodised aluminium. Its Skydeck, the highest observation deck in the United States, draws over 1.7 million visitors a year.

César Pelli designed this library in downtown Minneapolis with the local firm Architectural Alliance, and it opened on 20 May 2006. It is the largest library in the Hennepin County Library system. It replaced the city's second library on the same site, after voters approved $140 million for library services on 7 November 2000. The 353,000-square-foot (32,800 m²) building at 300 Nicollet Mall has two levels of underground parking and cost $250 per square foot. It has an atrium of 8,140 square feet, plenty of daylight, many energy-saving measures and a green roof of 18,560 square feet planted with low ground cover chosen to cope with sun and drought. Readers can enter the storage area without staff help, so almost the whole collection is open to them, and over 300 computers are for public use.

Now Hy-Vee Arena, this Kansas City venue went up in just 18 months in 1973–74 on the old stockyards site in the West Bottoms. Built to replace the smaller Municipal Auditorium for the city's professional sports teams, it held 19,500 people before becoming a youth sports and community gym. The German architect Helmut Jahn, later an important figure of his time, made it his first major project. Its simplicity and clear views, with no columns inside, were revolutionary: steel trusses hanging from three huge portals held up the reinforced concrete roof. Jahn reused this exposed outer frame widely. The American Institute of Architects gave it an Honor award in 1976. A later roof was welded rather than bolted and fitted with sensors to detect weak points. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.

This fountain, formerly known as the Williams Waterwall and as the Transco Waterwall, faces the south side of Williams Tower in Houston's Uptown District. John Burgee Architects with Philip Johnson designed both the fountain and the tower, and the Waterwall was running fully and regularly in 1985. It forms a half circle 64 feet (20 m) tall, one foot for each of the tower's 64 storeys, set among 118 Texas live oaks. Water pours down in broad, channelled sheets from the narrow rim at the top to the wider base, over both the inner and outer faces of the curve. Most of the structure is St. Joe brick, with Romanesque arches in Indiana limestone and a base of black granite. An internal system recycles the full 78,500 gallons of water every three hours and two minutes.

Made for the Texas Centennial Exposition, this hall in Dallas's Fair Park, first named the State of Texas Building, honours Texas history. It is considered among Texas's finest Art Deco buildings. Donald Barthelme was offered the role of chief designer; he presented his designs by 9 July, and the state's Board of Control in Austin approved them. Costing $1.2 million, it was dedicated on 6 September 1936. At the entrance, a curved exedra sets limestone pillars 76 feet tall against blue tiles that recall the bluebonnet, the state flower. The plan is a T, with four rooms standing for Texas's West, East, North and South. The main hall, 46 feet high, 94 long and 68 wide, has reeded columns of Cordova Cream shell stone, a Texas limestone. In 1981 it was made a Recorded Texas Historic Landmark.

Duke University's art museum, on its campus in Durham, North Carolina, used to carry the university's own name. In the early 2000s, helped in part by a gift from the alumnus Raymond Nasher, it took his name and moved into a new $24 million building of 2005 by the architect Rafael Viñoly. Since reopening it has drawn about 100,000 visitors a year. Its programme centres on contemporary art from many countries, giving special attention to artists who have been historically under-represented. The museum also holds a strong Pre-Columbian collection of 3,300 objects, with important Peruvian textiles and Mayan ceramics.

Home to the Nashville Symphony, this concert building was designed by the Washington, D.C., firm of David M. Schwarz, winner of the 2015 Driehaus Prize; the Nashville firm Earl Swensson Associates acted as architect of record. Its New Classical design borrows from other Classical and Neoclassical buildings in Nashville, among them the full-size copy of the Parthenon and the main public library. At its core is the 1,844-seat Laura Turner Concert Hall, a shoebox-style room lit by 30 soundproof, double-glazed clerestory windows. A 2-inch air gap circles the hall to stop sound passing in or out, and "chair-wagons" let it turn into a ballroom in about two hours. Its organ, made by Schoenstein & Co. of San Francisco, has 3,568 pipes. Leonard Slatkin conducted the gala that formally opened the center on 9 September 2006.

This pyramid by the Mississippi in downtown Memphis plays on the city's Egyptian namesake, known for its ancient pyramids. A local artist, Mark C. Hartz, first imagined a Great American Pyramid around 1954. Ground was broken on 15 September 1989, and it opened on 9 November 1991 as an arena for 20,142 people, run jointly by the city and Shelby County until the county sold its share in 2009. It stands 321 feet (98 m) tall, roughly 32 storeys, and each side of its base measures 591 feet. The city spent $30 million, with O.T. Marshall Architects hired to help with seismic retrofitting. In 2015 it reopened as a Bass Pro Shops store, with a hotel, restaurants, bowling and archery. America's tallest freestanding lift rises to the Lookout at the apex: viewing decks, a restaurant, a bar and an aquarium.

Florida's capitol in Tallahassee, dating from 1977, was designed jointly by two firms: Edward Durell Stone & Associates, based in New York, and Reynolds, Smith & Hills, based in Jacksonville. It is a concrete building in the New Formalist manner, its windows shaded by metal louvres, and the design was meant to stand for Florida's modern growth. It is usually described as 22 storeys and 345 feet (105 m) high, with an observation deck on the top floor. Four-storey Senate and House office buildings at each end connect to the Capitol by bridges at the second and third floors. The Historic Capitol of 1845 was threatened with demolition when the new one was built; restored to its 1902 form in 1982, it stands directly behind. The new design makes no reference to the old one's style.

Shreve & Lamb designed this Art Deco tower on East 4th Street in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, as the headquarters of the R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Company. The brief asked for an attractive building with an air of conservatism that avoided "flashiness". Finished in 1929 for $2.7 million, it rises 314 feet (96 m) over 21 floors with nearly 314,000 square feet of space, and it received a national award for its architecture. Like the far bigger Empire State Building in New York, built in 1931, it was planned for company offices above ground-floor shops, and it is well known as a source of inspiration for that design. It was added to the National Register in 2014. In 2016 the top 11 floors opened as apartments in March, and the lowest six followed in April as the Kimpton Cardinal Hotel.

Harry Weese designed this church in Columbus, Indiana, and it was completed in 1965. It was among the first church designs to bring Modern movement architecture together with a plan that breaks from the traditional church layout. The congregation chose a site of just over seven acres at the foot of a gently sloping hill because it left space to grow and room for parking. The red brick building falls into five clearly separate parts, set around a central courtyard: a narthex, the sanctuary, a chapel, a fellowship hall and a wing of offices. Very little has been altered since it was finished, so the building keeps its integrity, and it is one of seven National Historic Landmarks in Columbus.

Frank Lloyd Wright, a member of the First Unitarian Society and son of two of its founders, designed this meeting house in Madison, Wisconsin. The builder Marshall Erdman put it up between 1949 and 1951, and to save money members of the congregation carried limestone blocks for the walls. Wright based the design on triangles. The original upper meeting house has a prow-like roof of blue-green standing seam copper, its seams running both ways to stress the form. Hinged-arch trusses built from two-by-four and two-by-six framing members hold up the roof, spanning 64 feet (20 m) inside with no supports. People have read the shape as a ship's prow, a plough cutting the prairie or hands joined in prayer; Wright wrote that the triangle stands for aspiration. Its architecture earned it National Historic Landmark status.

The UTS Tower, also called Building 1, stands on Broadway at the southern edge of Sydney's city centre and holds many administrative units of the University of Technology across 27 occupied floors. A 1964 plan called for three towers of different heights plus a podium, but Commonwealth funding cuts by the mid-1970s left only this tower and the 11-level Building 2 beside it. Michael Dysart, working in the state's Government Architect's Office, drew the 1968 plan for the brutalist tower. Work began in 1969, the lower floors were in use from 1975, and NSW Premier Neville Wran opened it on 15 October 1979, when it was declared Australia's tallest educational building. It has often been named Sydney's ugliest building, including by the architect Frank Gehry, though others say its place on the skyline marks Sydney as a university town.

Nicknamed "the Coathanger", this steel through arch bridge links Sydney's city centre with the North Shore, carrying trains, road vehicles, bicycles and walkers. John Bradfield, of the state's Department of Public Works, directed the project, and the Middlesbrough firm Dorman Long designed and built it; it opened in 1932. The chosen tender was the firm's own design, partly drawing on its Tyne Bridge. Its arch spans 504 m, and its crown sits 134 m above mean sea level, rising by 18 cm on hot days as the steel expands. Six million Australian-made rivets, driven by hand, hold it together. At each end stand two 89 m concrete pylons faced in granite, designed by the Scottish architect Thomas S. Tait. Abutments below carry the arch; the pylons only frame it and give visual balance.

Charles Court, then State Premier, opened this building on 12 November 1976 under the name Westrail Centre. It serves as the terminal and administrative base for Perth's public transport system. Western Australian Government Railways commissioned it, built over and beside the platform of the railway terminal. It forms the heart of East Perth Terminal, a station for standard gauge trains and coaches next to East Perth station on Transperth's narrow gauge suburban network. The whole site, including both stations and this building, was once the East Perth Locomotive Depot. Renamed the Public Transport Centre, it now houses the Public Transport Authority and the Department of Transport.

This telecommunications tower and lookout, also called Black Mountain Tower and once known as Telecom Tower, stands above the top of Black Mountain in Canberra, Australia's capital. It rises 195.2 metres above the summit, the tallest structure in the city. The Department of Housing and Construction was responsible for its design, but a conflict arose with the National Capital Development Commission, then in full control of planning in the territory. During approval, people objected on aesthetic and ecological grounds, fearing that a tower on Black Mountain, inside a nature reserve, would dominate other Canberra buildings. Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser opened it on 15 May 1980. An indoor deck and two outdoor platforms look over the city and countryside. Its revolving restaurant, which turned once every 81 minutes, closed in 2013.

The University of Canterbury's main library building in Christchurch houses its Central Library, Te Puna Mātauraka. In 1963 the University Newsletter reported that the Ministry of Works would design the first stage of a large complex at Ilam for arts, library, administration and other uses. The 53-metre brutalist tower of exposed concrete has become a lasting symbol of the university and the most familiar sight on campus. Governor-General Sir Denis Blundell opened the library and arts block on 23 March 1974, when it was hailed as New Zealand's largest university building. By 1975 the library filled the lowest four floors, with departments from law to classics in the tower. Its original name, the James Hight Building, gained "Puaka" to reflect the university's bond with Ngāi Tahu, the mana whenua. The Christchurch earthquakes of 2010 and 2011 badly damaged it.

Marcus Barlow designed this Art Deco office and shopping building in Melbourne for the Manchester Unity Independent Order of Oddfellows, and it went up in 1931–32. Its stepped corner tower, facing the Town Hall across a prominent intersection, makes it one of the city's best-known buildings; the design clearly draws heavily on Chicago's Tribune Tower. Builders W E Cooper Pty Ltd took the contract for £215,000. Work began at midnight on New Year's Day 1932 with demolition, then ran day and night in eight-hour shifts, tracked with a construction progress schedule, a first in Australia. The steel frame is encased in concrete and clad in 250 tons of terracotta faience. The roof reached 132 feet, the city's height limit at the time, and the decorative tower and spire, as non-habitable parts, were allowed 78 feet more.

Built in 1965 in Floreat, Perth, this house ranks among the most familiar works of Iwan Iwanoff, an architect born in Bulgaria, and a well-known Australian example of mid-century modern design. The Paganin family traded in timber and marble, so Iwanoff used both materials generously throughout, most notably in a marble verandah at the front. The four-bedroom house has an open, practical plan. Phil Griffiths, who leads the Australian Institute of Architects in Western Australia, called it expressionistic, creative and brilliant, and in 2015 the WA State Architect, Geoff Warn, found it balanced European elegance with the open plans of the Case Study Houses around Los Angeles. In 2006 it was put forward for the State Heritage Register, and once returned to its architect's original design it featured in a March 2019 episode of Restoration Australia.

Francis Greenway, a convict architect, designed these Sydney barracks, put up from 1817 to 1819 to hold convict men and boys in a brick block and its compound. Governor Macquarie was so pleased with it that he soon granted Greenway a full pardon. The main block is a three-storey Georgian building of sandstock brick with a gabled roof and sandstone foundations, sills and string courses. Brick pilasters and ground-floor arched recesses order its plain, refined front, and the pediment holds an early colonial clock under a crown, inscribed with the governor's name and the year 1817. Inside, each floor had four rooms hung with two rows of hammocks and a 0.9-metre passage. It is one of 11 Australian Convict Sites on the World Heritage List. After an $18 million restoration it reopened in February 2020.

This centre in Adelaide is a public building with exhibitions on how wine is made and on the industry behind it. It sits where North Terrace ends to the east, in the parklands beside the Adelaide Botanic Gardens. Its design is credited to the firm Cox Grieve Gillett, who chose materials that echo the things used to make wine, and from outside the building reads as a slice of a wine barrel. Rows of vines in the grounds show seven grape varieties, so visitors who never get to a vineyard can compare them. The idea came from the National Wine Centre Act of 1997, and the centre opened in October 2001. After trouble with funding, management and profit, the University of Adelaide took over its running in September 2003 on a 40-year lease.

Brighton and Hove's largest public library was designed by Bennetts Associates with a local practice, LCE Architects (Lomax Cassidy & Edwards), whose lead architects had long worked together. It has been called among England's most energy-efficient buildings, with half the carbon footprint of a conventional public building its size. Sun and wind heat and cool it naturally, except in extreme weather. Daylight pours in through the glazed south front and is steered by a huge louvred screen, which, with steel and glass walkways, separates the outer glass from the interior. Large white concrete columns that flare at the top punctuate the two-storey, forum-like space. To the east, the staff and conference wing wears glazed blue tiles imitating mathematical tiles, an 18th-century feature common in Brighton but rare elsewhere. It was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2005.

This museum was at Mill Meadows beside the River Thames in Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire. Its three main permanent galleries dealt with the non-tidal Thames, rowing as a sport worldwide, and Henley itself. It was the first major British project of Sir David Chipperfield, a modernist architect, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it in November 1998. Old boat sheds and Oxfordshire barns inspired the building, which mixes modern and traditional shapes and materials. Concrete pillars lift its 2,300 square metres clear of floods. Untreated oak boards, like those of local rural buildings, clad it outside and partly inside; the roofs and sunscreens are stainless steel. Among its awards was the Royal Fine Art Commission's Building of the Year for 1999. The museum closed on 21 September 2025. In March 2026 the Twentieth Century Society applied to have the building listed.

Now called the Accu Stadium for sponsorship, this Huddersfield stadium is a multi-purpose ground for 24,121 people. Its design is credited to Populous; Alfred McAlpine built it, and it was named RIBA Building of the Year for 1995. The decision to build a new stadium for Huddersfield Town football club and Huddersfield Giants rugby league club came in August 1992, with work starting in 1993. It was ready for the 1994–95 season, when the clubs left Leeds Road, Town's home of 86 years, which the Giants had shared since 1992 after 114 years at Fartown. At first only the Riverside and Kilner Bank stands were open; the South Stand followed in December 1994 and the North Stand in 1998. It has been a venue for four Rugby League World Cups and the 1999 Rugby World Cup.

Kuggen, Swedish for "the cog", belongs to Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg and is owned by the property company Chalmersfastigheter. Wingårdh arkitektkontor designed it, and it was built between October 2010 and March 2011. It is round so that its outer skin is as small as possible for the floor area inside. Every floor gains two bays, so the building widens as it rises. Its glazed terracotta skin uses six reds and two greens. A movable sunscreen tracks the sun over the top two floors; neighbouring buildings shade the rest. Triangular windows carry daylight along the ceiling deep inside while making up only 30% of the facade. The target is energy use of 60 kWh per square metre a year, well under the usual green building level, with offices kept at 22 to 26 °C.

Charles Harrison Townsend designed this gallery on Whitechapel High Street, in the London Borough of Tower Hamlets. When it opened in 1901 it was among the first London galleries funded by the public purse and devoted to temporary exhibitions. It is cited as a notable example of the British Modern Style, and it is one of three original public buildings in London on which Townsend's reputation mainly rests, alongside the Bishopsgate Institute and the Horniman Museum. Pablo Picasso's Guernica hung here in 1938, in a touring show that Roland Penrose organised against the Spanish Civil War; This is Tomorrow followed in 1956 and Mark Rothko's first UK exhibition in 1961. Absorbing the next-door former Passmore Edwards library in 2009 doubled the gallery's size, nearly tripled its exhibition space and let it open all year.

Since 2001 mumok, the Museum moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig Wien, has been housed in a building by the Austrian practice Ortner & Ortner, reopening on 15 September that year in Vienna's MuseumsQuartier. The building is a cube clad in basalt lava. It holds 4,800 m2 of galleries for shows on one artist or one theme and for rotating displays from a collection of around 10,000 modern and contemporary works, and the museum is known for its large body of art linked to Viennese Actionism. In the MuseumsQuartier, new volumes were slotted into a large former stable complex to make a chain of courtyards, passages and venues instead of one museum building, and the way the modern blocks of mumok and the Leopold Museum stand against the old enclosure is central to the complex.

Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann designed this palatial complex with gardens in Dresden, one of the most important Baroque works in Germany. Built in stages from 1710 to 1728 as an orangery, garden and festival ground, it carries sculpture by Balthasar Permoser, and its pavilions and galleries, lined with balustrades, figures and vases, reflect the splendour of Augustus the Strong's reign as Saxon elector and elected King of Poland. The elector first imagined it as forecourt to a new castle reaching the Elbe, so the river side was left undeveloped, with only a provisional wall, until Gottfried Semper's gallery wing closed it in 1847–1855. The Kronentor of 1714, in dark wood and gold shaped like the Polish crown, asserted Augustus's claim to that throne. Bombing in February 1945 wrecked most of it; rebuilding began that year and was largely done by 1963.

Prince-Bishop Johann Philipp Franz von Schönborn commissioned the Residence in 1720 with his brother Friedrich Carl; Balthasar Neumann, the bishop's court architect, led the design, and it was completed in 1744. On a base of 92 by 167 metres, a central wing sits between north and south blocks, each built around two inner courts. The grand staircase rises under a pillarless 18 by 32 metre vault. Its first flight heads toward a blank wall, away from the reception hall, then splits into two flights that turn back, so a host on the landing above saw guests first as they walked away. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, his sons and helpers painted the vault in 1752–1753 with the world's largest continuous ceiling fresco, about 580 m2. Neumann's stone vaults held when the burning attic fell in. UNESCO listed the Residence in 1981.

Hans Scharoun, a German architect, drew the master plan for this nonprofit housing estate in Berlin's Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf district, built from 1929 to 1931 and also known as the Ringsiedlung. Six leading Weimar-era architects took part: Scharoun, Fred Forbát, Otto Bartning, Walter Gropius, Paul Rudolf Henning and Hugo Häring; the nickname reflects ties between some of them and the collective Der Ring. The landscape architect Leberecht Migge shaped the open spaces. Unlike other major public housing projects then, sponsored by the government cooperative Gehag, Siemensstadt was built by a private cooperative for workers at the nearby Siemens electrical factory, with its 60,000 employees. Its layout marked the moment Martin Wagner, Berlin's city planner, dropped a low-rise garden-city project with individual gardens in favour of far denser apartment blocks. UNESCO listed it in 2008 among Berlin's six Modernist Housing Estates.

This Baroque church on Vienna's Karlsplatz honours Saint Charles Borromeo, a key figure of the Counter-Reformation. In 1713, a year after Vienna's last major plague epidemic, Emperor Charles VI vowed to build it for his namesake saint, revered as a healer of plague sufferers. Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach took first place in the competition, beating rivals such as Ferdinando Galli-Bibiena and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt. After his death in 1723 his son Joseph Emanuel completed the church in 1737, modifying the plans. The centre of the front takes the form of a Greek temple portico, set between two columns by Lorenzo Mattielli that draw on Rome's Trajan's Column, and tower pavilions that show Roman Baroque influence. Fischer sought to combine the core ideas of the great churches of Western architecture, from Hagia Sophia to the Pantheon and Saint Peter's.

Known as the Wieskirche, or Meadow Church, this Roman Catholic pilgrimage church was designed during the late 1740s and finished in 1754 to an oval Rococo plan. It is the chief work of Johann Baptist Zimmermann and his brother Dominikus, who spent his last eleven years close by. A small chapel of 1740, built for a statue, could not hold the pilgrims it drew, so Steingaden Abbey commissioned a separate shrine, built from 1745 to 1754. The oval plan has a semicircular narthex and a long, deep choir. Twin columns set before the walls carry an elaborate cornice, with stucco painted by Johann Baptist, and trompe-l'œil ceilings seem to open to an iridescent sky. UNESCO added the church to its World Heritage List in 1983, and it was restored between 1985 and 1991.

Fritz Höger worked with Hans and Oskar Gerson on this nine-storey office building in Hamburg's Kontorhaus District, planned from 1925 and built between 1927 and 1943. The Gersons took inspiration from Venice's Doge's Palace and from Salamanca's Casa de las Conchas. Its frame is reinforced concrete, and the building is counted as an example of Brick Expressionism. When it went up it was the largest office building in Europe. Rhombic patterns of clinker stress its block-like character, and the facade carries further clinker and terracotta decoration. Hamburg's earliest underground car park was built in its basement. The Chilehaus stands just to the northeast, across the main road. Together with the rest of the Kontorhaus District, the Sprinkenhof gained World Heritage status from UNESCO in 2015.

Built between 1907 and 1909 as a cigarette factory in Dresden, Yenidze now serves as an office building. Its exterior is in the Moorish Revival style, borrowing elements from mosques and from the Alhambra in Spain. This "Oriental" look pointed to the distant origins of the Oriental tobaccos processed inside and doubled as advertising for the firm. The architect Martin Hammitzsch designed it in 1907. There are 600 windows in assorted styles, a dome 20 metres high and large coloured dome chimneys that look like minarets. Tiles are used throughout, both in complex colour patterns and in unusual three-dimensional shapes. During the carpet bombing of Dresden on 14/15 February 1945 most nearby buildings were wiped out, while Yenidze came through fairly lightly, losing some coloured glass in its dome.

Designed by the Bremen architect Thomas Klumpp, this science center opened in September 2000 near the University of Bremen. Its building is wrapped in 40,000 stainless steel scales, and its form is likened to a cross between a whale and a mussel. The exhibition covers more than 4,000 m2 and is grouped around three themes: mankind, the earth and the cosmos. Visitors are invited to interact with most of its roughly 250 exhibits. A newer addition, the SchauBox by Haslob Kruse and Partner, takes the opposite line: where the older building is curved and metallic, the SchauBox is a cube with a rust-red exterior.

Opened in Munich in 1992, the Goetz Collection is a privately owned body of contemporary art housed in a museum built for it by the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron. Ingvild Goetz, once a gallery dealer, owns the collection, keeps adding to it and presents it to the public through a series of themed exhibitions. On the building's lower level, exhibitions run alongside programmes of video and film. Its glass cladding diffuses natural light, and it was one of the projects through which the practice's international reputation grew during the 1990s.

St. Jakob-Park, credited to Herzog & de Meuron, is home to FC Basel and is Switzerland's biggest football venue. Work began on 13 December 1998 to replace the old St. Jakob Stadium, and the reopening match was played on 15 March 2001. The stadium is named after St. Jakob an der Birs, a village that once stood on the site. Four main blocks, A to D, each take one side of the stadium, and an upper balcony added later forms block G. Inside are 32 shops over three floors and two restaurants. Capacity rose to 42,500 for Euro 2008, co-hosted by Austria and Switzerland; seats were then removed to give more room between them, leaving 38,512 for Swiss Super League matches and 37,500 for international games. Building it cost around CHF 220 million.

Volkmar Burgstaller designed this building beside Salzburg Airport, which hosts events and serves as a gallery and museum. Red Bull GmbH built it as a place where art, aviation and the culinary arts meet. Its form is that of an airfoil, made from 1,200 tons of steel with 75,000 sq ft of glass; the Austrian specialists Waagner-Biro engineered and built the domed steel-and-glass structure, finishing it in 2003. It was planned to house the aircraft of The Flying Bulls, and its 40 m wide door was developed so the largest of them, a Douglas DC-6B, could fit inside. Rotating exhibitions show historical aeroplanes, helicopters and Formula One cars, alongside two bars, a lounge and Ikarus, a restaurant with a Michelin star. Writing on Salzburg's contemporary buildings outside the old town describes it as blob architecture.

Walter Gropius and The Architects' Collaborative (TAC) of Cambridge, Massachusetts, designed this nine-storey block with Wils Ebert of Berlin for Interbau, the first International Building Exhibition, in 1957. It holds 66 apartments at Händelallee 1–9 in the Hansaviertel, on the edge of the Grosser Tiergarten park. The block curves inward, with a textured facade and unusual short ends. Balconies are grouped in fours and alternate with windows and concrete plaster walls to form a checkerboard pattern. Linear Zeilenbau blocks usually have windowless ends, but here Gropius turned four apartments at each end to face east or west. The flat plans grow from his work at Siemensstadt in 1929–30, and because the structure is a concrete skeleton with few load-bearing walls, kitchens and living areas can be open plan. Seen as an important modernist landmark, it was listed in 1980.

Degelo Architekten, a Basel firm, won the competition launched in early 2006 to rebuild the University Library Freiburg, which serves the University of Freiburg, three other institutions in the city and the public. The shell was done in April 2013, and interior work then began along with 7,300 m2 of facade in glass and matt, dark chrome steel. Workspaces ring each floor and the books sit in the middle. Above the ground floor a glass wall splits every level, so crossing sides means going back down. The building has 20% less volume than the old one but 30,600 m2 more net floor area, with 1,700 workspaces. Low sun in spring and autumn reflects off the southeastern glass corner and dazzles road users, so canvas blinds cover it then. Handed over on 12 October 2015, it cost 53 million euros.

The Neues Museum Nürnberg shows modern and contemporary art and design in Nuremberg. It goes back to a decision by the Bavarian government in 1990 to build a museum for the 20th century. The architect Volker Staab designed the building, which went up between 11 September 1996 and October 1999 and opened officially on 15 April 2000. Some 3,000 m2 are given over to contemporary art and to art and design from the 1950s onward. In 2001 the building received the Deutscher Natursteinpreis, along with a special recognition in that year's Deutscher Städtebaupreis.

The Mossehaus, at 18–25 Schützenstraße in Berlin, is an office building that Erich Mendelsohn renovated between 1921 and 1923, adding a new corner. The original building held the printing works and offices of newspapers owned by Rudolf Mosse, mostly liberal titles such as the Berliner Tageblatt. Mendelsohn was hired in 1921 on the strength of his Einstein Tower to add storeys and a new entrance. The new upper floors were built in ferro-concrete, and the front used aluminium and modern lettering prominently. Bands and sculpted elements in the windows gave the building a dynamic, futuristic form, sharpened by contrast with the older Wilhelmine style. It was among the first streamlined buildings and a strong influence on Streamline Moderne. Richard Neutra was Mendelsohn's partner on the project and designed its interiors. The building was restored in the 1990s.

Werner March designed the Olympiastadion at Berlin's Olympiapark for the 1936 Summer Olympics. The wider complex was commissioned by the Nazi government and built from 1934 to 1936 with state money. March placed the new stadium on the foundations of the earlier Deutsches Stadion and again sank its lower half 12 metres below ground level. Between 1960 and 1962 he rebuilt the tower to its original drawings. To give football games a more intimate atmosphere, the playing field was lowered by 2.65 metres. The roof rises 68 metres above the seats, its transparent panels letting daylight through, and it stays open at the western end, over the Marathon Arch, so spectators can see the Bell Tower. The stadium's value as a historic monument, especially its natural stone blocks, was also taken into account.

The Neue Wache, or New Watchhouse, stands on Berlin's Unter den Linden. Karl Friedrich Schinkel, Neoclassicism's leading exponent, planned it as the Royal Palace's guardhouse and a Liberation Wars memorial; built from 1816 to 1818, it was his first major commission in Berlin. Four heavy corner projections frame a portico of baseless Doric columns in the original Greek form. Schinkel likened the free-standing plan to a Roman castrum, hence the sturdier corners and inner courtyard. Heinrich Tessenow, an architect, was commissioned in 1931 to make it a Great War memorial, turning the interior into a hall around a black granite block under an oculus. Since 1993 it has been Germany's central memorial to victims of war and tyranny, with an enlarged copy of Käthe Kollwitz's Mother with her Dead Son beneath the oculus, open to the weather.

Credited to Harald Deilmann, the Rheinturm, or Rhine Tower, is a concrete telecommunications tower 240.5 metres high in Düsseldorf, the capital of the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Building began in 1979 and ended in 1981, and the tower was inaugurated on 1 December that year. It contains 7,500 m3 of concrete, and the whole tower has a weight of 22,500 tons. A light sculpture on the shaft works as a clock. Designed by Horst H. Baumann, it is called Lichtzeitpegel, or light time level, and no digital clock anywhere in the world is larger.

The architect Erik Korshagen built this Modernist summer house for himself in 1960, at Korshage Fjordvej 1, just north of Rørvig in Denmark's Odsherred Municipality. He added a garage in 1965 and a guesthouse in 1984, and all three buildings were listed as protected in 1999. Each is made of timber under a steep thatched roof, in a Minimalist design that draws on Japanese architecture. The house sits on top of a former coastal cliff, while the other two stand at its foot. It has a single storey raised on poles, with cantilevered boardwalks on three sides and a rectangular plan of 18 by 4 metres. At the southern end a large living room is partly divided from the kitchen beside it by a central brick core that holds a fireplace and cupboards.

The Röhsska Museum in Gothenburg, also called the Design Museum, is devoted to design, fashion and applied arts. It was founded in 1904, funded by a donation made in 1901 from the estate of Wilhelm Röhss, with further gifts in the following years from others, among them his brother August Röhss. The Swedish architect Carl Westman, who also designed the Stockholm Court House, drew the original building in the National Romantic style and clad it in red hand-made brick. The museum opened to the public in 1916. Axel Nilsson, its first curator, also took part in building it. Today the collection holds more than 50,000 objects.

The Wenner-Gren Center, credited to Sune Lindström and Alf Bydén, is a tower and group of buildings in the Vasastan district of Stockholm, built from 1959 to 1961 and opened in 1962. It has three parts: Pylon, the tall tower; Helicon, a lower semicircular block wrapped around it; and Tetragon, a box-shaped building alongside. Helicon provides housing for scientists visiting Stockholm-area institutions, and a Wenner-Gren foundation owns it. The rest is let as commercial space, though some of it has traditionally gone to scientific bodies such as research funders. The name honours Axel Wenner-Gren, a businessman whose donation paid for construction, after Hugo Theorell, a Nobel laureate, had pressed for the housing needs of visiting scientists to be met.

Stavanger Concert Hall was designed by RATIO Arkitekter AS and opened officially by Crown Prince Haakon on 15 September 2012. It contains two halls, generous foyers facing the sea and a large outdoor amphitheatre, and a symphony concert and a rock concert can run in the two halls at once. The orchestra hall, named after the composer Fartein Valen, is designed for acoustic music and seats 1,500 across the stalls and three galleries; it was planned as the new home of the Stavanger Symphony Orchestra. The multi-purpose hall honours Jens Zetlitz, a poet and Lutheran pastor born in Stavanger. Its acoustics suit amplified music, and it can be set up as an amphitheatre, arena, catwalk or flat floor for banquets or standing crowds, with up to 1,700 seats.

Alvar Aalto designed Sähkötalo, the Electricity Building, in Helsinki's central Kamppi district; it serves as the head office of HELEN, the energy company owned by the city. Work began in March 1970. The office block is one of only two fragments of a larger Aalto plan to be realised, the other being the Finlandia Hall concert hall on Töölö Bay. Both use a Miesian language of geometric grids that Aalto also applied on other Helsinki sites: the Enso-Gutzeit headquarters and the Academic Bookstore, both from 1962, and, in 1969, the SYP Bank building. Since October 2007 the lower floors have held shops, linked to Kamppi Center by an underground pedestrian tunnel beneath Fredrikinkatu. After dark, neon lights lining the window frames slowly shift colour through the night.

Seinäjoki Library, built in 1964–1965, belongs to the Aalto Center, the civic and cultural core of this Finnish city. The center's six buildings, all by Alvar Aalto, were mostly completed between 1960 and 1968. In 1959 Aalto and Elissa Aalto, his wife, won a follow-up competition whose brief also covered a library, a theatre and state offices; the town hall followed in 1961–1962. As a whole, the center ranks among Aalto's most important works, and New York's Museum of Modern Art holds its wooden plan. Aalto also designed the courtyard between the buildings, with its fountain and outdoor lighting, and in 1988 this "citizens' square" was laid with granite slabs to his original plans. Finland's Ministry of the Environment protected the center in 2005, and in July 2026 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site with 12 other Aalto works.

Founded in 1872, the Finnish National Theatre had no permanent home until 1902, when this purpose-built theatre was finished in central Helsinki, on the north side of the Central Railway Station Square. The architect Onni Tarjanne designed it in the National Romantic style, drawing on romantic nationalism. Theatre, with Finnish language and art more broadly, formed the base of a cultural movement that started in the 1860s, took on political aims around 1900 and eventually led to independence in 1917. Besides the Main Stage, the theatre now includes the Willensauna Stage (1976), the Omapohja studio (1987) and the Small Stage (1954), the work of the architects Heikki and Kaija Siren. Out front stands a memorial to Aleksis Kivi, honouring his part in Finnish theatre, designed by Wäinö Aaltonen and raised in 1939.

No Nordic congress centre is larger than Tampere Hall, which sits at Sorsapuisto's southern edge in central Tampere, Finland. It grew from a first-prize competition entry by Sakari Aartelo and Esa Piironen, who set up an office together in 1978, and it is their main work: a hall for concerts and congresses that holds 2,000 people. The building was inaugurated on 29 September 1990. Its main auditorium seats 1,756. Both the Tampere Opera and Tampere Philharmonic Orchestra are based here, and in 2017 the complex gained the Moomin Museum. The University of Tampere's main building stands opposite, and the railway station is just half a kilometre away.

Completed in 1929 in Muurame, central Finland, this was Alvar Aalto's first church, and the sole one of his numerous 1920s church designs that was built. It marks his move from Nordic Classicism toward the Functionalism for which he is best known. The long single-aisled nave and the campanile reflect churches Aalto saw on his honeymoon in Italy a few years before. Because it sits between two phases, many critics have undervalued it among his works, and Aalto himself called it an "aberration of youth" (nuoruudensynti). A full restoration in 2016 returned the church to its original design, most visibly replacing the white and light wood interior, often linked with Aalto's minimalist style, with the original colours: a ceiling in bright blue and red, with dark grey fittings.

Alvar Aalto designed this complex in Seinäjoki to serve as headquarters for the Finnish Civil Guard's South Ostrobothnia division, a voluntary militia also known as the White Guard or Defence Corps, and for the linked women's auxiliary, Lotta Svärd. Drawn in the Nordic classical style, it counts among the main works of Aalto's earlier neoclassical period, before the modernism for which he is better known. Three buildings enclose a courtyard. The main building rises three storeys, with a masonry ground floor and two timber floors above; that ground floor sits partly below ground and holds a circular assembly hall. Since 1990 the building has housed the Suojeluskunta & Lotta Svärd Museum, part of the city's museum network, and in 2002 the Finnish Heritage Agency protected the complex as a nationally important built cultural environment.

Arto Sipinen designed this cultural centre in Tapiola, Espoo, completed in 1989 and best known as home to Tapiola's central library. It stands next to the Tapiola Central Tower, with the cultural square on one side and the central pool on the other. Sharing the building with the library are the Espoo music academy, Tapiola Sinfonietta (the city orchestra), Espoo's cultural office, a general service point for Tapiola and the Espoo folk high school. Of its two halls, Louhisali seats 300 and suits theatre, while Tapiolasali seats 800 and suits concerts. It ranks among Sipinen's best-known buildings, together with the cultural centres he designed for Mikkeli, Imatra and Kuusamo.

Westminster Cathedral, dedicated to the Blood of Jesus Christ, is the biggest Catholic church in England and Wales. John Francis Bentley designed it in a neo-Byzantine style based on 9th-century Christian building, so it is made almost entirely of brick, with no steel reinforcement. Bentley died a year before it opened in 1903. The building covers about 5,017 m2, and beyond the campanile its main feature is an open nave 18 metres wide and 70 metres long under domical vaulting. Shallow pendentive domes keep weight and thrust low. Huge, narrow buttresses braced by cross walls, arcades and vaults support the nave, much as in Gothic cathedrals, but all of them stay inside. Outside, bands of white stone run through the red brick. Interior decoration had barely begun at the consecration, since Byzantine ornament is applied rather than built in.

Daniel Burnham and Frederick P. Dinkelberg designed this 22-storey, steel-framed triangular tower at 175 Fifth Avenue in Manhattan, first called the Fuller Building and now 307 feet (93.6 m) tall. Its wedge of a site comes from Broadway cutting diagonally across the street grid, and the shape, like a cast-iron clothes iron, gave the building its later name. The construction firm Fuller Company bought the plot from the Newhouse family in May 1901 for its headquarters, and the tower opened on 1 October 1902 at 285 feet. Like a classical column, the facade splits vertically into three parts, with a three-storey limestone base and glazed terracotta above. The engineers Purdy and Henderson designed the steel frame for four times the area's strongest wind, yet doubtful locals once called it "Burnham's Folly". New York City made it a landmark in 1966.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this summer villa in Ashiya, Hyōgo, in 1918 for a wealthy Japanese sake brewer, maker of Sakura-Masamune, and it was finished in 1924. Arata Endo, who also saw the Imperial Hotel through to completion after Wright left in 1922, supervised the building work. It is Wright's only surviving residence in Japan. Set into a hilltop overlooking the Port of Kobe, the house is stepped to take in views of Osaka Bay; it has four levels, yet none rises above two storeys. Its exterior recalls Wright's textile block houses in Los Angeles, but the decorative blocks are Oya stone instead of concrete. No Taishō-period building in Japan had been named an Important Cultural Property before it was, in 1974. The Great Hanshin earthquake of 1995 damaged it; it was then repaired and reopened.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this chapel in Belvidere Cemetery, in Belvidere, Illinois; it was built in 1907. It honours Dr. William Henry Pettit, who died in 1899; his widow, Emma Glasner Pettit, commissioned Wright in 1906 and gave the chapel to the Belvidere Cemetery Association. It is the only funerary building by Wright built in his lifetime. The T-shaped plan, about 57 by 42 ft, puts a meeting room in the stem and two open porches in the crossbar, where Wright meant mourners to wait for their cars. A low hipped roof keeps the skyline quiet, as at his early Heurtley and Winslow houses, and the chapel gathers the elements of his Prairie Style: overhanging eaves, abstract geometric art glass, a raised floor and stucco against wood trim. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed One Charles Center, a 23-storey International Style office tower of aluminium and glass in Baltimore, built in 1962. A design competition preceded the tower, which took just 13 months to build and cost $10,350,000. It was Baltimore's first modern office tower and part of the downtown urban renewal movement, marking the start of the city's modern downtown buildings. A concrete-faced podium carries a paved plaza, and the T-shaped tower rises from it, finished in metal trim and gray glass. Its neighbour is the Fidelity Building, completed in the 1890s. In 2000 One Charles Center joined the National Register of Historic Places.

Rising 192 metres over 52 storeys in central Warsaw, Złota 44 is a residential tower designed by the Polish-American architect Daniel Libeskind together with the Polish practice Artchitecture. The name is taken from the address, on Złota, or "Golden", Street. People sometimes call it Żagiel, Polish for "sail", though Libeskind took his cue from an eagle's wing, symbolising a changing Warsaw, Poland and freedom. Its 287 apartments fill floors 9 to 52, and few residential buildings in Poland or the European Union are taller. Nearby stand Varso Tower, the Palace of Culture and Science and the Złote Tarasy shopping centre. Money trouble at the developer, a cancelled building permit and disputes with people living nearby halted construction in 2009; work restarted in January 2011, and the tower was topped out on 3 February 2012.

Kengo Kuma, a Japanese architect chosen through an international competition, designed this Paris Metro station north of the city in Saint-Denis. Part of the Grand Paris Express, it opened on 24 June 2024 at the end of Line 14; later it is to serve the orbital Line 15 and to be where lines 16 and 17 end. The station spans nine levels, with platforms 27 m underground, and should handle 250,000 passengers daily, roughly as many as Châtelet–Les Halles. All six tracks of the four lines will share one level, allowing cross-platform changes from Line 14 to Line 15, and from Line 15 to the track shared by lines 16 and 17. A new bridge over the Paris–Lille line links it with the Stade de France and RER D's Stade de France–Saint-Denis stop. Inside are 56 escalators and 17 elevators.

Toyo Ito and his firm designed this office building in the Zuidas district of Amsterdam, and the tower carries his name; ZZDP Architecten also took part in the design process. Building work ran from September 2002 to June 2005, within the first construction phase of the Mahler4 development. The tower rises 100 metres (328 feet), with twenty-five floors above ground and two below. Its load-bearing elements are reinforced concrete, combined with a steel frame. Outside, the form is angular and cut through with openings, and the facade alternates horizontal bands of windows with bands of aluminium panels. Four atria open up the interior, and a large terrace sits on the roof at the 16th floor.

The American architect Minoru Yamasaki received the design of this Madrid skyscraper in 1975 from its developer, Unión de Explosivos Río Tinto, and worked with Rafael Coll Pujol and Jorge Mir Valls. It stands by the Pablo Picasso Square in AZCA, a commercial complex on the Paseo de la Castellana. Begun late in 1982, the tower opened in December 1988. With 43 floors and a height of 157 m (515 ft), it was Madrid's tallest building until 2007. The rectangular block has chamfered corners and a facade clad in white aluminium. Its two-storey base has no windows; entry is through a wide round arch that carries the facade above and rests on steel below ground. Higher up, windows come in pairs split by a slim pier; the top two floors are blank, and the parapet flares into a cornice.

Hürrem Sultan, or Roxelana, wife and consort of Süleyman the Magnificent, the Ottoman sultan, commissioned this public bathhouse as a charitable work. Mimar Sinan built it in 1556 to serve the religious community of the nearby Hagia Sophia, on the site of the old Baths of Zeuxippus. At 75 m (246 ft) long, it follows the classical Ottoman bath type, with two matching sections for men and women. Both run north to south along one axis, which was new in Turkish bathhouse design. In each, a changing room leads to an intermediate cool room and then a hot room, whose large dome sits on octagonal walls and lets in half-light through small glass windows. Outer walls alternate one course of cut stone with two of brick. After a US$11 million restoration begun in 2008, the baths reopened in May 2011.

Victor Horta designed this Brussels town house in the Art Nouveau style for Armand Solvay, whose father Ernest Solvay was a chemist and industrialist; it was built between 1895 and 1900. Horta drew every detail, from furniture, carpets and light fittings to the tableware and even the doorbell, and used costly onyx, marble, bronze and tropical woods. Théo van Rysselberghe, a pointillist painter, helped him decorate the staircase. In 2000 the house joined the UNESCO World Heritage list with three other Horta town houses, his own house and workshop among them, works marked by open plans, the spread of light, and curved decoration joined to the structure. The Wittamer family bought it in the 1950s and kept the house and most of its contents intact. A facade renovation in 2022–2024 was directed by the architect Barbara Van der Wee.

This university in Bab-Ezzouar, a town 15 km (9.3 mi) outside Algiers, was designed by the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer and inaugurated in 1974. Known by the initials USTHB, it held the title of Algeria's largest university until 2013 and today has more than 20,000 students. The University Library occupies the centre of the campus, though it had no building of its own when the university first opened in 1974; in those early years it used temporary rooms set up in the classroom blocks. Its new building was officially inaugurated in 1986, twelve years after the university opened.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this Mayan Revival house for Charles Ennis, a businessman, and Mabel, his wife; it was finished in 1925 on a hilltop in Los Feliz. It is the largest of the four houses Wright designed in concrete textile blocks in 1920s Greater Los Angeles, built as he was moving from his early Prairie designs toward later Usonian ones. Its blocks were moulded from the site's degraded granite mixed with water, sand and gravel. A grid of 4-foot (120 cm) squares, each matching three blocks, orders the plan, and the outer walls step back as they rise, giving a massing like a Mayan temple. Its stained glass was the last Wright designed for a home. It is a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument and a California Historical Landmark, and is on the US National Register of Historic Places.

Part of the Süleymaniye Mosque complex in Istanbul, this bathhouse sits on a hill looking toward the Golden Horn. Mimar Sinan, a Turkish architect, built it in 1557; Süleyman the Magnificent, his patron, commissioned it, and the bath is named after him. Because many workers from nearby foundries bathed here, people sometimes knew it as the 'metalworkers' bath'. Inside, the rooms are arched and domed, and elaborate marble inlay covers the walls. A traditional bathhouse, it has cold, lukewarm and hot sections, and the hottest can climb to between 40 and 60 °C (104–140 °F). Sinan is said to have used a private cubicle here while he lived near the complex between 1557 and 1588, and it survives. The hamam was restored in 2001 to cater for tourists.

Paul Andreu's preliminary sketches for this museum showed a dome, and he suggested placing the building in the water itself. A basin of 300,000 m² was to be dug out of reclaimed land so that a spherical dome would seem to float in the bay, reached through a tunnel under water. Andreu based the dome's geometry on Viviani's curve. Arup engineered the dome and the internal structure that holds the exhibits, with the Japanese firm Tohata handling the entrance building and tunnel. Work began on site in March 1998, and the Mayor of Osaka City opened the museum on 14 July 2000. Because the dome had to withstand earthquakes, waves and wind, its completion earned a Structural Special Award from the UK's Institution of Structural Engineers in 2002. Financial problems and falling visitor numbers closed it on 10 March 2013.

Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and unveiled in 1920, the Cenotaph is the national memorial of the United Kingdom to those from Britain and the British Empire who died in the First World War. A temporary version came first, put up in 1919 for a parade at the war's end, when over 15,000 servicemen, among them French and American soldiers, saluted it. For the permanent one Lutyens added entasis, a curvature, and made few other changes. Its name is Greek for 'empty tomb': since the dead were mostly buried near where they fell, the monument marks their absence and gives mourners a focus.
