In Portland stone, a tomb chest sits on a rectangular pylon that narrows upward, with almost no decoration. It is Grade I listed, and it proved among the most influential models for First World War memorials.

Designed by the Israeli architect Yaakov Rechter, this centre for the performing arts stands in Tel Aviv, on King Saul Boulevard, and is also called the Golda Center. It first welcomed the public in 1994 and houses both the Israeli Opera and the Cameri Theater, which Rechter Architects added in 2003. Its programme spans opera, jazz, dance and classical music, along with exhibitions of fine art, and it draws about a million visitors each year. Neighbours include the Tel Aviv Museum of Art and Beit Ariela, the city's Central Municipal Library, while Dubnow Park lies at its rear. When the centre was renovated in the 2010s, its largest single donor was Charles Bronfman.

This Renaissance palace in Florence has a stone facade on Piazza degli Strozzi, diagonally opposite the grander Palazzo Strozzi's southeast corner. Older and smaller than its neighbour, it housed a cadet branch of the Strozzi family, and it was once called the Palazzo delle Tre Porte after its three street-level doorways. A renovation around 1457 had a design attributed to Filippo Brunelleschi, with other architects taking part. Michelozzo is credited with the lower facade, irregularly rusticated, and with the inner courtyard of about 1460, which had a columned portico. Giuliano da Maiano is credited with the first floor (c. 1456), where the rustication softens and the windows are double mullioned. A third floor in smoother stone came only in the 19th century. The courtyard was later lost to the Cinema Odeon, designed in 1920 by Marcello Piacentini.

One of the Seven Sisters, Moscow's Stalinist skyscrapers, this tower was designed by Mikhail Posokhin and Ashot Mndoyants. Laid down in 1950, it was finished in 1954, the final one of the seven to be completed. It rises 160 metres, with 22 floors in the central block and 18 usable floors in the wings. Standing where Krasnaya Presnya street ends, facing the Sadovoye Koltso, it was built mainly as high-end flats for the country's cultural leaders, not its politicians. The decoration is rich but mixed in style: the parapets follow ancient Roman models, pointed turrets around the spire recall Orthodox church domes, and sculptures of Soviet soldiers and workers stand on the stylobate roof. The building had central air conditioning and a central dust extraction system, with brushes and hoses in each flat and vacuum stations in the basement.

Forum Groningen, designed by NL Architects, is a cultural centre in Groningen, in the northern Netherlands. It gathers a library, a cinema, museums, study places, a restaurant and a rooftop bar under one roof. It sits beside the Grote Markt and the Nieuwe Markt, as part of a wider plan to rebuild the city centre. The design was chosen through a competition: residents ranked a top three from seven entries, and the municipal council picked the winner. Costs were projected at about €71 million, €35 million of it paid by the provincial government. Decades of gas drilling in the Groningen field have brought more induced earthquakes to the province, so new plans were needed to make the building earthquake-resistant, which pushed it over budget and two years late. It opened in November 2019 and receives 2.5 million visitors each year.

Edward and William Sutherland Maxwell, both of Montreal, designed this Beaux-Arts building in Regina, built from 1908 to 1912. It is home to Saskatchewan's Legislative Assembly and looks out over Wascana Lake. The design allows for growth: wings could run south from its east and west ends and meet around a courtyard, and the chamber was built for 125 members, although the assembly has never had more than 66 MLAs and now has 61. Red brick was planned for the outside, but after work had started, with the bricks already delivered, Premier Walter Scott chose Tyndall stone from Manitoba to make the building grander; the switch added $50,000 to the cost. In 1965 Clifford Wiens began a major renovation and restoration that took about fourteen years. The building and its grounds became a National Historic Site of Canada in 2005.

Nuevos Ministerios, or New Ministries, is a complex of government offices in the centre of Madrid. Its original project came from Secundino Zuazo Ugalde, one of the leading rationalist architects of his generation, who took the Escorial as an inspiration, and Indalecio Prieto, then Minister of Public Works, soon backed it. Work began in 1933, halted during the Civil War, and the whole complex was finished in 1942. Zuazo did not direct the building work: a team of architects close to the new regime completed it, cutting or changing major parts, such as a skyscraper intended for the northern edge. The ministries stand around a large central space of open areas, fountains and ponds, and a large arcade runs along the Paseo de la Castellana. Beneath the patio, the ground was dug out for what is now Nuevos Ministerios station.

Palmer & Hornbostel, a New York architecture firm, won a nationwide competition and designed this city hall in 1910. Completed in 1914, it replaced an earlier building that stood on today's Frank H. Ogawa Plaza. At 320 feet (98 m), it was the United States' first high-rise government building and, at the time, the tallest building west of the Mississippi River. The Beaux-Arts design climbs in three tiers that resemble a 'rectangular wedding cake'. The slimmer second tier is a ten-storey office tower whose top floor, the 12th, holds a 36-cell jail, unused since the 1960s, and above it sit a two-storey podium and a clock tower. Outside are white granite and terra cotta; inside, white and black marble. Rubber bearings later replaced cut steel columns in the foundation, letting the building shift 18–20 inches sideways in an earthquake.

Rosenbad, on Strömgatan in Stockholm, stands on the northern bank of the Norrström. Ferdinand Boberg, an Art Nouveau architect, designed it, and it was completed in 1902. In its early years the building held several different functions, including a restaurant that shared its name and stayed open until 1956. It now belongs to the Swedish state and is where the Government sits: both the Prime Minister's Office and the Government Offices work here. On the far side of the water of Stockholms ström lie the Royal Palace and the Parliament House.

Heureka, the Finnish Science Centre, stands in the Tikkurila district of Vantaa, north of Helsinki, where the Finnish Main Line meets the river Keravanjoki. Heikkinen – Komonen Architects designed it: a 1985 competition gave two first prizes, and the chosen one was the 'Heureka' entry by Mikko Heikkinen, Markku Komonen and Lauri Anttila. The building covers 8,200 m², 2,800 m² of it for exhibitions, and opened on 28 April 1989. Mirror glass on the side facing the railway is meant to keep out train noise. At the centre is a 14-metre-tall cylindrical hall, inspired by an exhibition Gunnar Asplund designed at the Stockholm city library, with about 200 science exhibits. Each part of the building has its own structural system, and it mixes concrete, steel and wood; some pillars are made of sub-pillars that show how load is shared.

Gabriel von Seidl, an architect, built the present home of the Historical Museum of the Palatinate in 1910, across the square from Speyer Cathedral, and a modern annex followed in 1990. Speyer made Seidl an honorary citizen on 14 April 1909 in recognition of this new building. The museum itself was founded in 1869, when three collections were combined: those of the city of Speyer, the former Rhine District, and the Palatinate's historical society. It traces the history of the Palatinate through about a million objects, the oldest a hand axe of roughly 190,000 years. Five permanent exhibitions over 8,000 m2 cover Prehistory, the Roman Era, the Cathedral Treasure, the Modern Era and the Wine Museum. A covered courtyard of 650 m2 offers space for concerts, workshops, theatre and discussions.

Robert Reamer, a 29-year-old architect working for the Yellowstone Park Company, an affiliate of the Northern Pacific Railway, designed the inn. He was hired for a far more radical design, rooted in the Adirondacks' rustic camps. The first building work was done in winter 1903–1904, largely using local lodgepole pine and rhyolite stone. A log lobby several storeys high sits between long frame wings of guest rooms. That log-and-limb lobby and an 85-foot (26 m) stone fireplace weighing 500 short tons (450 t) mark the inn as an example of rustic resort architecture's 'Golden Age', also called National Park Service Rustic. Twisted and curved branches carry the framing inside and out. It is the world's largest log hotel. The Old House section is turned 90 degrees to Old Faithful, so the entrance porch frames the geyser for arriving guests.

This large concert hall and convention centre in Zagreb takes its name from Vatroslav Lisinski, a Croatian composer of the 19th century. It grew out of a 1957 decision to give the city a new multifunctional hall, and the design contest was won by a team of architects under Marijan Haberle. Building began in 1961, but floods and money problems pushed completion into the following decade, and it was not until 29 December 1973 that the hall opened. Its big hall seats 1,841 people and its small hall 305, while a spacious lobby also serves for exhibitions. After a first major renovation in 1989, it hosted the 1990 Eurovision Song Contest, and in 1992 its copper roof covering was replaced in full. Over its first thirty years of operation it welcomed 10 million visitors.

The Jewish Museum Munich covers Munich's Jewish history and forms part of the new Jewish Center on Sankt-Jakobs-Platz, a group of three buildings. It sits between Ohel Jakob, the main synagogue, and a community centre that serves Munich and Upper Bavaria's Jewish community and contains a kindergarten, a public elementary school, a youth centre, a kosher restaurant and an auditorium. Wolfgang Lorch and Rena Wandel-Hoefer, the architects, won the contract through a competition on 6 July 2001. Built from 2004, the museum was inaugurated on 22 March 2007; it cost roughly €17.2 million, funded by the city of Munich, which also runs it. It is a freestanding cube whose ground-floor lobby is transparent. The permanent exhibition fills the lower level, and the two top floors hold changing exhibitions, a learning centre and a library.

This national museum in Leeds houses the National Collection of Arms and Armour, previously shown or stored at the Tower of London. It was among the first projects under the UK's private finance initiative: the Royal Armouries, a public body, contracted a private company, Royal Armouries International (RAI), to build the museum and run it for six decades, keeping the ticket revenue. Derek Walker and Buro Happold designed the building for RAI, Alfred McAlpine built it for £42.5 million, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it in March 1996. It sits at Leeds Dock on the River Aire's south bank. Planned from the inside out, it has ceilings up to 6.5 metres high so the longest staff weapons can stand upright. A giant staircase, the Hall of Steel, is lined with trophy displays of 2,500 objects.

Frank Lloyd Wright, born in Wisconsin, first proposed Monona Terrace for Madison in 1938, but the Dane County development board rejected it by one vote. Wright kept lobbying and revising the design until he died in 1959. In 1990 Madison's mayor, Paul Soglin, revived the plan. Opponents said it would not be a genuine Wright building, that it cost taxpayers too much, and that it would harm the environment, blocking the street-level view of Lake Monona from the Capitol Square's south side. The exterior follows Wright's design, while the interior as built is by Anthony Puttnam of Taliesin Associated Architects, a former Wright apprentice. The 250,000-square-foot (23,000 m2) convention centre opened on 18 July 1997, almost 60 years after the first proposal, and draws nearly 400,000 visitors a year. Its roof looks out over downtown Madison and the lake.

Originally named the Zénith Arena, the Zénith de Lille is an indoor arena for many kinds of events, with room for up to 7,000 people, which places it among the biggest venues in the city. Rem Koolhaas, the Dutch architect, designed it together with Cecil Balmond, and brought in Renz van Luxemburg for acoustics, dUCKS scéno for scenography and Arup Group for engineering. Pierre Mauroy, a former mayor of Lille, commissioned it as a long-term project, which began in 1980 and was not finished until June 1994. The arena belongs to Lille Grand Palais, a cultural complex, also designed by Koolhaas, that adds a congress centre and exhibition halls; together they hold three auditoriums, 28 meeting rooms and a banquet hall as well as the arena.

Tadao Ando, a winner of the Pritzker Prize, designed this privately funded non-profit museum in Shunde, Foshan, in China's Guangdong Province. Its name, He, meaning harmony, balance and mixture, comes from the surname of He Jianfeng, who founded it; his father, He Xiangjian, founded Midea Group. Of about 16,000 m² of floor space, some 8,000 m² is for exhibitions. Lingnan building traditions and patterns gave Ando the circle motif. Four concentric rings make up the exterior, widening off-centre as they rise like ripples on water; Ando said the design responds to the region's subtropical climate, giving it strong light and shadow. A circular reflecting pool tempers the summer heat and, reflecting the building, serves as its visual base. In the central atrium, a double-helix stair of fair-faced concrete cast in place takes daylight from the dome above.

The New Synagogue on Synagogenplatz in Mainz serves a Jewish congregation as synagogue and community centre. Built in 2010, it occupies the Hindenburgstraße site in Mainz Neustadt where the old main synagogue, destroyed in 1938, once stood. Manuel Herz, an architect from Cologne, won a 1999 competition for a new synagogue and community centre. The building reflects Kedushah, a Jewish liturgical term for sanctification and exaltation: Herz meant the five parts of the centre, used for community events, adult education and a Hebrew school for children, to stand for the word's five Hebrew letters. The horn-shaped roof over the assembly space points east toward Jerusalem and represents a shofar. The prayer hall seats about 450, five times the earlier capacity. After weather delays it was inaugurated on 3 September 2010, the anniversary of the former synagogue's inauguration in 1912.

Erick van Egeraat, an award-winning architect, designed this building for the University of Leipzig, and its construction began in 2007. It stands where the Paulinerkirche, the university's old church, stood until it was destroyed in 1968 during East Germany's communist era. The building holds the university's assembly hall, which includes an oratory, together with rooms for the faculties of information science and mathematics. The assembly hall rises on exactly the same spot as the old church; it shows figures and other objects from the Paulinerkirche and offers a room for common prayer. In memory of the original building, the facade draws on collegiate Gothic architecture.

This apartment complex in Ramat Gan, Israel, known in Hebrew as Beit HaSpirala, winds upward in a spiral. The architect Zvi Hecker designed it with Gil Bernstein, Rina Hering and Shmuel Groberman, and Jaakov Hai built it between 1984 and 1990. It applies the terracing of Arab villages, where roofs become part of the living space of the flats. The structure is concrete, faced in plaster, pink glass, stone fragments and corrugated tin. Hecker called it a 'miniature Tower of Babel'; one of his collaborators said it looked as if a storm had swept through Ramat Gan, gathered wreckage from roofs and yards, and formed the spiral at a stroke. Hecker lived opposite, in the Dubiner house, so he kept close control on site and revised the design repeatedly. It earned him the 1999 Rechter Prize for architecture.

Neutelings Riedijk Architects designed this building for the STC Group, whose headquarters are in Rotterdam. The group's founding school, the Shipping and Transport College, was formed in 1990 by merging all the maritime colleges in the Netherlands, and since then the group has opened many new buildings. This one stands in the Lloyd District, a port area in central Rotterdam that is both historical and contemporary. It contains every simulator and all the training materials needed to teach shipping and transport at secondary and higher levels, and it counts as one of Rotterdam's architectural landmarks.

MAR, the Museu de Arte do Rio, opened on 1 March 2013 in the historic centre of Rio de Janeiro, as part of a plan begun in 2009 to revive the downtown area. Jacobsen Arquitetura organised the whole architectural plan, drawing on ideas from three main architects: Thiago Bernardes, Paulo Jacobsen and Bernardo Jacobsen. The museum fills two buildings on Praça Mauá, which lies between the Zona Portuária and Centro. One is the Palacete Dom João VI, built in an eclectic style; the other, next door, was formerly the Mariano Procópio bus station and now holds the 'Escola do Olhar' and offices. A suspended walkway, described as a 'fluid cover', links the two. In its opening year the museum won the museum category of the Architizer A+ Awards, ahead of entries including the Heydar Aliyev Center and the New Rijksmuseum.

Seinäjoki City Theatre is the newest of six buildings in the Aalto Centre, the administrative and cultural centre of this Finnish city. Alvar Aalto and his wife Elissa won a follow-up competition in 1959 whose scope also took in a theatre, a library and a state office building. Aalto had the theatre plans ready by 1969, but construction waited almost twenty years. It finally went ahead in 1986–1987 under Elissa Aalto's direction, since Alvar had died in 1976. Its five neighbours all date from 1960 to 1968. Of the Aalto Centre as a whole, Finland's National Board of Antiquities lists it as nationally significant built heritage, Docomomo picks it out as an important example of Finnish modern architecture, and in July 2026 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site along with 12 other Aalto works.

Frank Lloyd Wright drew this two-storey organic house in 1959, and it became his last residential design. John Rattenbury of Taliesin Associated Architects, once Wright's apprentice, completed it in 1967. Wright picked the site for its view over Palm Canyon and shaped his sketches around it. From above, the plan reads as overlapping circles struck from five separate geometric centres, with a curved wing peeling off the round main block. It is one of 14 circular homes Wright designed, six of them around Phoenix. The house is built mostly of rose-tinted concrete. Where his houses often turn inward or away from busy areas, these windows look south to Downtown Phoenix, shaded by ledges against the heat, and a glass wall faces the patio and pool. A low foyer opens into larger rooms, showing Wright's idea of compression and release.

Completed in 1950 on the University of New Mexico campus in Albuquerque, this building was made to serve as both house and gallery for Raymond Jonson, a modernist painter. John Gaw Meem, who designed several other buildings for the university, gave it a fairly plain Pueblo Revival form. Set on a hillside, it shows one storey at the front and two at the back. Throughout, the windows are steel casements set on concrete sills. Jonson lived on the upper level, and the gallery occupied the floor below. Both while he was alive and after, the gallery acted as a hub for abstract and modern art across the state and held a large collection of his own work. In 2009 those collections were absorbed by the university's art museum, and the building became offices.

Franz Urbig commissioned this family villa in 1915, beside the Griebnitzsee at Babelsberg, just beyond Potsdam. It went up between 1915 and 1917 to designs by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, then a little-known architect. He would later change his approach radically, be recognised as a pioneer of modernism and, in 1930, become the Bauhaus School's final director, in Dessau. From 16 to 25 July 1945, Winston Churchill stayed in the house while he attended the nearby Potsdam Conference. For many years it lodged guests of the East German "Walter Ulbricht" academy of political and legal studies. After 1990 the villa went back into private hands, and in 2005 the businessman and property developer Theodor Semmelhaack bought it and carried out a full restoration.

Marcel Breuer designed Stillman House I in Litchfield, Connecticut, in 1950. It followed his "House in the Museum Garden", a demonstration house built a year earlier for the Museum of Modern Art and now standing at Kykuit, a Rockefeller estate. From 1950 to 1953 Breuer had three separate commissions on the site: the main house, a studio, and a redesign of the pool and porch. The sculptor Alexander Calder made an 18-by-10-foot mural wall for the pool, and Xanti Schawinsky, an artist from the first Bauhaus generation, made one indoors. Next door is John M. Johansen's Huvelle House of 1953; the pair were Litchfield's first and second modern homes, between a forest reserve and historic North Street. In reaction, the borough now limits modern design in its historic area to guard its Colonial and Greek Revival character.

When Josephine Crane married Harold C. Bradley, who taught biochemistry at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, her grandfather Richard T. Crane had this Madison house built for the couple as a gift. The design is credited to Louis H. Sullivan with George Grant Elmslie; it is among Sullivan's few houses and one of just two of his designs in Wisconsin. Elmslie sketched every drawing, with only the odd suggestion from Sullivan, and many details anticipate the style Elmslie later developed with William Gray Purcell. It was Elmslie's last design in Sullivan's office; he left in 1909 to partner with Purcell. The Bradleys thought the first scheme too big, so Elmslie scaled it down: two storeys on a T-shaped plan, two cantilevered sleeping porches upstairs and a porte-cochère at the back. The architects also designed its furniture, rugs, draperies and fixtures.

Adalberto Libera designed La Spezia's cathedral, built from 1956 to 1975. An earlier competition went to the architect Brenno Del Giudice, but work was put off for over 25 years and his scheme was never built. On its revival in 1956, Libera, a Rationalist, was chosen, and he used the raised site on Piazza Europa to heighten the building's monumental presence. He died in 1963 with the church unfinished; local architect Cesare Galeazzi took over, adding some changes of his own, and in 1975 it was finished and consecrated. Outside, a round plan and a windowless outer wall shaped as a hyperboloid of one sheet define it. Inside, light falls through an opening at the centre of the cupola, 50 metres across, carried on 12 heavy columns standing for the Apostles, and through a band of stained glass.

The clients behind Villa Kenwin at La Tour-de-Peilz engaged Alexander Ferenczy, an art director as well as an architect, to build it, and they moved into the new house in September 1931. Ferenczy died before the work was finished. Hermann Henselmann, who was working for him at the time, completed it and afterwards claimed the whole project as his own; his list of works dates the villa 1929–1931, with Ferenczy. Overlooking Lake Geneva, the house was planned as both a home and a film studio, although nothing shows it was ever used for filming. Its name was formed from the names Kenneth and Winifred. During the war years Bryher, one of the two clients, used Kenwin as a staging post for getting refugees out of Nazi Germany.

This 18,000-square-foot (1,700 m²) building stands at 200 N. 22nd Street in the historic Church Hill district of Richmond, Virginia. Philip Johnson designed it while he was working with the firm Budina and Freeman, and it was first built for WRVA, an AM station that was among Virginia's earliest broadcast radio stations. It is regarded as one of the most visible and important landmarks of mid-20th-century architecture in the city. Between 2007 and 2008 it went through a $5.4 million renovation so that ChildSavers could move in. Baskervill, an architecture firm based in Richmond, designed that adaptive reuse and changed very little of the structure.

Built in 1937 to replace an earlier building on the same plot, this school stands on Frankford Avenue at Stanwood Street in Holmesburg, part of Northeast Philadelphia. It belongs to the School District of Philadelphia and today teaches children from kindergarten to eighth grade. Irwin T. Catharine, the district's main architect at the time, designed it, and it is a model example of Art Deco and Moderne architecture. Catharine (1883–1944) served as chief architect for Philadelphia's public schools from 1920 until he retired in 1937. Work from his tenure runs from Gothic Revival, as at Simon Gratz High School, to the Streamline Moderne of this school, his last project. The building, at 8118–8120 Frankford Avenue, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Built in 1940 for Theodore Baird, an English professor at Amherst College, this Usonian house is the only design by Frank Lloyd Wright in Massachusetts. No nearby contractors could take on the job, so the building work was done by William Wesley Peters, a protégé of Wright. Some parts were made at a New Jersey factory, then brought to Amherst for assembly; it was the only Usonian whose materials were prefabricated before reaching the site. The single-family house has façades of brick, cypress wood and glass, under a flat roof that reaches far out over a carport. Hot water running through pipes in the concrete floor heats it. The property, on the National Register since 1985, also includes a woodlot of 4 acres (1.6 ha) stretching behind the house and its neighbours on Shays Street.

Completed in 1929 to designs by Alvar Aalto, this public building in central Jyväskylä is also called the Government Building (Valtiontalo). His competition entry, Intra Muros, placed only second, yet the committee still chose it as the basis for the project. He was only 28 and still building a reputation, and it counts among his earlier major works. Stylistically it turns from 1920s Nordic Classicism toward Functionalism, yet it is among the key surviving works of late Nordic Classicism. Planned for many tenants, it held a cinema, restaurants, shops, banking, sports venues and the Defence Corps' assembly hall. Inside are three-shade lights by the Danish designer Poul Henningsen and Mettlach tiles by Villeroy & Boch, rare in Finland then. The Finnish state took it over in 1934, and a full renovation and extension ran from 2017 to late 2020.

Designed by Theodor Fischer, this art building on Stuttgart's Schloßplatz has been the home of the Württembergischer Kunstverein since 1913. Founded in 1827, the Kunstverein is one of Germany's oldest art associations, and since moving here it has seen its role as engaging with contemporary art. In March 1933 the new regime shut a Kunstverein show, the first major retrospective of the artist Oskar Schlemmer, with his main work Bauhaus Stairs, before it opened. The Second World War left the building almost entirely destroyed. Rebuilding, tied to a modern extension, was finished only in 1961. The city of Stuttgart's gallery moved in alongside the Kunstverein. Today the complex joins the historic part, with its domed hall and galleries, to the newer so-called quadrangular hall, a design by Paul Bonatz and Günther Wilhelm, through a glass wing between old and new.

John Eberson designed this Marion movie palace as an atmospheric theatre for the Young Amusement Company. Costing $500,000, it opened on 30 August 1928 as the company's tenth theatre. The owner, V.U. Young, wanted "A Spanish Castle", and the style is best described as Spanish Colonial Revival. Patrons go from the lobby through wooden doors into an arcade behind the orchestra seats, then into what reads as a hilltop courtyard. From the balcony they look down on it, ringed by a Spanish town wall. During shows, stars laid out as constellations shine through holes in the ceiling plaster, while a hidden Brenkert Brenograph Jr. projector throws clouds across it. It was among the last American theatres built in the atmospheric style. After a local nonprofit took ownership, it was fully restored in 1975–1976, guided in part by Eberson's son Drew.

Andrew Carnegie's money paid for this library, which opened in December 1902 as Manhattan's first Carnegie library. James Brown Lord designed it in the Italian Renaissance style; it was among the last of his designs built before he died. Like many Carnegie libraries in Manhattan, it sits mid-block, with a footprint of 40 by 90 feet behind a limestone front three storeys tall. Construction cost $70,000. The city's Landmarks Preservation Commission has praised it as one of New York's most elegant uses of the Palladian style for a modern public building. The third floor first held German-language books for Yorkville's large German population. It has served as a library ever since, was renovated in 1960 and again in the late 1980s, and is a city landmark as well as being on the National Register of Historic Places.

Built in 1964–65 to plans by Gillespie, Kidd and Coia, this Roman Catholic parish church stands on Craigpark in Glasgow's Dennistoun district and holds category A listing. In 1966 the firm won the RIBA bronze regional medal and a Civic Trust Award for it. It belongs with a set of churches that also includes St Paul's in Glenrothes (1956), St Mary's in Bo'ness (1962, now demolished), St Joseph's in Faifley (1964) and St Benedict's in Easterhouse (1965). All are geometric buildings with sweeping roofs, and they made use of then-new building methods, glued laminated timber among them.

Edward Maufe's Gothic scheme in brick-faced concrete came first among 183 entries in a 1932 competition, and the cathedral, seat of the Bishop of Guildford, was built in 1936–1961. Maufe wrote that he sought a design clearly of its time yet following the great English cathedrals, depending on proportion, mass, volume and line instead of ornament. Narrow passage aisles, as at Albi, kept the nave broad and open with no flying buttresses. When cost ruled out stone, he brought home a medieval brick from Albi for Guildford brickmakers to copy. The 160-foot (49 m) tower holds twelve bells and a gilded angel that turns in the wind, and inside, with its pillars of pale Somerset limestone and floors of white Italian marble, it seems filled with light. It was the last Church of England cathedral consecrated on a new site.

In 1943 the architect Max Frisch was picked from 65 applicants to design a new swimming pool, the Letzigraben, in Zürich's Albisrieden district. The open-air pool, credited to Frisch together with Gustav Ammann, was later renamed Max-Frisch-Bad. The commission was large enough for Frisch to set up his own architecture studio with a couple of staff. Shortages of materials during the war held construction back until 1947, and the public pool opened in 1949. It is now protected by historic monument law, and a thorough renovation in 2006–2007 brought it back to its original state.

Erik Gunnar Asplund designed the Woodland Chapel (Skogskapellet) in 1920 for the Woodland Cemetery (Skogskyrkogården) in Stockholm, Sweden. The cemetery as a whole grew from a competition won by "Tallum", an entry by Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz, both young architects then. After changes the jury recommended, work began in 1917 on former gravel pits overgrown with pines, and the first stage was done three years on. The two designed the entire cemetery, from its landscape down to the smallest lamp, with sculptures by Carl Milles built in. UNESCO inscribed the cemetery as a World Heritage Site in 1994; its design shows architecture developing from Nordic Classicism into mature functionalism. In a later project, a team led by the directors Francesco Dal Co and Micol Forti brought together eleven international architects to reimagine the chapel for today's social and cultural setting.

Alvar Aalto and Elissa Aalto designed this pavilion, built in 1955–1956 as a temporary space for Finland's show at the 28th Venice Biennale and still in use. A prefabricated building on a trapezoidal plan, it is the only Alvar Aalto work in Italy finished while he was alive. It is built mainly of wood, a difficult choice for humid, flood-prone Venice, and its full coating and paint protect it from sun and water. After a shared Nordic pavilion was finished in 1962, it was lent to Italy, Argentina, Portugal, Iceland and others, and Finland has exhibited there again since 2007. Fredrik Fogh restored it in 1976–1982; another restoration followed in 1993. Its 2025 exhibition, The Pavilion – Architecture of Stewardship, used it to show how architects, engineers, builders, maintenance staff and cleaners all share in making and keeping a building.

Renaat Braem designed this house, known as "Huis Braem-Severin", in 1950 as a home for himself and Elza Severin, who helped with its interior design. It was built in 1955 at Menegemlei 23 in Deurne, Antwerp. Both its exterior and its interior are proportioned on the golden ratio, and its style is modernist. In 1999 the house was left to the Flemish Community together with everything in it, including Braem's archive, library and furniture. It was turned into a museum, Belgium's second such museum after Brussels' Horta Museum.

Konrad Wachsmann designed this wooden summer house in Caputh for Albert Einstein, and it was built in 1929. It is the only one of Einstein's homes in Germany that survives. Although he could not swim, Einstein loved sailing on the lake for pleasure, but he could use the retreat only until the Nazis took power in 1933. After German reunification the house was given back to the Einstein family, and it now belongs to the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. The Einstein Forum, led since 2000 by Susan Neiman, holds conferences, workshops and lectures there.

The architect Julio Vilamajó built this Montevideo house for his family in 1930. It came at a time of change, when he was shifting from a historical towards a humanist outlook and seeking a balance between logic and rationality in what he built. It gained National Historic Landmark status in 1990 and now houses the Vilamajó House Museum, the first modern home in Uruguay to open as a museum. The School of Architecture of the University of the Republic set it up by agreement with the owner, the Ministry of Education and Culture, and it opened to visitors in May 2012. Careful restoration brought back the original furniture, art and personal possessions, and the gardens were replanted with species first grown there. Besides a permanent display on Vilamajó's work, it hosts temporary shows on architecture, design and related subjects.

Hillside Terrace in Tokyo is less a single building than a sequence of projects that Fumihiko Maki carried out for the Asakura family, who commissioned the work. It grew in seven phases between 1967 and 1992, lining both sides of Kyū-Yamate avenue in the Daikanyama district. Over those years the complex took in homes, offices and cultural spaces, and it also came to house the Royal Danish Embassy. Maki stayed with the commission for close to a quarter of a century, and he said it shaped his thinking as an architect: as everyday life in Tokyo changed, the project changed with it. For students, it is a chance to study one architect adding to the same street, phase after phase, over decades rather than in one go.

25 bis rue Franklin is an apartment building in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, designed by Auguste Perret and built in 1904. Concrete had already appeared in Paris, but mostly dressed up to pass for stone; Perret was one of the first to explore the new forms it opened up. Here the concrete frame is shown openly as part of the street front. The plot was small yet had a fine view over the city, so the front is almost all glass: big windows set in ceramic panels by Alexandre Bigot, coloured neutrally to read like stone. By adding an excèdre to the facade, Perret fitted five flats on every floor, each with the view, where a flat front would have allowed four. For students, it is an early lesson in letting a concrete frame shape a facade.

The Granary Building at King's Cross in London is a listed warehouse complex, converted by Stanton Williams to house Central Saint Martins. The college moved there in 2011, when the renovated building opened on Granary Square, and most of it is now based on the site. The conversion cost £200 million. A year later the complex received a mayoral award for planning. Granary Square is one of five large new squares in the area, alongside Station, Pancras, Cubitt and North Squares. For students, it is a large-scale case of reuse: an old industrial structure, protected by listing, turned into a working school and set on a new public square.

The University of Ruhuna campus at Wellamadama, near Matara, was designed by Geoffrey Bawa. Its 30-hectare site covers three steep hills. The westernmost looks out to sea, and a low valley carrying the road towards Hambantota divides it from the others. Bawa used this ground as the plan itself. He set the vice-chancellor's residence and a guesthouse on the seaward hill, then flooded the valley so that water now separates the road from the main campus. Science buildings wrap around the northern hill, arts buildings around the southern one, and the hollow between them holds the library and shared facilities. The buildings answer the terrain, the planting, the views, light and shade, and the climate, which makes the campus a clear study in tying architecture to topography.

Dominus Winery stands in Yountville, inside the Napa Valley AVA in California. It serves Dominus Estate, a wine estate owned by Christian Moueix that makes Bordeaux style blends; before the building existed, the estate's earlier thirteen vintages were crushed and aged at Rombauer Winery nearby. The new winery was built by the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron, and it was their first U.S. project. Its walls are made of gabions filled with stone, which shelter the interior from the fierce heat of the day and from the cold at night. For students, the winery shows stone-filled gabions doing the work of climate control, with one wall material setting the character of the whole building.

ATIRA, the Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association, is a non-profit body for textile research in the Navarangpura area of Ahmedabad, India, and its building was designed by Achyut Kanvinde. Vallabhbhai Patel laid the foundation stone on 1 November 1950, and the finished complex was opened by Jawaharlal Nehru, then Prime Minister, on 10 April 1954. The outside of the building shows the influence of Walter Gropius. It stands on a large campus planted with more than 1,000 trees, which has become a favourite place for local people to walk and jog in the morning. For students, ATIRA is a research building of the early 1950s whose exterior draws on Gropius, and a reminder that a workplace can share its grounds with the city around it.

St. Johann von Capistran is a round church in Munich-Bogenhausen, built by Sep Ruf between 1958 and 1960. It is designed as two crescent-shaped shells, and the sacred rooms sit inside them. Above, a flat roof rests on a ring of glass and is topped by a glass dome. Outside, 22 pillars carry the roof, holding it free above the open room. For students, the church shows how a few clear moves can shape a place of worship: a circle split into two curved shells, a band of glazing between wall and roof, and a ring of supports that lets the roof stand apart from the enclosure below.

The Japan Pavilion at Expo 2000 in Hanover was a gridshell built from recycled paper tubes, which together formed a honeycomb-like building. Shigeru Ban designed it with consultants including the German architect Frei Otto, the British engineers Buro Happold and the structural engineering professor Stefan Polónyi. German authorities would not approve a structure of paper alone, held together at the joints by tape, so a second supporting structure of wood was added to win legal approval. Assembly took 3 weeks. The exhibit space measured 72 m long, 35 m wide and 15.5 m high, on a lot of 5,450 m² with 3,600 m² of building surface. For students, it shows how far a recycled material can be pushed, and how building rules can reshape an experimental structure.

The Cabanon de vacances at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin is a holiday cabin that Le Corbusier designed and built. He made it for himself alone, as a seaside retreat from life in Paris, and it is the only place he built for his own holidays. He spent every August there for 14 years. The cabin is built of wood logs and covers just 15 square metres. In July 2016 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list along with sixteen other works by Le Corbusier, and it is the smallest individual cultural structure on that list. For students, it is a lesson in fitting a whole way of living into very little room, and a rare look at what an architect chose to build for his own use.

The Bolgatanga Library in Ghana was designed by J. Max Bond Jr., an American architect whose work drew on Le Corbusier. Bond spent four years living in Ghana during the 1960s, and the library was the first large project he took on while employed by the national construction company. The building is shaped by climate. Its walls are perforated, letting air pass through, and it sits under an umbrella-shaped roof; together these keep the interior cool and well ventilated. For students, it is a compact lesson in cooling a building through its form, with the walls and the roof doing the work. It is also the first major project of an award-winning architect.

Diar es-Saâda is a housing estate in Algiers designed by Fernand Pouillon. When Jacques Chevallier became mayor of the city in 1953, he made Pouillon its chief architect and asked him for three residential complexes, this one among them; Pouillon had been brought to Algeria by the colonial government to help with its housing crisis. The estate holds 730 units. Its tower is built in massive precut stone, a method Pouillon developed after the war and called "pierre de taille" or "pré-taille". The tower rises 20 storeys in stone without reinforcement and has come through 70 years undamaged in an earthquake-prone region; an engineering study suggests the method copes well with earthquakes. For students, it shows cut stone, with no reinforcement, carrying a residential tower many storeys high.

The Edificio Basurto is an apartment building in Mexico City's Condesa neighbourhood, designed by Francisco J. Serrano and built between 1940 and 1945. Its design is described as post-Art Deco. At fourteen storeys it was unusually tall for the area in its day, and that height helped make it an emblem of Condesa. It stands on Avenida México, with Parque México half a block away to the south and Plaza Popocatépetl to the north, so it sits between two of the district's public spaces. For students, it is a case of a post-Art Deco block whose height, unusual for its time and area, made it a landmark of its district.

CapitaSpring is a skyscraper in the Downtown Core of Singapore, designed by BIG with the architect Carlo Ratti for the developers CapitaLand and Mitsubishi Estate. At 280 m it was, as of 2022, joint second-tallest in the city. Most of the tower is ordinary office space, with about ten percent given to coworking. Its lower levels hold a food centre on the second and third floors, including a hawker centre like the one in the old Golden Shoe Car Park that stood before it. Two gardens are built into the tower: one 100 metres above the ground, and a rooftop urban farm that is the highest in Singapore. For students, it shows how a commercial tower can make room for a food centre, gardens and a farm at several levels.

Hohenhof is an Art Nouveau villa of 1908 in the Gartenstadt Hohenhagen in Hagen, Germany, designed by the Belgian architect Henry van de Velde. He treated it as a Gesamtkunstwerk, a total work of art, in which the shell, fittings, furniture and landscape were all part of one design. The client was Karl Ernst Osthaus, a German industrialist and patron of the arts, who lived there with his family until he died in 1921. His children then sold the estate to the city of Hagen on condition that its overall character be kept. It has since been restored and is now a museum open to the public. For students, Hohenhof is a complete example of an architect designing everything from the walls to the furniture and garden as a single whole.

The paths around the Acropolis and Philopappou Hill in Athens are a landscape work by Dimitris Pikionis from the 1950s, perhaps the most important thing he made. Pikionis built few buildings, yet he is held in great regard for shaping these pedestrian routes beside the archaeological site. He laid rough-finished marble in pieces that look irregular but follow a strict geometry, and he planted the terraces and steps with carefully chosen local plants. The work has impressed visitors since it was made and is still highly valued. For students, it shows that a path, a step and the choice and setting of each stone can carry as much thought as a building, and how new work can be made beside ancient remains.

The National Museum of the Republic stands on the Eixo Monumental in Brasília, where it forms a cultural centre together with the National Library of Brasília. Oscar Niemeyer designed both buildings, and they were opened in 2006. The museum is covered by a single dome, and ramps lead to its entrance. Inside are 14,500 square metres of exhibition space, two auditoriums of 780 seats each and a laboratory. The building is used mainly for temporary art exhibitions. For students, it shows a full museum programme gathered under one dome, with ramps as the way in, and it is worth reading together with its neighbour, the library, as a pair of buildings by the same architect on the Eixo Monumental.

Cedar Rock, the Lowell Walter House in Quasqueton, Iowa, is a Usonian house by Frank Lloyd Wright. He finished the design in 1945, but shortages of materials held up construction until 1948, and the house was ready in 1950; the Walters then used it as their summer home for thirty years. The outside is brick, walnut and glass. As in his other Usonian houses, Wright left out a basement and an attic, which he saw as "dust collectors". The plan is split into zones, with a living and dining room and a bedroom wing. Wright used indirect lighting throughout, for example fluorescent tubes in coved ceilings under the clerestory glazing. Wright also shaped the land around the house, burying the utilities and leaving out stepping stones and tall trees.

The Azerbaijan Carpet Museum moved into a new building in Baku in 2014, set in the city's seafront park and designed by the Austrian architect Franz Janz. The form is meant to look like a rolled carpet, so the outside of the building pictures the collection held inside it. Plans to give the museum a purpose-built home began in 2010, and it opened on 26 August 2014. No museum in the world holds more Azerbaijani carpets. For students, the museum is a direct case of a building shaped to show what it contains.

The Library and Learning Center is the main building of Campus WU, the new campus of the Vienna University of Economics, which opened in October 2013 beside the city's fairground. It was planned by Zaha Hadid. The campus has 6 main building complexes on about 10 ha, by architects from five countries, and the Library and Learning Center is its dominant element. The building has five cores of complex geometry, with leaning walls and rounded corners whose radii vary. The campus sits close to the transport hub at Praterstern, with two stations on the U2 underground line and several buses. For students, it is a clear case of a parametric building set as the centrepiece of a campus shared with other architects.

Appleby Blue Almshouse in London was finished in 2023 for the United St Saviour's Charity, by Witherford Watson Mann working with Grant Associates. The design takes the traditional almshouse and rethinks it for today. It provides 57 affordable homes for older people, set around a planted courtyard that holds gardens, terraces and shared rooms meant to encourage life in common. Accessible routes and shared outdoor areas are built in, so that people can meet and look after their wellbeing. In 2025 it received the RIBA Stirling Prize. For students, it is a recent example of housing for older people that puts a shared garden at its centre, and of an old building type given a new form for a city.

Bodegas Ysios is a winery in Laguardia, Spain, designed by Santiago Calatrava and built between 1998 and 2001. It was conceived as a symbol of the Rioja wines the winery makes. The building sits on a sloping site with vineyards all around it, and it runs 196 metres in length. Its roof is aluminium, and its facade is clad in laminated wood panels that switch between convex and concave, and its roofline ripples like a series of waves. For students, Bodegas Ysios shows a long working building given a strong silhouette through its roof, and a winery treated as an emblem for its product. It is useful to compare with other wineries that let the landscape, not the building, lead.

The City Hall and Central Library in The Hague came from a 1986 design by the American architect Richard Meier and was finished in 1995, in the new city centre. Under one complex it gathers the council chamber, the city's main public library, cafés, rooms for exhibitions and a hall for weddings. A large atrium forms its heart, with a slab building on each side, one of 10 storeys and one of 12. The library occupies a semicircular building at the complex's northwestern tip. Because it is white, people call it "the Ice Palace" (IJspaleis). For students, it is a large civic complex organised around one shared atrium, and a way to see how many public uses can be gathered together in a single building.

The American Republic Insurance Company Headquarters in Des Moines was finished in 1965 as the insurer's head office, and it still serves that purpose. It was designed by Gordon Bunshaft, a prominent New York architect at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The Modernist building has eight storeys and rises to 107.34 feet. There are no windows at all on the east and west sides, while the glazing on the north and south sides lets daylight in and keeps radiant heat out. It joined the National Register in 2015. For students, it is a corporate headquarters whose window placement is set by daylight and heat, with the facades themselves taking on part of the work of climate control.

Casa de Vidro, the "Glass House", is the home Lina Bo Bardi designed in 1951 to share with her husband in São Paulo. It was her first built work, set in the new neighbourhood of Morumbi, on land that was then among the remnants of the Mata Atlantica, the rain forest that once surrounded the city. The name comes from its large glass panels and from the way the structure seems to hover above the ground. The house was also a place of work: Bo Bardi and her four staff gathered around the open fireplace instead of using a separate office. She died there on 20 March 1992. For students, it is Bo Bardi's first built work, and a house that joins living and working in one glass house.

Wells Fargo Center, once called Norwest Center, ranks third in height among the buildings of Minneapolis, Minnesota. César Pelli designed it in a modernized art deco style that echoes neighbours such as the CenturyLink Building and the Foshay Tower, and many read it as a homage to 30 Rockefeller Plaza. Completed in 1988, it stands 774 feet (236 m) tall. It replaced the Northwestern National Bank Building, which a fire damaged in 1982 and which was brought down by implosion two years on. The first plan was a 45-story tower on a square footprint that would have topped the city, but the site was halved and the design changed. In 2000 the US Environmental Protection Agency named it one of the 100 buildings in the country with the best energy efficiency.

The Aomori Museum of Art, designed by Jun Aoki, opened in July 2006 near the Sannai-Maruyama Site, and the building takes its idea from that neighbour: part of its structure is buried in the ground. The museum sets out to introduce the arts of Aomori to the world, collecting and showing work by artists from the region. Among its holdings are more than 120 works by Yoshitomo Nara, ranging from drawings to three-dimensional pieces. It is also busy with concerts, plays and workshops. For students, it is a case of a museum that answers the site near it by sinking part of itself into the earth, and of a regional museum that aims to carry the region's art to the world.

The Lyon Museum of Contemporary Art moved in 1995 into a building by Renzo Piano in the Cité Internationale, in the city's 6th arrondissement, beside a cinema and facing the Parc de la Tête d'Or. It opened on 19 December that year. The building pairs a 1930s facade with a modern brick volume, and it has two entrances at the sides and an area of 2700 sq.m. The museum asks artists to make their works directly on site, so between shows it closes for nearly six months a year to set up the next exhibition. For students, it is a case of a new gallery joined to an older facade, and of a museum that closes for months so that each show can be made in place.

Otaniemi Chapel is a Lutheran chapel on the Otaniemi campus in Espoo, Finland, part of Aalto University. The architect couple Heikki and Kaija Siren designed it for a 1954 competition; it was completed in 1956 and inaugurated in 1957. Students wanted something that would recall the wholeness of life amid their technical courses. The chapel sits on a small wooded hill among pine and birch trees, and is built of red brick and wood, linking it to the campus's other brick buildings, among them the main university buildings by Alvar Aalto. Its parallel walls lead visitors from an everyday to a sacred way of seeing nature, ending in an altar wall of glass that opens onto the forest, where a white cross stands among the trees. After an arson fire in 1976 it was rebuilt as before in 1978.

Accordia is a housing scheme in Cambridge, England, built on a 9.5-hectare site that once formed part of the grounds of a country house. It holds 378 dwellings, 166 flats and 212 houses, built in three phases, and 30% of the homes were to be affordable. Three practices shared the design: Feilden Clegg Bradley Architects did 65%, Alison Brooks Architects 10% and Maccreanor Lavington the remaining 25%. Alison Brooks drew four semi-detached villas on Brooklands Avenue, while Maccreanor Lavington drew a long terrace of four-storey houses. In 2008 its first phase became the first housing scheme to take the RIBA Stirling Prize, with the judges looking only at that phase. For students, it shows how several architects can share one large housing plan.

The Bauhaus-Archiv in Berlin is a state archive and design museum that collects and shows material on the Bauhaus School (1919–1933). Walter Gropius was the architect chosen, and in 1964 he drew plans for a museum on the Rosenhöhe in Darmstadt, which local politics stopped. The Senate of Berlin then offered both land and money. The foundation stone was laid in 1976 and was complete by 1979, but by then the 1964 design had been much altered; the semicircular, fin-like roofs over saw-tooth sheds remained its clear signature. The changes were made by Gropius's former colleague Alex Cvijanović together with Hans Bandel, a Berlin architect. The building was listed for protection in 1997. Its museum space allowed only 35 percent of the collection to be shown.

The Cairo Opera House, part of the National Cultural Centre, is the leading venue for the performing arts in Egypt's capital. It occupies the southern end of Gezira Island in the Nile, in the Zamalek district. The complex was paid for by Japan as a gift to Egypt, after President Hosni Mubarak travelled there in April 1983, and Nikken Sekkei designed it. Building began in May 1985, lasted three years, and the opera house opened on 10 October 1988. It holds seven theatres, a library of music, a gallery and a museum. The Main Hall has room for 1,200 people over four levels, with stalls, three tiers and a box for the president. A square open-air stage, designed for its acoustics, seats 600. For students, it shows a full arts campus planned as one complex.

The Children's Memorial at Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust authority in Jerusalem, was designed by Moshe Safdie and built in 1987. It remembers the children killed under Nazi rule. At the entrance stand white stelae of different heights, broken off to stand for lives cut short by the Nazis. The main room is lined entirely with mirrors that reflect the light of five candles, and the reflections create an illusion of space that stands for about 1.5 million children and young people who died in the Holocaust. As visitors walk through the dim room, a looped recording reads out the names, ages and places of death of the children. For students, it shows how light, reflection, darkness and sound can carry meaning in a memorial.

The de Young Museum is a fine arts museum in Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. Its old building was badly damaged in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake and replaced; Herzog & de Meuron won the competition in January 1999 against Tadao Ando and Antoine Predock, and completed the new building with Fong + Chan; it opened on October 15, 2005. The ground and the risk of earthquakes in San Francisco were a challenge for the design. The whole exterior is clad in 163,118 sq ft of copper plates, perforated and dimpled in varying patterns, which is expected to oxidize and turn greenish over time to echo the nearby eucalyptus. A 144-foot tower attached to the museum is the highest point in the park. For students, it shows a skin designed to change with the weather.

The McKim Building of the Boston Public Library stands on Copley Square in Back Bay, facing Richardson's Trinity Church across the square. The firm of McKim, Mead, and White won the commission in 1887, and a year later Charles Follen McKim put forward a Renaissance design modelled on a Paris library, the Bibliothèque Ste-Geneviève. The building was finished in 1895 and today holds the library's research collection; its vast reading room is called Bates Hall. In 1972 Philip Johnson added the Boylston Street Building, with similar proportions and the same pink Milford granite. The McKim Building became a National Historic Landmark in 1986. For students, it shows how a library can learn from a precedent, and how a later addition can respect the original.

The Museum of Sydney stands on a corner site where Bridge Street meets Phillip Street, over the ruins of the first Government House, home of Arthur Phillip, the first Governor of New South Wales. That house went up in 1788, was judged inadequate in 1832 and was pulled down in 1845–1846. In October 1983 the Premier, Neville Wran, said the ground would be preserved, with an international competition to find a building that acknowledged its past; the design that was built came from Denton Corker Marshall. The forecourt makes the archaeology part of the visit: inlaid stone traces the plan of Phillip's house across the plaza, and glass cases set into the paving show the old drains and privies where they lay. For students it shows a new building that keeps the remains of an older one on view.

140 Broadway is a 51-story office tower in Manhattan's Financial District, on the east side of Broadway between Cedar and Liberty streets. Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it in the International Style, and it went up between late 1964 and 1967. Early plans proposed a 36-story monolith; after Wolfson's death the architects changed course to a taller 51-story tower covering just two-fifths of the block, in line with the 1961 Zoning Resolution. The ground left open became a public plaza paved in white travertine, with Isamu Noguchi's Cube marking the entrance. By 1965 the tower had been reworked with a smooth, mostly black facade, meant to sit in harmony with the masonry buildings nearby while still standing apart from them. The city named it a landmark in 2013.

De Doelen is a concert hall and convention centre in Rotterdam and the home of the Rotterdam Philharmonic Orchestra. The first building went up in 1934 but was destroyed in May 1940, when German bombing struck the city. It was rebuilt in 1966, in the design credited to Kraaijvanger and Rein Fledderus, with a single hall at first; two more halls followed in the 1990s. Today the main space is the Grote Zaal, or Grand Hall, with 2,200 seats, joined by two smaller halls of roughly 700 seats each and a set of convention rooms. Since 2015 the building has been protected as a Rijksmonument. For students it is a post-war concert building that has grown by adding new halls over time.

The Gallery of Modern Art, known as GOMA, sits on Kurilpa Point inside the Queensland Cultural Centre at South Bank in Brisbane, next to the Queensland Art Gallery, with the State Library of Queensland also close by, looking across the river to the CBD. It opened on 2 December 2006 as the largest gallery in Australia devoted to modern and contemporary art, and it also contains the Australian Cinémathèque, a facility no other Australian art museum has. Its design centred on the idea of a pavilion in the landscape, acting as hub and anchor for the civic precinct around it, and it responds closely to the site: its natural topography, the existing pattern of the city and the river. In 2007 the design won the RAIA National Award for Public Architecture.

The Civic Center of Lima was planned as a civic and urban landmark for the Peruvian capital, bringing together government offices, a convention center and a hotel. The idea came in 1966 from Fernando Belaúnde Terry, an architect, during his first government, and the design is credited to Adolfo Córdova and team. Building started in 1970. The main tower has 33 floors and rises 109 meters, which kept it the tallest building in Peru for 34 years. The complex was Brutalist, a style then popular in Peruvian architecture, and it gave an impression of rigidity and firmness. During the Limazo of February 5, 1975, fire destroyed part of it. A later remodeling painted the walls and covered them in synthetic finishes, and the Brutalist surfaces were lost.

Baku Crystal Hall is an indoor arena in Baku, Azerbaijan, built to stage the Eurovision Song Contest 2012. Work started in August 2011 and was finished by April 2012, in time for that first major event. The design by gmp Architekten gives the building a crystalline form wrapped in a membrane façade lit by many LED lights. These were later upgraded so the lighting could change dynamically and set a different mood for each kind of event. Inside there are 12,000 seats, though the hall can hold 27,000 people, and the building is 24 m high at its middle. In 2015 the arena hosted boxing, karate, taekwondo, fencing and indoor volleyball for the first European Games. For students it shows an arena built in under a year whose façade also works as a lighting surface.

Genoa's Biosphere is a sphere of glass and steel set in the water beside the city aquarium. Renzo Piano designed it, and it was built in 2001 for the G8 summit that Genoa hosted. Inside, butterflies, iguanas, ferns and other tropical plants flourish because automated blinds lining the inside of the sphere let in just enough of the sun's heat. The sphere sits in an area that was completely redeveloped in 1992 to Piano's design, and he turned its old industrial buildings into a multipurpose centre. The Bigo, another Piano design, is a metal monument for Expo '92 Genoa that works as a panoramic lift, its form drawn from shipyard cranes. Students can read the two together as one architect returning to the same area across nearly a decade.

The former headquarters of the Central Bank of Ireland on Dame Street, now called Central Plaza, was designed by Sam Stephenson of Stephenson Gibney & Associates. It replaced a group of Victorian and Georgian buildings, among them the Commercial Buildings. Planners at first wanted an old facade on the site kept; it was taken down instead, and a replica was later built into the scheme. The project drew criticism from the start. In September 1972 the Architects' Journal called the proposal "an exercise in how to do the greatest urban damage", and the finished block stood higher than its planning permission allowed, a breach later fixed retrospectively. At ground level a paved courtyard gave walkers a shortcut from Merchant's Arch through to the Ha'penny Bridge. The bank moved out in March 2017, to North Wall Quay.

Aschanska Villa is a wooden house in Umeå, in the north of Sweden, designed by Ragnar Östberg and finished in 1906. It was built for Colonel Wilhelm Aschan, commander of the Norrlands dragonregemente. It follows the National Romantic style and is similar to Scharinska Villa, which the same architect had built in the town a year earlier. The timber house rests on a plinth and stone foundation. Östberg produced several buildings in Umeå, although he is best known for the Town Hall in Stockholm. Protected as a listed building since the 1980s, it now serves as a restaurant. Students can set it beside Scharinska Villa to compare two houses by one architect, built a year apart in the same town.

Vestersøhus is an apartment block on Vester Søgade in Copenhagen, designed by C. F. Møller and Kay Fisker and built between 1935 and 1939. The two architects worked in partnership from 1928 to 1942, and their apartment blocks include both this one and the earlier 2 Vodroffsvej of 1930. The building dominates its street. Its balcony-bay window concept became a model for later Danish residential design, and the block is still counted as a major influence on housing in Denmark. It has been a listed building since 1994. For students of housing, it shows how a single idea, here the balcony-bay window, can shape the housing that comes after it.

The Adria Palace stands on Jungmann Square in Prague. It was built for Riunione Adriatica di Sicurtà, an Italian insurance company, to designs by Pavel Janák working with the German architect Josef Zasche. Together with Josef Gočár's Legiobanka (the Legion Bank), it is counted among the main works of Rondocubism, and the two are considered the leading buildings of that style. Le Corbusier saw the building in 1926, while attending a conference in Prague, and described it as "a massive structure with an Assyrian appearance". For students, the Adria Palace and Legiobanka make a natural pair for comparing how two architects applied Rondocubism to buildings in the same city.

Alterlaa, or Wohnpark Alt-Erlaa, is a housing development in Vienna designed by Harry Glück. Planning started in 1972 under a pilot scheme to grow the city through satellite towns, and construction began in 1975. Glück aimed for a "city within a city", drawing on Le Corbusier's Ville Radieuse and on the terraced-house designs of Adolf Loos and Oskar Strnad. Three north-south lines of blocks step back in terraces over their lowest 12 storeys, then rise straight for 10 to 15 more. Every terraced flat has a big balcony fronted by a 4 m2 planter, which residents plant and look after themselves. Around 9,000 people live in 3,200 apartments, sharing rooftop and indoor pools, saunas and courts, and in 2008 the estate was reported to have the highest tenant satisfaction rating in Vienna.

Taranto's Roman Catholic co-cathedral, Concattedrale Gran Madre di Dio, was designed by Gio Ponti, with Archbishop Guglielmo Motolese giving the direction for it. Planning began in 1964 and it was built from 1967 to December 1970 in the fast-growing Città Nuova district, to back up Taranto's older cathedral. The design is closely tied to the city's place on the Mediterranean Sea. Three reflecting pools in front stand for the ocean, while the façade, 87 meters in length and 35 meters high, takes the shape of a sail. It is made of two concrete walls set a meter apart and pierced with geometric openings, which leave a Gothic outline. Inside, the floor and the accents in the nave are sea foam green.

Leeza SOHO (also called Li Ze Tower) rises 207 m as a commercial skyscraper in Beijing's Lize Financial Business District. Begun in 2015 and opened on 19 November 2019, it was the third of three buildings by Zaha Hadid Architects for the developer SOHO China, alongside Galaxy SOHO and Wangjing SOHO. The tower is split by a 194-metre atrium, the world's tallest, a record the Burj Al Arab in Dubai previously held. The atrium turns through 45° over the full height so that daylight reaches every floor. Every level has a structural ring, and four sky bridges plus double-insulated glazing join the tower's two halves. The building stands at the junction of Line 14 and Line 16 of the Beijing Subway, with an exit straight into the atrium.

Kevin Roche designed 1101 New York Avenue, a glass-clad office high-rise in Washington, D.C., completed in 2007. The block rises 50 metres over 12 floors, with 380,000 square feet of space in total. One design move is practical: the corners are notched so that more of the offices get a window. At that height it shares 20th place among the city's tallest buildings. Tenants include Google's public policy offices, and the National Retail Federation (NRF) has its headquarters there. For students it is an example of how one plan detail, here the notched corner, can give more people in an office building a room with a window.

Teshima Art Museum stands on the island of Teshima in the Seto Inland Sea, in Kagawa Prefecture, Japan, and holds just one work of art. Opened in 2010 and run by the Benesse Foundation, it was designed by Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA. The artwork inside, titled Matrix, is by the sculptor Rei Naito. The building is a single freestanding concrete shell, only 25 cm thick, spanning 40 by 60 meters and rising to just 4 meters at its highest point. For students it pairs a thin concrete shell with a museum that exists to host a single artwork.

Tate Modern is the London gallery that houses Britain's national collection of modern and contemporary art from around the world, made from 1900 onwards. It fills a former power station by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, who also designed Battersea Power Station, built in two phases between 1947 and 1963: a steel-framed, brick-clad building 200 m long with a central chimney 99 m tall. Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron were named winners of the commission in January 1995. Their conversion kept much of the original interior structure, including the vast turbine hall with its overhead travelling crane. The most visible change outside is a two-storey glass extension along half of the roof. The Queen opened the gallery on 11 May 2000, and 5.25 million people visited in its first year.

Running 1.45 miles above the West Side of Manhattan, the High Line is an elevated linear park laid out on an abandoned southern viaduct of the New York Central Railroad's West Side Line. In 1999 Joshua David and Robert Hammond formed Friends of the High Line to argue for saving the structure and reusing it as public open space. The design came from three teams working together, Piet Oudolf, Diller Scofidio + Renfro and James Corner Field Operations, who treated the old spur as a "living system" combining landscape architecture, urban design and ecology. Oudolf's planting draws heavily on species native to the region. Conversion began in 2006, and the park opened in stages in 2009, 2011 and 2014. Since June 2009 it has become a reference point for contemporary American landscape architecture.

The Pantheon in Rome is an ancient temple to all the gods, first built under the emperor Augustus and rebuilt under Hadrian, on the site of an earlier temple commissioned by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa. Its plan is round, apart from a portico of large granite Corinthian columns, eight across the front and two groups of four behind, under a pediment. Joining a domed circular cella to a conventional temple front had no parallel in Roman architecture. The interior is built on one measure: the height to the oculus equals the diameter, 43.3 metres, so a sphere of that size would fit inside. Nearly two thousand years on, the dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome anywhere. Continuous use, as a Catholic basilica since AD 609, has kept it among the best-preserved Roman buildings.

The New Museum stands on the Bowery at number 235, on Manhattan's Lower East Side, between Rivington and Stanton Streets. Its new building, designed by SANAA (Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa), opened on December 1, 2007, as a $50 million home. The museum shows new art and ideas, by artists still waiting for significant exposure, and SANAA's scheme was chosen because it suited that mission: a flexible building whose changeable atmosphere matches the shifting nature of contemporary art. Its form is a stack of white boxes, placed on the Bowery as a response to the neighborhood's gentrification. In April 2008 Conde Nast Traveler named it one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in architecture. For students, it shows how a stack of white boxes can answer both a brief and a street.

The Portugal Pavilion stands in Lisbon's Parque das Nações, on Alameda dos Oceanos. Designed by Álvaro Siza, it housed Portugal's national representation at the 1998 World's Fair, Expo'98. Its entrance is a large open square covered by a pre-stressed concrete canopy, conceived like a sheet of paper resting on two bricks, which opens the space to the city and leaves room for the many events such a place hosts. Once the exhibition closed, the building stood empty, waiting for a use. In May 2015 the minister Jorge Moreira da Silva announced it had been handed over for good to the University of Lisbon, now responsible for its upkeep. The plan adds a 600-seat auditorium together with exhibition rooms, offices, rooms for meetings and a restaurant. For students, the canopy shows how an everyday image can drive a structural idea.

Torino Esposizioni is an exhibition hall and convention centre in Turin, designed by Pier Luigi Nervi. It is built chiefly of glass and ferrocemento, a kind of concrete construction that Nervi pioneered in Italy and abroad. Ferrocemento uses thin sections of concrete with metal wire reinforcement, cast in forms that can be used again and again. For the 2006 Winter Olympics the hall was turned for a time into an ice rink for several ice hockey events, alongside Palasport Olimpico, and afterwards it went back to hosting fairs and exhibitions. For students it shows Nervi's thin ferrocemento at work in a hall that has served more than one use, from fairs to Olympic ice hockey.

Jongmyo is the Confucian royal ancestral shrine of the Joseon kings, in Seoul's Jongno District. Taejo, who founded Joseon and was its first king, had the main buildings raised when he moved his capital to Hanseong, today's Seoul; when new, the shrine was thought to rank among the longest buildings in Asia. King Sejong later enlarged the complex with Yeongnyeongjeon, the Hall of Eternal Comfort. Japanese invaders burned the original shrine during the invasions of 1592–1598, and the complex that survives today was rebuilt in 1601. The main hall, Jeongjeon, is a National treasure and the longest traditional-style building in Korea, and each niche of the shrine is simple and plain in design. In front lies the Woldae Courtyard, 150 meters long and 100 meters wide.

Rani ki Vav, the Queen's Stepwell, is a stepwell at Patan, a town in Gujarat, India. Its building is attributed to Udayamati, whose husband was Bhima I, an 11th-century Chaulukya king. It was conceived as an underground shrine, an inverted temple honouring the sanctity of water, and its panels carry over 500 main sculptures and more than a thousand minor ones, mixing religious, secular and symbolic subjects, many of them Hindu deities. The well is about 65 metres long, 20 metres wide and 28 metres deep. An interlocking post-and-beam frame of beams, brackets, walls, columns and pillars carries vertical loads and resists the pressure of the surrounding soil. Built in the Maru-Gurjara style at the peak of stepwell craft, it silted up, was rediscovered in the 1940s and was restored by the Archaeological Survey of India in the 1980s.

The Palestinian Museum in Birzeit, in the West Bank, opened on 18 May 2016. It was designed by Heneghan Peng, the firm behind the Grand Egyptian Museum. The building sits on top of a terraced hill looking out over the Mediterranean, and its design takes its cue from the rural landscape around it, so that building and land read as one. The facade is local limestone, and the gardens step down the slope, telling the history of Palestinian plants and farming. Builders laid the terraces by hand, drawing on craft knowledge and skill. Outdoor gardens continue the interior rooms, allowing exhibitions outside and tying the building to its setting. In 2019 it received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. For students it shows a museum whose design grows from the rural landscape around it.

The Pei Wing is the Exhibition Hall of the German Historical Museum in Berlin, designed by I. M. Pei and built between 1998 and 2003. It stands beside the museum's main home, the 17th-century Zeughaus, or armoury, on Unter den Linden, across the Spree River from Museum Island. The new building offers 2,700 m2 over four floors, with structural engineering by Leslie E. Robertson Associates, and it opened for temporary exhibitions in 2003. The same works brought glass roofing back over the Schlüterhof. While the Zeughaus has been closed for renovation, the Exhibition Hall has stayed open. For students it shows a new exhibition hall set beside a historic armoury.

Vancouver House, a residential skyscraper in the neo-futurist manner, stands in Vancouver, British Columbia. It was designed by the Danish architect Bjarke Ingels, with Buro Happold and Glotman Simpson as structural engineers. Work began in 2016; finishing was planned for late 2019 but slipped to the summer of 2020. The design reflects the limits of its site, a triangular plot just east of the Howe Street on-ramp of the Granville Street Bridge. Its form starts as a triangle at the ground and gradually becomes a rectangle as it rises. Box-shaped balconies on the east and west facades give the exterior a honeycomb texture. Spinning Chandelier, a public artwork, was installed nearby as part of the city's rezoning requirement. For students it is a lesson in turning a site constraint into a building's form.

Flamengo Park, also called Aterro do Flamengo, is the biggest public park in Rio de Janeiro and is described as the world's largest seaside park in a city.
