It stretches beside Guanabara Bay through the Flamengo district, between Downtown Rio and Copacabana, on almost 300 acres that were once part of the bay. Lota de Macedo Soares had the vision for it; Affonso Eduardo Reidy conceived and designed the scheme, and Roberto Burle Marx, landscape designer and artist, created its Modernist gardens and civic landscapes. The 296-acre park was finished in 1965. Within it stand the Carmen Miranda Museum, a memorial to those killed in World War II with Modernist sculptures, and the Rio de Janeiro Museum of Modern Art. For students it shows an architect and a landscape designer shaping a city's edge together.

Palazzo dello Sport, known today as PalaEUR, is a multi-purpose arena for sport and entertainment in Rome. Marcello Piacentini designed it in 1957, and Pier Luigi Nervi engineered its reinforced concrete dome. It was built in two years, from 1958 to 1960, ready for the 1960 Summer Olympics, where it hosted the basketball tournament. It was planned together with a smaller arena, the Palazzetto dello Sport, whose dome Nervi also engineered, so the two can be studied side by side. The arena seats 11,200 spectators for basketball. It was renovated between 2000 and 2003, and its original look has also been changed, especially the night lighting of the exterior. For students it is a clear example of an architect and an engineer sharing one building, with the concrete dome as the engineer's part.

Charles Rennie Mackintosh designed Scotland Street School in Glasgow between 1903 and 1906, to take 1,250 pupils. He based it on Falkland Palace and on Rowallan Castle in Ayrshire. It has a pair of Scottish baronial staircase towers lined with windows, and inside is a tiled Drill Hall. It stands as a key example of the Modern Style, Britain's version of Art Nouveau. Building it was not easy: Mackintosh argued often with the school board, which wanted something cheaper, and the final cost of £34,291 ran over budget. Today the former school ranks among Glasgow's foremost architectural attractions. For students it shows older Scottish buildings feeding the design of a new school, and what that cost an architect in arguments with his client.

Hyvinkää Church, or the New Church of Hyvinkää, is an Evangelical Lutheran church in Hyvinkää, Finland, built in the modernist manner. Aarno Ruusuvuori designed it, and it was built in 1961. Its pyramid-like form rises 32 metres and drew some criticism when it was new. The church covers 1,779 square metres and seats 630 people on the main floor, with another 250 upstairs. Light comes in through wide windows, and a large window is placed behind the altar. For students it is a Finnish modernist church whose pyramid-like shape was questioned when it was new.

Omar Khayyám's mausoleum is a white marble monument over the poet's headstone, on the south-east side of Nishapur in Razavi Khorasan province, Iran. The government under Reza Shah commissioned its rebuilding in 1934; the tomb was set apart from the shrine, and a new monument by Houshang Seyhoun, finished in 1963, was raised over it. Seyhoun drew together Khayyam's gifts as poet, mathematician and astronomer. A path from the garden leads to the tomb so that flowers fall on it each year, and a star-shaped feature opens to the sky, a nod to his geometry and to the heavens above Nishapur. Tiles bearing Khayyam's poems in Shekaste Nastalik calligraphy by Morteza Abdolrasul decorate the structure. It joined the Iran National Heritage List in 1975 and is regarded as a symbol of contemporary Iranian design.

Teatro General San Martín is a public theatre in Buenos Aires, on Corrientes Avenue, next to the cultural centre of the same name. Perón gave the commission to two local architects, Macedonio Ruiz and Mario Roberto Álvarez, and work began on 24 June 1954. It was inaugurated on 25 May 1960 but began operating a year later. Its 30,000 m2 are spread over thirteen floors and four basements, holding a cinema, several exhibition halls and three stages. The Italian-style stage has an opening that varies from 11 to 16 metres, and its centre section can rise or fall, whole or in parts, on nine lifts working together or separately. Theatre and cultural centre were both extensively renovated in 2010–2011. For students it shows a theatre stacked over many floors, with a stage that changes size and level.

The Temple of Heaven is a complex of imperial Confucian religious buildings in the south-east of central Beijing. It was first built in 1420 under the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who also built the Forbidden City, and its present layout dates largely from Qing reconstruction finished by 1749. Several of its features join two symbols, earth as a square and heaven as a circle. The outer wall is taller and semicircular to the north, for heaven, and lower and rectangular to the south, for earth. The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, a triple-gabled round hall 36 m across and 38 m tall on three marble levels, is entirely wooden, with no nails. Dark blue roof tiles stand for heaven, and the Circular Mound Altar is set out in rings of plates counted in nines, the Emperor's number.

The Le Corbusier Gymnasium in Baghdad grew from a commission by King Faisal II, who invited a number of Western architects; in 1956 he asked Le Corbusier for a sports complex that might serve the 1960 Summer Olympics. When Le Corbusier died in 1965 he left many drawings and studies for the complex, which was to include a large stadium, tennis courts, swimming pools and a gymnasium. The gymnasium is built of reinforced concrete. Its main roof spans 34 metres on a steel truss clad in corrugated aluminium sheets, and the trusses stay exposed inside, carrying the mechanical ducts. An enormous sliding door links the indoor 3,000-seat hall to an open-air amphitheatre beside it; when opened, it joins the two into one space. For students it is a Le Corbusier design completed after his death.

The World Forum in The Hague, first named Nederlands Congresgebouw, serves as a convention centre and concert venue, close to the buildings of the OPCW. It was designed by Jacobus Johannes Pieter Oud in the style of Dutch functionalism. Oud died in 1963 before it was finished, and Hans Oud, his son, saw the construction through; the building opened in 1969. It hosted many concerts and festivals, among them the annual North Sea Jazz Festival and the Eurovision Song Contest twice, in 1976 and 1980. In 2006 part of the centre, including the Statenhal, was demolished to make room for the Europol building. For students it is a building in the Dutch functionalist style finished by the architect's son, which later lost a part to make way for a new neighbour.

Grieg Hall (Grieghallen) in Bergen, Norway, seats 1,500 and stands on Edvard Griegs plass. It honours Edvard Grieg, the composer born in Bergen, who led the Bergen Philharmonic Orchestra as music director from 1880 to 1882. The Danish architect Knud Munk designed it. Building began in 1967 and was complete by May 1978. The hall stages concerts, ballet and opera every year; the Eurovision Song Contest came to the hall in 1986, and Eurovision Young Musicians followed in 2000. Each winter it is also home to the Norwegian Brass Band Championship. For students, it is a concert hall that took more than a decade to build and now serves concerts, opera, ballet and competitions.

The Peak Tower, a shopping complex, stands at Victoria Gap, near the top of Hong Kong Island's Victoria Peak. The building there now, completed in 1997 to designs by the British architect Terry Farrell, replaced an earlier tower that was demolished in 1993; the new one broke ground that same year. The architects wanted the tower to register on the skyline without cutting into the hills' natural line, so they set it in a dip along the ridge and kept its top at 428 m above sea level. The building was altered in 2005–2006 for $100 million, and it now has eight floors and a viewing terrace moved up to the roof, at the top of its 'wok' shape, facing Victoria Harbour and Aberdeen, though air pollution often hides the view.

Stadio San Nicola is a multi-use, all-seater stadium in Bari, Italy, designed by Renzo Piano and built in 1990 for that year's FIFA World Cup, when it staged five matches. It also took the place of Stadio della Vittoria as its club's home ground. Piano gave the bowl the look of a flower. The stadium is made of 26 'petals', and the upper tiers of its higher ring are separated by empty gaps 8 metres wide, enough to meet security needs. Holding 58,270 people, the ground is Italy's third largest for football, behind San Siro and Stadio Olimpico, and the largest used by a single team. Even so, it was full for the first time only at a Serie B playoff match in 2013–2014.

Set on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., the Smithsonian's Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden lies midway between the US Capitol and the Washington Monument, closing the southern end of the L'Enfant axis. Gordon Bunshaft shaped this art museum as an open cylinder lifted on four heavy legs, with a big fountain in its central court. It is faced in precast concrete with a pink 'Swenson' granite aggregate. The drum holds 60,000 sq ft of galleries; outside lie nearly four acres in a two-level Sculpture Garden and plaza. The 1.3-acre garden across Jefferson Drive sits 6–14 feet below the street, with ramps for access. Bunshaft's first idea for the garden, a long sunken strip with a reflecting pool crossing the Mall, was dropped amid controversy. Students can read it as a design unconcerned with the grandeur of the Mall.

The Oscar Niemeyer Museum stands in Curitiba, in the Brazilian state of Paraná, and its story has two stages. Niemeyer drew the first building in 1967 as an educational institute, in the style of that period, and it opened in 1978. Remodelling and a new annex followed, and the museum reopened on 8 July 2003 under the name of its architect, who finished the project at 95. The annex, a 30-metre reinforced concrete form that recalls a human eye, rises above a pool and links to the main building through an underground walkway. Inside, a large spiral stair joins its levels, while two diamond-shaped façades of glass and steel bring daylight into a gallery. Ramps, curved volumes set against rectangular ones, white-painted concrete and murals mark the museum, which sits in a garden by Roberto Burle Marx.

Fountain Place is a 60-storey tower of the late-modernist period in downtown Dallas, completed in 1986. Designed by Pei Cobb Freed & Partners and Henry N. Cobb, with Harry Weese Associates and WZMH Architects, it treats the tower as one large faceted prism: its sloping faces give it a different outline from every direction. The plaza at its foot gives the building its name, with 172 fountains and an automated water show. WET shaped this waterscape with the Pei office and with Peter Ker Walker and Dan Kiley as landscape architects, and it was the first fountain to use WET's open-jointed paving, where jets of water rise from gaps in the ground. A second tower, turned at a right angle, was planned for the neighbouring lot, but the 1980s collapse of Texas oil, banking and property left the scheme unfinished.

Opened in 1968, the Nordic House is a cultural institution in Reykjavík, run by the Nordic Council of Ministers to build cultural links between Iceland and its Nordic neighbours. The Finnish modernist Alvar Aalto designed it, and it gathers most of his signature traits in one building: the ultramarine tiled roof has an organic ridgeline that answers the mountains on the horizon, the library has a central well, and white surfaces, tile and wood run throughout. Aalto also designed the fixed furnishings, the lamps and nearly all the furniture. Elissa Aalto oversaw construction and, alongside Ilona Lehtinen, the project architect, finished the construction drawings. Its library holds more than 30,000 items in seven Nordic languages, though not in Icelandic. Students can study it as a building Aalto shaped from the roofline down to the lamps.

Salerno Maritime Terminal is a ferry and cruise station on a pier of the city's commercial port, tied directly to the new Piazza della Libertà and the waterfront. Zaha Hadid won an international ideas competition launched by the City of Salerno in 1999, and the building opened on 25 April 2016, weeks after her death. Its flowing lines mark the passage from land to sea, from solid to liquid, in both appearance and function. Passengers are steered along the length of the terminal by three fixed points, the ticket office, the restaurant and the waiting room, which act as natural landmarks. An area of 4,500 m2 on two levels is split into three linked blocks: administration, the ferry terminal and the cruise terminal. In 2013 Italy's culture ministry listed it among selected high-quality architectural works.

The Oscar Niemeyer International Cultural Centre stands beside the estuary in Avilés, Spain. Niemeyer conceived it in 2006 for the 25th anniversary of the Princess of Asturias Awards; building began in 2008, and it opened on 26 March 2011. Four buildings sit around an open plaza, housing among other things an auditorium, an exhibition hall, a cinema, a restaurant and an observation tower. Built mainly of concrete and glass, the white, curving forms read sharply against a setting long shaped by industry, and curves are its main feature. The centre also anchors a large urban regeneration plan meant to remake the town's entire waterfront. For students, it shows a cultural building placed at the centre of a plan to change a town's industrial waterfront.

Jean Nouvel's Tour Duo is a pair of towers in the 13th arrondissement of Paris, where the city meets Ivry-sur-Seine along the Boulevard Périphérique. Building began in late March 2017 and both towers were delivered in 2021. The scheme spans over 108,000 m2 of mixed uses: mostly offices, plus a hotel, a restaurant, an auditorium, shops, green terraces and a bar whose terrace looks across Paris. Tour Duo n°1 rises 180 m, which puts it third in the city's height ranking, below the Tour Montparnasse at 209 m and the Eiffel Tower at 324 m. The pair is meant to complete a 'belt' of towers and tall buildings at the city's gates, so students can study it as part of a ring of tall buildings at the edge of Paris.

The Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York City is both a history museum and a memorial to the victims of the Holocaust. Kevin Roche began the design in 1993, and his firm, Roche-Dinkeloo, designed both of its wings. The first, opened in 1997, is a six-sided building under a pyramid-shaped roof; it was designed to evoke the memory of the six million Jews killed, and it holds the core exhibition galleries. The Robert M. Morgenthau Wing followed in 2003, with offices, a theatre, classrooms and the Irving Schneider and Family gallery. A contemplative garden, meant to be revisited and experienced differently as the garden matures, can be seen from nearly every floor. Students can study how a simple geometric figure carries the meaning of a memorial.

Haus Wittgenstein, also called the Stonborough House, is a modernist townhouse on the Kundmanngasse in Vienna. Margaret Stonborough-Wittgenstein commissioned it from the architect Paul Engelmann, and brought in her brother Ludwig Wittgenstein, the philosopher, to help. Engelmann laid out a spare house in the manner of Adolf Loos, made of three rectangular blocks. Wittgenstein concentrated on the windows, doors, door handles and radiators, insisting that every detail match his specification until everyone on the job was worn out. Each window had a 150 kg metal screen, moved by a pulley he designed. The house was complete by December 1928. Following a campaign by Bernhard Leitner, the Vienna Landmark Commission rescued the house, and it was made a national monument in 1971. It is a lesson in how far precise detailing can shape a plain building.

The Atheneum is the visitor centre for New Harmony, Indiana, designed by Richard Meier and opened on 10 October 1979. The building sets a single route: visitors follow a set path through its three storeys and then out into the town itself. A ramp and layered grids frame repeated views of New Harmony and the surrounding countryside along the way. It won a Progressive Architecture Award on opening, an AIA Honor Award in 1982, and in 2008 the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award, which goes to no more than one building a year. It was praised as a pure example of the themes that recur across Meier's work, a classic Meier design. For students, it is a study of a planned route through a building, and of a building used as the doorway to a whole town.

Jørn Utzon built this one-storey house in Hellebæk, near Helsingør in northern Zealand, Denmark, for himself and his family in 1952, and directed the work on site without technical drawings. The long, narrow, flat-roofed block lifts a little above its gently sloping ground on a brick platform. Utzon closed the north side completely and made the south front entirely of glass, filling the open-plan living room, with its freestanding fireplace, with light. The same materials serve inside and out: yellow-white brick, Oregon pine and aluminium. Movable pinewood partitions and doors divide the other rooms, so the plan can be changed later. The design was widely copied in the 1950s, first in single-family houses and later at a larger scale, which makes it a useful case of a small house setting a pattern for many others.

The Perret Tower is an observation tower in Paul Mistral park in Grenoble, built from 20 May 1924 to 4 May 1925 as the orientation tower and emblem of the International Exhibition of Hydropower and Tourism. Auguste Perret won a city competition for it, and it became his first free-standing design. It was also the first tower in Europe built of reinforced concrete. Rising 95 metres, it is octagonal in section, with a frame of eight vertical poles, and its formwork was modular and repetitive. At 60 metres an orientation table, which the Touring club de France asked for, rings the shaft. Declared a national heritage site in 1998, it is an early lesson in how repetition in concrete construction can produce a tall structure.

Skagen Odde Nature Centre, in Skagen, Denmark, is a museum about the effects that sand, water, wind and light have. Jørn Utzon designed it in 1989, and his son Jan led it to completion in 2000. Utzon wanted the centre to rise out of nature, offering the silence, calm and reflection he felt were hard to find in the modern world. A four-metre brick wall wraps an activity area of 4,000 square metres, sheltering it from frequent storms. The grey concrete buildings carry black felt roofs, and a series of separate pavilions, each with a pyramid roof and a periscope-like skylight, document the four themes. An observation tower looks out across the dunes. Apart from a radar station nearby, no building in the area stands further north. Students can study it for its sheltered plan and top-lit rooms.

The Lisbon Port Control Tower stands on the end of a man-made peninsula in Lisbon, Portugal. Gonçalo Sousa Byrne's nine-storey, 38-metre tower leans towards the harbour entrance it watches over. Its lower part is wrapped in horizontal bands of copper, while the top three storeys are glass, so that the building looks like a lighthouse brought up to date. It opened on 16 July 2001 and won first prize in the TECU Architecture Awards on 9 May 2003. For students, the tower is a case of a working harbour building given the image of a lighthouse through its form and its materials, copper below and glass above.

The Pampulha Art Museum, first built as a casino, belongs to the Pampulha Modern Ensemble in Belo Horizonte, in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais. Oscar Niemeyer designed it at the request of Juscelino Kubitschek, then the city's mayor, with structural calculations by the engineer Joaquim Cardoso, and it was the first of the ensemble's buildings to go up. Its gardens are by Burle Marx and hold three sculptures, the work of Ceschiatti, Zamoyski and José Pedrosa. Gambling was banned across Brazil on 30 April 1946, and the building was then turned into a museum, a change completed in 1957, by which time it was called the Crystal Palace. It now holds 1,400 works, and since 2016 it has shared UNESCO World Heritage status with the rest of the ensemble. Students can follow how a building outlived its first purpose.

The National Monument in Jakarta is a 132 m obelisk at the centre of Merdeka Square, built to mark Indonesia's struggle for independence. Construction started in 1961 under President Sukarno, who turned to R.M. Soedarsono to carry the design forward, and it was opened to visitors in 1975. Soedarsono worked 17, 8 and 45 into its dimensions, for the proclamation of independence on 17 August 1945. The 117.7 m obelisk stands on a 45 m square platform raised 17 m, known as the goblet yard, and is clad in Italian marble, with a gold-leaf flame at the top. It carries the Lingga and Yoni philosophy, the pair resembling a rice pestle and mortar. Below, a marble hall holds the 51 dioramas of the Indonesian National History Museum. It shows how symbolism can be coded into proportion.

The National Stadium in Singapore opened in 2014 on the site of the earlier National Stadium, which stood from 1973 to 2010. Arup, DP Architects and AECOM designed it within a 35-hectare Sports Hub masterplan. The 55,000-seat venue sits under a steel dome 83 m tall and 75,000 m2 in area, among the largest domed structures anywhere, with a retractable roof. It relies on natural ventilation, and its insulated metal roof reflects the sun; rather than cooling the whole bowl, it feeds cool air to the seats, making pockets of comfort around spectators and saving energy. For football and rugby the lowest tier moves forward over the running track, a change of about 48 hours, and LED lighting lets the roof act as a large screen. It is a useful study in designing for a tropical climate.

The National Theatre in Lagos is Nigeria's main centre for the performing arts. Completed in 1976 ahead of the 1977 Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC), it was designed and built by the Bulgarian company Technoexportstroy, and repeats the design of the Palace of Culture and Sports in Varna, Bulgaria, at four times the size. Its outside was shaped to resemble a military hat. Inside, the Main Hall was built for 5,000 seats with a collapsible stage, alongside two cinema halls. Renovation began in 2020 as a joint effort between government and private partners. For students, it is an example of one design reused and enlarged in another country, with an outline drawn from a military hat.

The Negev Brigade Monument, by Dani Karavan, stands on a hill east of Beersheba and remembers the Palmach Negev Brigade soldiers who died in the 1948 Arab Israeli War. Built between 1963 and 1968, it is made of raw concrete in eighteen separate elements spread over 10,000 square metres, and is seen as a forerunner of land art. A perforated tower evokes a watchtower hit by gunfire, and the pipeline tunnel recalls the water channel in the Negev that the soldiers defended. The names of the 324 soldiers killed are cut into the concrete. It has become a symbol of the Negev and of Beersheba. Students can study it as a memorial made of many parts set across a hilltop rather than a single object.

Torre Reforma is a 57-storey office tower in Mexico City, rising 246 m (807 ft) to its roof. Designed by L. Benjamín Romano, it was started in May 2008 and became the city's tallest skyscraper when it was finished in 2016, the same year it gained LEED Platinum certification. Early plans would have cleared Casa Austin, a historic 1930s house near the site; instead the house was kept and now serves as the tower's main entrance. The building holds 45,000 m2 of offices, 2,500 m2 for shops and the same again for a gym, with a restaurant and entertainment areas, served by 28 lifts that travel at up to 6.8 metres per second. For students, it is a case of tying a new tower to an old house rather than erasing it.

Terminal 1 at St. Louis Lambert International Airport was designed by Minoru Yamasaki, of Hellmuth, Yamasaki & Leinweber, to cope with growing passenger numbers. Construction started in 1953 and the terminal was finished in 1956 for $7.2 million. Its roof of three domes came before the TWA terminal at JFK in New York City. A fourth dome followed in 1965, after a $200 million airport revenue bond was passed. On 22 April 2011 a tornado hit the building, wrecking jetways and shattering over half its windows. Today it serves 36 gates in two concourses, A and C. One proposal would slowly replace the old concourses with a single new one of 62 gates while keeping the domed terminal itself. Students can compare its domes with the later TWA terminal at JFK.

Menara UMNO, now called JKP Tower, is a 21-storey office building in the central business district of George Town, Penang, at the corner of Macalister Road and Jalan Zainal Abidin. Ken Yeang designed it for a government-linked developer on a 1,920 m2 plot of waqf land that had held a three-storey UMNO building; the new tower was proposed as the party's Penang headquarters, which it has been since. Built from 1995 at a cost of RM35 million, it opened in 1998. It is recognised as the first Malaysian skyscraper to use wing walls and other bioclimatic devices to draw natural ventilation through it, together with variable shading and a balcony on every floor. After UMNO lost federal power in the 2018 general election, it took its present name. It is a useful early case of a tower shaped by climate.

Nur Alem, the Kazakhstan Pavilion and Science Museum, was the central pavilion of Expo 2017 in Astana, the first world's fair held in Central Asia. The Chicago firm Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture won the lead design contract, and pavilion construction started in April 2014, involving 20 Kazakh companies and 49 from elsewhere. The building is a sphere, described as the world's largest spherical building. The Expo's theme was 'Future Energy'. Nur Alem now stands at the centre of a hub for technological innovation, where young investors develop start-ups, research inventions and carry out business ideas, and two years after the Expo a new Astana IT University opened on the grounds. Students can study it as an Expo building given a second life.

Standing at 49a Downshire Hill in Hampstead, London, the Hopkins House is a high-tech home and studio that Michael and Patty Hopkins designed in 1976 as the first project of their new practice, now Hopkins Architects. They expected architecture to merge with engineering and move toward prefabricated, very light construction. Described as a machine for living and working, it is a simple two-storey box of glass and steel with few fixed internal walls, and its steel frame is left fully exposed. From the street it is entered across a 'drawbridge' at first-floor level, so it looks only one storey high. It won a RIBA Award in 1977 and in 1979 a Civic Trust Award, and was listed Grade II* in 2018. Students can read the house alongside that belief in light construction and engineering.

The Museum of Byzantine Culture is in Thessaloniki, Central Macedonia, Greece. A nationwide architectural competition for the building was called in 1977 and won by Kyriakos Krokos. Construction ran from March 1989 to October 1993, and the museum opened on 11 September 1994. It collects, conserves, studies and shows works from the early Christian, Byzantine, medieval and post-Byzantine periods, and as of 2017 it had 11 permanent exhibitions. It also documents the stages from an object's excavation to its display in the museum. Since 1998 it has run education programmes for schoolchildren. For students, it is an example of a museum won through a nationwide competition and built after a long gap between design and construction.

Hotel Kazakhstan, completed in 1977, is a 25-storey hotel in Almaty, Kazakhstan, designed by Yuri Ratushny, Leonid Ukhobotov and Vladimir Kim. Its tall, ellipse-shaped block is the city's third tallest building and has become a landmark and symbol of Almaty. It was built to withstand a 9.0 earthquake on the Richter scale. Structurally it relies on a monolithic core of reinforced concrete, with transverse diaphragms also of reinforced concrete. At ground level, a curving canopy with a deep overhang and its own lighting marks the main entrance. Marble, granite, shell rock and other materials finish the façades and interiors. Students can study it as a late modern tower that pairs an oval form with an earthquake-resistant structure.

Queen Tamar Airport serves Mestia, in a valley among the Greater Caucasus mountains, 1,456 m above sea level. After the 2003 Rose Revolution put tourism at the centre of policy, Mestia was quickly chosen for a new airport with a paved runway. Jürgen Mayer, a German architect, designed the terminal as a modern take on the region's Svan towers, defensive towers from the medieval period. President Mikheil Saakashvili opened it in December 2010, flying in with his government to hold a cabinet meeting. Small and regional, with a 1,156 m paved runway and only domestic flights, it brings visitors to the mountains of Svanetia in summer and to the Hatsvali and Tetnuldi ski resorts. Students can study it as an airport building that borrows a local tower type for a new use.

Museo Enzo Ferrari in Modena tells the story of Enzo Ferrari's life and work; he founded the Ferrari sports car marque. The complex pairs two buildings: the house and workshop once owned by his father, and a new building by the practice Future Systems, completed in 2012. The new building, of 6,000 square metres, holds a large gallery with a permanent display of notable Ferrari cars, among them rare models from the 1950s and Formula One racers, plus Alfa Romeo and Maserati models and a large video projection about Enzo Ferrari's life. The gallery was substantially renewed in February 2014. For students, it is a case of one museum made of a new exhibition building and his father's former house and workshop.

Magdalene College in Cambridge officially opened its New Library on 2 July 2022, in the western corner of the Fellows' Garden. Níall McLaughlin Architects designed it, and work on site began in 2018. It is the first library the college had built in 330 years, and it offers three times the room of the old one. Until then, the college library, with the undergraduates' course books, sat on the ground floor and in the basement of the Pepys Building. In 2022 the building took the RIBA Stirling Prize, the first Oxbridge building to win it. For students, it is a recent example of a college adding a new building within its own garden, and of a library moving out of an older building into one designed for the purpose.

The Weald and Downland Gridshell at Singleton, finished in 2002, was designed by Edward Cullinan Architects together with Buro Happold for the Weald and Downland Open Air Museum. It is a structural timber gridshell, made of oak brought from Normandy and clad in cedar from the local area. Before building it, members of both teams made a prototype in their own time at weekends; that trial structure, likewise self-supporting, served as a temporary entrance canopy at the Pompidou Centre in Paris. The finished building won a RIBA Regional Architecture Award in 2002, a Gold Award at the 2003 Wood Awards, and a Civic Trust Award for improving the quality and look of its surroundings. Students can study it for timber structure and for the value of a built prototype.

Eliel Saarinen designed First Christian Church in Columbus, Indiana; his son Eero Saarinen and Charles Eames, an associate, oversaw some of its details. Finished in 1942, it was the town's first modern-style building and among the earliest churches in the United States to adopt a contemporary architectural language. The plan has four parts: east and west wings, a bridge joining them, and a freestanding campanile 166 feet (51 m) tall. The wings frame a sunken courtyard that once held a reflecting pool. Its facade of Indiana limestone and brick are set in a grid-like pattern, the roofs are flat, and leaded glass panels take the place of stained glass. Now a National Historic Landmark, it is an early case of a church that set aside traditional forms for a modern language.

Kingsgate Bridge, a footbridge of reinforced concrete, crosses the River Wear in Durham. It links Bow Lane, on the peninsula at the heart of the city, with Dunelm House on New Elvet, a building to which Arup's studio also contributed. Ove Arup designed it himself in 1963, and it was the last structure he designed; it opened in 1966. Its construction was unusual: each half was built running alongside the river and then swung through 90° to close the gap. Where the halves meet, a plain bronze expansion joint with a linear gear bearing marks the join. The bridge won a Civic Trust Award in 1965. It is thought to have been among Arup's favourite designs, and he spent many hours on each detail of the drawings. Students can study it for its unusual method of construction.

Opened in autumn 2020 in Tokorozawa, Saitama, Tokorozawa Sakura Town is a pop culture complex, a joint project of the Kadokawa Corporation and the city, and the Kadokawa Culture Museum is one of its parts. Kengo Kuma designed the museum as one monolith with an obtuse, shifting shape, its façade covered in more than 20,000 pieces of granite fitted to each of its shifts. Kuma described the building as the Earth's energy breaking up through the ground. Inside, an 8-metre double-height library holds over fifty thousand volumes and can turn into a 'bookshelf theatre' through projection mapping. TeamLab's permanent outdoor work 'Resonating Life in the Acorn Forest' sits outside. Students can study it for how a stone cladding system is made to follow a complex, shifting form.

Komazawa Olympic Park in Tokyo was built as a sports ground for the 1964 Summer Olympics, with redevelopment of the site starting in 1962. Japanese architect Yoshinobu Ashihara designed two of its buildings: an indoor gymnasium and a Control Tower that acts as the visual focus of the whole park. During the Games the gymnasium staged the wrestling events, and its arena holds 3,875 spectators. For students, the pairing is the point to study: one architect shaped both the landmark that anchors the park and an enclosed arena, and both were made for the same Olympic Games.

The Twist is an art gallery at Kistefos in Jevnaker, Norway, designed by Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) and opened on September 18, 2019. Kistefos needed more room for a growing art collection and also a second crossing to complete the route around its park. BIG's competition-winning scheme answered both needs in one structure: a gallery that bridges the Randselva river and rotates through 90 degrees halfway across. That rotation lets the building sit wide on the lower bank and long on the higher one, fitting the natural landscape of Kistefos. Ramboll engineered the 24-meter steel truss girder that carries the turn. Glazed sides follow the warp, giving side light at the north end, with views toward the old pulp mill, top light at the south, and a dark gallery on the lower level.

The main building of the National Palace Museum stands in Shilin, Taipei, where the museum, first founded in Beijing in 1925, was re-established in 1965. Huang Baoyu designed it, and it was built between March 1964 and August 1965. With too little space to display more than 600,000 artifacts, the museum was enlarged four times, in 1967, 1970, 1984 and 1996, and a US$21 million renovation in 2002 aimed to make it roomier and more modern. Within the compound lies a garden in the classical Song and Ming manner, covering 1.88 hectares, which draws on feng shui, the handling of water, landscape design, and Chinese folklore and metaphor. Students can follow how one building was extended again and again to keep pace with a vast collection.

The Ordos Museum in Kangbashi, Ordos, in Inner Mongolia, China, opened in 2011 and holds collections on the history of Ordos and the land around it. The Chinese practice MAD Architects, led by Ma Yansong, designed it because the local government asked for it, and Huhehaote Construction built it. Inside, the museum is one large open-plan space of about 41,000 square feet, with exhibitions spread over six levels. MAD drew on two sources for the design: the Gobi Desert and the work of Buckminster Fuller. For students, it shows a museum design that takes its cue at once from a desert and from the work of another designer.

Built between 1406 and 1420, the Forbidden City is the palace complex at the heart of the Imperial City in Beijing. From the Ming dynasty until the Qing dynasty ended in 1924 it was the emperor's palace and winter residence. The plan is a rectangle measuring 961 m north to south and 753 m east to west, enclosed by a 7.9 m wall and a moat 52 m wide and 6 m deep. The Outer Court to the south held ceremonies, while the Inner Court to the north housed the emperor's family and daily state business. A stone path, the Imperial Way, forms the central axis of both palace and city. Every scale of the design was planned to express philosophical and religious ideas and imperial power. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1987.

Frauenmuseum Hittisau is a museum devoted to women in Hittisau, Austria. It fills the upper floor of the Feuerwehrhaus und Kulturhaus, a fire brigade and culture house built by the local authorities from 1998 to 2000 to designs by Cukrowicz Nachbaur. The building stacks very different uses: the fire brigade takes the large basement, a seminar room sits on the ground floor, and a local brass band is based here too. The upper part is built in local silver fir, with a large glazed front. Exhibitions, events, workshops and children's programmes present women's cultural achievements, especially from the Bregenzerwald region. The building won several prizes, among them the national Österreichischer Bauherrenpreis in 2000 and the Vorarlberger Holzbaupreis in 2001, making it a useful study in mixed civic use and regional timber building.

Seville–Santa Justa is the main railway station of Seville, in Andalusia, Spain, designed by Cruz y Ortiz and opened in 1991. Before it, Plaza de Armas served as the city's first main station, a terminus beside the Guadalquivir river for trains heading north; the riverside tracks were removed and that land redeveloped. When the Madrid–Seville high-speed line opened in 1992, the new station was joined by a tunnel to the underground San Bernardo station, so trains could run through from north to south. Some 12.7 million people pass through each year. It is the centre of the Cercanías Sevilla local network and a stop for AVE trains to Madrid, Barcelona, Málaga and Granada. For students, it is a case of a city's main station built anew and linked underground to its network.

Riverside Centre, at 123 Eagle Street in Brisbane, Australia, is a heritage-listed office development designed by Harry Seidler in 1983 and completed in 1986 as Lend Lease's principal project of the decade. Costing more than $200 million, it combined a 40-storey tower with a public plaza opening onto the Brisbane River. The tower plan is a triangle with a third of a circle at each corner, which, Seidler explained, gives every beam the same span and a single repeated facade unit. Its pillars use a section that recalls a trestle by Studio Nervi. Seidler called the glass entrance canopy a version of the traditional verandah, a response to occasional downpours. Stairs and ramps he named 'stramps' lead down to a promenade along the 180m riverfront, edged by bollards and nautical chains.

Known locally as The Potter, the Ian Potter Museum of Art holds art and historical collections belonging to the University of Melbourne in Melbourne, Australia. Its current building, designed by Nonda Katsalidis of Katsalidis Architects, opened in 1998, the year the university's collection was given that name. The museum runs a curated programme of historical and contemporary art. In 1999 the building received the Victorian Architecture Medal from the Australian Institute of Architects as project of the year, as well as the Melbourne Prize for architecture, which recognised what it gave to civic life in the city. In 1975 the University Gallery had moved into the Old Physics Building, renovated to a design by Daryl Jackson. The museum closed for renovations in 2018.

On the Hobart waterfront, the building of the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) gathers several research bodies in one place. Designed by John Wardle Architects with Terroir, the 69,000 m2 building houses staff and students of IMAS alongside three partners: IMOS, the national marine observing system; the ACE CRC, a research centre on Antarctic climate and ecosystems; and TPAC, a partnership for advanced computing. It sits next to the CSIRO Marine Laboratories and is meant as a hub where marine and Antarctic research is shared. The project was an Australian Government initiative under the Education Investment Fund. The institute teaches and researches temperate seas, the Southern Ocean and Antarctic environments, and their part in the global climate.

The North Building of the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney came out of the 'Sydney Modern' expansion, whose design competition was won in 2015 by SANAA, the Tokyo office of Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa, working with Architectus. The scheme extended the gallery to the north and drew criticism on architectural and public-interest grounds; supporters of the adjacent Royal Botanic Garden opposed the loss of parkland in the Domain. Opened on 2 December 2022, the extension almost doubled the gallery's display area, which now totals 16,000 square metres. Its exhibition spaces cascade, with large windows facing Sydney Harbour, and a former underground oil bunker became a columned gallery called 'The Tank'. The new rooms show contemporary and installation art, with a focus on First Nations work.

Green Square Library and Plaza in Sydney, Australia, sits at the centre of the town centre of Green Square and pairs a 3,000 sqm library with an 8,000sqm public plaza. Studio Hollenstein, with Stewart Architecture, won the project through an anonymous international competition, and the jury, which included Glenn Murcutt, chose the scheme unanimously. The library lies underground, and because it sits within the water table it relies on a 3 layer waterproofing system. Air is supplied at low energy by displacement ventilation built into the bookshelves, and a central wastewater system adds to its sustainability measures. The Green Building Council of Australia gave it a 5-star rating. For students, it shows an underground library built to cope with wet ground, paired with a large public plaza.

Prime Minister John Gorton opened the National Library of Australia's present building in Parkes, Canberra, on 15 August 1968. The firm Bunning and Madden (Walter Bunning) designed it in a style classed as Late Twentieth Century Stripped Classical. Inside, the large building holds a range of reading rooms and collections. Marble lines the foyer, which also has three of Mathieu Matégot's tapestries and windows of stained glass by the artist Leonard French, and Lintel Sculpture by Tom Bass is set above the entrance. Since 22 June 2004 the building has been on the Australian Commonwealth Heritage List. For students, it shows a national library opened in 1968 that pairs a pared-back classical frame with artworks set into its entrance and foyer.

Halle Tony Garnier in Lyon, France, began life as a slaughterhouse and cattle market, nicknamed "La Mouche". Tony Garnier designed its market as a hall of about 17,000 square meters, 80 by 210 meters, and work ran from 1909 to 1914. He had first meant to build everything in concrete, but chose a steel truss for the main roof: a Fives-Lille type structure, resting on ball and socket joints devised by Victor Contamin, that spans the hall without resting on columns. Circulation runs in one direction, and all handling happens on a single level. Flooding was one of the technical concerns, and the whole 23-hectare site was raised by three meters. Listed as a Monument historique in 1975, the hall became a concert venue after the City of Lyon brought in Reichen & Robert and HTVS in 1987.

On Sloane Street in Chelsea, the Embassy of Denmark in London occupies a diplomatic complex built for the purpose, and the Embassy of Iceland shares it. Arne Jacobsen designed it; after his death in 1971 the office continuing as Dissing+Weitling finished the job, with Ove Arup Partnership as collaborators. Building started in April 1975, three foundation stones were laid that June, and the complex was completed in 1977. It combines the chancellery, flats for staff and a residence for the ambassador. The exterior was first clad in light sand-coloured aluminium, since repainted, and carries a geometric concrete mural by the Danish artist Ole Schwalbe. The Financial Times saw it as a grey modernist grid and an artwork in its own right. Held on a 99-year Cadogan Estate lease, it replaced older premises in Pont Street and in Cadogan Square.

Southwark tube station in London opened on 20 November 1999, as part of the Jubilee Line Extension. Richard MacCormac's practice, MacCormac Jamieson Prichard, was taken on in January 1991 by the extension's design team under Roland Paoletti. The site was cramped, with the platforms lying beneath the Victorian viaduct that links Waterloo East with London Bridge, a problem solved with two concourses on different levels. One is a space 16 metres high under a glass roof that carries daylight far down into the station, faced by a 40-metre wall of 660 cut pieces of blue glass by Alexander Beleschenko. MacCormac drew the concourses from a Magic Flute stage set by Karl Friedrich Schinkel. Another space has glass and steel 'beacons' at each end and deliberately unpolished stainless steel panels. In 2000 it won a RIBA Bronze medal.

Kleinhans Music Hall in Buffalo, US, opened on October 19, 1940, as home of the Buffalo Philharmonic Orchestra, to a design by Eliel Saarinen working with his son, Eero Saarinen. In 1934 an estate of around $1 million was left with a request that it fund a music hall. Local architects F. J. and W. A. Kidd assisted, with Stanley McCandless advising on lighting and Charles C. Potwin on acoustics. The hall is shaped so that listeners at the back of the balcony hear as clearly and immediately as those at the front of the main floor, while plain colours and simple lines keep attention on the music rather than ornament. Under a parabolic ceiling, the main hall has 2,441 seats, down from 2,839 before a 2015 renovation. It was named a National Historic Landmark in 1989.

The Power Center for the Performing Arts in Ann Arbor opened in 1971 as a proscenium-stage theatre for university and professional performances. Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates designed it, with Jo Mielziner on the theatre design, and, according to the university, it filled a gap: Hill Auditorium was too big and limited for many shows, while the smaller Lydia Mendelssohn Theatre lacked room. The building pairs steel-reinforced concrete with reflective glass. Six massive concrete columns read as a classical colonnade in abstract form, and a large rectangular lobby faces the park, its mirrored walls reflecting the trees so the green space seems bigger. Two freestanding spiral stairs rise to walkways above the lobby, while the auditorium and stage house form large windowless volumes. An orchestra pit that can be raised lets the stage change from proscenium to thrust.

Evans Hall houses statistics, economics and mathematics at the University of California, Berkeley. Gardner Dailey designed it, and it was built in 1971 at the northeast corner of the campus, a short way east of Memorial Glade. Its name honours Griffith C. Evans, who chaired mathematics from 1934 to 1949 and joined mathematics and economics together. The building is known for its many windowless classrooms, and it was given a gray-green coat of paint so it would merge with the Berkeley hills. Computing history was made here: the first version of the vi text editor was written in the building, and Berkeley Unix (BSD) and the game Rogue were born here too. In February 2022 the university said that, because of cost, Evans Hall would not be seismically upgraded and would be demolished instead.

Officially named Jim Ellis Freeway Park, this Seattle park joins downtown to First Hill and the Seattle Convention Center. It is built over part of Interstate 5 and over a big parking lot owned by the city, while 8th Avenue crosses above it on a bridge. Lawrence Halprin's office designed it, with Angela Danadjieva supervising, and the 5.2-acre park opened on July 4, 1976, having cost $23.5 million. It mixes brutalist architecture with planting. In 1982 an extension carried the park several blocks up First Hill, with a stairway and a ramp for wheelchairs. The Cultural Landscape Foundation credits it with helping to define a new kind of land use for American cities. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2019 and became a Seattle Landmark in 2022.

The Erasmus Bridge spans the Nieuwe Maas in central Rotterdam, joining the north and south of the city. Ben van Berkel designed the 802-metre crossing, built from 1986 to 1996 as a cable-stayed bridge joined to a bascule section. Its cable-stayed part hangs from a single asymmetrical pale blue pylon, 139 metres tall, with a prominent horizontal base that earned the bridge the nickname "The Swan". At the southern end, an 89-metre bascule span lifts for ships too tall to pass beneath. During development, back stays were added to reduce bending, and the planned 150-m concrete pylon became a 139-m steel one, yet the overall look held, which decided its selection. Architects and engineers worked as equals. Two box girder spines anchor the cables and carry a deck of four traffic lanes, with two tram tracks between the spines.

Sultan Mosque in Singapore was first built in 1826 and rebuilt in its present form in 1932 to designs by Irish architect Denis Santry of Swan & Maclaren. Between 1925 and 1931 parts of the old mosque were pulled down and rebuilt in stages, partly for lack of funds and partly so daily prayers could go on. Its classical style draws on Indo-Saracenic architecture. The prayer hall and memorial face Mecca, askew to Muscat Street and North Bridge Road. Two matching gold onion domes with crescent-and-star finials top the corners; their bases are set with the cut ends of glass bottles collected from the poor during the rebuilding. Two eight-storey minarets flank the eastern facade, the only ones in the country still allowed to broadcast the call to prayer. It was made a national monument in 1975.

Eero Saarinen designed North Christian Church in Columbus, US, for a Protestant congregation of the Disciples of Christ that shared its name; it held its first service on March 8, 1964. Alexander Girard worked on the interior, Dan Kiley on the landscape and Kevin Roche on parts of the design. The plan is a hexagon inspired by the Star of David, a reference to Christianity's roots in Judaism. Ribs split the slate roof, set over a glass curtain wall, into six parts that carry a central metal spire; the structure stands 192 feet tall. Saarinen put most rooms in the basement so that only the sanctuary rises above ground. The landscape was meant to limit views of the building until visitors came close, and the berm was nicknamed the Mount of Expectation. The sanctuary's shape suits concerts acoustically.

The National Library of Armenia is spread across four buildings in the Kentron district of Yerevan, and the oldest of them is the main building, built in 1939 to a design by Alexander Tamanyan. It was planned to hold around seven million books. Its spatial and architectural character gives a new reading to principles taken from early and medieval Armenian building, an approach that came to be called the 'Tamanyan style'. The main building has the status of a historical and cultural architectural monument. For students, the building is a way into the Tamanyan style, in which the architecture of early and medieval Armenia was given a new interpretation.

Home to São Paulo state's Court of Justice, the Palace of Justice stands in the old centre of São Paulo, Brazil, close to Praça da Sé and São Paulo Cathedral. In 1911 the office of the architect Francisco Ramos de Azevedo was hired, and its project, inspired by the Palace of Justice of Rome, was accepted by the court. Work began in 1920 on land once used by cavalry barracks, and Ricardo Severo and Arnaldo Villares later took charge of it. The delays made people doubt it would ever be finished, earning it the nickname 'unfinished symphony', but it opened in 1933, thirteen years on. Inside and out, the eclectic design mixes neoclassical and baroque elements, with rich finishes such as caryatids and judicial symbols. It was also one of the earliest Brazilian buildings with a metal structure.

Shaped as an obelisk, the Summit Minar stands at the centre of Charing Cross on Mall Road in Lahore, Pakistan. It marks the second Islamic Summit Conference, which the city hosted on 22–24 February 1974, and its first stone went down a year later to the day, on 22 February 1975. It is the work of Vedat Dalokay, a Turkish architect whose other designs include the Faisal Mosque in Islamabad. Construction took 20 months and cost roughly Rs.15 million. The 155-foot obelisk and a reflecting pool together finish the layout of an urban square. Beneath the ground are a museum display of art, paintings and gifts from the countries that attended the 1974 summit, along with a small auditorium and rooms for meetings. Students can study it as a memorial that also completes a public space.

Lahore Museum, on The Mall in Lahore, is Pakistan's largest museum and one of its most visited. Bhai Ram Singh worked with John Lockwood Kipling on the design of its present building, and Ganga Ram oversaw construction. It was raised to commemorate the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria in 1887 and paid for by a public fund collected for that occasion. Prince Albert Victor laid the foundation stone on 3 February 1890, and the collection moved into the building in 1894, during the British colonial period. The architecture follows the Indo-Saracenic style, and the collection is rich in Buddhist art of the Gandhara and Indo-Greek kingdoms. The entrance hall ceiling carries The Evolution of Mankind, a mural of 48 panels. The museum, with the Zamzama Gun before it, is where the opening scene of Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim takes place.

The Peter B. Lewis Building in Cleveland, US, was completed in 2002 to house the Weatherhead School of Management, and it was designed by Frank Gehry. It sits where Bellflower Road meets Ford Drive, rises five stories and covers about 150,000 square feet. The name honours the Cleveland philanthropist Peter B. Lewis, who gave $36.9 million towards building it. The plan is deliberately decentralized: faculty offices, classrooms and meeting areas appear on every floor, a choice meant to encourage informal encounters and to support the school's learner-centred teaching. For students, it is a case where the arrangement of rooms follows from how a school wants its people to meet.

In Weil am Rhein, Germany, the Conference Pavilion is part of the Vitra Campus. Tadao Ando designed it, and when it was built in 1993 it became his first completed work anywhere beyond Japan. It shows the minimalism he is known for, with gridded concrete walls and openings that bring in light, and it is surrounded by cherry trees. Inside are a set of conference rooms, while outside a series of paths was described as recalling Japanese monasteries. On the campus, the colourful sculpture Balancing Tools by Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen offers one kind of contrast and Ando's pavilion a quieter one. Students can study it as a first step abroad for an architect, made with the minimalism he was known for.

Esbjerg Performing Arts Centre stands in the City Park of Esbjerg, Denmark, beside the Esbjerg Art Museum, with which it forms one complex, and looks out over the harbour and the sea. Jan Utzon designed it working closely with Jørn Utzon, his father, and it was completed in 1997. The main hall sits inside a truncated pyramid clad in white ceramic tiles, joined to a generous foyer whose octagonal pillars look like mushrooms. The foyer leads one way to the theatre and concert hall, and the other way to the café and the art museum. The main auditorium, built for classical music, seats over 1,100 and has a ceiling that drops to tune the acoustics; the orchestra pit and the stage, of up to 400 m2, also adjust. A smaller hall seats 233.

Kunstnernes Hus is an exhibition building at Wergelandsveien 17 in Oslo, Norway, facing the Royal palace park. The artists' body Bildende Kunstneres Styre bought the site in 1927 to build its headquarters and ran a design contest in 1928. Entrants had to provide daylight from above, keep the building low and give it a façade in tune with its neighbours. From more than 60 entries, the winner was Felix, a scheme by Gudolf Blakstad with Herman Munthe-Kaas; it was pared back before work started in 1929. It opened its doors on 1 October 1930 and in 1931 received the Houen Prize. Its galleries spread over two floors. Seen as a key step from 19th-century Neoclassical architecture towards Functionalism, it was refurbished in 2000/2001 for about NOK 20 million.

The Museum of Central Finland in Jyväskylä has two roles: it acts as the museum for the Central Finland region and as the city's own municipal museum. Its present building, completed in 1960, is the work of the Finnish architect Alvar Aalto. It offers 1,328 square metres of exhibition space and stands beside the Alvar Aalto Museum; plans were made to join the two with a new wing, expected to open in late 2023. Between 2017 and 2020 the museum was thoroughly renovated, adding 80 digital information displays and many interactive audiovisual exhibits. For students, it is a chance to see an Aalto building serving as a regional and city museum, right beside the museum named after him.

Ympyrätalo, whose name means "Circle House", is a round office building in Helsinki, Finland, in the district of Hakaniemi. Heikki and Kaija Siren designed it, the work took eight years, and it opened in 1968 as the offices of Kansallis-Osake-Pankki. Outside stand three booths that worked as drive-through bank counters until low demand closed them in the 1970s. The building has been described as a high point of Finnish office architecture of the 1960s, and zoning rules protect its exterior, its entrances and stairways, and the inner courtyard. A renovation to bring it up to modern technical and functional standards ended in 2004. At one entrance sits a 3-meter steel ball called "The Symbol", by the architects' son, Hannu Siren, installed in 1985. Hakaniemi metro station's entrances are just outside.

Uspenski Cathedral in Helsinki, Finland, is the principal cathedral of Finland's Orthodox Church and the biggest Orthodox church anywhere in Northern Europe. The Russian architect Aleksey Gornostayev designed it, but it was built after his death, between 1862 and 1868, with Ivan Varnek leading the work; its formal opening came on 25 October 1868. Its 700 000 bricks came by barge from the Bomarsund Fortress, demolished during the Crimean War, and parishioners and private donors paid for most of the construction. The cathedral sits on a hillside of the Katajanokka peninsula, looking out over the city, and draws about half a million tourists a year. For students, it shows how material salvaged from a demolished fortress was reused to build a large church on a prominent site.

The Itatiaia Building is an apartment block in the Centro district of Campinas, in the state of São Paulo, Brazil. Oscar Niemeyer drew up the design in 1953, and construction finished in 1957. It was the first Modernist building in Campinas and, until the early 1960s, the city's only residential tower. The building takes up 1,569.8 square metres of a trapezoid-shaped plot on Irmã Serafina Avenue. It is often set beside another building of the same period, the Copan Building in São Paulo. For students, that comparison is a way in, and the Itatiaia is a chance to study the first Modernist building of a Brazilian city.

Also known as the Seidler Tower, Hochhaus Neue Donau is a housing skyscraper in Vienna, Austria, standing in Donau City and designed by Harry Seidler, an Austrian-Australian architect. Built from 1999 to 2001, it rises 150 m over 34 floors. Its plan is an elongated triangle, shaped with the aim of giving every apartment views of the water: the longer wing faces south to the Danube, and the shorter one turns east towards the Kaiserwasser and the Alte Donau. A facade of white aluminium cassettes is split into four parts, forming a triangular core with three wings around it. Offices for rent fill the lower floors up to the 8th; above them come two- and three-room flats, then smaller one- and two-room units, with penthouses at the top. Students can read the plan as a direct answer to the view.

Mimar Sinan, the Ottoman architect, built this mosque in Istanbul for Sinan Pasha, an admiral. Work began after the admiral died in 1554, and a gilded Arabic inscription over the arched gateway gives the completion as November/December 1555. A madrasa wraps the forecourt on three sides. The walls are built in alternating bands of ashlar and brick. The 12.6-metre dome rests on six arches, helped by two free-standing hexagonal piers. The north side once had a double portico; in 1749 its inner, five-domed half was absorbed into the prayer hall. The design has been compared with the older Üç Şerefeli Mosque in Edirne, of 1437 to 1448, which also carries its dome on six arches and two free-standing piers, making the pair useful for comparing one structural arrangement in two buildings.

The Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio in Oak Park, US, was built in 1889 by Wright, who made it his family home for twenty years and enlarged it several times. It has two linked parts: the house to the south is in the Shingle or Queen Anne style, and the studio to the north, added in 1898 after new rooms in 1895, is in the Prairie style. Brick, stone, battens and shingles clad wood frames, each part arranged around a central fireplace. The studio sets a double-height drafting room on one floor with a library, an office and a reception hall, and here Wright and his associates produced dozens of buildings. He tested many features here, favouring functional details over decoration. Its present managers, the Frank Lloyd Wright Preservation Trust, have restored it to how it looked in 1909.

Waldspirale, meaning 'forest spiral', is a housing block in Darmstadt, Germany, named for both its plan and its green roof. The Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser designed it, the architect Heinz M. Springmann planned and carried it out, and Bauverein Darmstadt built it; it was finished in 2000. The U-shaped building holds 105 apartments and a parking garage. Its planted roof of grass, shrubs, flowers and trees climbs like a ramp around the U, reaching 12 floors at the top. The facade ignores a regular grid, and its more than 1000 windows all differ, appearing to dance out of line. Gilded onion domes, earth-toned paint, colourful ceramic columns and an avoidance of straight lines and sharp corners complete it. For students, it is a housing block in which almost nothing repeats.

MAAT, the Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology, is a cultural project for Lisbon built around those three fields. The €20m museum lies on the River Tagus, west of the city centre, and was designed by Amanda Levete Architects (AL_A). The scheme ties the new building to the Tejo Power Station, which ranks among the most prominent works of industrial architecture in Portugal from the first half of the 20th century. MAAT launched its programme on 30 June 2016, with four exhibitions inside renovated parts of the power station, and the new building followed on 5 October that year. For students, it is a case of a new museum building tied to an older industrial landmark, with exhibitions in both.

Branded PAC NYC and also called 6 World Trade Center, the Perelman Performing Arts Center holds several stages at the northeast corner of the trade center site in Manhattan. The first designers were Snøhetta and Gehry Partners LLP, but their plans stalled and were dropped; the building that opened on September 13, 2023 is by Joshua Prince-Ramus with Davis Brody Bond. The 160-by-160-foot block rises 117 feet from a black-granite base 21 feet tall. Its windowless facade is made of 5,000 veined Portuguese marble panels, with lozenge patterns that turn amber at night; Ramus said this keeps the buzz of theatregoers at a distance from the memorial. Inside, walls can rotate and expand to give one of the three theatres extra space, and 1-foot pads separate the theatres from each other and from nearby structures to reduce subway vibration.
